News.title: Amazon unveils its Toys We Love list for 2026 featuring must-have presents with some bargains under £10
News.content:
FUN & GAMES Amazon unveils its Toys We Love list for 2026 featuring must-have presents with some bargains under £10







Next

AMAZON has unveiled its Toys We Love list for 2026, featuring the must-have presents expected to excite youngsters this festive season.

And while some of the biggest names in toys are battling for a place under the Christmas tree, parents will be relieved to hear that gifts start at under £10.



Among the standout picks are a mischievous new twist on the classic UNO card game, a Playmobil space rocket for budding astronauts and a Lexibook StarCam for children who fancy themselves as the next big thing in photography.

There are also creative building kits, surprise collectibles and imaginative playsets designed to keep children entertained long after the wrapping paper has been cleared away.



The list, hand-picked by Amazon’s toy experts, aims to take some of the guesswork out of Christmas shopping, with presents to suit different ages, interests and budgets.

And for the fourth year running, Amazon is donating hundreds of this Christmas’ most sought-after toys to families struggling with the cost of living through its partnership with charity The Multibank.

The presents will be delivered in a giant toy chest to six Multibank sites across the UK, including London, Greater Manchester, Birmingham, Tees Valley, Fife and Swansea, before being distributed to families in need.

The charity, which provides everything from nappies and toiletries to household essentials, has already distributed more than 23 million items, supporting over three million families across Britain.



Andrew Wright, EU director of toys at Amazon, said: “Our Toys We Love list brings together some of the year’s most exciting must-haves, giving shoppers inspiration to find the perfect Christmas gift.

“From family games and trending collectibles to toys that spark imaginative play, we’ve hand-picked something for different ages, interests and budgets.

“Once again, we’re proud to be donating hundreds of toys from this year’s list to Multibanks across the UK, helping families make Christmas that little bit more special.”

Bob Garmory OBE, chief executive officer at The Multibank, added: “For families facing financial pressures, this time of year can be particularly challenging, with the rising cost of everyday life making it harder to create special moments for their children.

“That’s why the continued support of Amazon is so important, helping us reach families who need it most.



“We’re delighted to be able to distribute some of the year’s most sought-after toys, bringing a little extra joy to families and helping more children experience the excitement and happiness that every child deserves.”

Amazon’s full Toys We Love 2026 selection is available here, alongside its downloadable Kids Toys Book, with fast delivery options available for shoppers hoping to avoid a last-minute Christmas panic.

News.title: Tech tycoon Adam Robinson’s heartbreaking post about ‘putting family first’ resurfaces after deadly Learjet plane crash
News.content:
Next

A TECH tycoon’s heartbreaking words about putting family before work have resurfaced after he was killed alongside his wife and two young children in a horror plane crash.

Adam Robinson, 45, had previously revealed how he made a conscious decision to prioritize spending time with his loved ones rather than chasing success at the expense of his family.



The founder of tech startup Retention was among nine people killed when a Learjet 60 plummeted to the ground near West Palm Beach, Florida, on Sunday.

His wife, Helen Sharp, 40, and their children, Emma, four, and Charlie, two, also died in the fiery crash.



Now, a poignant social media post Robinson shared in April has resurfaced, revealing how determined he was not to miss out on precious moments with his children.

Reflecting on his time working on Wall Street, the businessman recalled seeing colleagues sacrifice their family lives for demanding careers.



“People my age now (45) said they were working 70, 80, 90 hours a week for their families… but all their families actually wanted was their presence,” he wrote.

“They didn’t understand why their families resented how much they worked when they lived in a nice house and their kids went to private schools.”

Robinson said the experience shaped how he approached building his own company.

“I decided early in my startup journey that wasn’t going to be me,” he declared.



The entrepreneur explained that he and his co-founders introduced a policy of “quitting” work at 5pm or 5.30pm each day.

That meant shutting their laptops, ending work conversations and heading home to their loved ones.



He even admitted leaving earlier on occasions when he wanted to spend time with his children.

“My family life gives me energy for my work. My work gives me energy for my family life,” he wrote.

The heartbreaking words have taken on new significance following the tragedy that wiped out his young family.

Robinson and his loved ones had reportedly been heading from their home in Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas to celebrate his birthday.



Also onboard were the children’s nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

Pilot Jeff Gregory, 55, and co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras were also killed in the tragedy.

As investigators work to establish what went wrong, devastated relatives have paid tribute to Robinson and Helen as devoted parents whose children meant everything to them.

Emma and Charlie were described as “the light of their lives” in a joint family statement.



“Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever,” their loved ones said.

“Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.”



The families also remembered Rachael and Charmi as a couple who embraced life and adventure together.

“Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly.”

They also paid tribute to the children’s nanny, who had become an integral part of the family.

“Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.”

In a separate statement, Helen’s grieving relatives said the scale of the heartbreak reflected how deeply the couple had touched those around them.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“On behalf of friends and family, it is with a heavy heart that we share that our dearest Helen was taken from us too soon,” they said.

“To know Helen was to love her. The number of people grieving Helen and Adam is a testament to how many people were lucky enough to have them in their lives.”

News.title: Top military student spiked pregnant girlfriend’s protein shake with sedatives before shoving abortion pill in mouth
News.content:
POISON PLOT Top military student spiked pregnant girlfriend’s protein shake with sedatives before shoving abortion pill in mouth







Next

A CADET spiked his pregnant girlfriend’s smoothie with sedatives before forcing her to take an abortion pill.

Caleb Suh, who went to West Point academy, is being sued for assault and battery after shoving the drugs into his victim’s mouth and vagina – before enrolling in Columbia University.



The 25-year-old pleaded guilty to drugging and forcing pills on a cadet, a woman identified as “Jane Doe” in court documents.

The incident took place in 2022 when she was a freshman at West Point and Suh a sophomore.



Suh was charged in a federal court in June and pleaded guilty to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner.

While entering his guilty plea, he said he encouraged her to drink what he told her was a “prenatal protein shake,” the Daily Mail reported.



“I then waited for her to fall asleep, at which time I physically administered the abortion pills I had secretly obtained from the online pharmacy by impersonating her,” said the disgraced cadet.

“The next morning I learned that my girlfriend had been taken to the hospital where she, in fact, miscarried as a result of the abortion pills that I had administered without her knowledge and consent.”

The pair had started dating while enrolled at West Point in 2020.

The woman became pregnant two years later, and told Suh she wanted to keep the baby.



At first, he was staunchly opposed and “threatened to commit suicide if she did not terminate the pregnancy”- but then appeared to change his mind, the suit said.

Suh admitted setting up the fake account in his girlfriend’s name at the online pharmacy and obtaining Xanax to sedate her.

Court documents also claim that he “impersonated” his girlfriend in the pharmacy’s online forum.

There, he asked questions like: “I don’t want to swallow pills. Could I just break them up in my water and drink water?” and if he would “feel the pills in my vagina,” according to the civil lawsuit.

During the assault, his victim became “repulsed” by the taste – but Suh was “insistent”, and eventually forced her to drink it.



“Ms Doe became sick and fell asleep. For the next few hours, she was in and out of consciousness with severe pain,” the suit said.

It was then that he shoved the abortion pills in her vagina to ensure that she loses the baby.

After waking up, the woman was “profusely bleeding from her vagina” and fell seriously ill.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Despite his guilty plea, a judge has allowed Suh to delay his sentencing until January so he can finish the academic semester at Columbia, where he is currently pursuing a master’s degree.

Suh, who was due to be sentenced on November 12, faces up to five years in prison.

News.title: Man, 39, died after being swept out to sea and drowning in tragedy at pier in UK seaside town
News.content:
SEASIDE TRAGEDY Man, 39, died after being swept out to sea and drowning in tragedy at pier in UK seaside town







Next

A MAN sadly died after falling from a pier and being swept out to sea, an inquest heard.

Fred Croot, 39, was knocked from a support beam under Cromer Pier, Norfolk, at 6.30pm on May 11 and tragically drowned.



Fred had been enjoying a day out at the beach when he was knocked into the sea by a strong wave.

A chef at a nearby restaurant heard that a man had got into difficulty in the water and went to check on Fred.



He saw standing underneath the pier on framework “ankle-deep in water” when the weather was “extremely windy and wet”.

The chef then saw a large wave hit Fred and ran over to throw him a lifebuoy.

“This man tried desperately to get back to the shore,” the chef statement’s described to the court.

But another wave crashed over Fred and the chef lost sight of him after that.

Emergency services were called and at 7.25pm the coastguard helicopter spotted him in the water.

Fred was retrieved from the water where he was given CPR, but was sadly confirmed dead at 7.43pm.



Following a post-mortem, Fred’s confirmed cause of death was drowning, the court were told.

Norfolk Coroner’s Court heard that prior to the tragedy Fred had a “long-standing history of mental illness”.

According to an acting psychiatrist, he lived with schizophrenia and autism and had previously gone missing for four days in August 2023.

Following an overdose on co-codamol last year, he was eventually placed in Sunny Court residential care home in March.

He struggled to settle in and burnt a tablecloth at the home six days after his arrival.



Concluding the inquest, area coroner Yvonne Blake said: “A chef could see Fred was on the wooden support framework of the pier. He was swept into the sea by the waves.

“He tried to swim back to the beach, but it was exhausting. Various emergency services arrived, and they searched for Fred.

“Fred was retrieved from the sea and resuscitation began. Fred died from drowning.”

Fred’s sister said after the inquest: “He was very well-loved by his family. We are just devastated at his loss.”

News.title: Mystery as woman in her 60s found with ‘life-changing’ injuries in alleyway under bridge
News.content:
GRIM DISCOVERY Mystery as woman in her 60s found with ‘life-changing’ injuries in alleyway under bridge







Next

A WOMAN was found in an alleyway underneath a bridge with injuries believed to be potentially life-changing.

Cops are urgently appealing for information after the woman – aged in her 60s – was discovered in Dorchester, Dorset shortly after 10am on October 29.

Dorset Police said she was found with injuries under the bridge in an alleyway between Sawmills Lane and Herringston Road.

She is described as wearing a white bucket hat, dark-coloured coat, dark-coloured trousers and white shoes.





The woman was raced to hospital and her injuries are believed to be potentially life-changing.

Police Constable Jacob Chutter, of Dorset County CID, said: “We are carrying out enquiries into the circumstances of how this woman came to sustain her injuries and these remain ongoing.

“I would urge any witnesses or anyone with information that might assist our enquiries to please make contact with us.

“I would also urge anyone with home CCTV or doorbell cameras in the area of Sawmills Lane and Herringston Road to please review any footage from the morning of Thursday October 29 2026 to see if they have captured anything of relevance.



“I would also make the same request of any motorists with dashcam who were driving in the vicinity, including in the Manor Road area.”

Anyone with information or footage on the incident is urged to contact the force quoting occurrence number 55260169921.

News.title: ‘Mogging’ revealed as Collins Dictionary’s word of the year – but do YOU know what it means?
News.content:
Next

COLLINS Dictionary has officially named its 2026 Word of the Year, but many may not know what it actually means.

An eclectic list of words spread amongst youngsters have made the shortlist – from a term describing food that is both fruity and spicy, to an unusual viral phrase from the World Cup.

“Mogging” has taken the crown as Collins’ Word of the Year, with the trending term officially making the mainstream language.



The “fast growing slang” term, which means outperforming or outshining something or someone, has become an undoubted hit amongst Gen Z and Gen Alpha – those born since 1997.



It is said to derive from the acronym AMOG – standing for “Alpha Male of the Group.”

In 2026, use of the word “mogging” soared by 210 per cent, seeing names ranging from Arnold Schwarzenegger to Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg all adopting the term.



Managing director of Collins, Alex Beecroft, said: “The selection of ‘mogging’ as Collins’ word of the year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language.

“It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and ‘mogging’ the rest of us.”

Mogging saw off stiff competition to win this title, including “bixie”, a hairstyle shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut, and “fricy”, when a food is both fruity and spicy.



“Hydration break”, the unusual rule that took over this summer’s World Cup, also made the list, defined as “a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluid.”

News.title: Airport shut in Warsaw after bomb threat on flight from London sparks emergency landing as cops swarm plane
News.content:
BOMB SCARE Airport shut in Warsaw after bomb threat on flight from London sparks emergency landing as cops swarm plane







Next

A PASSENGER flight from London to Poland was forced to make an emergency landing after a bomb threat.

The Polish Airlines plane, with 181 people on board, was diverted to Warsaw Modlin Airport after the horror alert this morning.

It comes just hours after a fighter jet was scrambled to support a Wizz Air flight from London after a similar threat on Monday.



Emergency services rushed Warsaw Modlin this morning and the airport was locked down.



Bomb disposal teams were on site to inspect the aircraft and passengers’ luggage after the plane made an unscheduled landing at around 10am.

The Boeing 737 MAX 8 took off from London Heathrow Airport at 6.30am headed for Warsaw Chopin Airport.

But the flight was redirected at 9.54am “due to information on an explosive device on board”, Modlin airport said in a statement.



The airport in Poland’s capital will remain closed until further notice, a spokesperson added.

After landing, the aircraft was directed to a designated location while authorities assess the threat.

Passengers have reportedly begun evacuating the plane with authorities ushering families into the arrivals hall, according to local outlet onet warszawa.

“The safety of passengers, crew and airport employees is currently the highest priority,” Warsaw Modlin Airport said.



Another passenger aircraft heading into Warsaw was grounded this morning after a threat was made on board the plane.

The SAS flight from Copenhagen landed at Chopin Airport where masked officers are reportedly helping passengers evacuate.

“The captain said that a threat had been made to the plane,” a passenger told local outlet BT.

Fire trucks are on standby just over 100 meters from the plane, the passenger added.

“We are awaiting more information from the captain once he has handled the matter according to all procedures and passengers have disembarked,” an SAS spokesperson told the outlet.

News.title: Brit pensioner, 73, faces prison after reversing over wife, 56, & killing her at Spain home following day-long binge
News.content:
OAP KILLER Brit pensioner, 73, faces prison after reversing over wife, 56, & killing her at Spain home following day-long binge







Next

A BRIT pensioner faces up to four years in prison after reversing over his wife and killing her outside their Spanish home following a day-long drinking session.

Michael John Carter, 73, dodged a potential 25-year stretch behind bars after jurors cleared him of murder and convicted him of manslaughter instead.



Public prosecutors in the south-east region of Murcia accused the OAP of deliberately attacking wife Vanessa, 56, after an all-day beer and wine bender in local pubs.

But Carter insisted she died in a tragic accident, claiming he did not realise he had run her over while reversing his car outside their property in Camposol, near the Costa Calida resort town of Mazarron.



Late on Monday evening, all nine jury members unanimously cleared him of his partner’s aggravated murder.

The expat was instead convicted of manslaughter, meaning he will serve just a fraction of the 25 years demanded by prosecutors and a private lawyer acting for Vanessa’s family.

Both are now pushing for the maximum four-year term Carter can receive under Spanish law.

They have also urged the trial judge at the Audiencia Provincial Court in Murcia to slap him with a six-year driving ban and order him to pay £18,300 (€21,940) in compensation to his grieving sister-in-law.

After the verdict, Carter’s lawyer Zoraida Garre called on the judge to free his client as soon as possible, pointing to the time he has already spent behind bars on remand since Vanessa’s death in December 2022.

She added that his voluntary payout of part of the compensation should count as a mitigating factor.



In a shocking pre-trial indictment, public prosecutors accused Carter of battering Vanessa in a “sudden” attack, before “kicking her forcefully all over her body several times” with the “intention of inflicting great pain and severe physical and psychological suffering”.

They also claimed he jumped on her chest and clamped his hand over her mouth.

Two forensic experts who carried out the autopsy told the court Vanessa’s horrific injuries – including multiple broken ribs – could not have been caused by a low-speed reversing accident.

They insisted the wounds were instead compatible with a brutal beating, including violent kicks and punches.

Vanessa’s sister gave evidence via video link from Cardiff, revealing how the victim had previously confided in her about how Carter had allegedly mistreated her throughout their relationship.



A neighbour also told the jury the pensioner acted “without compassion” as his wife lay dead on the ground.

But Carter’s defence lawyer offered a completely different version of events, insisting he should be acquitted because he had no “will to kill” and there was a total absence of “any conduct aimed at causing the victim’s death”.

She described a manslaughter verdict with mitigating factors including alcohol consumption as the only “legally possible outcome”.

And Carter insisted when he took the stand last Friday: “I am not capable of kicking or punching anyone.”

He said he suffered from Buerger’s disease – a rare inflammatory condition that causes blood vessels in the arms, legs, hands and feet to swell – adding: “I can’t even stand on one leg.”



Carter told the court his wife died after “entering their house to secure the dogs”.

He said: “I stayed in the car for two minutes and didn’t see any lights come on, so I backed the car up to get a better look.

“When I got out of the vehicle, I saw Vanessa in front of the car. As soon as I saw her lying there, I rushed over as quickly as I could and tried to wake her.”

By a majority 7-2 verdict, jurors concluded that Vanessa fell behind the car, before her husband reversed over her and caused her death “without the intention of killing her”.

They rejected the claim he deliberately ended her life by physically attacking her, instead ruling that Carter remained inside the BMW vehicle while his wife entered their property.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Cops confirmed Carter had previously been reported for domestic violence – but there was no active file on Spain’s VioGen database, which was created in 2004 as part of a national law against gender violence.

News.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
News.content:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see Â£5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for Â£200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for Â£25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.

"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.

Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.

News.title: Mahmood refuses to detail cost of revised settlement plans
News.content:
The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save Â£10bn.

Under revised plans, some foreign care workers will wait five years and others will be able to seek a five-year extension, in what the Tories have called a "U-turn".

While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC the state would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.

In March, the Home Office said, external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at Â£10bn under existing rules.

Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.

Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least Â£25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.

Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.

She said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.

"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.

"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.

The Conservatives said her "U-turn" will cost the state billions of pounds.

News.title: Scientists detect signals from the zeptoverse - the smallest scale of nature ever explored
News.content:
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

News.title: Watch: Just how small is the zeptoverse?
News.content:
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored â 100 billion times smaller than an atom. A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

The BBC's science correspondent Pallab Ghosh explains just how small the zeptoverse is.

Learn more about this new scientific discovery.

News.title: 'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?
News.content:
"Mogging", a word used playfully to mean outshining, outperforming or upstaging someone or something, has been named as word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary.

A fast-growing slang word among members of Generations Z and Alpha - both online and in everyday conversation - mogging went mainstream in 2026 with a 210% increase in its usage.

Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft said its lexicographers look at "how often words are used" and also "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.

The selection of mogging as word of the year, he said, "shows how each generation leaves its mark on language".

News.title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European supermarket fridges
News.content:
After hackers targeted refrigeration systems in supermarkets and food suppliers across Europe, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK".

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

He said it had alerted "handfuls" of bodies, and that it was aware of a "couple of impacts".

It comes after supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges being hiked in temperature on Monday.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

News.title: PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
News.content:
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.

As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.

The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.

"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.

The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda, but other leaders insisted they should be.

This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.

"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery, external. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.

Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.

They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.

"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video, external, is something "the British government are open to".

He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right or feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."

News.title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
News.content:
Investigators believe parts of a private jet which crashed in Florida and killed all nine on board may have broken off in the air.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.

A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died on Sunday.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to a huge crater on the road in Palm Beach which was formed by the jet.

The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time.

"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.

The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, was partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.

Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.

"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.

"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."

Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.

Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".

They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.

An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

Seven passengers died on board the flight - named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.

The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.

One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.

News.title: Family of girl murdered by ex given law change hope
News.content:
The family of a murdered schoolgirl says the government has told them it plans to create a new law defining teenage abusive relationships because of their campaigning.

Micala and Lee Trussler met the Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls minister Satvir Kaur at the Home Office in London on Monday, where they were given an outline of the plans.

Their daughter, Holly Newton, was 15 when she was stabbed to death in an alleyway in Hexham in January 2023 by her ex-boyfriend Logan MacPhail.

Kaur said: "Stories like Holly's are why we are deploying the full power of the state to halve violence against women and girls in a decade."

MacPhail was 16 when he killed Holly and could not accept the relationship was over. He had been controlling and stalked the teeanger in the run up to her death.

Police recorded her murder as knife crime because the law does not recognise those under 16 as victims of domestic violence.

This is something her mum and stepdad, Micala and Lee Trussler, have been campaigning to change.

News.title: DUP leader 'very sorry' Carla Lockhart has quit the party
News.content:
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson has said he is "very sorry" that MP Carla Lockhart has quit the party.

Robinson said he would not be criticising the Upper Bann MP, who left the party on Monday over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute, and expressed hope they would continue to work together in the future.

Lockhart had been calling for the DUP to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force Sinn FÃ©in First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.

Speaking on Tuesday, Robinson said the disagreement was over strategy not sentiment.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn FÃ©in figures have been interviewed by police investigating the Garvaghy Road demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn FÃ©in in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.

But Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.

Speaking on the Good Morning Ulster programme he said: "We share exactly the same sentiment - all of us are angered, all of us believe the position of Michelle O'Neill and her willingness to break the law, to ignore the courts, to breach her pledge of office requires sanction.

"So while we share the same sentiment, we have not been in agreement when it comes to how you deal with it.

"The Democratic Unionist Party is firmly of the view that it is Michelle O'Neill who should face the consequences of her actions, not the rest of the people of Northern Ireland.

"Northern Ireland needs a functioning government, Northern Ireland needs a budget - those important discussions will continue on Thursday I believe with the secretary of state."

Robinson said he believes "there is a role for this government to come forward with a sanctions regime that will punish those who break the pledge of office".

News.title: Police admit unlawful home entry and assault of couple
News.content:
A couple have been awarded Â£9,000 in damages after police admitted its officers unlawfully entered their home and assaulted them nearly four years ago.

Andrew and Sabrina Fearn had a house party in their home in December 2022. Earlier, Sabrina had called police and officers attended before leaving. They then returned, believing someone was injured inside and wanted access.

Sabrina refused, but officers forced entry and used physical force on her, according to legal documents. Andrew then stepped in before "unnecessary force" was used on him.

Both were arrested and charged with assaulting an emergency worker, but their trial was halted when police admitted the forced house entry was unlawful.

Andrew and Sabrina, from Alvaston in Derby, pursued a civil claim against the force, and the case has now been settled for Â£9,000, the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) said.

According to the legal claim submitted by the couple, a gathering at their home ended when they discovered one of the guests had a knife.

Sabrina called the police, which attended and then left shortly after.

But soon after, several officers returned wanting to gain entry, believing someone was injured inside and needed urgent medical attention.

Sabrina, 31, refused to let police in, saying the party had finished and no guests remained. She tried to stop police from entering her house, before officers forced entry and used physical force on her.

Andrew, 40, stepped in to protect his wife, fearing she was being hurt, before "unnecessary force" was used on him, according to the legal papers.

Extracts from police bodycam footage describes Andrew being held by the throat against a wall, while Sabrina was held by the neck as officers forced entry.

Andrew was warned he would be Tasered if he did not comply, was sprayed in the face with an incapacitant spray, handcuffed, taken away in a police van and held for 15 hours.

According to the LDRS, as the couple made physical contact with officers during the incident, both were arrested and charged with assaulting an emergency worker.

However, the pair were found not guilty in the middle of their trial, after police gave evidence to admit the forced entry to the home was unlawful.

News.title: Major study into 'forever chemicals' in people's bodies launched in UK
News.content:
The government is launching its first study into the levels of so-called 'forever chemicals' in the UK population.

By taking blood and urine samples, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) hopes to gain a better understanding of any potential health risks caused by the substances also known as PFAS, as well as other potential contaminants like lead and arsenic.

It said current evidence suggested the possible health impacts associated with PFAS are likely to be limited, but said the strongest links found in large population groups have been to raised cholesterol and lower birth weights.

The first results are expected next year.

PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have been used prolifically since the 1940s and 1950s because they are resistant to water, oil and heat.

It is why they have been placed in thousands of items such as pots and pans, clothing and foams used to fight fires.

But because they do not break down easily in the environment - hence the name 'forever chemicals' - they have raised health concerns in recent years.

Two are already banned in the UK - PFOA and PFOS - because prolonged exposure to them can increase the risk of cancer, according to the World Health Organization., external

But the study of PFAS is an emerging field with more than 15,000 types to research.

The UKHSA will take blood and urine samples collected through the existing Health Survey for England, external to establish baseline levels of PFAS, lead, arsenic, bisphenols, phthalates and flame retardants in the population.

News.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
News.content:
Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity.

The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland.

The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men.

This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp.

Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail.

She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added.

The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity.

The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn.

David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world."

News.title: Two boys arrested after Halloween party stabbings
News.content:
Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.

Officers said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.

Police said two boys remain in hospital having suffered serious injuries, with one 17-year-old victim in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.

A 17-year-old and 16-year-old, both from Southampton, have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and remain in police custody.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie said: "Whilst the two arrests are a significant development in our investigation, which has moved at pace since the incident was first reported to us, we still urge our communities to contact us with any information, no matter how small it may seem."

She added: "If you were at the party and have not spoken with officers yet, or you have any CCTV, mobile phone, dash cam or doorbell camera footage covering Park Road and the surrounding area, then please get in touch."

News.title: Police question Steve Wright about unsolved cases
News.content:
Serial killer Steve Wright has been questioned about a series of cold cases but is "not currently a suspect" in any of them, the police have told the BBC.

The 68-year-old was jailed for life in 2008 for the murders of five women in Ipswich between October and December 2006.

In February, he was given a further life sentence after pleading guilty to the kidnap and killing of 17-year-old Victoria Hall, from Trimley St Mary, in September 1999.

Suffolk Police said his admissions prompted the force to consider whether Wright may have been involved in other unsolved disappearances or murders.

"Following his sentencing for the murder of Victoria Hall earlier this year, he has been interviewed in prison about other unsolved cases," a spokesperson said.

"In the cases where we have DNA we have sought to use it to eliminate him from inquiries."

News.title: Dry and chilly start to November after wet but sunny October
News.content:
High pressure has seized control of the UK weather meaning largely dry, settled but chilly autumn conditions will continue this week.

Days will bring a mix of patchy cloud, sunny spells and a few showers, with frost and fog expected to form at night - especially in northern and western areas.

Temperatures will generally be around or a little below the seasonal norm and it will feel particularly chilly in southern England and south Wales where there will be a brisk easterly breeze.

The relatively quiet start to November follows a decidedly mixed October which - according to Met Office data just released was wetter, warmer and sunnier than average.

News.title: Bernie Taupin says he no longer feels ‘even remotely British’ after decades in the US
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bernie Taupin has said he no long feels “even remotely” British, having lived in the US for five decades.

The songwriter, known for his decades-long career as Elton John’s lyricist, accompanied the “Rocket Man” singer to the US on a tour years ago, and decided to move there shortly afterwards. He became a US citizen in 1990.

Speaking to The Guardian, Taupin admitted that he no longer feels connected to his British roots, admitting: “I have no British tendencies whatsoever.

“None of my friends or people I interact with in the States think of me as British because I’m so assimilated into American culture.”

open image in gallery Bernie Taupin in September ( Getty Images for Americana Music )

Before moving to the US, the Lincolnshire-born celebrity was an ardent Americanophile, and had drawn on US iconography in his music, in songs such as “Ballad of a Well-Known Gun” on John’s 1970 album Tumbleweed Connection.

Recalling his initial trip to the US, Taupin explained: “I immediately thought, ‘I could live here for the rest of my life.’ I moved there as soon as I could afford it, living very, very cheaply in places I rented that were pretty appalling. I just loved it. I never, ever, ever got homesick.”

He also spoke about his daughter – a professional bull rider and “rodeo star in Texas” who “barrel races” and is “100 per cent cowgirl”.

“You couldn’t pry her out of Texas with a crowbar,” Taupin joked.

open image in gallery John and Taupin pose in the press room during the 2020 Oscars ( AFP/Getty )

Elsewhere in the interview, Taupin spoke about the origins of John’s 1983 hit “I’m Still Standing”, a track released amid a turbulent time in John’s personal life that served as an affirmation of his own resilience.

“‘I’m Still Standing’ was a sort of kiss-off to an ex-girlfriend, but I didn’t tell Elton that,” Taupin recalled.

“I wanted him to do his own take and it sounded like Elton singing about himself because it was on our big comeback album, Too Low for Zero. So it felt like him talking about his own resilience.”

Speaking about his comparatively low profile – when juxtaposed with John – Taupin said: “Elton’s probably one of the most recognisable people in the world.

“I understand why he has to have a security team, but I could not live like that. I live in a very very small community, near Santa Barbara: everybody knows me, I know everybody, nobody treats me in any way other than as a friend. I’ve gone way past being regarded as somebody remotely special and I love that more than anything.”

Taupin is now releasing an album titled The Sea Has No Mercy, his fourth solo album and first since 1987’s Tribe.

News.title: The bizarre hidden health benefits of voting in the midterm elections
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Most people know the basics of healthy living that become more important as you grow older: Eat plenty of vegetables, exercise regularly, sleep well, have a social life, limit your alcohol consumption and don’t smoke.

As an economist and social psychologist who study altruism and health, we wondered whether civic engagement might play a role as well.

In 2022, the American Medical Association, an organization representing doctors, noted that voting could potentially have health benefits.

So we conducted a study that directly tested this idea: We examined whether older Americans – people who are 65 and up – who vote live longer than nonvoters.

Older adults vote at a higher rate than younger adults in the United States. In Wisconsin, the focus of our study, the voting rate of older adults is even higher.

We used data from the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, a study which has followed a randomly selected sample of Wisconsin high school graduates since 1957.

We compared the long-term health of older adults who voted in the 2008 presidential election to those who did not vote in that election.

Using objectively verified voting records from Catalist, which tracks Americans’ voting behavior, along with official National Death Index records, we found that voters were 45% less likely to die within five years after the 2008 election, 37% less likely to die 10 years after the election, and 29% less likely to die 15 years later.

We also examined voting in the 2004 and 2012 presidential elections and found that the results were stronger for more recent elections – those held in 2008 and 2012 – compared to the earlier one held in 2004.

You may wonder whether this is just because healthier people are more likely to vote in the first place.

( AFP/Getty )

It’s easier to vote when you’re healthy than when you’re not, but this does not fully explain our results.

Voters still had a lower risk of dying when we controlled for demographic factors such as gender, marital status and income, other forms of civic engagement such as volunteering, and a voter’s health status prior to voting.

We also found that those in poorer health to begin with benefited more from voting 15 years later than those who had been healthier before they voted.

Here’s another finding: How someone voted didn’t matter. When we compared what happened to older adults who cast their ballots in person to those who mailed their ballots, we found that both groups had about an equally lower risk of dying over the 15-year period.

About the authors Sara Konrath is an Associate Professor of Philanthropic Studies at Indiana University. Femida Handy is a Professor of Social Policy at the University of Pennsylvania. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

It also did not matter whether a voter’s preferred candidate won. We found that although it can be stressful when the candidate you support loses, the people we studied experienced similar long-term health benefits of voting regardless of their political affiliation.

Why it matters

Scientists have long known that people who volunteer for nonprofits experience many health benefits, including a longer lifespan.

Voting is, arguably, also an altruistically motivated act. That’s because individual voters are aware that their one vote will not change the outcome of a national election.

What still isn’t known

If you are wondering why voting predicts lower mortality risk, well, so did we.

One possibility is that as with other civic engagement activities, including volunteering, voting may trigger positive biological responses that support well-being. Other researchers have found ample evidence showing that volunteering can boost the brain’s reward system, reduce stress and even slow some aspects of aging.

Although we didn’t test for these in the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, they may help explain why people who vote tend to have better health outcomes than those who don’t.

Voting might also improve health through a sense of self-efficacy, civic duty and social connection, since it is both an altruistic and shared activity.

Although the exact explanations aren’t known, studies consistently show a link between volunteering and a lower mortality risk, which suggests that participating in civic life – even something as simple as casting a ballot – may be good for your health, like going for a run or eating vegetables.

News.title: Michael Douglas issues midterm election plea after predicting Trump ‘massacre’
News.content:
Lifelong Democrat Michael Douglas has urged Americans to defend the Constitution after predicting that Donald Trump’s supporters face a “massacre” in the midterm elections.

Addressing election officials directly on Tuesday (3 November), the Wall Street and Basic Instinct star asked them to “honor” the Constitution by “making sure every vote is counted accurately and securely.”

“Please stand firm against any directive that would undermine our constitutional right to a free and fair election,” he added.

Last week, the Oscar-winning actor told the BBC’s Today programme, while in the UK to promote his autobiography One Helluva Ride: “I’m hoping for a massacre, and we’ll see … overwhelming Democratic votes across the board.”

News.title: James Blunt says Celebrity Traitors didn’t show ‘full extent’ of ‘heavy’ James Acaster roundtable
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Celebrity Traitors’ recent series saw James Acaster do something no one on the show has ever done before, when he prematurely confessed to being a Traitor at a roundtable – and now co-star James Blunt has revealed the build-up to that moment that didn’t make the edit.

The “You’re Beautiful” singer has claimed that viewers “didn’t see the full extent” of Acaster being interrogated at the roundtable and that the comedian “didn’t fall on his sword”.

In the penultimate episode of the BBC competition, Acaster revealed himself to be a Traitor before the votes were cast after being questioned by Michael Sheen over his role in Ross Kemp’s murder-in-plain-sight. Unsurprisingly, Acaster was banished and the Faithful – Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian Croft – went on to win Celebrity Traitors 2026.

Speaking to BBC News about the jaw-dropping moment, Blunt – a Faithful who made it to the final episode before being banished by Ranganathan and Croft – said: “He didn’t fall on his sword. That’s what you saw, that’s what you feel, but he didn’t.

open image in gallery James Blunt on ‘Celebrity Traitors’ ( BBC/Studio Lambert )

“You didn't see the full extent of the interrogation. It was heavy in there and it was clear-cut. He was pinned to a post. We got him. We really, really got him.”

He added that the true sequence of events “hasn’t really been revealed” to viewers. “He didn’t just say, ‘Oh guys, you got me.’” According to the BBC report, Blunt hinted that Acaster was caught in a fib about a perfume bottle used in the murder.

Addressing the editing of the series, Blunt said that there were elements of the show where he was “screaming at the screen for a different reason than” viewers. “No matter what really went on in that castle, you’re a victim to the edit.”

The Independent has contacted the BBC for comment.

It was reported that filming of the penultimate episode was halted so producers could intervene when Acaster became distressed at the roundtable. In a statement, the BBC said that its “highest priority is always the safety and welfare of everyone taking part”.

A spokesperson added: “Players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team.”

open image in gallery James Acaster declared himself to be a Traitor before the roundtable voting began in the penultimate episode of ‘Celebrity Traitors’ ( BBC )

Blunt isn’t the only Celebrity Traitors star to speak out about the moment; Acaster’s fellow Traitor Maya Jama said in a recent interview that the game was “a lot” for the comedian.

“Bless him,” she said. “Never in a game would you expect that you’re going to be put in a situation where you absolutely hate being a Traitor. And I obviously had no idea beforehand that he didn’t want to be a Traitor, I just thought everyone’s kind of up for it.

“But yeah, it was hard. I don’t think anybody knows how it would feel once you’re in the situation, and that’s going to impact everyone completely differently. As he said, for him it was a lot,” she added. “You’re like, ‘OK, this is a game, we’re playing for charity.’ But then these people have real feelings, and trying to find the balance between it is tougher than it looks.”

Over 11.2 million people tuned in to watch Ranganathan and Croft split the £83,000 prize pot on Friday, making it the highest-ever overnight audience for the show.

News.title: Bomb alert on London Heathrow plane closes Warsaw airport
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A flight from London to Poland had to make an emergency landing after a bomb threat on Tuesday.

The plane, with 181 people on board, was diverted to Warsaw Modlin Airport after the alert. The airport remains closed until further notice.

Warsaw Modlin Airport , which is around 25 miles north of central Warsaw, reported the unplanned landing of a plane from London Heathrow Airport due to information on an explosive device on board, it said in a statement.

The plane has landed safely and security services are verifying the reported threat.

Flight tracking website Flight Aware shows a Boeing 737 MAX 8 departing London Heathrow at 6.54 am on Tuesday and arriving at at Modlin-Warsaw at 9.59am local time.

open image in gallery The flight was diverted to Modlin-Warsaw ( Flight Aware )

This LOT Polish Airlines flight was originally heading to Nowy Dwór Mazowiecki, a town in east-central Poland before it was diverted. Warsaw-Modlin said that at 10.01 am local time, passengers started disembarking.

Once off the aircraft, passengers were told to wait in the arrivals hall.

“Further actions are being carried out in accordance with established safety procedures,” the airport said. “At this time, no additional information regarding the specific operations of the emergency services will be provided.”

News.title: Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns
News.content:
Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

News.title: US dairy worker dies from bird flu as outbreak rages in cattle
News.content:
“People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States. Public health officials are continuing to monitor individuals who had close contact with the patient for symptoms,” the health district said in a statement.

Experts say the US bird flu outbreak is not only costing the dairy industry millions of dollars but also raises the risk that the virus could mutate to spread more easily between mammals. They are also concerned that authorities are doing little to check the spread.

Marc Johnson, a virologist at the University of Missouri, told the Telegraph last week that the outbreak in dairy cattle was “completely preventable”.

“Cattle infections last only a few weeks before the animals recover. If infected herds were simply isolated until the outbreak fizzled out, it would stop.

“But cattle keep being moved around, spreading it into new states,” said Dr Johnson, referring to the way the US dairy industry operates, in which cows are routinely transported across state lines, whether to join new herds, for breeding, or to replace animals at large milk-producing operations.

A bird flu outbreak has also been raging on a mink farm in Utah for the last couple of months, according to news outlet ProPublica.

Jonathan Ball, professor of molecular virology at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, said allowing a virus to rage unchecked raises the risk of it mutating.

“Viruses like influenza are constantly exploring new hosts, and more often than not, it burns out. It’s not quite got the right combination of genetic changes to allow it to efficiently infect, efficiently replicate, and then efficiently transmit to the new host. But the longer these steps - adaptive changes, so genetic changes - are happening in these sporadic outbreaks, the more likelihood you’ve got of it mutating. It’s a bit like a one-armed bandit machine - if you keep pulling that handle, eventually you’re going to get three cherries,” he said.

News.title: First ever trial of long-acting injection against malaria to launch in Africa
News.content:
Dr Cristina Donini, executive vice-president of research and development at MMV, said the compound would be “complementary” to existing tools, rather than replacing them.

“The vaccine is doing a fantastic job in infants but if you could add onto that another tool that can cover a broader population with a longer regimen then we would be in a very good position to eliminate the disease,” she said.

Children in malaria-endemic regions are already given prophylactic drugs during the malaria season and studies have shown that these combined with the vaccine are highly effective. However, resistance has developed to these drugs and they have to be given monthly.

The malaria season in Africa varies by region but usually peaks after periods of rainfall. If the season lasts longer than three to four months it’s likely that people would need two injections. However, Dr Donini and her colleagues are working on a second generation LAI which they hope would provide year-long coverage.

Full costs have not yet been worked out but Dr Donini said affordability was an important factor in assessing the LAI’s suitability.

“It’s too early to say whether it will be cheaper than an injection - hopefully, yes. The beauty of it is that if you simplify it and decrease the number of injections needed you decrease the cost,” she said.

LAIs are gaining traction in the fight against infectious diseases - Lenacapavir, now being rolled out after being approved in 2025, provides almost 100% protection against infection from HIV and many believe it could help end the HIV pandemic. There are also LAI candidates in development for the prevention of tuberculosis, treatment and prevention of which usually relies on daily pills being taken over many months.

Lottie Renwick, global campaign director at Malaria No More UK, welcomed the launch of the trial.

“Thanks to sustained investment in malaria science including here in the UK, we are now on the brink of a number of breakthroughs which could turn the tide on the fight against the disease. And the long-acting injectable, specifically, could be a valuable addition to this toolbox as it has the potential to provide sustained protection from a single shot, avoiding the need for repeat doses.

“This phase of the trial also builds on earlier research conducted in the UK, highlighting the importance of the UK’s ongoing role as a malaria science superpower and the value of continued investment in malaria R&D. We look forward to the trial progressing further and eagerly await the results.”

News.title: Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win
News.content:
It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

News.title: Tears flow for Antonelli after becoming youngest champion in F1 history
News.content:
Welcome to our coverage for the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix from the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. Today could be the day for Kimi Antonelli, the day he becomes a Formula One world champion. In fact it is very likely. All he needs to confirm the drivers’ championship is to finish ninth or higher. If George Russell or Lewis Hamilton do not claim victory then he is champion whatever happens. Given his season so far, it is difficult to see the title fight going to Brazil next week.

What chance of a decent race here today? The first few laps are often entertaining as the pack bunches up and there are plenty of chances to overtake early on. Generally the top four teams have been close together (last week in Austin excluded) and it is possible to overtake here, though it is not exactly easy.

Qualifying yesterday as an intriguing and close session. Hamilton secured his first grand prix pole for Ferrari, by just 0.009sec from the Mercedes of George Russell, with Charles Leclerc of Ferrari a little behind him in third. Then came Max Verstappen, Antonelli, Norris, Hadjar and Lindblad. Liam Lawson was disqualified on a technicality.

Ferrari have been an up-and-down team this season but have been strong without really delivering on it fully in the last few rounds. Could they secure a third victory of the season today? They do not really need to worry about losing second in the constructors to Red Bull or McLaren and Mercedes are too far out of reach in any case.

In any case, the biggest story is likely to be Antonelli’s coronation in Mexico. Hamilton has won titles here before for Mercedes, will the Italian give the Silver Arrows another fiesta in Mexico City? The race starts at 8pm GMT and we will be here for all the build-up, live updates and reaction from it.

News.title: Lewis Hamilton becomes oldest driver to claim pole position in 44 years
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for qualifying for the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix from the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico City, obviously. The big story this weekend is that Jimi Antonelli is almost certain to become the youngest world champion in Formula One history. To guarantee it he needs just two points, but if George Russell or Lewis Hamilton fail to win here then the title is his whatever he does. It has been a superb, strong and consistent season from the man who began the year as a teenager. He has not quite been faultless, but he has not been far away.

There are other stories floating around the paddock, too. Notably, Esteban Ocon has been dropped by Haas today for final practice, qualifying and the race, to be replaced by reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the weekend. Whether Ocon will continue in any other races has yet to be confirmed but you have to say that it seems extremely unlikely. More on that later.

Another line is the ongoing tension between Liam Lawson and Max Verstappen after their crash in FP2 yesterday. It was certainly a strange one in which neither driver backed down, which resulted in contact, debris being strewn across the track and a red flag. Both drivers seemed unrepentant, though admitted it was clumsy. Lawson and Verstappen each receive a one-place grid penalty for the incident, which feels about right given how silly and unnecessary it all was.

But what about the competitive order on track? Since the summer break, and a little before in fairness, things have been unpredictable at the top. Mercedes have still, on average, been the best team but Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren have all had their moments.

What happened in final practice? It was Lando Norris who topped the timesheets by just 0.001sec ahead of Mercedes’ Antonelli. Charles Leclerc was a further tenth or so back for Ferrari followed by Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren, who was 0.195sec off his team-mate’s pace. Then came Verstappen, Hamilton, Russell, Isack Hadjar, Lawson and Arvid Lindblad. All drivers were within 0.6sec off Norris, which promises a close qualifying session. Let’s hope we get it.

News.title: Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points
News.content:
Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

News.title: Alex Mitchell injury blow for England but Northampton dig deep to win
News.content:
England were dealt a fresh blow ahead of their Nations Championship opener with Australia after scrum-half Alex Mitchell was forced off early in Northampton’s victory over Gloucester.

Mitchell left the field gingerly 20 minutes into the action after picking up a suspected hamstring injury following an innocuous coming-together with Gloucester winger Will Joseph.

The Saints scrum-half has suffered a series of hamstring issues this year – this would be a fourth time he has picked up a problem – and he looked visibly disappointed as he limped off.

He suffered a left leg hamstring tear during England’s Six Nations defeat to Ireland which left him sidelined for two months and, in a cruel twist of fate, sustained another on his right leg during an England three-day training camp in Bagshot last May. He suffered the injury for a third time in England’s 73-8 rout of Fiji in July.

With Mitchell’s club-mate, Archie McParland, nursing an unspecified knock that forced him to miss Saints’ high-stakes clash with Gloucester, Jack van Poortvliet is likely to start at nine against the Wallabies next Sunday. McParland was the third-choice scrum-half in England’s Nations Championship squad, but Steve Borthwick may be forced to look elsewhere if Mitchell’s prognosis is serious.

Sports.title: England told to 'keep pressure on' with Australia at risk of 'imploding'
Sports.content:
Australia have got problems.

A No 3 batter in Marnus Labuschagne who has gone 49 innings without a Test century and looks certain to be axed ahead of the impending home series against New Zealand.

Batting issues besides that, too, with the team rolled for 99 and 111 during the recent 2-1 loss in South Africa that saw their opponents displace them at the top of the Test rankings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from day five of the series-deciding third Test between South Africa and Australia as the Proteas won by 176 runs to go top of the rankings.

Selectors in the firing line after persisting with Labuschagne and also recalling Nic Maddinson, who had not played a first-class game since March 2025 and went on to total just 56 runs in four knocks in South Africa, including a 33-ball duck, before he was jettisoned.

A generational, certainly, but aging bowling attack that must cram in that four-match assignment versus New Zealand around Christmas, five Tests in India and the day-night 150th anniversary Test at home to England in March prior to the away Ashes next summer.

Michael Atherton can envisage an "implosion" before Australia arrive in the UK, telling the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast: "You could see it going horribly wrong, couldn't you?"
