Ghana News.title: Vehicles do not commit crimes: Registered-Owner liability, the presumption of innocence, and the legality of TRAFFITECH-GH
Ghana News.content:
By: Albert Gyamfi, Esq.

Abstract

On 1st November, 2026, the Ghana Police Service commenced full implementation of TRAFFITECH-GH, an automated traffic enforcement programme under which Electronic Notices of Violation are issued to registered vehicle owners detected committing road traffic offences. This article contends that the programme, as presently operated, rests on an unexamined assumption: that the person in whose name a vehicle is registered is the person who committed the offence. It argues, first, that criminal liability in Ghana attaches to persons by reason of their own conduct and not to vehicles or to the holders of title in them; second, that Ghanaian law recognises no general doctrine of vicarious criminal liability capable of fixing a registered owner with the offences of employees, agents, borrowers or unregistered transferees; third, that the identity of the driver is an element of the offence which the prosecution must establish beyond reasonable doubt; and fourth, that an enforcement regime which in substance presumes the owner's guilt, absent a clear Act of Parliament reversing the onus of proof, is ultra vires its parent statute and inconsistent with Article 19 of the 1992 Constitution. The article closes by considering the principal objections and proposing a lawful legislative framework.

Keywords: automated traffic enforcement; vicarious liability; presumption of innocence; reverse onus; subsidiary legislation; Article 19, 1992 Constitution of Ghana

I. Introduction

A camera can record a number plate. It cannot record a guilty mind, nor, in most deployments, the identity of the person at the wheel. This limitation, trivial as a matter of engineering, is fundamental as a matter of criminal law, and it lies at the centre of the legal difficulty presented by TRAFFITECH-GH.

The programme went live nationwide on 1st November, 2026, after a one-month postponement announced to allow further public sensitisation. Its objective is beyond reproach. Ghana's road fatality figures are grave, and technology that deters speeding and the disregard of traffic signals is a legitimate instrument of public policy. The question this article addresses is narrower and juridical: whether the State may lawfully treat the registered owner of a vehicle as the offender and require that owner to exculpate himself, without an enabling Act of Parliament that clearly provides for it.

The argument proceeds in seven further Parts. Part II describes the scheme and its legal architecture. Part III restates the principle that criminal liability is founded on personal conduct. Part IV demonstrates the absence of any general doctrine of vicarious criminal liability in Ghanaian law. Part V examines the allocation of the burden of proof. Part VI identifies the constitutional and administrative-law infirmities that follow. Part VII engages the strongest objections, drawing on comparative practice. Part VIII proposes a lawful framework, and Part IX concludes.

II. The TRAFFITECH-GH Scheme and Its Legal Architecture

Operation

Fixed, vehicle-mounted, tripod and handheld devices capture alleged violations. Following review at a back office, an Electronic Notice of Violation (ENV) is transmitted by SMS to the registered owner at the telephone number held on the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA) record. The recipient may, within 14 days, pay the fine electronically or lodge an online contest; the matter proceeds to court only if contested. Default attracts a surcharge of one per cent of the fine for each day, and, until payment, the DVLA will decline to renew a driving licence, register or transfer a vehicle, or conduct a roadworthiness inspection. Regulation 242 of the Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519) prescribes the fines: ten penalty units for each of the first three offences, rising thereafter, with a sixth offence within 24 months referred to court.

B, The Locus of Liability

Official and semi-official guidance on liability has not been consistent. Public explainers issued before the rollout stated that the registered owner bears liability irrespective of who was driving; that a seller who has not registered a change of ownership remains responsible; that a company is answerable for its employees' use of its vehicles; and that an owner may rely on theft only where it was reported to the police before the alleged offence. The Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) subsequently characterised the owner's liability as initial, explaining that the owner may thereafter identify the driver, and that the relevant regulation defines the responsible person as the owner or the person driving at the material time.

C. Statutory Foundation

The primary legislation is strikingly sparse. The Road Traffic (Amendment) Act, 2005 (Act 1153) addresses automated enforcement only by extending the definition of "spot fine" to include an automated fine. Owner liability, the daily surcharge, licence consequences and the evidential status of camera records are left to L.I. 2519. That instrument is subsidiary legislation made by the Minister under the regulation-making power conferred by the Road Traffic Act, 2004 (Act 683). The structural significance of this allocation, between Act and instrument, is developed in Part VI.

Ill. Personal Conduct as the Foundation of Criminal Liability

The first proposition is elementary but frequently obscured in public debate: vehicles do not commit offences; persons do. A motor vehicle possesses neither will nor knowledge and cannot be the subject of a criminal prohibition. Offences such as exceeding a speed limit, disregarding a traffic signal or using a mobile telephone while driving are offences of conduct, and the relevant conduct is the act of driving. The offender is the person in control of the vehicle at the moment of the prohibited act.

This proposition has constitutional footing. Article 19(11) of the 1992 Constitution forbids conviction for a criminal offence unless the offence is defined, and its penalty prescribed, in a written law. Road traffic offences are defined by reference to what a person does. Evidence that a vehicle bearing a given registration mark travelled above the limit establishes the actus reus in the abstract; it says nothing about whose act it was. Both elements; the offending act and the offender, must be proved to establish criminal liability.

Registration does not bridge that gap. The DVLA register is an administrative record of title and of the person responsible for licensing a vehicle. It was never designed to record, and does not purport to record, who drives a vehicle on any given occasion, neither does it contain a restriction that a registered vehicle must be driven by the registered owner at all times. In the Ghanaian context the divergence between owner and driver is endemic rather than exceptional: commercial vehicles are owned by one person and driven by several in rotation; private vehicles are shared within households; and vehicles change hands informally, often more than once, without registration of the transfer. To treat registration as proof of driving is to convict on a document incapable of proving the fact issue.

IV. The Absence of Vicarious Criminal Liability in Ghanaian Law

A. The General Principle

Criminal responsibility is personal. A person is liable for what he does, and for what he counsels, aids, abets or procures; he is not liable in the criminal courts for another's act merely by reason of a relationship with that other. The contrast with tort law is instructive. An employer is vicariously liable in damages for torts committed by an employee in the course of employment, and a vehicle owner may be joined as a defendant in civil proceedings arising from a collision. These rules allocate the burden of compensation. They have never been rules allocating guilt.

At common law, which Ghanaian courts treat as highly persuasive, vicarious criminal liability is exceptional. It arises only where a statute, expressly or by necessary implication, imposes liability on one person for the acts of another, as the House of Lords emphasised in Vane v Yiannopoullos. Even the classic instances of statutory vicarious liability, such as those recognised in Mousell Bros Ltd v London and North-Western Railway Co, depend on the construction of particular statutory language. No Ghanaian Act of Parliament renders a registered owner criminally liable for speeding or signal offences committed by another person.

B. Employees andCommercialDrivess

The owner of a commercial vehicle whose driver exceeds the limit has committed no offence. He did not drive, did not authorise the excess, and may have prohibited it. A corporate owner stands in no different position: although a company is a legal person capable of criminal liability for its own acts, the company does not drive; the driver does. To fine the company for the driver's conduct is vicarious liability in its purest form.

C. Agents, Relatives and Borrowers

Lending a vehicle is lawful. A parent who lends a car to an adult child, or an owner whose vehicle is road-tested by a mechanic, does not thereby become a party to offences later committed by the user. Absent proof of participation, such as encouragement or knowing permission to commit the specific offence, the general principles of secondary liability provide no basis for attributing the user's conduct to the owner.

D. Unregistered Transferees

L.I. 2519 requires notice of a change of ownership within 14 days. A transferor who fails to give that notice may be answerable for that default, a discrete regulatory breach carrying its own consequence. It does not follow that he becomes criminally responsible for every offence the transferee commits thereafter. A failure to update a register cannot be transmuted into participation in another person's subsequent crime.

E. The Disjunctive Definition

On the MTTD's own account, the regulation defines the responsible person as the owner or the driver at the time of the offence. That formulation is disjunctive. It identifies the classes of person who may be charged, depending on the facts proved; it does not provide that the owner is guilty when the driver offends, and it does not deem the owner to have been the driver. Had the legislature intended to fix owners with criminal responsibility for the conduct of others, it was required to say so in unmistakable terms. It has not done so.

V. The Burden of Proof and the Presumption of Innocence

A. The Governing Rules

Article 19(2)(c) of the Constitution provides that a person charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved or pleaded guilty. The Evidence Act, 1975 (NRCD 323) gives that guarantee procedural content: in a criminal action the prosecution bears the burden of producing evidence, and the burden of persuasion, as to every fact essential to guilt, and must discharge the latter beyond reasonable doubt. Section 22 of the Act is especially significant. Where a presumption operates against an accused person as to a fact essential to guilt, the accused need only raise a reasonable doubt as to the presumed fact. The principle, traceable to Woolmington v Director of Public Prosecutions, has been consistently affirmed by the Supreme Court of Ghana, which has held that the burden of proving guilt remains with the prosecution throughout and never shifts to the accused to establish innocence.

B. Identity of the Driver as an Essential Element

The identity of the driver is a fact essential to guilt; without it there is no offender. The prosecution must therefore prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that the person named in the ENV was the person driving. A photograph of a registration mark, together with an extract from the DVLA register, establishes ownership. It does not establish driving. To infer the latter from the former is to supply by assumption the very element the law requires the State to prove.

C. Nomination as a Reversal of the Onus

The scheme's practical mechanism treats the owner as liable unless he identifies another person as the driver. Whatever its administrative convenience, this places on the accused the burden of disproving an element of the offence. It is in substance a legal, not merely evidential, reverse onus. It also sits in tension with Article 19(10), which protects a person tried for a criminal offence from being compelled to give evidence at the trial. An owner cannot be required, on pain of penalty, to construct the prosecution's case against himself or against a member of his household or workforce without any express legislative requirement.

D. The Illusion of Voluntary Payment

It may be said that no one is convicted, since the recipient may simply pay, and that the option of contesting in court preserves every procedural right. The answer is that payment under the pressure of a compounding daily surcharge and the withdrawal of DVLA services is not a free admission of guilt. And the motorist who elects to contest is entitled to insist that the State prove its case in the ordinary way, without the benefit of a presumption that Parliament has not enacted.

VI. Constitutional and Administrative-Law Infirmities

To the extent that TRAFFITECH-GH operates on a presumption that the registered owner is the offender, it depends on a reversal of the onus of proof that Parliament has not enacted. Four consequences follow.

A. Constitutional Supremacy

Article 1(2) renders void any law, and any act, inconsistent with the Constitution. The presumption of innocence in Article 19(2)(c) and the guarantee of a fair hearing in Article 19(1) bind the Police Service and the DVLA no less than the courts. An administrative practice that infers guilt from title cannot be sustained against them.

B. The Limits of Delegated Legislation

L.I. 2519 derives its validity entirely from Act 683. Subsidiary legislation is valid only within the four corners of the enabling power; what the parent Act does not authorise, the instrument cannot do. The Road Traffic (Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 1153) brought automated fines within the definition of a spot fine. It is silent on owner liability for another's driving, silent on any presumption that the owner was the driver, and silent on the burden of proof. A general power to regulate road traffic is not, on any ordinary reading, an authority to create vicarious criminal liability or to displace presumption of innocence.

It must also be noted that Act 1153 did not amend section 118 of the Road Traffic Act, 2004 (Act 683), which requires that spot fines, which were later defined to include an automated fine payable upon the commission of a traffic offence, were only to be imposed on the person who commits an offence. Section 133(1) of Act 683 only enabled the Minister to make regulations "providing for the payment of spot fines and offences for which spot fines are payable". The parent Act clearly does not envisage the imposition of a spot fine on another merely because he is the registered owner of the vehicle involved in the commission of the offence and a fortiori for the person to prove that he was not in operation of the vehicle at the time of the offence or to identify or produce the offender to exculpate himself. A legislative instrument made thereunder that provides for the transfer of criminal liability on a person other than the person who committed the offence is clearly inconsistent with the Parent Act and therefore unlawful. The parent act clearly required that the police identify the offender and impose the spot fine on him; an attempt by a legislative instrument to transfer the liability or a shift of the criminal burden on another, other than the police, to identify the offender is clearly in conflict with, or amounts to an amendment of, the parent Act.

This was the exact act prohibited in the case of Mensima and others v Attorney-General and others. In that case, reg 3(1) and 21 of the Manufacture and Sale of Spirits Regulations, 1962 (L.I 239) required as a condition to the grant of a distiller's licence that an applicant was to be a member of a registered co-operative and also requiring that a distilled gin be sold to specific persons. The Plaintiffs challenged the regulations on grounds, among others, that it was inconsistent with the parent act as it provided no such requirement for registration. The Supreme Court, per a majority decision, held that The Manufacture and Sale of Spirits Act, 1962 (Act 154), subsequently repealed by the Liquor Licensing Act, 1970 (Act 331), under which LI 239 was made did not specifically provide for the making of regulations for the issuing of distiller's licence conditioned on one being a member of a co­operative society. LI 239 had thus clearly amended its enabling or parent Act. And since Act 331 did not provide that the regulations made under it should have the same effect as if enacted in the Act, regulation 3(1) of LI 239 was in conflict with Act 331. The Court accordingly struck it.

It is my contention that, under the principle of legality, fundamental rights may be overridden only by express words or necessary implication, so that the legislature must squarely confront what it is doing and accept the political cost. [23] General words in a regulation-making power do not meet that standard.

C. The Scope of Articlei9(i6)(a)

The strongest textual answer available to the State is Article 19(16)(a), which saves from invalidity a law that imposes on a person charged with a criminal offence the burden of proving particular facts. Three points may be made in reply. First, as an exception to a fundamental right, the provision must be construed narrowly. It contemplates the proof of particular facts, characteristically facts peculiarly within the accused's knowledge such as the possession of a licence or lawful excuse, and not a presumption as to the identity of the offender, which is the very core of guilt. Second, comparative jurisprudence counsels caution. The House of Lords in R v Lambert read down a statutory reverse burden to an evidential one in order to preserve the presumption of innocence; the Constitutional Court of South Africa in S v Coetzee struck down reverse-onus presumptions that permitted conviction despite reasonable doubt; and the Supreme Court of Canada in R v Oakes held that a provision requiring an accused to disprove an element of the offence infringed the presumption of innocence.

Third, while I do not intend by this paper to postulate that an onus reversal offence is prima facie unconstitutional under our law, it is my contention that where the law maker intended to create an onus reversal offence, same is clearly stated in the law. This principle was espoused in the case of Donkor v The Republic where Wiredu J (as he then was) held as follows, "Where a statute creates an offence, it is the duty of the prosecution to prove each and every element of the offence which is a sine qua non to securing conviction. Unless the same statute places a particular burden on the accused, the fundamental and cardinal principle as to the criminal burden of proof on the prosecution should not be shifted even slightly." Again, even if Article 19(16)(a) could in principle sustain an owner-liability presumption, a derogation of that gravity ought to be enacted by parliament in an Act, after open debate, and not inferred from a ministerial instrument read together with press statements.

D. Penally Without Adjudication

The refusal of licence renewal, vehicle registration and roadworthiness certification, together with a compounding daily surcharge, are penalties. They are imposed before any court has found the recipient guilty, based on a notice sent to a telephone number that may be years out of date. Contests are lodged with, and resolved by, the department that issued the notice. This process is difficult to reconcile with the fair-hearing guarantee in Article 19(1) and the duty of administrative bodies and officials under Article 23 to act fairly and reasonably.

VII. Objections and Responses

A serious argument must meet the best case against it. Five objections merit consideration.

A. "A Legislative instrument Is Law"

Article 11 includes subsidiary legislation among the laws of Ghana, and the State may contend that L.I. 2519 is itself the "law" contemplated by Article 19(16)(a). The response, developed in Part VLB, is that an instrument's status as law is conditional on its being intra vires. If Act 683 does not authorise owner liability for another's conduct or a reversed onus, the instrument cannot supply that authority for itself.

B. "The Owner May Simply Nominate the Driver"

The MTTD presents nomination as a safeguard. Yet a safeguard that requires the accused to identify the offender is itself the reversal of onus complained of. It also fails the owner who genuinely does not know who drove a shared or fleet vehicle at a particular moment, and it may compel an owner to give evidence against a relative or employee.

C. "Comparable Jurisdictions Use Owner Liability"

Owner-liability camera schemes are common. The instructive feature of the leading examples, however, is that each rests on specific primary legislation. New South Wales amended its Motor Traffic Act by statute in 1986 to make owners liable for camera-detected red-light offences, coupled with a statutory defence for an owner able to show he was not the driver. Queensland's 1996 amendments provided expressly that owner liability does not displace the actual offender's liability, and that owner and offender cannot both be punished. New York created owner liability for red-light camera violations by statute, framed as a civil liability. South Africa operates a statutory presumption under section 73 of its National Road Traffic Act within a separate administrative adjudication regime. These examples do not show that owner liability is inherently impermissible. They show that it is a choice for the legislature, to be made expressly and accompanied by defences, often by decriminalising the owner's exposure. Ghana has skipped that step.

D. "The Fines Are Small and Payment is Voluntary"

The magnitude of a criminal penalty does not alter its character, and Part V.D has explained why payment under escalating sanctions is not voluntary in any meaningful sense.

E. "Road Deaths Demand Urgent Action"

They do. But urgency is a reason to legislate properly, not a warrant to dispense with the presumption of innocence. A scheme vulnerable to constitutional challenge serves road safety poorly.

F. Residual Considerations

The State's position is not without force. It may point to the express permission in Article 19(16)(a); to the practical impossibility of photographing every driver; to the general acceptance of strict liability for regulatory offences; to the fact that the owner, not the police, is best placed to know who had the vehicle; and to the salutary incentive owner liability creates for owners to supervise drivers and register transfers. The ultimate resolution will depend on the precise text of L.I. 2519 and on how the courts construe Article 19(16). This article submits that, on the present legislative footing, those considerations do not suffice.

VIII. Toward a Lawful Framework

Automated enforcement can be placed on a sound legal footing. The following reforms are proposed:

Primary legislation. Owner liability, if adopted, should be created by Act of Parliament, specifying whether the owner's liability is criminal or civil, the defences available, and the incidence of each burden. Decriminalised owner liability. An owner who was not driving and who fails to identify the driver should face at most, a civil or administrative penalty. Criminal liability, with its attendant record and licence consequences, should remain with the person proved to have driven. A fair statutory defence. Owners should be able to establish, on the balance of probabilities, that the vehicle had been sold, stolen, hired or taken without consent, without the defence being confined to thefts reported before the offence. Independent adjudication. Contests should be determined by a body independent of the MTTD, with surcharges and DVLA sanctions suspended pending determination. Register integrity. The State should rectify the DVLA register, through a simplified transfer procedure and verification of owners' contact details, before relying on it to imposeliability.

IX. Conclusion

The legitimacy of an enforcement system depends not only on the soundness of its objectives but on the lawfulness of its methods. TRAFFITECH-GH pursues a vital public purpose, yet in its present form it substitutes a register of title for proof of conduct and asks the citizen to prove his own innocence. Ghanaian criminal law knows no general doctrine of vicarious liability that would justify the former, and the Constitution and the Evidence Act forbid the latter absent clear legislative warrant. Until Parliament supplies that warrant, a registered owner who receives a notice for an offence he did not commit is entitled to require the prosecution to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that he was the driver. Vehicles do not commit crimes. Persons do, and the law must identify the right person before it punishes anyone.

Ghana News.title: 2026 CAF Awards: Black Queens nominated for Team of the Year
Ghana News.content:
Ghana's senior women's national team has been named among the nominees for the 2026 Confederation of African Football (CAF) Awards.

The Black Queens are nominated in the year under review following their performances in friendly and international competitions.

The nomination is a recognition that highlights the team’s impressive resurgence and outstanding performances over the past year.

Ghana is joined by Algeria, Cape Verde, Cameroon, Cote d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mali, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa.

Led by Kim Lars Bjorkegren once again, the team competed at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON), which was staged in Morocco.

Ghana exited the competition in the quarterfinals after losing to Malawi, missing out on an automatic qualification to the 2027 Women's World Cup.

However, the Black Queens beat Côte d'Ivoire to book a place in the Inter-Confederation Play-Off tournament, which is scheduled for later this month in Morocco.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Sudan’s displaced return to new challenges in war-battered Khartoum
World.content:
The Sudanese was one of the first areas to be affected, and one of the worst hit, by the war between the SAF and the RSF.

Khartoum, Sudan – Mohamed Mahdi Makki Farah, 51, returned home near the Sudanese capital in August 2025 after the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) declared the entire state of Khartoum free of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters. But it was not the end of his family’s struggles.

The 51-year-old had left his home in Jabal Awliya, south of Khartoum, for el-Fasher in North Darfur in June 2023.

He returned home to find it destroyed and ransacked, with even the household utensils stolen.

“Everything had been completely destroyed. Now we sleep on the floor, and some of us are living in rented houses,” Makki Farah told Al Jazeera. “We have not made any decision to repair our home because the costs are extremely high, and we have not been able to start.”

His years as a trader appeared to have been wasted, with his possessions gone and his business capital reduced to almost a third of its pre-war level because of the Sudanese pound’s depreciation.

The journey of displacement and return exhausted his remaining resources, while children’s medical expenses and the family’s daily needs added to their financial burden.

This meant he was unable to generate the funds needed to repair his home, so rent became an additional burden, while access to water, electricity and healthcare services is still difficult.

They had also lost important documents during the war and had to start from scratch to replace them.

“Everyone knows about the water and electricity problems; Khartoum is almost entirely in darkness now. As for healthcare, only government health centres are operating, thank God,” Makki Farah said.

The family’s experiences are those faced by millions of Sudanese families returning to their homes after years of displacement.



Fighting between the SAF and the RSF, which began in April 2023, continues, particularly in the southeast of the country. But large parts of Sudan are more stable after government victories, particularly around Khartoum. Sudanese displaced from these areas during early years of fighting are beginning to return home now that the situation has improved.

According to the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix report, as of September 30, approximately 5.27 million displaced Sudanese returned to their homes in nine states.

Of those, 82 percent had been internally displaced, while 18 percent had crossed the borders. Children accounted for about half of all returnees.

According to an assessment published by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in August 2026, approximately 2.5 million people had returned to their homes in Khartoum state.

But the agency warned that returning did not necessarily mean people had the conditions needed to rebuild their lives. Many found their homes damaged or uninhabitable, while work opportunities remained limited. Access to water and basic services was also inadequate due to damage to infrastructure during the war.

Many returnees are still renting as they cannot afford to repair their homes.

Abubakr Ishaq Hamed Ibrahim, 40, returned to Khartoum in February 2026 after being displaced to River Nile state in May 2023.

Like Makki Farah, he also found his home destroyed, with the furniture, bedding and basic household belongings they had accumulated over the years gone.

They had to move to Omdurman, neighbouring Khartoum, renting a home in the al-Thawra neighbourhood, but this became difficult to afford without a regular income.

“Our homes were looted and destroyed. We found nothing inside. Everything was wrecked, and we had no furniture, no bedding, nothing at all. We were unable to pay the rent for several months, and rents are quite expensive. We have been through extremely difficult conditions, and even now we have no stable source of income,” he said.

Before the war, Hamed Ibrahim had relied on self-employed work, but now depends on any casual work he can find.

His family had exhausted all their savings and borrowed money from family and friends to cover basics such as food, housing and school fees.

“Thank God, we are now doing casual jobs. The income is not enough to meet the cost of living and the daily burdens. We have exhausted all the money and savings we had, and we have borrowed money from individuals,” he said.



Things are slightly improving. His children have returned to school with support from relatives.

The family also receives in-kind assistance from organisations such as the World Food Programme, including supplies of sorghum (a cereal grain), flour, wheat, oil and sugar.

But overall, the situation in Khartoum remains dire for most residents. There have been fuel shortages and repeated power cuts in recent weeks, disrupting public transport. Fares have increased on some routes and commuters are often forced to wait hours for a bus. There are also long queues outside bakeries in some areas due to shortages of flour.

Families with limited resources, few employment opportunities and homes in need of costly repairs have been the worst affected.

On Saturday, Khartoum state authorities announced measures to address the transport crisis. Governor Ahmed Osman Hamza chaired a meeting that agreed to supply public transport services with fuel and give buses priority.

Government departments were also instructed to give residents lifts when travelling to and from work. Members of the Popular Resistance of Sudan, a coalition of SAF-aligned armed factions, help manage traffic in the capital.

Economic journalist and specialist Khalid Takes said the public transport crisis in Khartoum highlights a need for the state to take more responsibility for managing a centralised process, away from a reliance on private minibuses.

“No country has left the public transport sector entirely in the hands of the private sector, which relies on small vehicles,” he told Al Jazeera. “This results in ongoing costs for the state, both directly and indirectly, particularly in importing spare parts and fuel, which require foreign currency.”

Makki Farah says although he has managed to return to his home city of Khartoum, it is not enough to return his life to how it was before the war. He does not see a future in the capital for his family unless they receive more support.

“We have lost everything we had before the war. Now we need assistance because everything we need – housing, healthcare and education – has been destroyed,” he said.

World.title: Surging ICE raids shadow final weeks of California congressional race
World.content:
Local organisations and representatives say immigration raids have spread fear and uncertainty through communities.

Bakersfield, California – In a nondescript car park, a memorial with orange marigolds and prayer candles has been erected in honour of recently deceased labour organiser and civil rights leader Dolores Huerta.

Huerta was a well-known figure in California’s Central Valley, where she helped found the United Farm Workers union (UFW) and win better wages and working conditions for migrant and Latino labourers, who were vital to the state’s huge agricultural sector in the 1960s and 1970s.

The term “si, se puede”, coined by Huerta and translating to “yes, it can be done”, has also been placed on the display of a local theatre in her honour.

If Huerta represents a tradition of social and economic justice and labour organising that continues to resonate, an uptick in immigration raids across the valley over the last month has underscored the degree to which insecurity, both economic and political, remains a stubborn reality for many of the region’s agricultural workers.

Since early October, federal immigration agents, often masked and in unmarked vehicles, have fanned out across the Central Valley as part of a 45-day effort titled “Operation Save California” by the Trump administration.

Those raids, part of the administration’s mass deportation campaign, have become a flashpoint in the race for California’s 22nd congressional district, one of several contests in the state that Democrats hope will help deliver them a majority in the United States House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3.



While Republican incumbent David Valadao has been a fixture of the Central Valley for years, winning six of his last seven races, progressive challenger Randy Villegas is seeking to capitalise on popular frustration over the rising cost of living, healthcare cuts and immigration raids.

In a small building down the road from the Huerta memorial in Bakersfield, one day before the election, a room full of volunteers chant her slogan, encouraged by labour leaders and Democratic representatives such as California Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, before they knock on doors.

“I’ve spoken to local business owners who have told me how their businesses are now struggling as a result of these ICE raids, and many of them have now pivoted to delivering things like groceries,” Villegas told Al Jazeera, noting that some residents are afraid of leaving their homes amid the increase in raids.

“It’s having an impact on people who just want to go to work, want to go to school,” he added.

‘Unlawfully targeted’

Immigration authorities say the raids have targeted criminals and deny that they are racially discriminatory.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the Department of Homeland Security said in an email. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the US – NOT their skin colour, race, or ethnicity.”

But the administration’s depiction of targeted operations focused on people with serious criminal backgrounds is at odds with accounts from farmworkers, labour organisations, local officials, and advocacy groups, who describe aggressive methods and a dragnet approach.

“These are not criminals. These are hard-working, long-term members of our communities being unlawfully targeted simply for looking Latino and working class,” Teresa Romero, president of the UFW, whose members have campaigned for Villegas, said in a statement on October 10.

“We are seeing car windows being smashed and farm workers dragged from vehicles in the middle of the road while on their way to work.”

A woman who spoke with Al Jazeera over the phone on condition of anonymity said her husband, a farmworker in Fresno County, had been detained by immigration agents while returning home from work during the first week of October.



“I understand that if they [those arrested] are criminals or have done bad things, they have brought it on themselves,” the woman said of immigration arrests over a phone call. “But my husband has not done anything. The only thing he has done is work.”

She adds that her four children, all of whom are citizens born in the US, became anxious after the incident, and that some now begin to cry when they hear a knock at the door and fear that their mother will be taken away as well.

‘Word spreads’

Local officials say such stories have reverberated through their communities.

“When you have a small community like ours, and folks are actually detained, word spreads,” said Olivia Calderon, mayor of the city of Arvin.

“I had pastors ask me whether ICE takes a day off on Sunday because people don’t want to go to church,” she added.

Villegas has drawn a link between the raids and Valadao’s vote in favour of a bill that is set to transform ICE, often accused of excessive force and disregard for civil liberties in its operations, into the most well-funded law enforcement agency in the country.

Asked about the impact of the raids in a debate with Villegas in early October, Valadao responded by mirroring the government’s claims that many of those targeted have criminal backgrounds and that “it is what it is.”

As Republicans and Democrats jostle for control of the House, the race has also received national attention.

Prominent figures such as leftist Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson have visited in recent months to rally in support of their respective candidates.

Labour organisations, such as UFW, have also mobilised members to knock doors for Villegas.

But polls suggest a tight race between Valadao and Villegas, even after a partisan redistricting measure passed by California voters in 2025 resulted in a series of newly drawn maps, including parts of the 22nd district, meant to favour Democrats.

Valadao has proven himself to be a resilient candidate. His upbringing in the Central Valley, where his Portuguese parents settled and worked as dairy farmers, has helped him build close ties with ranchers, growers, and conservative voters who play an influential role in the region. While California in general is a bastion of support for the Democratic Party, rural areas are often favourable terrain for Republicans.

While Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris defeated Donald Trump in California by nearly 20 points in 2024, Trump carried Kern County, where Bakersfield is located, by a similar margin.

Still, Villegas and his supporters are hoping that concerns over the rising cost of living, driven in part by the Trump administration’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has sent energy prices soaring, will help him dislodge the resilient Republican incumbent.



Priscilla Ortega, a 23-year-old in the city of Lamont, said she is “annoyed and very angry” about rising prices and the impact of immigration raids.

“It was really unnecessary,” she said of the war on Iran, adding that rising fuel costs have made her commute to her job as a warehouse worker in the region much more expensive.

“That could have gone to food for my household or bills that need to be paid,” she added. “People are sick of the prices increasing.”

World.title: Cricket World Cup: India vs Pakistan gets more ticket requests than final
World.content:
ICC receives 8.4 million ticket requests for 34,000 seats at the October 10 group stage match in Johannesburg.

Share Cricket World Cup: India vs Pakistan gets more ticket requests than final on social media

The International Cricket Council (ICC) says it has received nearly 8.5 million ticket requests for a group stage match between India and Pakistan at next year’s Cricket World Cup in South Africa.

A World Cup cricket match between the South Asian rivals traditionally draws the highest ticket requests, barring the final, but the demand for the October 10 match has surpassed that for the final of the ICC Cricket World Cup, the sport’s global governing body said on Monday.

The South Asian neighbours will meet at the Wanderers cricket ground in Johannesburg during the initial round-robin-style phase of the tournament.

“The clash between India and Pakistan has drawn 8.4 million ticket requests, with the tournament’s final on November 21 in the same city trailing close behind with nearly eight million,” the ICC said in a statement.

The bitter rivals could meet for a second time in the Super Seven stage of the competition and for a third time in the final, should both qualify for it.

It will be the fourth consecutive 50-over World Cup in which the most lucrative group stage match of the tournament has been guaranteed by drawing both India and Pakistan in the same group in a ballot held behind closed doors, unlike other major global sporting events.

The 12 nations are split into two groups:

Group A: Australia, India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe, qualifier

Group B: New Zealand, South Africa, Sri Lanka, England, Bangladesh, qualifier

The 57 matches during the tournament will be held at 12 venues across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia from October 7 to November 21, 2027.



An online ballot for tickets opened on October 1 and will close at midnight Central African Time (22:00 GMT) on November 21.

The total ticket requests, which came from 2.8 million unique fan accounts in 193 countries, surpassed the 120 million mark on Sunday.

Applications from South Africa, the United Kingdom, India, the United States and Australia lead the charge in ballot registrations, according to the ICC.

Fans from Africa, including those from the host nations, accounted for 14.9 million of the ticket applications.

Namibia will stage men’s ICC Cricket World Cup matches for the first time, and Zimbabwe will showcase its new stadium at Victoria Falls.

The World Cup will return to Africa for the first time in 24 years. South Africa, Zimbabwe and Kenya were the hosts in 2003.

Six years later, South Africa hosted the ICC Champions Trophy, which was won by Australia in a final played at SuperSport Park in Centurion.

Australia won the 2003 edition, defeating India by 125 runs in the final at the Wanderers.

South Africa was also the venue for the inaugural edition of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup in 2007 when India clinched a thrilling final against Pakistan at the same venue.

World.content:

NewsFeed Georgia Senate candidates make final appeals ahead of US midterms

World.title: FIFA to share documents related to World Cup sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA Council members may view documents related to Gianni Infantino’s doomed plan, but only in person in Zurich

FIFA will release details of President Gianni Infantino’s aborted plan to sell off stakes in future World Cups to private investors, but they will not be shared with the public.

Reports in the British media said members of the FIFA Council, the main decision-making body of football’s world governing body, will be given access to “key documents” related to the proposal, named FIFA Forward Enterprise.

However, they can only view them under “strict protocols to preserve confidentiality”, the reports said. Those include the 37 members of the council having to register for an in-person appointment to view selected paperwork in Zurich, Switzerland, in the next two weeks.

The news came out late on Monday, the deadline European football’s governing body, UEFA, had set for FIFA to release details about the $4.2bn scheme and answer questions about how the proposal came about and who approved it before the plans were dropped in July amid a worldwide backlash.

UEFA set the deadline after a tense council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the proposal but provided no details about how the plan was formed. He asked council members to submit their questions in writing.

UEFA is leading attempts to remove Infantino before or at the FIFA presidential election on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco. Infantino, who was elected in 2016, is seeking a fourth term through 2031.

World.title: The US midterms will test the limits of Trump’s power
World.content:
Control of Congress is at stake, but so is the ability of American institutions to withstand presidential pressure.

Share The US midterms will test the limits of Trump’s power on social media

On November 3, as Americans vote in the midterm elections, the United States faces a defining test of presidential power, constitutional accountability and democratic resilience. The election will determine control of Congress, but its stakes extend far beyond partisan fortunes. At issue is whether constitutional checks and balances can constrain President Donald Trump, whether election officials can withstand political pressure, and whether the government will respect the voters’ verdict when the outcome threatens its interests.

The battle for control of elections

The administration’s efforts to reshape election procedures have encountered substantial judicial resistance. According to an October 20 review by the Brennan Center for Justice, at least 34 federal district court decisions had temporarily or permanently blocked administration initiatives involving election procedures and demands for voter registration records. The rulings included decisions by judges appointed by presidents of both parties, including Trump himself.

These decisions demonstrate that judicial oversight remains an important constitutional safeguard. Yet repeated litigation exposes a vulnerability: courts often intervene only after disputed measures have been introduced, leaving states to challenge policies that can generate uncertainty close to Election Day.

The controversy intensified on October 26, when a federal appeals court declined to order California to set aside ballots from approximately 20,000 registered voters whom the Justice Department alleges may be noncitizens. The court ruled that the lower court had not been given adequate opportunity to consider the government’s request. The underlying dispute remained unresolved.



The administration maintains that its actions protect electoral integrity. But investigating credible allegations of wrongdoing is fundamentally different from restricting eligible voters on the basis of unverified suspicions. Election security requires accurate voter rolls, but it equally requires protecting citizens from erroneous challenges.

Repeated allegations of fraud can undermine confidence even when evidence fails to establish that an election has been compromised. The danger is that routine election administration becomes suspect in the public mind, regardless of the facts.

Congress as a constitutional check

Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress, placing control of the House and potentially the Senate within reach of Democrats.

A Democratic House majority would strengthen the opposition’s ability to investigate administration policies, subpoena officials and scrutinise executive decisions. Immigration enforcement, election procedures, federal spending and the implementation of executive orders could face intensified oversight.

Such scrutiny could expose misconduct where evidence supports it and compel officials to explain decisions otherwise shielded from meaningful examination. Yet investigations do not automatically produce accountability. Subpoenas can trigger prolonged legal battles, and congressional hearings alone cannot force policy changes.

Control of the Senate would give Democrats greater influence over presidential nominations and judicial appointments. Nevertheless, Trump would retain his veto power and substantial executive authority. Even unified Democratic control of Congress would not automatically reverse his agenda.

The deeper question is whether Congress will exercise its constitutional responsibilities independently or allow partisan loyalty to take precedence over institutional accountability. Checks and balances cannot function effectively if one branch declines to challenge another when circumstances demand it.

The test after election day

Perhaps the most consequential confrontation will come after the ballots are cast.

Trump’s response to his 2020 presidential defeat remains a critical precedent. He challenged the result, made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud, and pressured Georgia officials to find enough votes to reverse his loss. On January 6, 2021, a mob attacked the Capitol as Congress met to certify the presidential election.

That history does not establish that similar events will recur in 2026. It does, however, make scrutiny of potential election disputes essential.



The danger may lie not in a single intervention capable of changing the result, but in successive confrontations: challenges to ballot counting, pressure on state officials, demands for investigations and attempts to portray ordinary procedures as evidence of fraud. Even unsuccessful efforts can delay resolution and weaken public confidence.

Candidates have every right to pursue legitimate legal challenges. Courts must consider credible evidence, and election officials must correct documented irregularities. But allegations are not proof, and no president can simply declare an unfavourable result invalid.

An election can also be damaged without a single vote being changed. Intimidation of election workers, unfounded accusations and efforts to discredit established procedures can erode public acceptance of legitimate outcomes.

The distinction between lawful scrutiny and political interference is therefore fundamental. Electoral integrity depends on evidence, consistent procedures and respect for the law – not on whether the outcome favours the governing party.

Courts cannot defend democracy alone

Judicial intervention demonstrates that constitutional safeguards remain operational. Courts can invalidate unlawful executive actions, but they cannot independently administer elections across thousands of jurisdictions or guarantee that political leaders will respect every ruling.

Nor can judicial decisions alone restore public confidence after sustained efforts to discredit electoral institutions. Democracy depends on Congress exercising oversight, election officials counting ballots accurately, courts acting impartially and political leaders respecting lawful outcomes.

The willingness of judges appointed by presidents of both parties to rule against administration initiatives reinforces a fundamental principle: constitutional protections cannot depend on partisan alignment. Their effectiveness rests on whether institutions apply the same rules regardless of who benefits.

The broader danger is institutional erosion. Repeated confrontations can weaken public confidence, discourage election workers and normalise the idea that constitutional constraints are obstacles to political power rather than obligations governing its exercise.

A verdict beyond the ballots

The November 3 midterms will not resolve the struggle over presidential power. If Republicans retain Congress, Trump will continue to benefit from congressional majorities, although judicial and state-level checks will remain. If Democrats gain one or both chambers, the administration will face greater scrutiny, but substantial executive authority will persist.

Neither outcome guarantees effective constitutional government. The decisive issue is whether institutions exercise their lawful responsibilities and whether political leaders accept that presidential power is neither unlimited nor permanent.

American democracy has survived profound crises, but resilience should not be confused with invulnerability. Checks and balances work only when institutions enforce them and political leaders respect their limits.



The midterms are therefore about more than congressional arithmetic. They will test whether votes are counted according to law, disputes are resolved through established procedures and electoral outcomes are respected regardless of partisan consequences.

The ballots will determine who controls Congress. What follows will reveal whether American institutions can still uphold a principle fundamental to democratic government: no president stands above the law, no party owns the electoral process, and no exercise of political power is beyond accountability.

On November 3, Americans will vote to determine the composition of Congress. The aftermath will test something more enduring: whether the constitutional restraints that have sustained American democracy remain binding when their enforcement carries the highest political stakes.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Two helicopters crash near Everest base camp, killing Indian tourist
World.content:
NewsFeed Two helicopters crash near Everest base camp, killing Indian tourist

Two helicopters have collided while preparing to land in Nepal’s Mount Everest region. An Indian tourist was killed, while a New Zealander was rescued. The accident comes amid peak trekking season in Nepal’s Solukhumbu district.

World.title: French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.
World.content:
Pinned

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Here’s what else to know.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often clash with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

World.title: Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapter
World.content:
With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.

And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.

Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.

Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.

He made his closing pitch on Monday in front the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".

But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.

His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.

"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.

"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.

World.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
The US has launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported several explosions on the island on Monday.

The US officials described the strikes as limited and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing upon a US aircraft. The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom), the part of the US military responsible for operations in the Middle East, for comment.

It comes ahead of the US midterm elections, which will determine whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.

Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Earlier on Monday, he told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
