World.title: Mali: Still No Accountability Six Months After Abduction of Pro-Democracy Politician Mountaga Tall and His Son
World.content:
Malian authorities must urgently disclose the fate and whereabouts of lawyer and pro-democracy politician Mountaga Tall and his son Cheick Mamadou Tall, Amnesty International said six months after their abductions.

On the night of 3 May 2026, just days after a series of attacks by armed groups across Mali, Mountaga Tall, leader of the National Congress for the Democratic Initiative (Congrès national pour l'initiative démocratique), was abducted from his home in the capital, Bamako, by armed and hooded men driving vehicles without registration plates.

Cheick Mamadou Tall, his eldest son, went missing on 16 May after allegedly receiving a telephone call from his father asking him to bring personal effects. He left his home to deliver the effects and never returned. His fate has remained unknown since then.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The Malian authorities cannot continue to evade their responsibility to independently, impartially and transparently investigate the disappearances of Mountaga and Cheick Mamadou Tall. Six months of uncertainty and anguish for their family must end. The authorities must urgently disclose what happened to them and ensure that those suspected to be responsible are held accountable," said Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International's Regional Director for West and Central Africa.

"If Mountaga Tall and his son are detained by the authorities, their whereabouts and proof that they are alive must be disclosed immediately. They must be granted prompt access to their families, their lawyers, doctors, and to any medication they may require."

"If they are suspected of having committed an offence, they must be promptly brought before a judge, informed of the specific charges against them and afforded all fair trial guarantees. Otherwise, they must be immediately released."

Multiple calls for urgent clarification remain unanswered

In a statement released on 3 May, Mountaga Tall's family denounced his abduction, and the lack of information about his fate and which they consider to be detention.

Amnesty International called on the Malian authorities to clarify the fate and whereabouts of Mountaga Tall on 4 May, and raised concerns about the disappearance of Cheick Mamadou Tall on 18 May.

On 26 May, the International Bar Conference, which brings together bar associations from 42 countries, demanded that "the full truth be brought to light immediately regarding the fate" of Mountaga Tall and his son, and that "they be released immediately and unconditionally, or at the very least brought immediately before a judicial authority."

In July, the United Nations Committee on Enforced Disappearances called on Mali's authorities to "take immediate measures to search for, locate, and protect" Mountaga Tall and Cheick Mamadou Tall.

We have documented a pattern of enforced disappearances carried out by agents of the National Agency for State Security in Mali. We reiterate the extreme gravity of the crime of enforced disappearance.Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International's Regional Director for West and Central Africa

Political figures targeted in May 2026 amid escalating conflict

On 25 April 2026, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims, also known as Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front attacked Bamako, and five other cities in Mali, targeting military camps and the residences of Malian politicians and military figures.

On 1 May, the military court in Bamako announced that an investigation into the attacks was underway and that several individuals, including politicians and members of the army, had been arrested with further arrests expected. In a video released a few days after Mountaga Tall's abduction, a former soldier appeared on camera accusing him of involvement in the attacks.

However, neither Mountaga Tall nor Cheick Mamadou Tall has been formally charged with any offences or brought before a court since May.

Other political figures were abducted in early May, including Youssouf Daba Diawara, Aboubacar Soumaré, and Moussa Djiré, who were taken from their homes in Bamako, while social media activist Ibrahim Taméga was arrested on 23 May.

On 16 May, the African Commission of Human and Peoples' Rights expressed deep concerns over the abductions of Mountaga Tall, Youssouf Daba Diawara and Moussa Djiré, and called on the Malian authorities to start immediate searches to find the people abducted.

After several months without information about their fate, Youssouf Daba Diawara and Moussa Djiré were charged on 20 October with "undermining the credibility of the state, criminal conspiracy, and attempting to destabilize the institutions of the Republic," according to media reports. They were all remanded into custody at the Bamako prison after being interrogated by a judge.

Enforced disappearance: a crime of extreme gravity under international law

Under international law, the crime of enforced disappearance is the arrest, detention, abduction or any form of deprivation of liberty by state agents, followed by the authorities' refusal to acknowledge the detention or to reveal the fate or whereabouts of the disappeared person, placing them outside the protection of the law and under a high risk of torture and other human rights violations.

Close 

"We have documented a pattern of enforced disappearances carried out by agents of the National Agency for State Security in Mali. We reiterate the extreme gravity of the crime of enforced disappearance, which no circumstances, however exceptional, can justify," said Marceau Sivieude.

"The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, which Mali has ratified, prohibits invoking a situation of war, the threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency as a justification for enforced disappearances. The authorities must put an end to these violations, protect civic space and uphold the country's international human rights obligations and the rule of law."

Background

69-year-old Mountaga Tall was a key figure in Mali's political democratization during the 1990s. Over the last three years, he challenged the dissolution of political parties by the military-led authorities in Malian courts and tribunals and defended in court several political figures who were arbitrarily detained, including former Prime Minister Moussa Mara.

World.title: South Africa: U.S. to Drop South Africa, Rwanda from AGOA Duty-Free Trade Initiative
World.content:
The Trump administration has said South Africa and Rwanda are breaking the rules of the AGOA free trade initiative, a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.

South Africa and Rwanda are set to be removed from a US trade initiative that has provided duty-free access to the US market for thousands of products from sub-Saharan African countries for 26 years.

On Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said US President Donald Trump intends to "terminate" the two countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program starting in January 2027.

The program, which comes under regular review, was extended in February by Trump.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In a statement, Greer said that "the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria."

Greer said these practices include "barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region."

The statement did not provide any specific examples of the trade barriers or security and foreign policy issues in question.

What is AGOA?

AGOA was introduced in 2000 by former US President Bill Clinton, and it has become a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.

Duty free access to the US market is seen as a critical economic boost for the more than 30 AGOA countries. Over 1,800 specific products are covered under AGOA.

Requirements for membership include eliminating barriers to US trade and investment, while maintaining an open market economy along with democratic principles like the rule of law, human rights and labor protections.

South Africa largest AGOA partner

South Africa has been AGOA's largest beneficiary, with $1.7 billion (€1.5 billion) worth of goods like car parts, citrus fruit and wine, exported to the US under the program in 2025.

South Africa's Trade Ministry said last week that it was prepared for the decision, adding that AGOA exports comprise only about 10% of its total exports to the US and 1% of its total global exports.

"AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the ‌United States," it said in a statement.

In recent weeks, President Cyril Ramaphosa has also said South Africa must prepare for being excluded from AGOA by seeking new markets and trade deals with partners like China.

On Monday, the South Africa government said the US remains an important trade partner and it would provide support for affected sectors.

Close 

South Africa's export-dependent citrus industry warned that its entire value chain "on both sides of the Atlantic, is now under threat," and warned that jobs and the economic security of entire communities is now at stake.

Rwanda sanctioned for alleged M23 ties

The US has been putting economic pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support of the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Washington sanctioned Rwanda's Defense Ministry last week, which denies any ties to M23, along with several individuals, institutions and a gold refinery.

Major Rwandan exports to the US include coffee and minerals.

World.title: Uganda: Uganda Begins Withdrawing Troops from Somalia After Two Decades
World.content:
Ugandan troops first deployed to Somalia in 2007 as part of an international military coalition to battle Islamic insurgents. But the mission has faced mounting pressure since a US decision to withdraw funding.

Uganda announced on Monday that it had begun pulling its troops out of Somalia, where it has been a key player in efforts to counter insurgents for almost two decades.

"The first cohort of troops under the phased withdrawal operation have already arrived back in Uganda," a statement from the Ugandan military said.

Uganda was the first country to send troops to Somalia as part of an African Union peacekeeping force set up in 2007 to support the Somali government battling Al-Shabab Islamist militants.



Uganda "will gradually withdraw all its forces in Somalia, including those currently deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) by the close of 2027," the military's statement added, referring to the latest African Union mission.

Around 4,500 Ugandan troops are stationed in Somalia as part of AUSSOM, as well as about 2,000 deployed under bilateral agreements.

The Ugandan army said its withdrawal "will mark the end of Uganda's enduring 20-year peace and stabilization support operations in Somalia, permitting the Somali Armed Forces to assume full responsibility for security in the country."

An initial contingent of 109 Ugandan soldiers left the Somali capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, local media reported.

Why is Uganda withdrawing its troops from Somalia?

The future of the African Union mission, AUSSOM, has been thrown into doubt following a recent US decision to end funding for a UN logistics office the military coalition relies on.

Washington, the coalition's biggest donor, has voiced frustration with a lack of progress in the fight against Al-Shabab, which continues to control large swaths of central Somalia. The US has also accused the Somali government of failing to unite the country and implement political reforms.

Uganda's withdrawal announcement on Monday also came as the UN ended its political mission in Somalia.

The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia closed on Saturday after more than three decades of peacebuilding in the East African country, transferring responsibility to the Somali government and various UN agencies.

Somalia is due to hold elections in May next year, but insecurity and opposition disputes are threatening to derail the process.

Somalia has been gripped by a deadly insurgency led by Al-Shabab for more than two decades. While Ugandan forces have played a crucial role in driving the militants from the capital and several major towns, the group has recaptured territory in recent years and now controls significant areas in the center and south of the country.

Close 

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: The battle for Congress is just the beginning. Here's what's at stake on Election Day
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

It's Election Day in America, with voters heading to the polls to determine control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years.

Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate for the final two years of his presidency.

"We're going to win and let's make the next two years bigger and better and stronger than ever before," Trump told supporters Sunday night at a rally in Kansas.

But Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The GOP is also facing a potential turnout deficit, with public opinion polls indicating Democrats are more energized than Republicans to cast ballots in the midterms.

Early voting in the midterms has shattered previous records, with more than 54 million people already casting ballots, according to the Associated Press. That's nearly nine million more ballots cast in early voting than in 2022, the previous midterm elections.

With early voting traditionally favoring Democrats, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, pointing to Election Day turnout, recently told Fox News Digital, "If our voters turn out, we win."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The political climate has the GOP playing plenty of defense on the campaign trail, as the president tries to energize the GOP base.

Trump's event in red-leaning Kansas, which he touted as his 30th rally over the past month, came hours after the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the state's Senate race from Lean Republican to Toss-up. Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, who is challenging GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, is aiming to become the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a Senate election in Kansas.

The Fox News Power Rankings, as well as many of the leading nonpartisan political handicappers, point to Democrats retaking control of the House, with the majority in the Senate a toss-up heading into Election Day.

"Think of what is possible tomorrow: Democrats can flip the House, take back the Senate, and stop Trump’s harmful agenda," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin spotlighted, in an Election Eve social media post.

Also up for grabs in this year's elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states. Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast.

The big question with Election Day upon us — have the public opinion polls that point to a potential blue wave undercounted Republican voters?

LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP DEFYING MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS HE BARNSTORMS COUNTRY

We'll find out in the coming hours.

Until then, here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026.

SENATE

Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, which means Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority. The GOP needs to hold at least 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate.

Besides Kansas, Republicans are also playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat.

Democrats are on defense in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire.

HOUSE

The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, with Democrats needing a net gain of just three seats to reach 218, which would hand them the majority.

A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber, according to the Power Rankings. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party.

The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future.

"Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said.

GOVERNORS

There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors.

The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up.

The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings. Meanwhile, the showdowns in Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Oregon are rated Lean Democrat.

BALLOT MEASURES

Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia.

Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024.

But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race.

Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release.

California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines.

The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare.

Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax.

Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations.

Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions.

California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development.

POLL CLOSINGS

The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET.

7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close.

World.title: Ex-Chicago FBI chief sues DOJ, claims he was ousted over failed anti-ICE prosecutions
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The former chief of the FBI's Chicago field office said he was forced out of his job after he says he was wrongly blamed for the failed prosecution of six people who protested against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Windy City, according to a lawsuit he filed on Monday.

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence, according to the lawsuit. He said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer.

"I saw the writing on the wall," DePodesta told The Associated Press.

DePodesta accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros, of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Hours after the lawsuit was filed, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed "Broadview Six" case.

"There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court," Perry wrote in the order.

Federal prosecutors brought charges against roughly 30 protesters during the federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, but many of those charges have since been dropped or dismissed.

DePodesta’s lawsuit alleges that Boutros faced pressure from the DOJ throughout the immigration crackdown to slap protesters with felony charges.

"Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration," DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the complaint.

Boutros often pressured assistant U.S. attorneys to press charges "before investigating the objective evidence," according to the lawsuit, which says he wanted felony charges when assistant U.S. attorneys "favored misdemeanors or no charges at all."

Last October, Boutros charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, in connection with their actions during a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

Grand jury transcripts later turned over to the court showed that grand jurors twice declined to indict the six people as prosecutors sought charges, according to The Associated Press. Boutros dropped all charges against the six people in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.

Boutros "repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington" that the failure was DePodesta's fault "to deflect attention from his own malfeasance," DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.

DePodesta denied Boutros’ claims to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out of his job due to the "political pressure Boutros created," according to the suit.

The complaint alleges Boutros told DOJ leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, "conspired to destroy" the case.

PRITZKER CALLS FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATIONS INTO ICE AGENTS OVER ‘MIDWAY BLITZ’ CONDUCT

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug," Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to The Associated Press, adding that it is "both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by" Boutros.

In September, one of the prosecutors on the "Broadview Six" case abruptly resigned, writing in a resignation letter that Boutros had "scapegoated and publicly vilified" her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party moving forward.

The former defendants have asked the judge to appoint a special counsel to probe possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further "fact-finding" about communications between Boutros’ office and DOJ leadership.

Boutros has previously denied that politics played a role in charging decisions.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump admin over ICE's use of city-owned lots for immigration enforcement
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations without the city's authorization.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations," which the mayor said is unauthorized and illegal.

"This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property," Mamdani wrote in the letter. "If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property."

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

According to the mayor's letter, ICE agents have reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots, including in a parking lot at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx as well as in parking lots along 111th Street on the west side of Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens, which is located next to a city-run preschool and several cultural institutions welcome hundreds of children and families every day.

"ICE has not secured any authorization from the City to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the City does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner," Mamdani wrote.

"Parking lots connected to City parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks," he continued. "Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations."

Mamdani added that New York City "deeply values its immigrant communities and will continue to use all available lawful means to ensure their safety, well-being, and ability to navigate the City and its resources without fear."

MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Last month, Mamdani and other New York Democratic leaders pushed for the city’s private parking lot owners to ban ICE from their properties.

"In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the mayor wrote in a letter to property owners and operators.

MAMDANI SAYS EVEN IF HE CAN GET ALONG WITH TRUMP, HE STILL DEMANDS THAT 'ICE SHOULD BE ABOLISHED'

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., were among more than 100 elected officials who signed on to Mamdani's October letter.

Mamdani has previously pushed for ICE to be abolished, including after an ICE agent shot and killed Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July and after another ICE agent shot and wounded Dominican national Oscar Belgal during an enforcement operation in New York City last month.

World.title: Bears prove they are NFC North's most complete team with commanding win over Seahawks
World.content:
Don’t let the standings fool you: the Chicago Bears are the darling of the loaded NFC North, and they proved why on "Monday Night Football" against the Seattle Seahawks.

Lumen Field and the "12s" never make it easy for a road team to play against the Seattle Seahawks, and it doesn’t help that this group just gave the Kansas City Chiefs its first loss of the season in Week 7.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But the Bears, led by head coach Ben Johnson and quarterback Caleb Williams, don’t seem to care where their games are held each week.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Their offense, and a defense that saw All-Pro Jeffery Simmons show out in his first game with the club since he was traded, made problems for the reigning Super Bowl champions in a 34-17 victory to improve to 6-2 on the season.

The Minnesota Vikings are still in first place in the division at 6-1, but there are a lot of questions about their offensive struggles compared to a suffocating defense that has kept them on the right side of close games thus far.

The Detroit Lions gave the Vikings their first loss to move to 5-2, while the Green Bay Packers got the job done against the Carolina Panthers on "Thursday Night Football" to get to 5-3.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

It’s loaded from top to bottom, but the Bears appear to be the most complete team out of this pack.

Just look at what Williams and company accomplished against the league’s best defense in terms of yards allowed per game (233.9). The Bears totaled 363 yards, 237 of which were through the air on big chunk plays including a 23-yarder to Luther Burden III, who caught Williams’ only touchdown pass of the contest, and a 24-yard strike to Rome Odunze, who led the team with 87 yards on four receptions.

Williams became the first quarterback to eclipse 200 passing yards against this vaunted defense.

Then, there’s the ground game, Johnson’s bread and butter as he continues to draw up the right concepts with a disciplined offensive line that executes who D’Andre Swift can plow his way into the end zone three times in the game.

But the Bears’ defense are no slouches either, coming into the game ninth in yards allowed and points allowed. With Simmons on board, Chicago was proving there are all-in for this championship window, and the veteran defensive tackle was present throughout his first-ever Bears game.

He finished tied for the team lead in combined tackles (6), while collecting a sack and two tackles for loss. James Lynch also forced a key interception when it was 27-17 with six minutes to play, leading to Swift’s third touchdown of the game.

Meanwhile, Sam Darnold and the Seahawks have shown spurts of that Super Bowl-level play that got them the Vince Lombardi Trophy last season. However, it hasn’t been as consistent as they would like.

They made a trade themselves before the Bears landed Simmons, acquiring left guard Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts to beef up their offensive line, help the run game and keep Darnold upright. And with rookie Jadarian Price back from injury, and Zach Charbonnet making his season debut after recovering from an injury last season, the run game was supposed to be better heading into Week 8.

World.title: Trump calls Iran conflict a 'soft war,' insists US holds the cards ahead of midterm elections

President Donald Trump sought to reassure voters the day before the midterm elections that Iran is not a "forever war," but a "soft war" that the United States could end at any time.

"We're not fighting a war … When was the last time we fired anything? This isn't a war, this is a very soft war," Trump said Monday on "Hannity."

Iran could be a key deciding issue as voters go to the polls on Election Day Tuesday as Americans continue to grapple with surging gas prices and the economic fallout from the United States’ conflict, which began eight months ago.

AMERICANS 'FRUSTRATED' ABOUT IRAN WAR GOING INTO MIDTERMS AS TRUMP ADMIN HAS DECISION TO MAKE: GOP LAWMAKER

"What’s a war? A war is fighting. Take a look at World War I, World War II. When was the last time you saw us fighting with them? We go months and months, we talk," Trump told host Sean Hannity.

"This is not much of a war, Sean, because there hasn't been shooting for months."

TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION

Trump’s comments come shortly after the United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz Monday after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft. Officials confirmed to Fox News that the "defensive" strike does not indicate a return to full-blown U.S. military strikes in Iran.

The president said Monday that he was in no hurry to resume military strikes against Iran but warned that the U.S. will give Iran "the hammer" soon if the latest round of peace talks are not fruitful.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN

"With [Operation] Midnight Hammer, we bombed out all of their potential nuclear power. Now we have might have to go after Pickaxe [Mountain], but that's not a big deal. We can do it in literally one hour," Trump told Fox News.

"This isn't like a war that's going on, there’s no war raging," he added. "It could happen if they don't make a deal. But they want to make a deal very badly, and there is a very good chance we make a deal."

FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR

The financial toll of the Iran conflict has emerged as a political liability for Republicans ahead of Election Day as the Pentagon estimates the war has cost taxpayers more than $47 billion.

President Trump, however, dismissed criticism of the staggering price tag, describing the expense as "peanuts" and saying that the war was necessary to disarm Iran from building a nuclear weapon.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS ‘DEAD’ — EXPERTS POINT TO THE REAL SIGN TEHRAN IS NEARING THE BRINK

"Their military is gone, their navy is gone, their air force is gone, their anti-aircraft is gone, and they have some missiles, but they don't have many of them – very little capacity to build more. They have drones, but they don't have very many, they have very little capacity to build more," he said.

World.title: Child’s measles death marks New York state’s first in more than 30 years amid outbreak
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years amid an ongoing measles outbreak, officials announced on Monday.

Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death.

"As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement.

"Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease. This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," she added. "In New York, we will continue to stand by proven public health measures and do everything we can to keep New Yorkers safe and healthy."

DEADLY MEASLES OUTBREAK HITS NORTHEAST AS STATE RECORDS FIRST DEATHS IN 35 YEARS

The Trump administration has made changes to federal vaccine policy, including revising the childhood immunization schedule and reviewing how vaccines are recommended. The CDC, however, continues to recommend two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine for children and says two doses provide the best protection against measles.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services for a response to Hochul's comments.

The child's death comes four weeks after Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states, expanding the pool of eligible people who can administer measles vaccines and providing quick access to additional resources if needed.

The governor said last month she planned to seek federal assistance to combat the outbreak.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The New York State Department of Health said it is working with county health departments and local partners to provide the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to any unvaccinated people who request it and to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases.

As of Oct. 24, New York had recorded 178 measles cases this year — 170 outside New York City and eight in the city.

State health officials urged New Yorkers to protect themselves by making sure they are up-to-date on their measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines and be aware of health advisories if traveling with unvaccinated people, especially young children.

"We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child's family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time," the New York State Department of Health said in a statement.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The department said measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious complications and death, stressing that vaccination is the "best protection against measles."

"The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts – both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak," the department's statement reads. "We urge New Yorkers to ensure they are up-to-date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and speak to their healthcare provider about immunizations."

World.title: Christian Yelich says 'Brewer Ball' is hard to replicate for this season after World Series triumph
World.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers’ celebration continues, and it likely won’t be stopping for quite a while.

After all, the organization and its fan base have never celebrated a World Series title, and the entire state, let alone the city itself, is still on cloud nine after the five-game victory over the Tampa Bay Rays.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Christian Yelich has been waiting for this moment since he landed in Milwaukee in 2018, and since that last out was made at Tropicana Field, he understood immediately how much it means to the loyal fan base as well as his teammates.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"It’s been awesome," Yelich told OutKick just before celebrating once more with Brewers fans at Raising Cane’s for a victory "shift" in Greendale, Wisconsin. "We’ve been busy kinda bouncing around everywhere. Not a whole lot of sleep, but I think that’s kinda how it should be. Still taking it all in and celebrating with everybody still. It’s been an awesome couple days."

But, while the Brewers relish their first-ever title, all 29 other MLB teams might be trying to rethink how to play the game itself after "Brewer Ball" took over this season.

Milwaukee’s style of play, which emphasizes fundamentals and situational baseball — think compared to the launch angle, raw power mindset others have adopted in today’s game — earned the moniker whilst winning 103 regular-season games. Then, they made a postseason run that shocked some, especially after sweeping the back-to-back-champion Los Angeles Dodgers and almost doing the same to the Rays in the World Series before a Game 4 walk-off by Tampa Bay saved them for another day.

MILWAUKEE BREWERS BROKE BASEBALL ON THEIR WAY TO REMARKABLY DOMINANT WORLD SERIES RUN

Does Yelich believe the league will follow suit and get back to fundamentals being top priority? "Brewer Ball" is clearly successful, but there’s a caveat for Yelich.

"Yeah, I think everybody tries to do it, but it’s really hard to do it," he explained. "It takes a team that’s together and everybody’s bought in and going in the same direction. I think that was one of our biggest strengths – the togetherness of everybody and everybody sharing a common goal. Being willing to do whatever it took to accomplish that."

Perhaps Yelich’s point is the biggest part of "Brewer Ball" – having a team bought into doing the little things needed to win those close matchups. It takes a special group, which is what Milwaukee had been all season long through the highs and lows.

Now, Yelich and the rest of the crew are reaping the benefits of that selfless style of play that other teams may be trying to replicate down the road.

While they try, Yelich will keep interacting with fans like he did on Monday, surprising more than 400 fans at Raising Cane’s following Friday’s victory parade through the streets of Milwaukee. World.title: Associated Press Top 25 poll voters hit a new, ridiculous low with this week's results
World.content:
At this point, it's reasonable to wonder if the voters who determine the Associated Press Top 25 poll are even trying anymore.

It's been a recurring problem in recent years, with the first part of the 2026 season showing once again that many poll voters are either not paying close enough attention, or are hopelessly consumed, or confused, by specific pro-conference or pro-team biases.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

That observation was even more evident with the release of this week's poll, which has conclusively demonstrated, yet again, that preseason polls are given far too much importance and that no other conference gets the special treatment the SEC receives.

YES, THE SEC IS STILL GETTING RIDICULOUS PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN THE AP TOP 25 POLL

First? The Texas Longhorns. Texas has two poor quality losses this year, to the Oklahoma Sooners and a home loss to the Florida Gators. They have the miraculous escape over Ohio State, and a win over Ole Miss. They're No. 10 in the country. Texas Tech has just one loss, a bad one at Cincinnati, but two "ranked" wins in a surprisingly strong Big 12 Conference. They're No. 13.

We've had an entire offseason and half a season with SEC coaches, cough Lane Kiffin cough, complaining about moving to a nine-game schedule and demanding preferential treatment for their schedules, all while they're already getting it.

Missouri is No. 19, for some reason, despite an extremely unimpressive resume of providing losses for other SEC teams. They were blown out 31-3 by Ole Miss, lost to what's clearly a mediocre Mississippi State team, though at least that was with Kamario Taylor, but their big win over Florida now looks much less impressive considering the Gators' collapse.

But the biggest problem? Their ridiculous handling of that Florida team and the South Carolina Gamecocks. Exclusively because of their conference affiliation.

Florida has two impressive wins, over Ole Miss and Texas, but has three awful losses. Not one, not two, but three losses. They were blown out 45-17 at Missouri, blown out 38-19 by South Carolina, and blown out 27-8 by Georgia. That 27-8 loss was just on Saturday. Why are they ranked?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

You could make the case that the Gators deserve to be in the top 25 had their three losses been even remotely close. They weren't. This is a deeply flawed team that is capable of flashes of brilliance against some opponents. They shouldn't be ranked. And they wouldn't be, if their jersey patch didn't have the SEC logo on it.

Meanwhile, Northwestern isn't ranked, despite having just two losses. Two close losses, to Indiana and a still-feisty Oregon Ducks team.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

South Carolina also has three losses, yet not only are they ranked, they're No. 23. At least Florida can point to Ole Miss and Texas, but the Gamecocks jumped into the top 25 after beating a very mediocre Oklahoma team. They lost to Mississippi State, Kentucky, and were blown out 49-18 by Alabama. While they did beat Tennessee, there's little to justify being ranked with three losses this early in the season.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

To be fair to the SEC, the voters' handling of Notre Dame is also bizarre. The Irish have taken advantage of an easy schedule this year, going 7-1 with wins over Wisconsin, Rice, Michigan State, Purdue, North Carolina, Stanford and Navy. They lost their only "tough" game on the road at BYU. So why are they No. 4, ahead of an undefeated UCLA and one loss Indiana team? The Hoosiers, after all, lost in close fashion to Ohio State, with starting QB Julian Sayin. They've won everything else.

UCLA hasn't lost at all, the only team in the Big Ten or SEC able to say that. Sure, they've had a pretty easy schedule, but they have wins over Wisconsin at home and Oregon on the road...how's that any different from Notre Dame? Especially considering, again, they haven't lost?



The reality here is that poll voters are hopelessly committed to brand names. Whether those brand names are at the team or conference level. After Kiffin and Sarkisian have spent weeks complaining about the SEC's schedules and how they're handled, it's clear that the AP Poll is giving them an enormous amount of deference, likely undeservedly so.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The reality is that the SEC this year, and the Big Ten for that matter, are filled with teams that are far less talented than in years past. NIL and the transfer portal have flattened out college football, and brand names matter less than ever. You'd think that watching Indiana win a national championship would show voters that the traditional pathways and powerhouse programs should not be given the benefit of the doubt.

Some of this will sort itself out as November plays out, but there's no question that the AP Poll will impact the College Football Playoff selection committee rankings. The ones that actually matter. It's clear that they shouldn't.

World.title: How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains how a pair of controversies in Michigan and Alaska could impact the broader battle for Senate control. Plus, Rebecca Shabad examines President Donald Trump’s election eve message.

— Adam Wollner

How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

An “October surprise” and a “November surprise” have rocked the Senate races in Alaska and Michigan, which are critical chess pieces in the battle for the majority.

To understand why these contests are so important, consider two scenarios.

The “red wall” scenario: Picture this: Democrats are having a good night and hold every seat they are defending, including in Michigan. They flip North Carolina. And they accomplish their long-held goal of unseating GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. That would leave Democrats with 49 seats.

Other targets would include five states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. There’s a plausible scenario where Democratic candidates in those states overperform by 10 points compared to the 2024 presidential margin, and still lose all of them.

The “blue tsunami” scenario: Now consider this: Michigan and Maine tip into the Democratic column and, one by one, all five of the red states start to fall. The blue wave turns into a tsunami and breaches the walls of MAGA country.

Through some mix of depressed Republican turnout, swing-voter movement and high Democratic enthusiasm, Democrats win Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. That’s their dream scenario, and it’d result in a 54-46 Senate majority. And if South Carolina flips, that’s 55 seats.

The Michigan and Alaska scenarios: That brings us to two states that have sparked controversy lately.

In Michigan, Haley Stevens, the runner-up in the Democratic primary, defected from her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the election. It’s a race where Democrats already were experiencing anxiety over progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s prospects.

If Democrats lose Michigan, their path to the majority gets steeper: They would need to flip at least three double-digit Trump states, rather than two.

In Alaska, a New York Times report that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan jolted the race, and the saga is under state and federal investigation. Peltola has denied any involvement in the effort. (Over the weekend, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and first-time candidate.)

There’s a scenario where Senate control comes down to Alaska. And if the race is close, it may not be decided for a while.

Alaska law allows up to 15 days for absentee ballots to arrive, as long as they’re postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3. That means counting can continue through Nov. 18, and the target date to certify the election is Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving.

If it’s very close, a candidate could demand a recount. There could be a court fight. That would put the country into December without knowing which party will control the Senate.

🏃 Related read: ‘A genuine toss-up’: Senate battle comes down to red states and Republican voters, by Bridget Bowman

Ahead of Election Day, Trump sets the stage for potential Republican losses

By Rebecca Shabad

In an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said that Republicans “gave this a very strong shot,” while acknowledging that historically, the president’s party “doesn’t win the midterms.”

“This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime,” Trump said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump’s “closing message” before voters make their final trips to the polls, the president spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool.

Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs, and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, D.C., a key focus and fascination of his second term.

Speaking about the election, the president touted what he considered economic wins. But, he said, “it all doesn’t matter if we’re going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election.”

Trump’s speech today came after he held his final midterm rally in Kansas last night — one of 28 for him over the last month, Peter Nicholas notes.

“I’m closing the sucker down,” Trump told the crowd, standing in a chilly evening breeze. “I’m getting out of here. I got to get a little sleep. I’ve been doing a little too many of these.”

World.title: U.S. military carries out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
World.content:
The U.S. military carried out limited strikes Monday on Iran’s Qeshm Island, according to two U.S. officials.

The officials said the U.S. attacks, which came on the eve of crucial U.S. midterm elections and as the Middle East is anxious about the possibility of a return to all-out war, were not a resumption of major combat operations in Iran. They described the attacks as self-defense in response to Iran’s ongoing efforts to target maritime shipping and U.S. assets.

The U.S. continues to intercept drones and missiles that are targeting shipping every day, one of the U.S. officials said.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has routinely targeted and shot at U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz and in the area over the past few weeks, one of the U.S. officials said.

The U.S. is occasionally striking Iranian missile launchers in self-defense when the Revolutionary Guard shoots at U.S. aircraft, the official said.

Iran tried to target a U.S. aircraft again, leading to the U.S. strike on Qeshm to take out the launcher, the official said, calling it part of ongoing operations.

A third U.S. official said, “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.”

Iranian state media reported that five explosions were heard Monday on Qeshm Island.

President Donald Trump had said the U.S. would not launch strikes on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

The administration was last known to have carried out some attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from getting to the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal can still be struck to prevent Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, few details of which have been offered by the White House. Trump told reporters the letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.”

Vance suggested Monday that there was reason to believe the U.S. and Iran could still come to an agreement.

“We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he told reporters when he was asked about the letter, adding that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.”

The region remains on edge about the prospect of the U.S.’ resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The back-channel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way forward in the eight-month-old war, which has rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election last week as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.

But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war appeared to show signs of progress.

Trump noted the drop Monday in a speech in Washington, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion.

“I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Earlier he posted on Truth Social that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.”

He has frequently asserted that the two sides are close to a deal to end the conflict, though one has so far failed to materialize.

Iran has repeatedly said it is open to a diplomatic resolution, but has largely stuck to its demands.

Tehran “has delivered a firm and rational response to the American side and the ball is now in America’s court to prevent a war,” Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tuesday.

World.title: New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years
World.content:
New York health officials Monday reported the state’s first measles-associated death in more than 30 years.

A child in a rural county in northern New York died.

“We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child’s family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time,” state health officials said in a statement.

The statement did not provide additional details about the child.

So far this year, 178 measles cases have been recorded in New York, according to the state Health Department. The vast majority — 170 cases — were outside New York City. Fifteen cases have been reported in Lewis County.

In October, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared the outbreak an emergency.

“Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease,” she said in a statement after the death was announced Monday.

In neighboring Pennsylvania, health officials are fighting the country’s worst outbreak in 30 years. As of Monday, there have been 1,433 cases, according to the Pennsylvania Health Department, including 269 hospitalizations. Six people have died.

As of Friday, there have been 4,852 measles cases nationally, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

New York health officials said people should make sure they are current on their measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations.

The first dose is typically given at around 1 year of age and another at around age 5. Two doses offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life.

During outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old are eligible for a dose ahead of those two recommended shots.

World.title: With AO3 down, fanfic readers are in survival mode
World.content:
When the internet’s biggest fanfiction repository vanishes from reach, there’s one thing you can still count on: a network of fellow fans.

Just ask the massive community of Archive of Our Own readers, who in the past few days have gone from panic to ingenuity after their beloved fanfic haven went dark.

AO3 is home to more than 18 million works, including many sexually explicit stories (affectionately referred to as “smut”), and writing inspired by popular IP, such as “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry.”

But last week, the Organization for Transformative Works, the nonprofit behind AO3, announced the site would be down for two to four weeks, citing a “security incident.”

The prospect of weeks without AO3 sent shock waves through a community devoted to the platform’s uncensored storytelling and meticulous tagging system. Some went as far as likening the outage to life in prehistoric times or descending into madness.

But their desperation also gave way to solidarity, with readers sharing tips with each other on how they can still get their fan fiction fix.

In the r/AO3 community on Reddit, moderators have set up megathreads for the purpose of helping members find and share copies of their favorite stories. Some AO3 writers are uploading new chapters of their fanfiction stories to their Tumblr blogs. Others are creating shared Google folders.

“There are always debates, different opinions and occasional fights within and between fandoms. But during the outage, I have seen people from completely different fandoms and backgrounds helping one another and working toward shared solutions,” said Ashmita, a 23-year-old AO3 reader and fanfiction writer from India who built a web tool to make it easier for users to connect Google Drive folders and navigate the hundreds or thousands of files inside.

“It has been a beautiful reminder of how much these communities care about each other,” Ashmita, who requested to be identified by first name only to preserve her online privacy, added.

Another public Google Drive link to a “Fanfic Emergency Fund,” created by author Berklie Novak-Stolz, has already accrued a deluge of works across a wide range of fandoms and genres.

“The horrors may persist, but so do we,” Novak-Stolz wrote in a letter to readers. “We’re all going to be okay thanks to the wonders of humanness and community and storytelling.”

As of Sunday, the Organization for Transformative Works said there are no further updates regarding the outage.

The organization encouraged users to review certain recommended safety practices as the outage persists, such as clicking links from trusted sources, being wary of scammers and creating unique passwords for every website.

In a statement to NBC News, a spokesperson for the Organization for Transformative Works said it will share further updates on the “security incident” as soon as verified information becomes available.

“AO3 and the OTW were founded by fans, for fans. That ethos remains at the heart of our mission today, and we love seeing how fans mobilize and support one another, both through and beyond AO3,” the spokesperson said. “As fan[s] ourselves, we deeply empathize with the frustration and despair of losing access to AO3—and we’re heartened by the creativity, humor, and sense of community reflected in the flood of memes.”

AO3’s absence has prompted other fanfiction websites and adjacent platforms to seize on an opportunity to attract more users.

“We’re here to support you during this difficult time,” a post from Wattpad on X read.

“while our spouse ao3 is still resting drop your fav fanfics and authors to fill the void,” the X account for Tumblr wrote.

The audio erotica platform Quinn also enticed readers by offering a discount code citing AO3’s blackout.

But some die-hard readers said there’s nothing like AO3, a space they laud for being entirely community-funded and free of s.

“To me, AO3 feels heartfelt,” Ashmita said. “It is a huge platform, but it still has the feeling of a niche community built by people who care deeply about what they are creating and sharing.”

World.title: 17-year-old arrested in Spirit Halloween shooting that killed pregnant woman, injured 6 other people
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy has been arrested in last week’s shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in California that killed a pregnant woman and injured six other people, police said Monday.

The suspect, whose name will not be released because he is a minor, will be charged with one count of murder but could face an additional murder count because 31-year-old victim Constance Hages was pregnant, Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall said.

The teen was arrested in Suisun City, a municipality adjacent to Fairfield, where the shooting took place at Solano Town Center mall around 8:30 p.m. Friday, police said at a news conference Monday.

A 16-year-old boy and two men, ages 19 and 32, were left in critical condition, Marshall said. A 23-year-old man was stable in critical condition at a hospital, and two other men, ages 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and later released, according to authorities.

All but one of the victims still hospitalized Monday had been stabilized, with one still in critical condition, Marshall said.

The shooter entered the store and targeted someone specific inside when he opened fire, said Officer Michelle Belyea, a police spokesperson. Marshall said that the shooter used a handgun and that there may have been a previous altercation between him and a victim.

The suspect opened fire on a vehicle at a local high school last year and was in custody for a few months as a result, Marshall said. He bemoaned what he characterized as a lack of accountability in that case.

“This event shouldn’t have even occurred,” Marshall said. “California has gotten extremely soft on accountability with youth.”

He said detectives identified a suspect hours after the attack but didn’t want to tip him off. The teen was arrested at his home Monday afternoon, Marshall said.

The suspect is believed to have acted alone, he said.

Fairfield, a city of more than 122,000, is about 45 miles northeast of San Francisco.

World.title: Indicted ICE officer had been on the job a little over a year as Trump’s hiring surge comes under scrutiny
World.content:
ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales turned himself in Monday after being indicted last week in connection with running over a man who was on foot. The case has put Morales’ work record under scrutiny and called attention to the administration’s hiring surge last year to fill in immigration enforcement posts.

Morales, 33, was released on a $30,000 bond after a hearing before District Judge Matthew Peneguy in Harris County, Texas. He had been indicted Friday on a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

The case has escalated criticism of the administration’s attempt to quickly increase the ranks of ICE officers to fulfill President Donald Trump’s mass deportation pledge, just as voters are heading to the polls for midterm elections.

ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales after his first court appearance in Houston on Monday. KPRC

Last year, several Department of Homeland Security officials told NBC News some of the ICE recruits had failed to meet the standards for hire, including having disqualifying criminal backgrounds or lacking physical or academic requirements. The DHS told NBC News at the time that most of its new recruits are former law enforcement officers.

Earlier this month, the agency said it would be retraining thousands of its officers who had received expedited training due to the hiring surge.

The Oct. 10 incident involving Morales and Miguel Parra Hernandez was captured by several cameras. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said the footage led investigators to believe that Morales deliberately ran over Parra to stop him during a chase.

Parra is in rehabilitation, overseen by ICE officers, recovering from multiple injuries.

If a similar incident occurred in a Harris County agency, Teare told NBC News on Monday, “every one of those people, whether or not they had gotten into any trouble or not, would be taken off the street and sent back through the full academy.”

Morales was hired by ICE in August 2025 and had more training than other hires, his attorney, David Lindenmuth, said. He accused Teare of character assassination.

“This Democratic district attorney has great issues with the conservative Republican Party government’s ICE agenda, and he’s trying to pick a fight with them, but he’s smashing this individual to do so,” Lindenmuth said.

Lindenmuth said the car strike was accidental and happened as Morales reacted to avoid hitting a car that was in front of him.

In response to criticism of Morales’ actions and to the training of ICE officers, an ICE spokesperson said in an email that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE.”

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” the ICE spokesperson stated.

Miguel Parra Hernández. Courtesy FIEL

Video of the collision captured by cameras from local businesses and bystanders recorded Morales pursuing Parra, who exits a stopped truck and begins running. Morales’ vehicle makes a quick left turn in front of a stopped vehicle and hits Parra.

Morales’ body camera video captures the officer saying, “You got hit with the car, bro,” turning Parra over, straightening his leg, trying to pick him up from under his arms and telling others he should be moved into the car.

Teare said Morales’ attempt to move Parra was “careless.”

“These are not things that a law enforcement officer would ever do to someone that they had detained, with or without force, if they were complaining of injury,” Teare said.

According to the DA’s office, Morales had two handcuffed arrestees sitting in the back of his car without seat belts when the vehicle hit Parra. To Teare, that was illustrative of the problems with the agency’s tactics and lack of proper training and vetting of ICE officers.

Morales is the first ICE agent indicted in Texas. In May, prosecutors in Minnesota charged ICE enforcement officer Christian Castro in connection with the January shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis, and he was indicted on federal charges in September for making false statements to investigators about the case.

Before joining ICE, Morales, originally from Brownsville, Texas, on the U.S.-Mexico border, worked several stints as a guard. One of those jobs was at the Port Isabel Detention Center, an ICE facility that has historically been the final stop before an immigrant is shuttled out of the country, Lindenmuth said.

The scene in west Houston where a vehicle driven by an ICE officer hit Parra during an enforcement operation. KPRC

Morales started young, working from August 2012 to January 2013 as a corrections officer for Cameron County in Olmito, Texas, Lindenmuth said.

He then joined the military and worked as a military police officer, though was not deployed during his two years of Army service, Lindenmuth said. An Army spokesperson said Morales left in 2014 with the rank of private first class.

Morales then spent seven months with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice as a mid-level correctional officer overseeing the care and custody of inmates with limited supervision, according to Amanda Hernandez, a TDCJ spokeswoman.

He resigned in 2018 while on probation with the agency for falsification of records, specifically documenting security rounds as completed when they had not been conducted, Hernandez said in an email.

Lindenmuth said he did not immediately have further information about the probation.

On Friday, Teare said he was “not familiar with a single agency that would have hired” Morales, after seeing his work record.

Lindenmuth said his client is an ordained pastor of a Christian-based church. He said Morales studied to be a police chaplain at Universidad Cristiana Internacional El Shaddai in Dallas and has done missionary work in other countries.

“He is a faith-based person,” Lindenmuth said. “You know, he is a good person who tries to help people.”

Polling times vary by state. The lists below show each state's earliest opening and latest closing times. States will begin reporting election results after their polls close.

Forty-seven states and the District of Columbia offer early voting options, with the exception of Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire. Eight states and Washington, D.C., automatically send a mail-in ballot to every registered voter, although voters generally can still choose to vote in person. Over 57 million voters have already cast their ballots early this year.
