World.title: Two economists studied California's billionaire tax. They reached wildly different conclusions
World.content:
Two economists studied California's billionaire tax. They reached wildly different conclusions

toggle caption i PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.

As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled California since the tax was proposed.

Sponsor Message

On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter and podcast ). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires . Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.

"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money.

On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.

Sponsor Message

" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."

It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report in The New York Times.

A golden opportunity in the Golden State?

The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.

A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. That said, most of the wealth held by California billionaires is in publicly traded stocks, whose value is easy to determine.

Zucman, together with Jasper Boll and Emmanuel Saez, released an analysis of the California billionaire class and this proposed wealth tax.

Sponsor Message

"California billionaires' wealth has reached $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, as large as all the annual income reported on income tax returns of all Californians," they wrote. They found that California billionaire wealth had exploded by 144% between 2023 and 2025, thanks largely to the AI boom. "Over the longer run, the real wealth of California's billionaire class — the top 0.001% richest households — has been multiplied by 25 from 1982 to 2026, while average real family income in California has only doubled."

Zucman says a crucial problem with the existing tax system in California, America, and beyond is that the superrich have been seeing their wealth snowball bigger and bigger while paying relatively little in income taxes. Billionaires can structure their finances to generate little or no taxable income, making the income tax rate "totally irrelevant," he argues. Zucman believes a wealth tax will help address this, thereby helping to fight rising inequality, counteract the political power of "the oligarchs," and raise much-needed funds for everyone else.

Zucman, Boll, and Saez estimated that the state wealth tax proposed by Prop 40 could raise "about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax revenue." They arrive at that figure by taking 5% of their $2.3 trillion estimate of billionaire wealth, then reducing the projected revenue by 10% to account for avoidance, evasion, and the possibility that some billionaires ended their California residency before January 1, 2026.

Rauh argues that this 10% reduction to account for billionaires avoiding the tax is too optimistic.

Why past wealth taxes have been "abject failures"

As we've previously reported in the Planet Money newsletter , wealth taxes have been tried before around the world and they have had a dismal track record. Even Zucman, a wealth tax champion, writes in his new book that past wealth taxes "by and large, have been abject failures."

Zucman and his coterie of other (typically French) economists have spent a lot of time studying why past wealth taxes failed and have sought to design new ones that address those failures.

Sponsor Message

One crucial problem was that wealth taxes tended to have loopholes that allowed the rich to shelter their assets, making these taxes a leaky bucket. For example, before France scrapped its wealth tax back in 2018 , it exempted qualifying business assets, including shares in companies their owners ran. That, Zucman says, was a big loophole that drastically reduced the amount of revenue it raised.

Another crucial problem — which is at the center of the debate on this California wealth tax proposal — is that some superrich people move to avoid the tax. France became a cautionary tale, with critics often pointing to estimates that tens of thousands of millionaires left while its wealth tax was in place. However, how much of that exodus was caused by the wealth tax remains disputed.

Zucman acknowledges that the flight of rich people has been an issue with past wealth taxes, but he also argues that this problem has been overblown. He, for example, pointed to a recent working paper about Norway, which has had a wealth tax since 1892 . It found that recent increases to this existing wealth tax, alongside other tax increases on the rich, drove at most 100 rich people to leave. But, it found, those departures didn't do much to dent the resulting gains in wealth-tax revenue. That said, Norway is a nation, not a state, and moving to another country is a bigger deal than, say, moving from California to Nevada.

To avoid the failures of past wealth taxes, Prop 40's designers have tried to plug potential leaks. Unlike France's old wealth tax, it would tax business holdings, including shares in companies that billionaires run. And by making it a one-time, retroactive tax tied to where billionaires lived on January 1, 2026, they hope to prevent billionaires from escaping the bill by simply moving away.

Sponsor Message

However, whether these provisions will actually work is at the heart of the debate.

Are Prop 40 supporters just California Dreamin'?

Rauh recently released a competing analysis with a provocative conclusion: instead of raising $100 billion, as Zucman and the measure's supporters claim, this wealth tax could ultimately cost the state billions.

First, Rauh argues, at least seven famous billionaires had already left California before the January 1, 2026, residency cutoff, putting their fortunes beyond the tax's reach. Those billionaires are Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, and David Sacks.

Those departures alone, Rauh says, reduced the potential revenue from this wealth tax by "around $30 billion."

Zucman, however, disputes that those fortunes are beyond California's reach. He says the legal experts he trusts believe it's unlikely that any of these billionaires successfully ended their California tax residency before the cutoff. Ending your residency, he argues, takes more than a last-minute move across state lines. Prop 40 was designed with this in mind. It was announced in late October 2025 , giving billionaires only about two months to establish residency elsewhere before January 1, 2026. Talk about a New Year's Day hangover.

Take Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Sure, he's moved just across the border to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe — and meanwhile spent more than a hundred million dollars trying to defeat Prop 40. But, Zucman says, he still frequently commutes to work in Silicon Valley. A quick change of address, he argues, doesn't necessarily mean you've left California behind for tax purposes. Rauh counters that Brin, backed by what we can only assume are the best accountants and lawyers, has likely succeeded in establishing Nevada residency. He stands by his assumption that Brin and the others are beyond the tax's reach.

Like much of the debate over how much this tax will ultimately raise, this dispute has as much to do with the law as it does economics.

Sponsor Message

Which leads us to the second reason Rauh believes this proposed wealth tax will raise much less money than its supporters hope: the courts. Billionaires, armed with the best lawyers money can buy, will mount a slew of constitutional challenges to this tax. And given this wealth tax's novelty — and the Supreme Court's conservative majority — there's a real risk that at least part of Prop 40 could be struck down.

For example, Prop 40's controversial retroactive provision. It would tax some billionaires based on where they used to live. Rauh argues that could violate the Constitution's due process protections, although the Supreme Court has upheld other retroactive taxes in the past. The tax also reaches beyond California's borders, targeting wealth held around the world, which could create legal issues. Rauh also raises legal concerns about how the tax would value privately held companies. He says that venture capital deals can put a price on a company that overstates what it's actually worth. Taxing an owner's share of that inflated value, he argues, could create constitutional problems.

The architects of Prop 40 designed the law with legal challenges in mind, and it has all sorts of fallback provisions meant to keep the tax working if the courts strike down any part of it. But how much revenue would survive those legal battles? This is another big disagreement between Rauh and Zucman.

Rauh and Jaros estimate a big range of possible outcomes. But their central estimate, which has generated plenty of headlines, cuts the remaining projected revenue in half to account for legal uncertainty. That is a strong assumption — not a certainty about how the courts will rule — and Zucman disputes it.

After accounting for billionaire departures and the anticipated legal challenges, Rauh and Jaros estimate the wealth tax would bring in only "around $30 billion."

Sponsor Message

But that's not the end of their gloomy estimate. Because Rauh and Jaros expect even more billionaires to flee the state if Prop 40 passes, taking their existing income tax payments with them.

Zucman questions that prediction: if moving won't necessarily get billionaires out of paying this retroactive, one-time tax, why would they leave? They're already on the hook, and this isn't an annual tax.

Rauh's answer: because they will rationally fear that this won't be the last wealth tax that California passes. The sense that California is becoming a hostile environment for the superrich could drive departures even if another wealth tax never materializes, he argues. After all, Zucman and many other supporters of Prop 40 see this one-time tax as only the beginning. Zucman advocates for an annual wealth tax in his book, and he told us, yeah, he doesn't really want this to be a one-time tax.

The way Rauh sees it, Prop 40 trades a stream of income-tax revenue in the future for a more immediate payout of wealth-tax revenue today. His calculation assumes those income tax losses continue indefinitely. All of which is how he and Jaros arrive at their shocking conclusion: "On net, the state loses $39 billion in expectation because of this tax," Rauh argues.

Zucman objects that their calculation factors in future income tax losses from billionaires fleeing feared wealth taxes — but none of the revenue those hypothetical wealth taxes would bring in.

"That's absurdly one-sided," Zucman says. "You can't just count the loss and not the gain."

Zucman also argues that the income tax losses from departing billionaires would be smaller than Rauh predicts. Using public financial disclosures, his team estimates that some of the richest billionaires — including Larry Page and Sergey Brin — pay relatively little in income taxes.

Rauh defends their calculation, arguing it follows standard procedures for scoring tax proposals. "It would be absurd to count revenue from not yet proposed taxes," he says. He also argues that the public financial disclosures Zucman and his team focus on give an incomplete picture of how much billionaires pay in income taxes.

Sponsor Message

The pull Of Silicon Valley

How much income tax revenue California could lose depends not just on what billionaires currently pay, but also on how many leave if Prop 40 passes. And the state has a powerful magnet that could keep them there: its thriving tech ecosystem.

For years, conservatives have been painting California as a progressive basket case, predicting that Democratic mismanagement would plunge its economy down the tubes and send rich people fleeing. Yet the state has become the epicenter of the AI boom. In 2025, Bay Area companies attracted three-quarters of all U.S. AI funding — and more than half the worldwide total — according to the Bay Area Council Economic Institute.

Economists refer to this industrial clustering as "agglomeration." Companies, workers, and investors in the same industry benefit from being near one another. It's like a gigantic magnet for economic activity. Zucman suggests these agglomeration effects are so strong that billionaires will still want to live and work in California even if there is a wealth tax.

Zucman points to Mark Zuckerberg as an example. Rather than simply leaving California, Zuckerberg reportedly struck a deal with Meta's board that would let him pay the tax without sacrificing control of his company. Essentially, the deal would let him sell nonvoting shares to cover his potential wealth tax bill while holding on to enough voting shares to keep control of the company. In return, he agreed to stay in California for eight years, subject to conditions, including Meta remaining headquartered there.

Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, told Bloomberg in January that he was "perfectly fine" with paying the wealth tax envisioned by Prop 40. Under it, he would be on the hook for something like $8 billion. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Huang said. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."

Sponsor Message

Rauh, however, doubts that California's tech ecosystem has enough gravity to keep billionaires there if the tax passes. "Agglomeration effects are fragile," he argues. A wealth tax could saddle startup founders with big tax bills based on their companies' valuations, even before they've cashed out. Prop 40 includes provisions that would allow qualifying taxpayers with illiquid wealth to defer payments, but Rauh argues those protections are inadequate.

" You have to understand that the entire startup ecosystem of California is threatened by taxes like this," Rauh argues. He predicts that "investors will pull out of California if the wealth tax is passed."

Zucman hears echoes of an earlier fight in all these warnings about taxing wealth: the fight over taxing income back in the early 20th century. Back then, he says, critics argued that an income tax would drive people away and hurt the economy.

He points to Wisconsin's adoption of a progressive income tax in 1911 as a crucial turning point. Two years later, America adopted the federal income tax we know today. Zucman hopes California can play a similar role for taxing wealth.

"I have little doubt that it will work very well for the state of California," he says. "And then very quickly you'll see other states doing the same."

Ultimately, Zucman hopes this movement will lead to a federal wealth tax. He acknowledges that billionaires are less likely to move to avoid a national wealth tax than a state one.

Rauh also expects less flight under a national wealth tax. But he argues that such a tax would still discourage investment and threaten the U.S. economy.

California voters are now being deluged with ads and glossy mailers in what has proven to be one of the most expensive ballot fights in the state's history. If wealth tax supporters have their way, the rest of America could face a similar choice in the near future. For now, it's up to Californians to decide whether this wealth tax is a golden opportunity or a costly mistake.

World.title: How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?
World.content:
How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?

toggle caption i mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images

How you brush your teeth — and what you use to do it — matters.

Recently, dentist Dr. Jin-Ho Phark says he's noticed patients asking about fluoride-free toothpaste options. Phark is an associate professor of clinical dentistry at the Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry of University of Southern California.

"There's a lot of interest from the patients," Phark says. "I hear that also regularly from students."

One product that patients are asking about in particular is a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite. Many patients, Phark says, may have seen the products on social media, "being pushed by influencers and other people quite intensively."

Sponsor Message

The traditional fluoride toothpaste became common in the late 1950s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when Procter & Gamble Co. released Crest nationally. Over the next few decades, oral care products with fluoride as their active ingredient became widely available around the world. These products help protect the outer layer of teeth from cavity-causing bacteria.

And dental health is important because it's related to so many systems in your body, from your heart to digestion.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

"There are these connections made between your oral health, and the bugs that you have in your mouth, and systemic health and even the composition of your gut microbiome," says Dr. Livia Tenuta, a dentist who specializes in preventing tooth decay and associate professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.

The claim

The promise of hydroxyapatite? Many of the things you care about when it comes to toothpaste: cavity protection, whitening, enamel-strengthening. But without fluoride.

Health experts widely agree that fluoride — a naturally occurring mineral — is beneficial to health. But curiosity is growing about fluoride-free options.

"There is an increasing number of people who are refusing fluoride totally, or hesitant to take it, especially for their children," says Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

Sponsor Message

That hesitancy stems from a history of skepticism about fluoride. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has blamed the fluoridation of water for a number of health problems, including arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer, IQ loss, neurodevelopmental disorders and thyroid disease.

Low levels of fluoride are generally considered safe and key to preventing cavities. Amaechi says there's no concrete evidence about potential harms of fluoride when it comes to children's IQ. And research that has found associations between fluoride and IQ has looked at very high levels of fluoride — over twice what's recommended in the U.S. water supply. The CDC previously named the addition of fluoride to public drinking water one of the top 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century, alongside vaccinations and family planning. They also say fluoride in water reduces cavities by 25%.

Still, Kennedy's criticism of fluoride seems to have made its way to toothpaste — and opened up space for products that use hydroxyapatite instead.

So what is hydroxyapatite?

The hype around hydroxyapatite is, in part, due to its similarity to tooth enamel. There's also some research that suggests hydroxyapatite can help with tooth sensitivity.

Tooth enamel is mostly made of calcium and phosphate. Those minerals form the outer layer of your teeth, which protects the internal layers of tissues, nerves and blood vessels, from damage.

Your enamel is stronger than your bones, but still susceptible to damage over time from things like sugary foods and dental plaque. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars, and produce acids that eat away at the outer layer of your teeth. Tenuta says over time, that process sets the stage for tooth decay, often referred to as caries, or eventually cavities (a hole in a tooth that comes from this decay).

She says fluoride toothpaste helps protect teeth by "remineralizing" them with calcium and phosphate.

Sponsor Message

"When [fluoride is] available in our saliva, in the dental plaque that we were not very perfect in brushing, that fluoride that is left over after brushing with the fluoride toothpaste will actually bring minerals back to the tooth," Tenuta says.

Fluoride works with those minerals to form a new compound that protects teeth. It acts like a shield for your enamel. But you need to brush with fluoride toothpaste consistently. Dentists recommend twice daily to keep those minerals around in our mouths.

Hydroxyapatite is thought to work in a slightly different way. These products seem to get into tiny crevices in the tooth enamel.

Many hydroxyapatite products use a form called nano-hydroxyapatite, which has smaller particles that, in theory, can more easily penetrate pores in enamel, though research data is limited.

The evidence

Amaechi, who studies hydroxyapatite use, says fluoride is extensively researched, especially in long-term studies. But he says early research on hydroxyapatite is positive.

"When it comes to remineralization and preventing caries manifestation, it is as effective as fluoride," Amaechi says.

Amaechi was an author on a 2021 study in the journal Scientific Reports, that followed 177 children for almost one year, and compared hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste. The researchers tracked tooth decay in each group, and found that both groups had similar outcomes. That study included funding from Dr. Wolff Group, a German company that owns two brands that make hydroxyapatite toothpastes.

That company contributed funding to another study, published two years later in the journal Frontiers in Public Health. Researchers found similar results after tracking 171 adults, comparing tooth decay in participants using a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to those using a fluoride toothpaste for 18 months. Both groups showed similar outcomes, suggesting that hydroxyapatite worked as well as fluoride in the study. However, the participants in the study were mostly healthy young adults without any severe oral health problems.

Sponsor Message

Tenuta says she'd want to see more long-term studies, especially in people with high risk of tooth decay.

"There are very few studies and they recruited participants of low caries risk," she says.

One shorter-term study in 2019, published in the Journal of Investigative and Clinical Dentistry, did compare a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste in 133 people who were at higher risk of caries. After a little over five months, the researchers found both toothpastes performed similarly.

The bottom line

Hydroxyapatite toothpastes tend to be more expensive than fluoride ones — some over a dollar more expensive per ounce.

For patients who are open to both options, "I will advise them to use fluoride because fluoride has more evidence supporting its efficacy," Amaechi says.

Tenuta agrees.

"I would recommend as a best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's what we have a lot of evidence behind," she says.

The American Dental Association, a professional group for dentists, said in an email to NPR they acknowledge more people are using products with forms of hydroxyapatite and that some evidence suggests those products can contribute to remineralization.

However, research on the ingredient is new, "and evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous, especially regarding clinical indications," wrote ADA Consumer Advisor spokesperson Dr. Ada Cooper.

Instead, the ADA recommends you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, floss daily and regularly visit a dentist.

World.title: 6 things to watch for on election night
World.content:
6 things to watch for on election night

toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images

It can be hard to know what to focus on in midterm elections. There are so many races, from elections for governor and senator to the House and state legislatures. For a better idea of how the night might go to see which party might control Congress, here are six things to watch:

1. The early bellwethers for Republican turnout and the Latino vote

There are two states, Indiana and Kentucky, that will see results in the 6 p.m. ET hour. And then there's Florida, which is split between the Eastern and Central time zones. But most of the state is on Eastern time. So lots of House race results will be coming in during the 7 p.m. ET hour, even if statewide contests like the Senate and governors races won't be called at the earliest until 8 p.m. ET.

Sponsor Message

Some races to watch for early indicators of what might come later in the evening — Indiana's 5th Congressional District, Kentucky's 6th and Florida's 22nd and 27th. Indiana's 5th and Kentucky's 6th are seats held by Republicans that are more competitive now than at the beginning of the cycle. If these are close or tipping to Democrats, it could be a sign of low Republican turnout and a bigger Democratic wave.

Florida's 22nd is held by a Democrat but redrawn to tip in Republicans' favor. Trump won Florida's 27th by double-digits so this heavily Latino district could be an indicator of how this key subgroup votes.

2. Do Republicans get 46% with independents?

Independents are a key swing group, but they are also a lower-propensity voting group in midterms.

It used to be that Republicans had to win a bigger share of independents before the Trump era. Mitt Romney, for example, won 55% of independents in 2012 but lost the presidential election. But there's been a political realignment in this country with blue-collar white voters trending toward Trump, fewer people identifying as Democrats and better-educated white voters shifting toward Democrats.

So in the decade since Trump has been on the political scene, Republicans have done well when they win at least 46% of independents. When they haven't, they've lost.

Sponsor Message

3. Black voter turnout in key states

The Michigan Senate race is important for control of the Senate. If Republicans flip it, the magic number for Democrats goes from four to five, meaning Democrats would have to win five seats held by Republicans to win control of the Senate.

For Abdul El-Sayed (D) to win in Michigan, a key is going to be Black voters in Wayne County. If he runs up the score in and around Detroit, he has a path to victory, but if he doesn't, it becomes that much harder — and it's been an area of vulnerability for him.

During the Trump era, Democrats have needed 68% or more in Wayne County to win Michigan unless, like Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024, they can overperform in the suburbs.

Wayne County Democratic margins

2024 Slotkin 63% Win (11% share)

2024 Harris 62% Loss

2020 Biden 68% Win (12%)

2020 Peters 68% Win

2018 Stabenow 69% Win (15%)

2016 Clinton 66% Loss (13%)

4. The margin with young voters

Voters 18 to 29 see a drastic drop off in turnout between presidential and midterm elections. During presidential races since 1992, 43% of registered young voters cast ballots. But in midterms, that falls to 21%, just 1 in 5 who show up at the polls.

But they are crucial to Democratic success. In the last 20 years, when Democrats won this group by more than 20 points, they have done well, winning presidencies or making gains in midterms. The only exception was 2022, but arguably, the strong margin Democrats won with young voters that year, helped them stem what could have been a much larger Republican tide. That year, Democrats lost nine House seats, but gained a Senate seat.

Democratic margin with voters 18-29, election result

2024 +11, Trump wins presidency

2022 +28, Republicans win House, Democrats gain Senate seat

2020 +25, Biden wins presidency

2018 +35, Democrats win House

2016 +19, Trump wins presidency

2014 +11, Republicans expand House majority, win Senate

2012 +23, Obama wins re-election

2010 +17, Republicans win House

2008 +34, Obama wins presidency

2006 +22, Democrats win House

Sponsor Message

5. In Texas, the keys will be the difference between Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and Ken Paxton's (R) vote totals – and the Latino vote in South Texas

Given past polling errors in Texas that underestimated the Republican vote, there's a healthy skepticism that Democrat James Talarico's margin of error lead in polling averages is enough to win.

There was lots of enthusiasm in 2018 for Beto O'Rourke's (D) 2018 bid against an unpopular Republican senator in Ted Cruz, but Cruz still won, although by less than 3 percentage points. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and no Democrat has been elected to the Senate from Texas in 38 years.

For it to actually happen in this state Trump won by 14 points in 2024, two groups are key – Republicans and Latinos. Ken Paxton (R) is unpopular. Republican Gov. Greg Abbot is also facing a tight race, but he's thought to be in better shape than Paxton. In 2018, Cruz won about 400,000 fewer votes than Abbott, but Cruz still won by more than 200,000 votes. So watch if the difference between Abbott and Paxton is more than 400,000 for Talarico.

toggle caption i Christian Moorman/AFP via Getty Images

The second part of Talarico's path to victory runs through South Texas. Statewide, O'Rourke won 64% of Latinos in 2018, and they were 26% of the electorate, according to exit polls. If Talarico is north of both of those, that's how he wins the seat. Talarico would need to improve on O'Rourke's totals in these Latino-heavy counties: Cameron 63%, Hidalgo 69%, Webb 71%, Nueces 51%. As a bonus, watch the fast-growing and heavily populated Dallas suburbs – Collin 47%, Denton 46%, Tarrant 51%.

6. Party identification

Because of the political realignment that's taken place in the Trump era, watch how people identify in exit polls.

The percentage of those saying they were Democrats hit a low in 2024 at 31%. That trend is happening as the base of the Democratic Party has become more liberal and more disaffected with their own leadership. This year, though, Democrats were among the highest in enthusiasm levels, according to the latest NPR poll, but they are likely going to have to be far higher than 31% as a share of the electorate to do well.

Sponsor Message

Democrats as a share of the electorate

2024 31%

2022 33%

2020 37%

2018 37%

2016 37%

2014 35%

2012 38%

2010 39%

2008 39%

That's quite possible given the opposition to Trump in this election is sky high – 53% of likely voters in the latest NPR poll said they strongly disapproved of the job he's doing. That is very likely to be a unifying force for the left in this election. As the saying goes, the enemy of my enemy is my friend.

Along these lines, it's going to be important to watch races like the Michigan Senate race and the contest for Michigan's 7th Congressional District, both of which have very progressive Democratic candidates trying to win in purple places. Democratic unity – and the party's ideological future – is going to be a key storyline of the 2028 presidential primary and could define the American left for years to come.

World.title: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's midterm election day in the U.S.

Just a small handful of battleground states and districts will decide whether power in Congress shifts from the Republicans to the Democrats for the remainder of U.S. President Donald Trump's time in the White House.

The Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to get a majority in the 435-member House of Representatives, a target that polling analysis suggests is well within reach.

What's less certain is whether the Democrats will take the Senate.

To achieve a 51-49 Senate majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats. That requires flipping at least two states Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas or Kansas.

Here's a look at the pivotal races to watch in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Senate: Maine

U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican representing Maine, speaks with gun shop owner Rick LaChapelle at a campaign stop in Lewiston, Me. on Oct. 21. (Robert F. Bukaty/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Susan Collins vs. (D) Troy Jackson

Collins has held this seat for 30 years, even though Maine has not voted for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988.

Collins has kept winning elections by persuading enough Democrats that she gets results for Maine in Washington. Most recently, she took credit for Trump's moves to exempt certain Canadian products used by Maine businesses from the crushing 50 per cent tariffs he'd imposed in late August.

The question is whether Maine voters will punish Collins for being a Republican this time or reward her for the occasions when she stood up to Trump.

Her Democratic Party opponent is a former logger turned politician from a small town in northern Maine. Jackson entered the race only in July after the original nominee, Graham Platner, stepped down amid allegations he had sexually assaulted a former partner.

Key issues: Trump's posture toward Canada has led to a sharp drop in Canadians crossing the border to visit Maine. His war in Iran triggered a 74 per cent jump in the price of furnace oil, which roughly half of all households in the state use to heat their homes.

Senate: Michigan

Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is putting U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada on the ballot in Michigan in the midterms. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

Candidates: (D) Abdul El-Sayed vs (R) Mike Rogers

This seat was thrown open by incumbent Democrat Gary Peters' decision not to seek re-election. If Democrats can't hold Michigan, their path to a Senate majority becomes significantly tougher.

El-Sayed is a medical doctor and staunch progressive who was born in the U.S. to Egyptian immigrant parents. Since winning the Democratic nomination in August, he has become a frequent target of Trump's attacks.

Trump launched an Islamophobic rant against El-Sayed during a rally in the border town of Port Huron, Mich. on Oct. 25, calling him a "jihadist" several times. Trump warned that a Democratic win in the midterms would bring "hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror."

Rogers, a former FBI agent who served in the House for 14 years, has attempted to put some distance between himself and Trump on Canada-U.S. relations. He launched a new ad this month in which he said, "We need to end this tariff war now," while sitting in a sports bar with a Labatt beer.

Key issues: Trump's tariffs on Canadian products and the breakdown in trade talks are causing upheaval in the auto industry, Michigan's economic engine. Michigan residents have faced higher tariff costs per household than any other state, according to a recent study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

Senate: Ohio

Trump listens as Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio speaks at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Oct. 12. (Gene J. Puskar/THe Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Jon Husted vs (D) Sherrod Brown

Husted was appointed to the seat in 2025 to replace JD Vance when Vance became Trump's vice-president. Before that, Husted had a lengthy career in state politics, holding elected office since 2001.

Trump has recently commented frequently on the 59-year-old Husted's athletic physique, including at events outside of Ohio.

"I examined his ass," the president said at a rally in Kentucky on Oct. 17. " I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I'm still recovering."

Brown has been in politics for more than 50 years, first elected to the state legislature just before his 22nd birthday. He held Ohio's other U.S. Senate seat from 2007 until losing his re-election bid in 2024.

Brown has long advocated targeted tariffs to protect U.S. manufacturing jobs but has consistently criticized Trump's sweeping tariffs, including those on Canadian goods, as ineffective and inflationary.

Key issues: Ohio is a often considered a bellwether state, so the issues top of mind for voters there mirror those resonating across the country: the rising cost of living and whether Trump's war against Iran and his tariffs are to blame. Concern over the spread of data centres is also emerging as a local issue that could affect the statewide race.

Senate: Texas

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, right, greets a supporter at a campaign rally in Allen, Tex. on Oct. 19. Paxton is the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, running against Democrat James Talarico. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Candidates: (R) Ken Paxton vs (D) James Talarico

Democrats haven't won a U.S. Senate election in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born.

Yet polls suggest Trump himself has put the seat at risk by rejecting incumbent Sen. John Cornyn and endorsing Paxton — the state's scandal-ridden attorney general — as the Republican candidate.

A Republican loss in Texas would be the most significant midterm repudiation of Trump in the country. Paxton seems to realize the burden.

"I'm not exaggerating when I say if we lose Texas, we lose America," he told an Oct. 19 rally in Fort Worth.

In their campaign stump speeches, the rivals describe each another in extreme terms. Talarico calls Paxton "the most corrupt politician in Texas," while Paxton says a vote for Talarico is "a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now."

Key issues: The Latino community accounts for roughly one in every five eligible voters in Texas. It supported Trump in record numbers in the 2024 presidential election, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) targeting thousands of non-criminals who've been in the U.S. for years could swing many of those voters toward Talarico.

Senate: Iowa

Iowa Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee Josh Turek on Oct. 13 in Des Moines, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Ashley Hinson vs (D) Josh Turek

Both parties believe they've nominated appealing candidates in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst.

Hinson was a TV reporter and anchor before winning a House seat in 2020. Turek is a three-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball who was born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam.

Both candidates have tried to persuade Iowa voters they aren't beholden to their party or its leadership. Hinson has said she will stand with Trump on issues such as border security but stand up to him when she believes his policies are wrong for Iowa.

Turek, campaigning in a state that hasn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 16 years, has described himself as "proudly a moderate" and said he and Trump could agree on many issues.

Key issues: Farmers are a major voting bloc in Iowa and rely on diesel to fuel their equipment. For months, Trump brushed aside concerns about soaring fuel prices, driven largely by the war with Iran. Less than two weeks before election day, he announced $8 billion US in one-time payments to farmers to offset diesel costs.

Other notable Senate races

North Carolina appears poised to be the mostly likely state for Democrats to flip.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is retiring, Trump only carried the state by three percentage points in 2024, and Democratic candidate Roy Cooper served 16 years as North Carolina's attorney general and two terms as governor.

His opponent Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, is a political backroomer who has never held elected office.

Alaska has sent only one Democrat to the U.S. Senate in the past 50 years. But there are clear signs the Republicans are worried this time.

At Trump's behest, the Department of Justice launched a lawsuit seeking to bar the state from certifying the election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. The ostensible reason: there is also an independent candidate on the ballot named Daniel J. Sullivan.

The tight Alaska race took on even more uncertainty last week after a bombshell New York Times report that Sullivan the independent was recruited into the race by a Democratic operative from Ohio.

The Democratic candidate is Mary Peltola. She and Minnesota Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan could become the first Indigenous women elected to the U.S. Senate.

In Kansas, no Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election since 1932.

Yet polls suggest that could change in 2026. Similar dynamics are at play in Kansas as in Iowa: farmers are upset by soaring diesel prices triggered by the Iran war and rising input costs resulting from tariffs.

Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is up against Democrat Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a megachurch.

WATCH | What a Democrat sweep of both House and Senate would mean for Trump: What happens to Trump if the Democrats crush the midterms | Duration closed caption 4:57 With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections threatening Republican control of Capitol Hill, CBC’s Ellen Mauro breaks down how a shifting balance of power could challenge President Donald Trump’s agenda — and the key tools he can use to counter Democratic opposition.

House races to watch

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for election.

However, various websites that analyze U.S. politics — including the Cook Political Report, the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, Decision Desk HQ and 270toWin — currently rate no more than 53 of them as truly competitive.

Here are a few of the key Republican-held districts Democrats are targeting in their effort to take control of the House.

Virginia 1st district: (R) Rob Wittman (incumbent) vs (D) Shannon Taylor

Polls close in Virginia at 7 p.m. ET, so this race could provide one of the earliest indications of what kind of a night it will be for Republicans and Democrats. The district, which stretches from the suburbs of the state capital, Richmond, to the historic city of Williamsburg, was flagged by the Washington Post as one of the "bellwether races to watch" in the midterms.

Pennsylvania 7th district: (R) Ryan Mackenzie (incumbent) vs (D) Bob Brooks

This district, centred on the working-class city of Allentown, has swung between Democrats and Republicans four times since 2006. Latinos make up nearly one-quarter of eligible voters. Mackenzie won the seat in 2024 by a one-point margin. Brooks is a former firefighter who has never held elected office.

New York 17th district: (R) Mike Lawler (incumbent) vs (D) Cait Conley

Lawler's pitch to voters in this Hudson Valley district includes what he has called his "strong working relationship" with Trump as a way to get things done in Washington. Conley is a West Point graduate who served in Iraq and Afghanistan and is making her first run for office. She has put her military background front and centre in her campaign advertising.

Democrat Bobby Pulido, a famous singer among the Latino community, is trying to unseat Republican Monica De La Cruz in the race for the 15th Congressional district of Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Texas 15th district: (R) Monica De La Cruz (incumbent) vs (D) Bobby Pulido

Democrats recruited a star candidate for this South Texas race: Pulido is a two-time Latin Grammy Award winner. De La Cruz tried to dismiss him as unserious by saying the election " isn't about who you want performing at your niece's quinceañera." Pulido seized on the remark by taking his campaign to quinceañeras, the traditional celebration of a girl's 15th birthday.

Ohio 7th district: (R) Max Miller (incumbent) vs (D) Brian Poindexter

This district in Cleveland's western suburbs wasn't originally a prime target for Democrats. That changed after Miller's ex-wife — the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno — accused him of physical abuse, including throwing boiling water at her and holding a gun to her head. Miller has denied the allegations.

Poindexter is an ironworker and city councillor in the working-class community of Brook Park.

Michigan 10th district: (R) Michael Bouchard vs (D) Christina Hines

This race in Detroit's northern suburbs is open because incumbent Republican John James is running for governor. Bouchard is an Army veteran whose ads have focused on being tough on crime and securing the southern border.

Hines is a former prosecutor who boasts of having put " hundreds of predators, murderers, and pedophiles in jail ."

World.title: Ottawa wants us all to have emergency supplies for 3 days. The good news is, that number hasn't changed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Public Safety Canada is maintaining its longstanding advice for Canadians to be prepared to go at least three days without running water or electricity, following recent calls in the U.K. and other countries for their residents to do the same.

"Canadians have been encouraged for many years to ... be ready to take care of themselves and their households for a minimum of 72 hours during an emergency," Zarah Malik, a spokesperson for Public Safety Canada, said in a statement to CBC News.

Some U.K. retailers reported spikes in sales of essential goods after London launched its Be Ready campaign on Oct. 22. Officials warned that cyberattacks and severe weather could disrupt essential services, and encouraged residents to stockpile 72 hours of supplies including non-perishable food and bottled water.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house."

Officials in Normandy, France, posted on social media on Oct. 27 that residents should prepare a bag containing essentials for 72 hours. "Don't wait for the emergency: prepare now!" the post reads.

And Japan launched a new national agency focused on disaster management on Monday which, as one piece of a much broader plan focused largely on earthquake preparedness, urged residents to evaluate their evacuation procedures and stock up on water and portable toilets for at least three days.

There is no indication that any of those announcements were co-ordinated or are connected to a particular expected event, but the timing has set off some speculation online.

Prep for one week: expert

Suzanne Bernier, faculty member of the Disaster Recovery Institute of Canada, says governments have been putting out the same messaging for at least three decades but it's a good time for an update.

She says it makes sense that the messaging is becoming more prominent, as natural and human-caused disasters are increasing, people are living in areas that used to be unpopulated and cyberattacks are becoming common.

A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food, echoing a similar ‌attack in France last month.

"We're just seeing that it doesn't really matter where we are, everywhere is a target. But particularly of concern is the cyberattacks on critical infrastructure," said Bernier.

"It's just a matter of time before everybody is either indirectly or directly affected by a cyberattack."

She encourages Canadians to aim for at least seven days' worth of supplies.

WATCH | Expecting the unexpected: Getting prepped to deal with emergencies | Duration closed caption 4:11 Emergency Preparedness Week aims to educate people about how to ready themselves for the unexpected, whether it’s a house fire, severe weather or a power outage. Thunder Bay Fire Rescue encourages residents to take a few simple steps now that could make all the difference later.

"We need to really be preparing people for ... potentially not being able to have anybody respond to you or save your family within that first week," she said, adding people should also have a go-bag ready in case of evacuation.

Public Safety Canada says 72 hours is a minimum recommendation and notes it could take more time for some areas to restore basic services, or for emergency workers to reach all affected residents.

The government agency gives more detailed preparedness advice on its website.

Europe has generally ramped up its emergency preparedness messaging over the last two years. The European Commission's Preparedness Union Strategy, released in March 2025, warns of growing geopolitical tension and threats from natural disasters.

Scott Cameron, co-founder of Emergency Management Logistics Canada, says Canadians should also be paying more attention to emergency preparedness, given talk of national sovereignty and growing climate-related concerns, including recent mass evacuations from wildfires and floods.

Cameron says stockpiling for 72 hours is a good idea for personal preparedness, but more work needs to be done on a community level, like identifying local supply chains and resources.

"Where is our local, our community capacity and resilience, to move beyond 72 hours?" he said. "And what are we as Canadians all prepared to be able to help with, as opposed to being the recipients of aid?"

World.title: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Russian President Vladimir Putin recently declared to a television reporter that inflicting a "strategic defeat" on Russia is "unrealistic," it may have sounded like standard wartime bravado.

Instead, his boilerplate rhetoric may signal something deeper: positioning ahead of a diplomatic endgame as international pressure grows to end the war in Ukraine.

"It is impossible to defeat Russia on the battlefield," Putin told the reporter on Oct. 22.

He continued that "historical Russia" includes all Ukrainian territories and as such, the idea that Moscow could ever relinquish land it has conquered in Ukraine is impossible.

Analysts who've reviewed the Kremlin leader's comments suggest they're part of a deliberate strategy to shape an eventual peace settlement.

"Putin is using history to make a political statement and a political claim," said Eugene Maikinkov, a Canadian-Latvian scholar of Russian history who lectures at the University of Swansea, in Wales.

British Kremlin-watcher Mark Galeotti regularly parses Putin's speeches on his In Moscow's Shadows podcast and agrees Russia's leader is sending important signals.

"Everyone is moving into that kind of preparatory position of establishing their negotiating stances," he told CBC News.

Putin speaks with state television correspondent Pavel Zarubin following an event at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, on Oct. 22 . (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Reuters)

Maikinkov says Putin's message to Russia's adversaries — Europeans especially — is that inflicting a humiliating defeat that fundamentally changes the trajectory of the Russian state will not happen and, one way or another, Russia's demands to end the war will have to be reckoned.

"Russia isn't going anywhere. It will have to be a partner in the future," said Maikinkov, suggesting there is no realistic way to rob Putin of negotiating power.

Intractable demands

After four and half years of combat, the war on the ground has largely bogged down into a stalemate, with Russia making only incremental territorial gains in Ukraine's Donbas region.

Some Western estimates suggest its military has suffered as many as half a million deaths and up to 700,000 wounded.

But despite the bloodbath, Putin has not noticeably moved on any of his key demands to end the invasion: Ukraine must turn over the last remaining 15 per cent of the territory of eastern Donbas region; it must demobilize its army; it must have nothing to do with NATO and must "de-Nazify," as the Kremlin puts it.

That last condition, along with the Nazi reference, reflects Putin's long-held position that the current Ukrainian government of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — who is Jewish — is illegitimate and must be replaced.

Most Ukrianians believe Putin's real intention is to totally subjugate their country and erase Ukrainian statehood.

Ukrainian soldiers fire rockets toward Russian positions on the outskirts of the front-line city of Kramatorsk, in Ukraine's Donetsk region, on Sunday. (Iryna Rybakova/Press Service of the Ukrainian Armed Forces/Reuters)

The belief in Russian exceptionalism — that Russia is a historic empire which will always emerge victorious no matter how hard its enemies try to tear it apart — is one of Putin's most dominant narratives.

It's also one of the most intensely contested.

"There is a myth that has been successfully planted in the West that Russia always wins," said Poland's Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, in response to Putin's comments.

"But things don't always go their way."

People carry candles past The Motherland Calls, a statue commemorating the Russians killed during the German invasion in the Second World War, in Volgograd, Russia, on June 21, 2021. Putin often cites the German defeat as an example of Russia's military prowess. (Kirill Braga/Reuters)

Russia was defeated in the Crimean war in 1856 which blocked its territorial ambitions in Europe.

In 1905, the country's Baltic navy sailed more than 25,000 kilometres around Africa to confront the Japanese navy in the Pacific only to be literally blown out of the water.

And the brutal Soviet-Afghan war, which started in 1979, turned into a decade-long quagmire that ultimately contributed to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Curated history

Still, the rambling lectures that Putin frequently delivers to foreign guests and leaders, particularly Europeans, are always more curated.

His often sermon-like discussions tend to emphasize the defeat of invaders such as Napoleon and Hitler. Putin has also celebrated Czar Peter the Great who captured the territory that now makes up modern-day Estonia and St. Petersburg.

"Putin scours the historical landscape for legitimacy," said Maikinkov.

"One way to gain legitimacy is to create and sustain the narrative of victory and military success. That's why this narrative [of Russia's invincibility] is powerful and why it sticks."

European divisions

In recent days, Europe has been divided over engaging with Putin.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb took the lead and called Russia's leader last week — the first direct European outreach in years. The move was met with heavy criticism in many European capitals including those of Sweden and Italy, but Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Fredrickson was especially vocal, expressing deep skepticism over the overture.

Galeotti says the divisions revert back to a core disagreement over whether its possible to inflict an Afghanistan-style collapse on Putin that fundamentally changes the power dynamics of Europe.

"Putin is trying to inject himself into the debate, more or less saying, 'You can be serious [about negotiating] or you cannot be serious, it's your choice.'"

Municipal employees work at the site of private houses which were damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine November 2, 2026. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has tried to incentivize Putin into a ceasefire, including by waiving sanctions on diesel exports. The Wall Street Journal has also reported some of his officials are trying to convince Europe to start buying Russian natural gas again.

So far, despite Trump's overtures, European nations have expressed little to no interest in re-establishing commercial ties with Russia before there's an end to the war. Nor are there any indications that restoring commercial ties could entice Putin to stop fighting.

Indeed, Maikinkov — the University of Swansea analyst — believes the likelihood the war will end with a peace agreement is remote and a "frozen conflict" akin to the situation on the Korean peninsula, is more likely.

North and South Korea are still technically at war and their border is one of the most heavily fortified and volatile places on the planet.

"At the end of the day, [it] may resemble something like the situation in Korea where we have a robust successful democracy backed by the West, and perhaps part of Ukraine that is under the Russian sphere of influence."

WATCH | Exodus from Oleshky: This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive | Duration 2:32 Buses full of residents from Oleshky arrived in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Oct. 31 after a marathon journey from the besieged Russian-occupied town through Russian-annexed Crimea, and Belarus. Residents have been struggling with severe food shortages, mined routes and drones in recent months. Melania Trump, wife of U.S. President Donald Trump, is credited with brokering the rare, limited ceasefire earlier in October. Some residents would only provide their first names due to safety concerns.

While Zelenskyy has hinted he could live with such an outcome, Putin has insisted all of his maximalist demands must be met — including that Ukraine's army must leave the remaining parts of Donbas that it holds, and turn the territory over to Russia.

However, the area which includes the city of Kramatorsk, is arguably the most heavily defended part of the front. Known as the "fortress belt", if it falls into Russian hands, Ukrainians fear Putin's military would have an open path to capture Kyiv and other other Ukrainian cities.

The Donbas issue "is still an absolute block," said Galeotti.

It is a reality that leaves other seasoned observers warning against false optimism.

"I struggle to imagine any scenario in which any Ukrainian leadership would agree to Putin's terms for ending the conflict,' wrote renowned Russia analyst Tatiana Stanovaya.

Instead, she predicts more dangerous geopolitical behaviour from Putin as the economic costs of the war on Russia escalate and the country's elites fight among themselves for survival.

She concludes with a bleak warning.

"I believe we should prepare for the worst," she said, suggesting there could more hybrid attacks or other Russian aggression.

"What appears to be a red line today may become the new normal tomorrow," she said, meaning potentially dangerous confrontations with European countries could become far more common.

Which is exactly why the Kremlin's projection of "battlefield invincibility" matters and why Russia's leader is heavily leaning into the narrative now — to shock exhausted Ukrainians and its Western allies into a state of resignation.

World.title: Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota released after federal court ruling
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Canadian dentist detained by U.S. federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Minnesota during a green card interview is back home after being ordered released by a federal judge.

U.S. District J udge Michael J. Davis wrote in his ruling that the arrest and detention of Dr. William Lizardo, 32, originally of Mississauga, Ont., violated his constitutional rights.

Lizardo moved to the U.S. on a student visa in 2019 to study at the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry, according to court documents. He graduated in 2023 and married an American that same year. They had a daughter two years later.

Lizardo's wife filed a petition for an alien relative in September 2023, while Lizardo applied to adjust his status to permanent residency. The relative petition was approved in January 2025, according to the court.

Lizardo practised dentistry in federally-designated shortage areas until his work authorization was revoked, at which time he started volunteering at a low-cost clinic in Burnsville, Minn., according to the court documents.

WATCH | ICE shooting in New York captured by bodycam: New bodycam video shows aftermath of ICE shooting in NYC | Duration closed caption 2:49 Police bodycam footage shows the aftermath of an ICE shooting that wounded a man in New York. His lawyers are challenging his detention as protests grow and federal officials defend the agents’ actions.

Hearing orders sent to wrong address

In January, his request for permanent residency was denied because he had failed to provide a certified document from Ontario.

Orders to appear at subsequent hearings were sent to the wrong address. Lizardo missed the hearings and was subsequently arrested by ICE on Oct. 23, detained at Sherburne County Jail and ordered removed from the U.S.

The judge called the facts of the case "appalling" — noting that while the couple moved several times, each time Lizardo "filed changes of address" with the post office and with U.S. Citizen and Immigration Services (USCIS). "In turn, USCIS communicated with Petitioner at each new address."

The judge also noted that Lizardo had never been arrested during his time in the U.S.

Lizardo filed to have the order of removal rescinded as he had never received the notices for the hearings. That request was granted by an immigration court on Oct. 28 after it found he had provided sufficient evidence of lack of notice.

ICE argued Lizardo should be kept in custody while the green card case was being decided.

The judge ruled ICE agents had no reason to believe Lizardo was a flight risk and ordered him immediately released.

"Because the facts presented here are so appalling and so well supported, the Court could issue a long order, complete with colorful details about, and commentary on, the abuses suffered by Petitioner," the judge wrote.

Instead, he said he simply wanted to make sure Lizardo didn't spend another night in jail.

'This was a paperwork error'

Lizardo's lawyer, Hassan Ahmad, confirmed to CBC News that his client was finally released Sunday evening, hours after the judge's order.

Lizardo is now waiting for a USCIS decision on his green card application, and Ahmad says he hopes that given what his client has been through, that decision will come soon.

"This was a paperwork error," Ahmad said. "That's all it was. And they literally made a federal case out of it."

Ahmad says Lizardo cannot be detained again by ICE while he is waiting for the decision on his green card. "I made sure to put that in the order when I filed and, and the judge signed on," he said.

"This whole removal proceedings was tainted from the very beginning," Ahmad said, adding that he hopes ICE will just let it go.

World.title: Ryan Wedding's $40M US motorbike collection to go up for auction
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A $40-million US collection of rare and high-performance motorcycles seized from Canadian alleged drug lord Ryan Wedding will go up for auction next week in Mexico.

The 61 bikes include models from Ducati, Honda, Kawasaki, MV Agusta, Suzuki and Yamaha. Some were previously used in professional racing, according to the FBI.

The motorcycles were uncovered during raids in the Mexican capital and nearby Mexico state last December at addresses linked to Wedding, who was then one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives.

The former Team Canada Olympic snowboarder was arrested in Mexico City the following month and flown to the U.S., where he remains in custody.

The Mexican public agency known as INDEP — translated as the institute to return stolen assets to the people — shared pictures of the motorcycles on its website and social media accounts ahead of next week's auction.

A red Ducati motorcycle — set to be auctioned off — was among those seized in raids on properties linked to Ryan Wedding in Mexico last December. (INDEP)

Proceeds from the agency's auctions typically go to fund social services.

INDEP didn't name Wedding, but announced the motorcycles were now subject to forfeiture after they were seized by law enforcement last December. Some of the models pictured on the auction site match those seen in images previously shared by the FBI.

Mexican media also reported the link to Wedding.

Following last year's raids, the FBI said in a social media post the "large number" of motorcycles seized were believed to be owned by Wedding, with an estimated total value of about $40 million US. The U.S. agency said the operation was the result of co-operation with Mexican authorities, the RCMP and the Los Angeles Police Department.

Mexican authorities said more than 60 motorcycles, as well as medals, artwork and drugs were seized in a series of raids in December 2025. The FBI later said the operation targeted Ryan Wedding, then considered a most-wanted fugitive. (Mexican government)

'Amazing collection'

Racing enthusiasts who examined pictures of the seized bikes last year said some were identical to those used in Grand Prix road races, including a Ducati driven by Spanish world champion Marc Márquez.

The FBI previously confirmed to CBC News some of the models had been used in professional racing.

"There are maybe 10 or 15 of them that are literally the two-wheeled equivalent of Formula 1 cars," said Simon Patterson, a North Ireland-based journalist who covers MotoGP, told CBC News.

"All in all, [this is] just an absolutely amazing collection of machines that Wedding has somehow been able to amass."

The FBI said the December raids resulted in the seizure of a 'large number' of motorcycles. (FBI)

The U.S. Treasury Department has said Wedding laundered his vast wealth through an "extensive transatlantic network" involving associates, businesses and luxury assets including cars and motorcycles.

The FBI in Florida also seized an ultra-rare 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK-GTR Roadster, said to be worth $13 million US. The silver two-seater had been purchased by Toronto-area jeweller Rolan Sokolovski — described by U.S. authorities as one of Wedding's two chief money launderers.

Big-ticket assets seized by U.S. federal law enforcement are also often auctioned off, but it's unclear what will happen to the Mercedes.

An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on Monday when CBC News asked whether more Wedding-linked items would be sold off.

Canadian Ryan Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January 2026 and flown to California to stand trial. (U.S. Embassy in Mexico, FBI Los Angeles/X)

Bids start at $1,600

As for the motorcycles, INDEP said in a news release the models going up for auction range from the 1960s to the 2020s, with starting bids going from roughly to $1,600 to $192,000 Cdn., depending on the bike.

Bidders must register by Nov. 10. The live auction is set to begin the following morning.

The raids last December also netted other items, including Canadian snowboarding medals, artwork and two vehicles, authorities said at the time.

Next week's auction, set to be held at a banquet hall in the Mexican capital, will feature 620 lots in total, including armoured vehicles, boats and aircraft. It's unclear whether any of the other goods may be connected to the Canadian.

U.S. authorities have said Wedding — also known as "El Jefe" (The Boss) — fled to Mexico around 2015, when the RCMP in Montreal sought his arrest. The Thunder Bay, Ont., native then allegedly expanded his purported cartel-linked drug-smuggling operation to a $1-billion US empire.

WATCH | Motorcycles seized last year linked to Ryan Wedding: Motorcycles seized from Ryan Wedding used for pro racing: FBI | Duration closed caption 2:02 The FBI recently seized dozens of high-end motorcycles believed to belong to Canadian fugitive Ryan Wedding with an estimated value of $40 million US. The FBI is now confirming some of the motorcycles were used in professional racing.

Wedding has pleaded not guilty to charges related to drug trafficking, money laundering and murder.

The 45-year-old is set to stand trial in Los Angeles next year.

Prosecutors have linked Wedding's purported criminal network to multiple killings, including the mistaken-identity shooting of a family in Caledon, Ont.

CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle has covered the case of Ryan Wedding extensively. He can be reached by email at thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Millions of fish died at an Ontario nuclear plant in 2025. Now its operator faces federal charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The private company that operates the Bruce Nuclear Generating Station faces two federal Fisheries Act charges after millions of fish died in the plant's cooling water intake system in 2025.

The charges against Bruce Power come after a CBC News investigation revealed publicly, for the first time, the extraordinary scale of what happened.

An estimated 8.1 million gizzard shad massed near the power plant during a sudden cold snap on Feb. 13, 2025, according to an internal report from Bruce Power. The small, cold-sensitive fish were drawn to the warm water discharged into Lake Huron near Tiverton, Ont., by the nuclear power plant over a two-month period, between February and March of 2025.

The fish subsequently became trapped and died against the plant's intake screens in such large numbers that one reactor had to be shut down and another had to reduce power, straining the province's electrical grid during a prolonged winter cold spell.

The company's own findings said the massive fish kill was the result of an "organizational failure" to adapt to changing environmental conditions caused by climate change.

Dead gizzard shad lie along the Thames River in 2021. The same temperature-sensitive species washed ashore along Lake Huron for days during the 2025 fish kill at Bruce Power. (Colin Butler/CBC)

Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) estimates between 3.3 and 4.3 million fish died between February and March of 2025 — more than 200 times Bruce Power's annual authorized limit by weight.

Gizzard shad carcasses washed ashore in nearby communities for days, while Bruce Power used a crane to scoop millions of dead fish from the plant's cooling water channels before hauling them to a landfill, provincial records showed.

Under the federal Fisheries Act, Bruce Power was charged last month with causing the death of fish through non-fishing industrial operations and violating the conditions of its environmental permit, which limits the company to 6,600 kilograms of dead fish annually.

" As this matter is before the courts, we cannot comment on how we intend to plead or provide additional commentary relating to the charges," Megan Adams, Bruce Power's director of corporate communications, wrote in an email.

The company will appear in Ontario provincial court on Nov. 24.

Fines pay for environmental restoration

In a recent news release, Bruce Power said it was transparent with regulators, including DFO and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, as well as nearby First Nations and municipalities about the fish kill.

An aerial image of the Bruce Power site located near Tiverton, Ont. (Submitted by Chad Richards)

Still, prosecutors don't have to prove the company meant to kill fish in order to establish an offence, according to Theresa McClenaghan, a lawyer and the executive director of the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA).

"The courts consider Fisheries Act offences to be serious offences," she said.

Fines for a first offence can range from a few thousand dollars to $200,000, she said, and are intended to deter violations and express the court's condemnation.

When a fine is issued by the court, the money goes into the federal Environmental Damages Fund to support conservation, habitat protection or restoration, McClenaghan said.

The court can also recommend directing the money to a particular organization or project, including an Indigenous nation or for environmental research.

'A giant fish trap'

Since the fish kill, Bruce Power has spent more than $10 million on mitigation measures, including nets to keep fish out, acoustic and strobe-light deterrants, sonar, cameras and artificial intelligence to monitor fish movements, along with expanded lake research.

WATCH | Fish gather in the warm waters off Bruce Nuclear Station: Rare 'fish city' footage reveals hidden world | Duration 2:01 Using a $250,000 underwater drone, documentary filmmakers Yvonne Drebert and Zack Melnick are capturing footage from parts of the Great Lakes that are often too deep or remote to observe directly.

Ryan Lauzon, a fisheries biologist who advises Saugeen Ojibway Nation, whose traditional territory includes the nuclear plant, said during a recent onsite visit last year he saw gaps in the mitigation measures.

"I did see fish that were swimming right up to that sound and acoustic deterrent system. There was gaps in the nets that were being used to exclude the fish. They ended up having to take the net out because they were so full of algae and dead fish."

Invasive zebra and quagga mussels have depleted the plankton that supports Lake Huron's food web, Lauzon said, leaving less food for other species and making the loss of millions of gizzard shad concerning. They are a prey species for trout, pike and walleye.

Lauzon, who has written a paper on the fish kill, said smaller die-offs happened at the plant in 1977 and 2023. He said while Bruce Power may have spent millions on mitigation measures, they don't address the warm-water discharge that attracts the fish in the first place.

"Unfortunately, the plant acts as a giant fish trap," he said. "Until we establish the effectiveness of mitigation measures and try to deal with this attractant issue, I still think there's real danger."

The cooling systems that draw those fish also face growing challenges as the climate changes, said McClenaghan, who noted the incident may point to a need to rethink how nuclear plants are cooled in a changing climate.

"On the list of possibilities are cooling towers or cooling loops as opposed to what happens right now," she said. "The lakes are acting as a heat sink."

World.title: Lockdown at University of Toronto Mississauga partially lifted
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A shelter-in-place order issued as police responded to a dangerous weapons call at a University of Toronto dormitory in Mississauga has been partially lifted.

The school announced the update in an alert early Tuesday, adding that the lockdown remains in effect for McLuhan Court residence.

The alert says the situation has been contained to a single residential unit and that there have been no reports of physical injuries.

Peel Regional Police have said the immediate area was evacuated late Monday and urged the public to stay away.

On social media, the force described the matter as a dangerous weapons call, though further details have not yet been shared.

The university says on its website that McLuhan Court provides beds for hundreds of first-year students.

Police were called about the situation at 9:11 p.m. In alert issued by the university after 9 p.m., students were told to shelter in place at the UTM campus due to an "active threat."

The school said it had received reports of police activity at McLuhan Court residence, 3330 Residence Road.

"Active threat. Take shelter immediately and secure doors," it told students in a post on social media platform X.

World.title: 24 hours in Antigua: Mark Carney's priorities at this year's Commonwealth Summit

Prime Minister Mark Carney's oft-stated determination to keep his government focused on what Canadians can control could be tested today, as he meets with leaders from the 55 other member countries of the Commonwealth in Antigua.

As he boarded his flight with his wife Diana on Monday, Carney gestured as if he couldn't hear reporters yelling for clarification on where things stand following his conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend.
