Trade negotiations could return to a full boil, but for now they remain on a back burner while the White House focuses on the verdict about to be rendered by American voters in their midterm elections .

The future of the Canada-U.S. relationship hangs so heavy over the Carney government's agenda that it could be hard to focus on anything else. But this week's Commonwealth talks are the first in a series of multilateral summits this month where Canadian officials will pursue alternative partnerships in trade, security and diplomacy.

Here are five things to watch for:

1. Push to double intra-Commonwealth trade

The Commonwealth has three main priorities leading up to 2030: democratic resilience, economic resilience and environmental resilience.

On that first priority, ministers, including Foreign Minister Anita Anand, met Sunday to welcome the restoration of an elected government in Gabon, the central African country which had its membership partially suspended following a military coup in 2023.

But the main focus at this summit is trade partnerships: specifically the association's ambition to lower trade barriers and double trade between member countries by the time they meet for their next biennial summit.

That dovetails perfectly with the Carney government's attempt to pivot away from the U.S.

"I think people don't realize the economic clout of the Commonwealth. There's almost a trillion dollars of trade," said Arif Lalani, a former diplomat who served as a senior official the last time a Canadian prime minister attended the Commonwealth Summit, in 2022.

"There are studies which show that it's cheaper to do business between Commonwealth countries because we have the same practices, same language, generally the same set of regulations. So it's definitely a place to pursue the economic diversification agenda," Lalani said.

WATCH | What the Commonwealth could offer Canada: Carney should see Commonwealth as trade opportunity: secretary-general | Duration closed caption 0:57 With Prime Minister Mark Carney heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting, Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey tells CBC's Janyce McGregor that Canada should consider the association of 56 member states as an alternative trading option.

His fear, however, is that the Commonwealth's "relevance is growing faster than its capacity to deliver."

Leaders need to get more outcome-oriented on trade, he said. He agrees with Carney's efforts to expand this focus to defence and security co-operation too.

At a time when conflicts over choke points like the Strait of Hormuz are restricting global trade, "Commonwealth countries have a lot of coastline, they have strong navies, and so I think there's something that can be done to increase maritime co-operation," Lalani said.

2. Evolving Caribbean relationships

This is Carney's first trip to the Caribbean as prime minister.

That diplomatic deficiency will be addressed this morning in a bilateral meeting with this year's Commonwealth host, Antigua and Barbuda's Prime Minister Gaston Browne, followed by a working breakfast Canada is hosting for all the Caribbean leaders attending this year's summit.

While not a complete gathering of CARICOM leaders, officials briefed reporters that this breakfast is a chance to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Diana Fox Carney are met by a greeting party as they arrive in Antigua. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Vandana Kattar, who worked in the prime minister's office under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, says Carney's approach so far makes sense to her.

"Multilateralism is important to him," she said. Carney went after some of the bigger pieces of his puzzle first, she reckons — pursuing the "low-hanging fruit" of a closer relationship with Europe , attempting to resolve tariff tensions with China .

"Those are big pieces of the puzzle that he's been able to put together," she said. But he also needs to fit smaller pieces into that puzzle, like nurturing Canada's relationships in the Caribbean, "otherwise that doesn't complete the whole picture."

3. Climate finance commitments

"You can't go to the Caribbean countries and not talk of climate resiliency," Kattar said. "They're the ones impacted the most."

Canada's already contributed $4.65 million over three years to the Commonwealth's climate finance access hub to help small island states. It's also made a bigger $13-billion commitment to support all developing countries adapt to the consequences of climate change — like stronger and more frequent hurricanes — over the next five years.

Canada hopes to amplify the voices of smaller Commonwealth partners on climate issues, officials told reporters prior to the trip.

"That's what actually builds the trust, and that's what ensures that Canada is seen as a reliable and a trustworthy partner that actually listens to the concerns of their partners and [is] not just forcing their own agenda onto them," said Climate Action Network's Soomin Han.

Han believes conversations on climate financing between big and small Commonwealth partners might be more productive than at United Nations climate conferences, where a few large countries can block progress.

"Countries should not have to take out more debt simply to survive a crisis they contributed comparatively little to creating," she said.

4. Tensions, debate on reparations

While the Commonwealth has 56 members, King Charles is the head of state in only 15 of them. Half of those are Caribbean countries, and for the week leading up to this summit, he's been touring the region , amid ongoing political pressure for the Crown and the government of the United Kingdom to apologize for its historical role profiting off the slave trade in British colonies .

So far, the King has acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond," but he has not apologized.

Canadian officials briefing reporters prior to the trip said Canada acknowledges the generational and lasting impact of slavery, and supports "open and respectful dialogue" on reparations, but noted there are a "diversity" of perspectives on reparatory justice among Commonwealth members.

WATCH | Britain's role in transatlantic slavery under scrutiny: King Charles will confront 'shameful aspects' of Britain's role in slavery | Duration closed caption 8:13 King Charles III will confront 'shameful aspects' of Britain's history with 'unflinching honesty' when he addresses Commonwealth leaders next week, amid renewed scrutiny of Britain's role in historical transatlantic slavery. The comments resurfaced after Prime Minister Andy Burnham revealed he was open to the U.K. formally apologizing for its role in the trade but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Nicholas Marcus Thompson, an advocate for reparations for Canada's Black communities , says the current U.K. government's opposition to negotiating reparations for slavery is "simply a non-starter" for Caribbean nations.

"Reparations is not giving away a freebie. It's repaying what you took, right? Wealth extracted from enslaved Africans built businesses, financial institutions, universities," said Thompson, who is also the president and CEO of the Black Class Action Secretariat.

"It would have been billions of dollars in today's currency."

5. The Trump factor

Former diplomat Lalani said he believes Canada is heading into this summit with more credibility than it's had in the past, thanks to the "provocative vision" Carney laid out in his speech on middle powers at the World Economic Forum in Davos last winter.

Carney's conversations today won't be limited to people he's close to, like Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. It's also a chance to talk to leaders with whom he doesn't have full agreement — without being overshadowed by superpowers like the U.S. or China.

"Canada can have a discussion with other countries without the baggage of having the United States at the table," he said.

"The biggest destabilizing power in the world right now is the United States. … That requires a candid discussion."

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics
World.content:
The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:29 UTC Full article

Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”

Pope Leo XIV will arrive in Buenos Aires on Sunday on a visit that Javier Milei’s government presents as strictly pastoral, but which takes place amid tension with Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy, one of the most critical voices against the president’s austerity policies. The pontiff will begin a tour in Uruguay on Friday that will continue in Argentina from November 8 to 11 and end in Peru.

“The Pope belongs to all Argentines, not to a political party or a political colour,” presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, who led negotiations with the Church and the Vatican, has repeatedly said. The secretary of worship, Agustín Caulo, insisted it is “an apostolic tour” and that “this should not be politicised”. Authorities expect some 7 million people to follow the Pope in Buenos Aires, Claypole, Luján and Córdoba, in what Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva described as “the largest operation in our history”.

The underlying differences are well known. Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”. A study by sociologist Sol Prieto of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet) of documents published by the Argentine Bishops’ Conference between January 2024 and September 2026 found that 42 of the 44 referring to public policy, or 95%, take “a critical position”, on issues such as the social situation, the environment, institutional quality, the lowering of the age of criminal responsibility and a decree curbing migrants’ rights.

Ten days ago, when Milei questioned the idea that many people cannot make ends meet, the president of the Bishops’ Conference, Marcelo Colombo, replied: “That people cannot make ends meet is a fact of reality, not something that needs to be proven.” The Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge García Cuerva, said the Pope “will find a wounded Argentina”. “There is no affinity, but a very strong aversion between most Argentine bishops and Milei’s government,” said researcher Fortunato Mallimaci, who identifies opposition to abortion as one of the few points of agreement.

According to El País, the government sought to limit mass gatherings but the Vatican’s position prevailed, and the Pope will celebrate open-air Masses. Two events are particularly uncomfortable for the government, according to the newspaper: the meeting with trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina and the visit to the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities, one of the sectors hardest hit by spending cuts. The place of Vice President Victoria Villarruel, estranged from Milei, at official events also remains undecided.

World.title: Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”
World.content:
Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:18 UTC Full article

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government

The president of the Madrid regional government, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, on Monday awarded the region’s International Medal to Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who is in the Spanish capital for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government. “On both sides of the Atlantic we defend the same things,” Ayuso said at the ceremony.

“We are free nations and we defend our governments and liberal democracies and the rule of law, which will not yield to authoritarianism,” said the People’s Party leader, who contrasted Chile with Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Ayuso praised Chile as “an example of what a nation can achieve when it trusts its citizens” and highlighted Kast’s “commitment to freedom, security, prosperity and the defence of institutions”. “We do not want citizens dependent on power; we want them to be masters of their own lives,” she added.

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government. “It is the first duty of the state. And when the state fails in that duty, the most vulnerable pay. Without security there is no order, without order there is no peace and without peace there is no freedom.”

The Community of Madrid’s International Medal, created in 2017 and purely honorary, is awarded on the regional president’s personal initiative. Previous recipients include Argentine President Javier Milei and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa; Venezuelan opposition leaders Juan Guaidó and Edmundo González; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky; Pope Leo XIV; and the United States, for the 250th anniversary of its independence. Manuela Bergerot, spokeswoman for Más Madrid in the regional assembly, accused Ayuso of turning the award into “the membership card of her far-right international”. A group of demonstrators protested outside the regional government headquarters.

Kast began the day with a private meeting with Vox leader Santiago Abascal, with whom he has close ties, and plans to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during the summit, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra.

World.title: Corruption joins the cost of living as a top concern for US voters
World.content:
Corruption joins the cost of living as a top concern for US voters

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 00:31 UTC Full article

A Fox News poll published in October found that 88% of voters say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about corruption in government

The United States votes on Tuesday in midterm elections in which corruption has emerged in the final stretch as one of voters’ main concerns, second only to the cost of living, according to several polls. At stake are all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of the 100 Senate seats and numerous governorships and state legislatures.

A Fox News poll published in October found that 88% of voters say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about corruption in government. Another survey, by Harris for Britain’s The Guardian, found that nine in ten Americans consider it a problem and that 76% believe public officials care more about enriching themselves than improving people’s lives. According to that study, only the cost of living weighs more heavily than corruption in voting decisions, ahead of immigration and healthcare.

“Just six months ago, corruption was not a top issue for voters. A few days out from the midterms, it has absolutely become one of the issues,” pollster Frank Luntz said. The Brennan Center for Justice estimates that references to government ethics in campaign ads have reached their highest level in 14 years: about 24% in House races and 16% in Senate races.

Democratic candidates have focused their criticism on the business dealings of President Donald Trump and his family, particularly in cryptocurrencies, and on private donations of more than US$300 million for the ballroom being built at the White House, including US$25 million each from Apple and Nvidia. Ethics allegations also extend to candidates from both parties: Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, the Democratic Senate candidate in Minnesota over alleged welfare fraud, and the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola in Alaska, under investigation for allegedly promoting a candidate with the same surname as her rival.

More than 51 million people have already voted early, 25% more than in the 2022 midterms. Polls favour the Democrats, who need four more seats to control the House and at least four more to take the Senate, with close races in Michigan, Alaska, Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Texas. Trump closed his campaign on Sunday with rallies in Iowa and Kansas.

World.title: Falklands representative in London honours the Islands’ fallen at Westminster
World.content:
Falklands representative in London honours the Islands’ fallen at Westminster

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 00:08 UTC Full article

Falkland Islands Government Representative, Richard Hyslop, placing a commemorative cross at the House of Commons Garden of Remembrance

The Falkland Islands Government Representative to the UK and Europe, Richard Hyslop, has placed a commemorative cross at the House of Commons Garden of Remembrance in London in memory of Falkland Islanders killed in both world wars and those who lost their lives in 1982.

The cross commemorates the 22 Islanders killed in the First World War, the 25 killed in the Second World War, and the 255 British Armed Forces personnel and three Islanders killed in the Falklands War, according to a statement from the Falkland Islands Government Office in London.

The Garden of Remembrance, installed each year in New Palace Yard outside the Palace of Westminster, was started in November 2021 by the Speaker of the House of Commons, Sir Lindsay Hoyle, in partnership with the Royal British Legion. It allows parliamentarians and representatives of Commonwealth countries and UK Overseas Territories to plant memorial crosses honouring Armed Forces personnel.

“I was honoured to place a commemorative cross in the House of Commons Gardens of Remembrance in memory of those Islanders killed in both World Wars and those killed in the liberation of the Islands in 1982,” Hyslop said. “We must remember the service and sacrifice of those individuals who gave so much to protect the freedoms we enjoy today, we will remember them.”

World.title: An Oxford professor to sit as the UK's chosen judge in the Falklands dispute in Hamburg
World.content:
An Oxford professor to sit as the UK's chosen judge in the Falklands dispute in Hamburg

2nd Monday, November 2026 - 15:23 UTC Full article

British jurist Vaughan Lowe, emeritus professor of public international law at the University of Oxford, will be the judge ad hoc chosen by the United Kingdom in the case between Argentina and London before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea over hydrocarbon exploitation north of the Falklands. Lowe will make his solemn declaration on Monday, November 9, the day before the hearing.

According to a statement from the Hamburg-based tribunal, the public sitting will be held at 10 a.m. in the main courtroom, where Lowe will make the declaration required under article 9 of its Rules. The tribunal's Statute allows a party that has no judge of its nationality among its members to choose one for a specific case. Lowe, who held the Chichele Professorship of Public International Law at Oxford, is one of Britain's most prominent experts on the law of the sea.

The hearing on provisional measures in the case officially named the Case concerning hydrocarbon exploitation in the South-West Atlantic Ocean (Argentina v. United Kingdom) will take place on November 10 and 11. Argentina requested four measures on October 13, including that the United Kingdom prevent exploitation of the Sea Lion field and refrain from granting new permits. London has said it will take part and challenge any attempt to use the proceedings to settle sovereignty. The sittings will be public and broadcast live on the tribunal's website.

World.title: Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns
World.content:
Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns

2nd Monday, November 2026 - 00:57 UTC Full article

The expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the elections

Argentina’s case against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands “could fall at the first hurdle”: the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, which cannot settle territorial sovereignty disputes, according to Australian law of the sea expert Donald R. Rothwell. The tribunal will hold hearings on Argentina’s request on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg.

In an analysis published by The Interpreter, the Lowy Institute’s publication, Rothwell, professor of international law at the Australian National University, notes that under Article 286 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea the tribunal is only competent to settle disputes “concerning the interpretation or application” of the treaty. Territorial disputes have traditionally fallen to the International Court of Justice.

The problem, he argues, is that Argentina’s case cannot be separated from the underlying question. “If the UK has sovereignty over the islands, then Sea Lion is a legitimate act of exploration and exploitation of the continental shelf. If the Argentine claim over the islands is valid, then the UK’s conduct is in breach of UNCLOS,” he writes. Argentina alleges that the UK is illegally exploiting the continental shelf, that the project will cause environmental damage and that issuing licences aggravates the dispute over the maritime areas. “Absent the underlying territorial dispute, these would all be legitimate issues for ITLOS determination,” the expert says.

Rothwell compares the case with the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, in which the Philippines “neatly sidestepped” the question of sovereignty over disputed features and focused on China’s maritime claims, so there was never a need to determine who owned what. That, he warns, will not be possible in the case of the South Atlantic islands. Even so, he acknowledges that the tribunal “has generally been reluctant to take a narrow view of its jurisdiction” and recalls that, in the maritime boundary dispute between Mauritius and the Maldives around the Chagos Archipelago, it reached a full determination even though sovereignty between Mauritius and the UK was not fully resolved at the time.

The legal expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that President Javier Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the 2027 elections. He adds that US President Donald Trump could intervene, unhappy at the limited British support over Iran; Washington officially remains neutral in the dispute, although Trump has said that position is “under review”. “London will inevitably robustly defend its position on all fronts,” Rothwell predicts, adding that if the case proceeds it will be historic: the first time any aspect of the dispute has gone before an international court.

Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, lies about 200 kilometres north of the archipelago. Argentina bases its claim on succession to Spanish rights and on its occupation of the islands between 1820 and 1833, when they were taken by the United Kingdom; London cites its continuous presence since then and the islanders’ right to self-determination, confirmed in the 2013 referendum by 99.8% of voters.

World.title: Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 15:52 UTC Full article

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of France and Germany on Saturday to protest against the cost of living and deteriorating public services, in mostly peaceful demonstrations that ended in clashes between police and masked groups in several cities. In France, where the third day of protests in a month took place, 565 people were arrested.

According to France’s interior ministry, some 320,000 people took part in about 150 demonstrations across the country, down from an estimated 410,000 the previous weekend. In Paris, 70,000 marched along boulevards on the outskirts to avoid the city centre, some in Halloween costumes. The protests, called by students, trade unions and former members of the “yellow vest” movement, passed off calmly until the end, when masked groups hurled paving stones at police in Paris, who responded with teargas and baton charges. There were also incidents in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, where water cannon were used. Four police officers and a gendarme were injured in the capital. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who had deployed 70,000 officers, denounced an “extraordinary” level of violence and described a petrol bomb attack on a riot officer as “attempted murder”.

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living. The first major day, on October 17, ended with the looting of hundreds of shops in several cities. Students announced new blockades of high schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday, ahead of a trade union demonstration called for November 5.

In Germany, thousands of young people demonstrated in dozens of cities at the call of the group “Gen Z regelt!” (“Gen Z has got this”) “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life”. After largely peaceful marches, police used water cannon in Cologne against protesters throwing fireworks; in Frankfurt at least two shops were looted, according to a Reuters witness, and in Hamburg burning barricades were set up, according to the newspaper Bild.

There were also clashes in Tirana, the capital of Albania, at a new protest demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Police were on alert in Barcelona, over calls from an anonymous TikTok network, and in Italy, after recent clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

World.title: Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London
World.content:
Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension

Nearly a hundred Argentine intellectuals, jurists, historians and politicians have signed a declaration rejecting the transformation of the Falklands dispute into a “national cause” that “admits no dissent”, and criticising Javier Milei’s government for acting with “flagrant opportunism” amid escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

The declaration, entitled “Malvinas and dissent” and published in early October in the newspaper Perfil, is signed by, among others, jurist Roberto Gargarella, constitutional lawyer Daniel Sabsay, former justice minister Ricardo Gil Lavedra, former minister Graciela Fernández Meijide, economist Pablo Gerchunoff, writer Santiago Kovadloff and historians Luis Alberto Romero, Hilda Sabato and Federico Lorenz.

The signatories do not deny the dispute. They accept “the existence of this international disagreement”, with its “diplomatic and legal” dimensions, and acknowledge differing views among themselves, for example on whether the islanders should take part in any negotiations. But they warn that the issue “long ago ceased to be essentially a dispute and became a supposed national cause” that “admits no relevant dissent” and brands anyone who strays from it a “bad Argentine”. “The national cause is, in short, an abuse of state, political, social and cultural authority,” they argue. They particularly criticise Article 111 of the sovereignty defence bill, which in their view established “a vague criminal offence and the criminalisation of dissent”; the government acknowledged in mid-October that it would have to be removed. “On Malvinas, this is all we ask: that unanimity stop speaking in our name,” they conclude.

One of the signatories, Alejandro Cowes, who describes himself as a lawyer, went further in a text posted on Saturday in English and Spanish in a public Facebook group about the islands. Cowes accuses the government of using the “sacred national cause” as “a tool for internal state coercion and domestic political consumption” and revives Argentine political scientist Carlos Escudé’s thesis of the “malignant lie”: the idea that a tough policy will raise Britain’s costs, when to do so Argentina would have to multiply its own against a power with far greater resources. He criticises the sanctions on companies linked to hydrocarbon exploitation and the purchase of F-16 fighters, and concludes that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have “the inalienable right to self-determination”, a position not reflected in the collective declaration.

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension. The sovereignty defence bill secured committee approval on October 27, after sanctions were narrowed in response to US objections, and the ruling party plans to debate it in the Chamber of Deputies on November 12. Two days earlier, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will hold the hearing in Hamburg on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. Milei has reiterated that “the Malvinas are Argentine”, while ruling out “military solutions”.

The claim to sovereignty over the islands is enshrined in a transitional provision of Argentina’s Constitution and enjoys broad public support, as the declaration itself acknowledges.

World.title: A new road opens in Cancún, better connecting the airport with the hotel zone
World.content:
With an inauguration ceremony led by Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama, the Kukulcán Interchange opened to traffic at 6 a.m. Sunday, cutting travel time between the Cancún International Airport, the Nichupté Bridge and the hotel zone.

The new federal government-led improvement follows the opening of the 11.2-kilometer Nichupté Bridge in May. The bridge, which consists of three lanes and a two-way bike path, connects the city’s residential area to its hotel zone, cutting commuting time by up to 50 minutes. It is thought to handle around 12,000 vehicles a day.

The new connector allows vehicles traveling on Kukulcán Boulevard toward the airport to use an elevated one-way road, while those heading to downtown Cancún can use it to merge onto the Nichupté Bridge.

Traffic heading from the airport to the city’s bustling Punta Cancún area will be directed to a one-way street behind Plaza Kukulcán, while traffic from the Nichupté Bridge to the airport will continue along Kukulcán Boulevard.

The U-turn next to La Joya Hospital will remain closed to general traffic, with access only for local vehicles.

During the opening ceremony, Lezama emphasized that the new road project complements the Nichupté Bridge project and stressed that an opposite lane of the interchange is expected to open in the coming weeks.

President Claudia Sheinbaum has supported the city road project throughout, following in the footsteps of her predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who approved the development of the Nichupté Bridge.

“We secured it; you never hesitated; you always said yes,” Lezama said in reference to President Sheinbaum’s support of the Kukulcán Interchange project.

With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and Excelsior

World.title: Ex-TV host wanted in Mexico for fraud arrested by ICE; she and husband face same charges
World.content:
Inés Gómez Mont — a former Mexican television host who is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement — is in immigration detention in the United States after she was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Miami, Florida, on Friday.

According to ICE, Gómez Mont, a former telenovela actress who became an entertainment show presenter, is being held at the Broward Transitional Center, located in Pompano Beach, Florida. Although she is wanted in Mexico, she was arrested for overstaying her U.S. visa, according to media reports.

La #FGRinforma que, derivado del intercambio de información con el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos de América, este día, en Miami, Florida, fue asegurada Inés “N”, quien cuenta con una orden de aprehensión vigente en nuestro país, por su probable participación en el delito de defraudación fiscal equiparada. Más adelante, daremos mayor información — FGR México (@FGRMexico) October 30, 2026

The Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) acknowledged Gómez Mont’s arrest in a social media post on Friday.

“The FGR informs that, as a result of the exchange of information with the Government of the United States of America, Inés “N” was apprehended today in Miami, Florida,” the FGR said, adding that Gómez Mont is the subject of a valid arrest warrant in Mexico “for her probable participation in the crime of tax fraud.”

Gómez Mont is also wanted on money laundering and organized crime charges.

The charges are related to Gómez Mont’s alleged participation in a shell company scheme aimed at evading taxes, embezzling public money and laundering ill-gotten funds.

The former TV presenter’s husband, Víctor Manuel Álvarez Puga, allegedly led the scheme.

The newspaper Reforma reported that he and Gómez Mont allegedly received 17 million pesos (US $915,000) through a scheme that diverted funds from prison construction contracts. The couple is accused of involvement in an alleged embezzlement scheme linked to Interior Ministry prison contracts worth 2.95 billion pesos (US $159 million).

Álvarez Puga, a lawyer and native of the southern Mexican state of Chiapas, was arrested by ICE in September 2025 over alleged immigration violations. However, he was subsequently released pending further immigration proceedings.

Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga have been subject to arrest warrants in Mexico since 2021. The FGR is seeking the extradition of both suspects, who have lived in Florida for years.

Reforma reported that the U.S. Department of Justice hasn’t begun the required legal proceedings to extradite the couple more than a year after Mexican authorities requested their transfer to Mexico.

Since 2021, Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga were each the subject of an Interpol Red Notice — a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action — but President Claudia Sheinbaum said in September that Interpol had withdrawn the notices. She said Mexican authorities would seek their reinstatement.

Sheinbaum described Gómez Mont and Álvarez Puga as “well-known factureros,” or issuers of fraudulent invoices.

Gómez Mont seeks release from immigration detention

On Saturday, lawyers for Gómez Mont filed a habeas corpus petition seeking her release from immigration detention. They also filed an emergency motion aimed at preventing her transfer to another immigration detention center.

Federal Judge Jeffrey Kuntz ordered ICE and other authorities to justify the need to keep Gómez Mont in detention. He ruled that they must do so by this Wednesday. Kuntz denied the request aimed at preventing Gómez Mont’s transfer to another immigration detention facility, saying that he lacked the authority to block such a move.

Reforma reported that Gómez Mont’s habeas corpus petition includes reports about the medical care required by one of her daughters. The purpose of including those reports, Reforma reported, was to justify the need to keep her in the Miami area and to release her from detention while her immigration status is assessed.

Álvarez Puga was released from immigration detention after his lawyers presented a habeas corpus petition in late 2025. He is scheduled to appear before a U.S. immigration judge this month. It remains to be seen whether Gómez Mont’s case will follow a similar path.

With reports from Reforma, El Financiero, La Jornada and EFE

World.title: Mexican-American news executive assumes top Vatican role
World.content:
A 39-year-old woman born in Mexico City and raised in the United States has become the Vatican’s new communications chief — the first laywoman to lead a ministry-level department in the church’s central administration.

María Montserrat Alvarado, whose appointment took effect Sunday, previously served as president and chief operating officer of EWTN News, the news division of the largest Catholic television network in the United States.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Archbishop Nelson Perez (@archbishopperez)

She succeeds Italian journalist Paolo Ruffini, 70, as prefect of the Dicastery for Communication.

Pope Leo XIV, hailed by Mexico when he was elected, announced her appointment in June.

Alvarado takes over an operation encompassing Vatican News, Vatican Radio, the newspaper L’Osservatore Romano and the Holy See Press Office, along with publishing, television, photography and other services.

“It’s enormous,” she told EWTN News.

Alvarado, who goes by the nickname Montse, said she was about 7 or 8 when her family moved from Mexico to the United States. She grew up in Miami and holds Mexican and U.S. citizenship, according to AFP.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in political science from Florida International University, she moved to Washington, D.C., to study for a master’s in political management from George Washington University.

In 2009, she joined the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a Washington-based nonprofit law firm that handles religious freedom cases. She started in communications and rose to vice president and executive director in 2017.

Her work included advocating for Becket’s clients in the media, including Univision, Telemundo, CNN en Español and EWTN (Eternal Word Television Network).

In 2021, she joined EWTN as the founding host of “EWTN News In Depth,” a weekly program. Two years later, she was named president and chief operating officer of EWTN News, overseeing its global, multilingual news operations across television, radio, print, digital platforms and social media — work that brought her into direct contact with Pope Leo XIV and Vatican officials.

She helped prepare the Pope’s live video conversation with young people attending a National Catholic Youth Conference in Indianapolis last year, and also worked with the Vatican on a video introducing the Pope’s first encyclical.

Leo later approached her about leading the department, she said. Though she had not applied, Alvarado said she believed Leo wanted a professional equipped to bridge traditional and digital communications.

“In no way am I imposing a vision,” she said. “I’m very much receiving one and executing it.”

Her appointment comes after years of friction between the conservative Catholic network and Pope Francis. Some EWTN programs criticized Francis, who publicly complained about an unnamed Catholic television network’s attacks on him.

Former Francis collaborators told BBC Mundo that tensions had largely eased after Alvarado took charge of the news operation.

Alvarado is not the first Mexican or woman to lead a Vatican department. Mexican Cardinal Javier Lozano Barragán headed its health care department from 1996 to 2009, and Italian Sister Simona Brambilla has overseen religious orders since January 2025.

With reports from N+, Uno TV, BBC and EWTN News

World.title: Record crowd greets Checo Pérez at Mexico City Grand Prix
World.content:
The return of Mexican driver Sergio “Checo” Pérez to Formula 1 with Cadillac electrified the grandstands at Mexico City’s Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez this past weekend, where the three-day Grand Prix drew a record-breaking 405,363 fans.

According to official reports, attendance surpassed the previous record — set in 2024 with 404,958 — by 405 admissions. It also eclipsed the 401,326-person attendance seen at the 2025 Mexico City Grand Prix, at which Pérez was absent following his departure from Red Bull.

Fans’ enthusiasm began to take shape during the lead-up activities, including Checo’s Show Run along Reforma Avenue on Oct. 28, which drew over 100,000 people.

On the grandstands, Friday saw 102,122 attendees for the practice sessions; Saturday brought in 147,889 for qualifying; and Sunday drew 155,352 spectators for the race.

Pérez marked his 300th Grand Prix with a flying start, but trouble in the pits and a penalty hindered his chances of staging a comeback. After starting in 20th position on the grid, he gained six places during the opening laps, reaching as high as 13th position, but a slow pit stop around lap 32 and a 5-second pit-lane speeding penalty dropped him to 19th.

After Valtteri Bottas’s crash brought out a red flag, Pérez climbed to 14th, but he slipped back to cross the line in 17th position. However, following a 10-second penalty handed to Pierre Gasly for speeding under a yellow flag, he moved up to 16th — though still outside the points. Checo’s former Red Bull teammate Max Verstappen came in first, while 20-year-old Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli finished third, becoming the youngest-ever champion of the F1 season.

Checo acknowledged that Cadillac’s problems during pit stops hindered his participation in the race, especially after having gained several positions after the start.

“We had a very good initial start, but then we had a very bad pit stop — the right-side wheel gun broke down and we lost 4 or 5 seconds — which meant we effectively lost the positions we had gained over the other drivers at the start,” Pérez said after the race.

However, he noted that racing in Mexico City again “was a very special moment.”

“I really missed it last year,” Pérez added.

With reports from El Financiero and Telediario

World.title: Medical tourism lifts Mexico’s Caribbean coast as beach tourism falls 7%
World.content:
While overall tourism in the state of Quintana Roo has contracted this year, medical tourism has demonstrated remarkable resilience, according to data from the Medical Tourism Commission of Coparmex Quintana Roo.

Traditional sun-and-beach tourism has declined almost 7% during the first nine months of 2026 — representing approximately 959,000 fewer travelers — whereas 25,000 healthcare tourists are expected to travel to the Caribbean state this year, generating an estimated economic impact of 200 million pesos (US $10.76 million).

Andrés Jurado Viera, director of the specialty firm My Medical Vacations and president of the Medical Tourism Commission, explained that these visitors are not drawn by the beaches, so problems like sargassum do not affect their travel decisions.

“Their main objective is to access high-quality healthcare treatment at competitive prices, as well as first-rate hospital infrastructure and top-quality medical staff,” he said.

Jurado said the average cost per patient rose from US $11,000 to $13,500 in the last year, a 20% increase due to the exchange rate, but one that still represents savings of up to 80% compared to costs in the United States.

When the trend began 16 years ago, medical tourism focused on plastic surgery and dentistry. Today it encompasses more complex procedures thanks to positive reports of hospital experiences in Cancún.

A Commission report found that the visitor profile stands out for its socioeconomic impact. Visitors register average stays of 11 days or more, which generates higher hotel occupancy and boosts sectors such as gastronomy and transportation.

As a result of sustained demand in this sector (following a decade of double-digit growth), the commission will participate in the first joint working group meeting involving the state Tourism Ministry, the Hotel Association and airport representatives will be held this month to promote the destination in strategic markets in North America and Mexico.

This medical tourism has also triggered hospital investment in the region — both foreign and domestic — as new clinics are being built (including a Wyndham Group medical center in the Riviera Maya), international certifications have been procured and diversification of specialties has noticeably increased.

The United States remains the leading source of patients; Canada saw a slight decrease due to the exchange rate against the dollar.

With reports from Animal Político and El Economista

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: How the water crisis is affecting local businesses, fewer dengue cases and a new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal
World.content:
This past week, business leaders and government officials sparred over whether the ongoing water crisis in the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA) will affect business investment in Jalisco, so we looked at the facts.

Meanwhile, as the rainy season winds down, dengue cases have fallen sharply across the state compared to 2025, and a new “Hecho en Jalisco” (“Made in Jalisco”) seal aims to boost the visibility and cachet of select local products.

Business leader warns investment will suffer due to water quality issues

Speaking to local journalists on Oct. 23, José Medina Mora, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), issued a stark warning to Jalisco state officials.

Medina Mora said he expects investment projects in Jalisco to be negatively impacted by Guadalajara’s ongoing water crisis, noting, “There will be investment decisions in Jalisco, and in Guadalajara particularly, that will be halted until we can offer quality water.”

Medina Mora also blamed local politicians for their failure to anticipate and solve these issues before they became acute.

Later clarifying his comments, Medina Mora said the CCE does not expect the water crisis to spark capital flight from Jalisco but expects new investments to be put on hold due to the increased business risk posed by water contamination.

State and federal government officials swiftly pushed back on Medina Mora’s comments.

Government points to strong FDI as local businesses adapt

Ximena Escobedo Juárez, undersecretary of industry at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce of the Ministry of Economy, cited strong business investment across Jalisco in 2026 as evidence that the business community remains undeterred.

In the first half of 2026, Jalisco attracted US $1.41 billion in new capital, surpassing the US $1.2 billion invested in the state for all of 2025. This contrasts with a sharp decline in foreign direct investment in Mexico’s first half overall.

Yet some economic disruption is undeniable.

With municipal water supplies being rationed over the next six months, many local businesses are scrambling to arrange deliveries from private water trucks to avoid major disruptions to area restaurants, hotels, hospitals and other local service providers.

In addition, manufacturers around Guadalajara have reportedly been supplementing operations with more sophisticated filtration protocols, including on-site chlorination systems, sediment micro-filters and reverse osmosis units. These enhancements are needed to remove heavy metals, sediment and fecal matter from the municipal water that enters their facilities and keep contaminated water from damaging their industrial equipment.

Rainy season ebbs with dengue cases in Jalisco down by 90%

Through Oct. 11, Jalisco has 242 confirmed dengue cases in 2026, ranking 12th nationwide. This represents a massive improvement over 2025, when Jalisco ranked third nationwide for dengue, behind Sonora and Veracruz.

Year to date, there have been two confirmed deaths, with five more under investigation. Last year, the state recorded 10 dengue deaths.

Dengue cases in Jalisco

Year Confirmed Cases Percent change, year over year 2023 941 N/A 2024 20,907 2,122% 2025 2,317 -89% 2026 (through Oct. 11) 242 -90%

Source: Secretaría de Salud

Some strains of dengue are more virulent than others. One of the serotypes that is spreading in Jalisco right now is the most virulent form (serotype 2), which causes dengue hemorrhagic fever. Year to date, both serotypes 2 and 3 of the virus are circulating in Jalisco.

It is a mistake to think that most people get infected with dengue in remote, jungle areas. Rapid urbanization and increased population density have created conditions ideal for mosquito breeding and infection.

Yordi Raúl Portillo Montes, who heads Jalisco’s National Public Health Service, noted that the highest incidence of dengue in the state has occurred in Cocula and Teuchitlán, with coastal areas, including Puerto Vallarta, also at high risk. In the GMA, central Guadalajara, Tonalá and Tlaquepaque have recorded the most cases this year.

While dengue is less common outside of the rainy season, the risk does not fall to zero.

Due to the water crisis affecting Guadalajara, hundreds of families have resorted to storing water in buckets, drums or other containers, which has increased dengue risk in urban areas. In response, health authorities have reiterated the importance of covering these containers to discourage mosquito breeding.

While there is a vaccine for dengue, it can be difficult to access in Mexico, so your best bet is to be proactive and avoid infection.

The new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal aims to promote and protect local products

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Desarrollo Económico Jalisco (@sedeco.jalisco)

In a bid to strengthen the marketing of products made in the state, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) recently announced the launch of the “Made in Jalisco” seal.

The initiative aims to increase visibility for Jalisco-made products with protected designations in foreign markets while ensuring that the economic benefits flow through to local communities where they are made.

The new seal is expected to recognize at least 40 businesses that make products with a designation of origin or geographical indication. Participation will be free, and eligible businesses include companies, cooperatives, workshops and individual producers of tequila, raicilla, Yahualica chili or Sayula cajeta that have authorization from the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI).

However, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) and the civil association El Telar will decide which products are eligible to display the new seal. Applicants will be judged on their history and roots in Jalisco, their products’ distinctive qualities, organizational preparedness and desire for designation of origin protection.

According to state figures, the tequila supply chain supports more than 100,000 families, while raicilla involves more than 80 artisanal producers. Yahualica chili peppers are cultivated by roughly 250 small farmers and collectives, and Sayula cajeta is produced in 21 family workshops.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: More than 2,000 join Uruapan mayor in march for peace and justice in Michoacán
World.content:
Listen to this article

Uruapan Mayor Grecia Quiroz led a “justice and peace” march in Uruapan on Sunday to mark the first anniversary of the assassination of her partner, Mayor Carlos Manzo.

Manzo, an outspoken, tough-on-crime mayor, was killed on Nov. 1, 2025, during a Day of the Dead event in Uruapan’s main square. The person who shot Manzo was a 17-year-old boy who was killed by a municipal police officer after he was detained.

More than 30 people — including seven of Manzo’s bodyguards — have been arrested in connection with the assassination, which was allegedly masterminded by Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala (aka “R1”), alleged leader of a criminal cell affiliated with the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

On Sunday, around 2,500 people accompanied Quiroz — who had two children with Manzo — during the “March for Justice and Peace.”

The march set off from the Monument to General Lázaro Cárdenas in Uruapan, the second largest city in the state of Michoacán, and concluded at Plaza Morelos, the square where Manzo was assassinated. A statue of the murdered mayor was unveiled in the square at the end of Sunday’s march.

Quiroz, who succeeded her partner as mayor just days after he was murdered, wore a T-shirt featuring Manzo’s image during Sunday’s march. Some marchers wore sombreros like those the slain mayor used to wear.

Quiroz called on President Claudia Sheinbaum to ensure that an “exhaustive” and “independent” investigation into Manzo’s assassination takes place. The Michoacán Attorney General’s Office is conducting the now one-year-old probe.

“I call for an exhaustive, independent, and transparent investigation, free from any constraints imposed by political or personal interests; I call for everyone — absolutely everyone — to be investigated, and if the evidence points to individuals with political, economic or any other kind of power, the investigation must not be halted,” Quiroz said.

“I don’t want revenge. I’m not asking for anyone to be convicted without evidence. I’m asking for something that should be standard practice in any country governed by the rule of law: that the authorities investigate this matter thoroughly and that those found responsible be brought to justice,” she said.

“… Arresting someone does not necessarily mean that a crime has been solved, because an investigative file alone does not mean that a family has found justice,” Quiroz said.

Julia Lila, an aunt of Manzo, told reporters in Uruapan that the purpose of Sunday’s march was not just to honor the memory of her nephew and call for justice for his murder, but also to speak out on behalf of other victims of homicides and abductions.

Zayda Zuloaga, a resident of Uruapan who took part in the march, told the news outlet Expansión that she was confident that Mexico would one day have a government like that led by President Nayib Bukele in El Salvador. Manzo was nicknamed “The Mexican Bukele” because of his hardline stance against organized crime.

“I believe that God has a Bukele for Mexico,” Zuloaga said.

“In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, we declare that Grecia [Quiroz] is our Bukele. God will open the way so the entire nation changes, so that we, through Grecia, can have a government like that of Bukele,” she said.

Quiroz could run as a candidate for governor in next year’s state election in Michoacán, but she told the newspaper El Universal in a recent interview that she hasn’t yet decided if she will.

The federal government responded to the assassination of Manzo and general insecurity in Michoacán with “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice,” a 57-billion-peso (US $3.1 billion) initiative that has been credited with driving a significant decrease in homicides in the state this year.

Quiroz: ‘We can’t normalize violence’

In addition to marching through the streets of Uruapan, Quiroz marked the first anniversary of the assassination of her partner with a social media post titled, “The saddest first year of my life.”

EL PRIMER AÑO MÁS TRISTE DE MI VIDA 💔 “La última foto tuya Carlos con nuestro pequeño Plutarco como tú lo llamabas, recuerdo ese día y me duele hasta las entrañas, tu solo querías un mejor futuro para nuestros hijos y para todas las familias de México. Un año donde tu ausencia en casa se siente todos los días, en donde todos los días sigo esperando que entres por esa puerta como lo hacías gritando por toda la casa para que los niños te escucharan, un año dónde sigue habiendo una silla vacía a la hora de comer, un año en donde los recuerdos irrumpen en todos lados porque todo me recuerda a ti, extraño nuestras pláticas, extraño tus abrazos, tus besos, tu voz, extraño verte caminar por el centro con nuestros hijos, puedo decir que es lo más doloroso que he tenido que enfrentar en toda mi vida. Ese 1 de noviembre del 2025 quedaste en la historia de México Carlos Manzo, fuiste un hombre valiente, fuerte y entregado a tu gente, fuiste el mejor presidente que Uruapan haya tenido y estoy segura ibas a ser el mejor presidente de México. No podemos normalizar la violencia, no podemos normalizar que más alcaldes tengan que ser asesinados por querer hacer las cosas bien, no podemos seguir viviendo con miedo a que nuestros hijos sean desaparecidos, ya basta de tanta sangre derramada en nuestro querido Michoacán. Te seguiré honrando Carlos Manzo y seguiré de pie como muchas veces vi que tú lo hacías en medio de la adversidad solo te pido que nos cuides desde donde estás. Descansa en paz Amor de mi vida y recuerda: un día nos volveremos a encontrar y esta vez será para siempre 🕊️🤠❤️” GQ — Grecia Quiroz Michoacán 2027 (@GreciaMich2027) November 1, 2026

Above a photo of Manzo holding their young son in his arms shortly before he was killed, she wrote:

“The last photo of you, Carlos, with our little Plutarco as you called him. I remember that day and it hurts me to my core. You only wanted a better future for our children and for all the families of Mexico.”

Quiroz also wrote that she had felt Manzo’s “absence at home” every day during the past year.

“… Every day I still wait for you to walk through that door like you used to, shouting through the whole house so the kids could hear you. [It was] a year with an empty chair at mealtime, a year in which memories burst in everywhere because everything reminds me of you. I miss our talks, I miss your hugs, your kisses, your voice, I miss seeing you walk through the center [of town] with our children. I can say it’s the most painful thing I’ve ever had to face in my entire life,” she wrote.

“On November 1, 2025, you went down in Mexico’s history, Carlos Manzo. You were a brave, strong man, dedicated to your people. You were the best mayor Uruapan has ever had and I’m sure you were going to be the best president of Mexico,” Quiroz wrote.

“We cannot normalize violence; we cannot normalize more mayors having to be assassinated for wanting to do things right; we cannot keep living in fear that our children will be disappeared. Enough of so much blood spilled in our beloved Michoacán. I will continue honoring you, Carlos Manzo, and I will keep standing tall like I saw you do so many times in the face of adversity. I only ask that you watch over us from wherever you are. Rest in peace, love of my life and remember: one day we will meet again and this time it will be forever.”

With reports from La Jornada, Eje Central, Expansión and El Financiero

World.title: Bayern Munich hints at future Azteca match
World.content:
England captain and Bayern Munich star Harry Kane has fond memories of Estadio Banorte (formerly Azteca).

After all, he netted what turned out to be the game-winner in what was arguably the most entertaining match of the 2026 World Cup, a 3-2 victory over host Mexico. Now the German giants — one of the most important clubs in Europe — are reportedly considering playing a game in the iconic stadium in southern Mexico City.

In an interview with Fox Sports on Saturday, Rouven Kasper, marketing director of the Bavarian club, confirmed the institution’s interest in staging a match in Mexico.

“The connection with Mexico is special,” he said. “The league has gained ground on television there, and the arrival of more Mexican players in the future could accelerate a visit … to the country.”

Kasper said Mexico represents a significant link for the Bundesliga and the teams participating in it, while also recognizing that the addition of Mexican players to the league could be a key factor in strengthening ties with the Mexican market.

The last time a Mexican international toiled in the Bundesliga was during the 2018-2019 season when defender Carlos Salcedo and midfielder Marco Fabián played for Eintracht Frankfurt. Other notable Mexicans to play in Germany include “Chicharito” Hernández and Andrés Guardado (both with Bayer 04 Leverkusen).

A Bayern Munich appearance in Mexico would also boost the Bundesliga, which is intent on consolidating its presence in various international markets. Bringing its teams and players closer to Mexican fans would reinforce the interest generated by TV broadcasts and open new commercial opportunities, he acknowledged.

The team boasts a renowned international track record and a fanbase that extends far beyond Germany’s borders, so playing a match on Mexican soil could become an attractive event for European football fans.

A hypothetical Bayern Munich match at Estadio Azteca would represent the ideal scenario for the Ballon d’Or winner to retrace his steps on the pitch where he and his England mates experienced glory.

With reports from Excelsior and Infobae

World.title: US Midterms Shape Africa and Latin America
World.content:
US MIDTERMS · LATIN AMERICA · AFRICA

Updated Tuesday 3 November 2026
