World.title: Why financial empowerment is the UK’s next great economic opportunity
World.content:
Ask a 22-year-old and a 70-year-old in the UK today whether they use digital tools to manage their money, and the answer is increasingly the same: yes. Ask them whether they feel confident doing so, and you get two very different answers.

Financial empowerment is the term we use to refer to the knowledge, skills, tools and opportunities that allow an individual to take control of their financial life and improve their financial wellbeing over time.

Britain increasingly banks, budgets and borrows online — a shift made possible at scale by advances in digital technology and the data and analytics behind it. But how confident people feel doing it is the real story of financial empowerment in Britain right now, and it offers valuable insight for policymakers and industry alike.

Different lives, shared financial ambitions

For a decade, Lloyds Banking Group’s Consumer Digital Index has tracked how people across the UK engage with digital technology and the confidence they have in doing so. Its analysis shows that more than 75 percent of 18- to 24-year-olds have used artificial intelligence (AI) for personal finance in the past year — the highest adoption of any generation. Yet they’re also the least confident using the tools they’ve adopted: just 64 percent of 18- to 24-year-old digital tool users feel confident using them, rising steadily to 85 percent among 65- to 74-year-olds.

Britain increasingly banks, budgets and borrows online — a shift made possible at scale by advances in digital technology and the data and analytics behind it.

Look across the UK and the picture shifts again. According to the index, London is the UK’s AI finance capital — 49 percent of digitally engaged respondents use it weekly, reporting the nation’s highest average savings of £562 after following AI-powered recommendations.* Yet Londoners who use digital tools feel less confident doing so than anyone else in the country. Wales leads the UK on financial engagement and knowledge — how actively people manage their finances and how well they understand them — with the highest proportion nationally of those surveyed saying digital tools have helped them grow their pensions and investments. Yorkshire and the Humber leads on digital budgeting, and Northern Ireland shows some of the lowest adoption alongside some of the strongest outcomes among those who do engage.** How people use digital tools to manage their money across the UK is as varied as the lives, places and ambitions behind it.

These insights insist that financial empowerment should be a national priority. While people across different generations and in different places are engaging with digital money tools differently, the ambition is the same — to have confidence, capability and control over their financial future.

It can’t be enabled in the same ways to everyone. A 20-year-old in Croydon, a 45-year-old in Leeds juggling debt and family costs, and a 70-year-old in Cardiff drawing down a pension will need different things to feel confident in managing their money online.

While people across different generations and in different places are engaging with digital money tools differently, the ambition is the same — to have confidence, capability and control over their financial future.

But strip away the age and the postcode, and what people want is remarkably consistent: the confidence to decide, the capability to act, and the control to plan ahead without being derailed by the next bill.

That’s the common connection between a Gen Z Londoner testing an AI budgeting tool and a Boomer in Edinburgh checking her pension pot on an app before bed.

Financial access is only the starting point

The UK has made big steps toward building digital access — nearly nine in ten digital tool users across the UK (88 percent) now manage their money online weekly. That’s a real achievement, but access was never the finish line and cannot be taken for granted.

A second goal is to turn that access into outcomes, in ways that reflect how differently people actually experience money. That means building financial education into schools and workplaces earlier and closing the trust gap around AI-generated advice for the younger users adopting it fastest. Places with the least developed financial habits should be given support designed for their circumstances, not advice scaled down from somewhere else.

As the UK’s largest digital bank, with around 22 million customers now managing their money through our apps, we have as much reason as anyone to get this right — and a role to play in doing it. Our ambition is to make finance simpler, smarter and more connected for every moment that matters, which is why we’re using AI, data and digital tools in practical, purposeful ways to help customers make better financial decisions and protect themselves from harm. By using our reach, technology and connectivity, we can help more people and businesses build stronger financial futures and realise their ambitions.

Financial empowerment is a national economic opportunity

The size of the prize is substantial. Independent research commissioned by Lloyds Banking Group and led by the University of Nottingham puts the value of turning digital access into financial confidence at up to £100 billion for the UK economy over the next decade — roughly £3,500 per household.

Our ambition is to make finance simpler, smarter and more connected for every moment that matters, which is why we’re using AI, data and digital tools in practical, purposeful ways.

Confidence changes what people do with their money. Instead of just getting through the week, they start to plan, adapt and invest in what comes next. Multiply that across millions of households, and the effect stops being personal and starts being national.

Digital access got the UK this far. Confidence, capability and control are what will get it the rest of the way — and building them should be a national priority.

Notes:

*Savings figures are self-reported estimates and are not verified against transactional data. They should be interpreted as perceived impacts rather than guaranteed outcomes.

**The Northern Ireland outcome findings are based on a small sample, n<100, and should be interpreted as indicative rather than statistically representative of the wider population.

World.title: Crisis over top court shapes Poland’s battle lines before 2027 election
World.content:
The clash comes to a head on Tuesday, when the eight judges backed by Tusk’s ruling parliamentary coalition plan to hold a meeting to approve the tribunal’s budget and consider disciplinary proceedings against its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański.

They need a quorum of 10 of the court’s 15 judges to be present — meaning they need to peel away at least two justices chosen under the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023.

The fight over the control of the tribunal is helping bring right-wing opposition parties together ahead of next year’s parliamentary election.

The crowd outside the tribunal protesting against Tusk’s government included PiS co-founder Jarosław Kaczyński alongside Grzegorz Braun, an extreme-right Polexit campaigner and antisemite whom Kaczyński had previously ruled out governing with. This time round, they took a selfie. Other right-wing leaders at the rally included former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki and libertarian Sławomir Mentzen.

“There are plenty of differences between our programs. But ending Prime Minister Tusk’s government is the fundamental common goal,” Anna Bryłka, vice president of Mentzen’s Confederation party, told POLITICO.

Tusk’s Civic Coalition leads POLITICO’s Poll of Polls, but its smaller partners might not make it into the next parliament, opening the way for PiS and other right-wing parties, provided their leaders are able to work together.

World.title: Why Europe shouldn’t celebrate a Democratic midterm victory
World.content:
“It would be a mistake for Europeans to assume there will be warmer transatlantic relations,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the veteran German diplomat and former chair of the Munich Security Conference. “My assumption is the exact opposite will happen.”

A recent EU-wide survey found 58 percent of respondents rooting for the Democrats, compared with just 18 percent for Donald Trump’s Republicans. But while opinion polls suggest the U.S. president’s European critics will get their wish, they’d better avoid any triumphalism or crowing, counsels Ischinger.

“There will be voices here in Europe, some important ones, who’ll want to celebrate and congratulate the Democrats, but I think that would be poisonous,” he told POLITICO.

“I’d advise my European friends to be restrained and avoid creating any pretext for the White House to be mad at Europe — that is any more than it already is,” he added with a chuckle.

Others are skeptical that reticence will make any difference. They include Nathalie Tocci, a former adviser to two EU foreign policy chiefs.

“To be honest, I don’t think Trump really needs any reasons or excuses to lash out at Europe,” she said. And it will be hard not to celebrate, she argued, if you “care about democracy,” given the ties between Trump’s MAGA movement and populist, far-right politicians in Europe.

World.title: Les lobbies du tabac mettent le paquet à Bruxelles, alors que l’UE se penche sur le secteur
World.content:
Philip Morris International, le fabricant des cigarettes Marlboro, dont le nombre de réunions est le plus élevé parmi toutes les entreprises du secteur du tabac, a souligné sa contribution à l’économie européenne et a indiqué qu’être “engagée dans une profonde transformation vers un avenir sans tabac”.

“Nous sommes fiers de contribuer au dialogue démocratique et de dialoguer avec tout député européen, quel que soit son groupe politique, qui soit disposé à discuter en s’appuyant sur la science et les faits, ainsi que sur notre détermination à faire partie de la solution”, a déclaré le groupe, qui commercialise également des sachets de nicotine, des cigarettes électroniques et des produits du tabac chauffés.

Débat sur les traités internationaux

L’une des craintes soulevées par Tilly Metz et d’autres députés européens est de savoir si les règles antitabac de l’OMS sont correctement respectées.

Sa Convention-cadre stipule que les politiques de santé publique doivent être protégées contre les intérêts commerciaux de l’industrie du tabac. Elle n’interdit pas le lobbying, mais les lignes directrices relatives à la mise en œuvre du traité précisent que les décideurs politiques doivent limiter leurs interactions avec ce secteur au strict nécessaire aux fins de sa réglementation, et garantir la transparence de ces réunions.

L’industrie affirme qu’elle respecte les règles et expose son point de vue en toute transparence. Elle invoque également un arrêt rendu en 2022 par la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne, selon lequel le traité n’interdit pas sa participation à la mise en œuvre de la lutte antitabac ; il “vise uniquement à empêcher que les politiques de lutte antitabac des parties à la convention ne soient influencées par les intérêts de cette industrie”.

Par ailleurs, le secteur fait valoir que la Convention-cadre de l’OMS ne couvre pas les produits à base de nicotine sans tabac. Ces produits sont particulièrement visés par un durcissement de la réglementation, alors que l’Europe s’apprête à revoir les règles relatives aux produits du tabac et à la publicité, ainsi que les taxes minimales au niveau du continent.

World.title: Streeting: Burnham is better than Blair at talking to the public
World.content:
Streeting — who has long been a pro-EU voice within his party — backed Burnham’s drive to reopen the conversation about membership.

He said the British public is “perfectly capable of engaging with complicated arguments, if they've got a political leader brave enough to have that conversation with them."

“And I do think … he is an extraordinary political communicator," the defense secretary said of Burnham. "And the way in which he has a conversation with the public is unlike anything I've seen before.

"Even Tony Blair, who was such a generational political leader with a gift for communication — he would confront the public with arguments — but I don't think even Tony Blair had Andy Burnham's conversational style, which the public warm to.”

Streeting reiterated that he is personally in favor of rejoining the EU: “My position on the EU was clear in 2016. It was clear when I had a tilt at the leadership, and I haven’t changed my view.”

However, he warned that renegotiating Britain’s relationship — including rejoining — would not be simple. “Leaving was a very complicated process, and rejoining would also be a very complicated process,” he added.

World.title: Spanish footballer Jesús de Miguel dies after collision with goalkeeper, club says
World.content:
Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel has died as a result of injuries he suffered in a sickening collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono in their second division match, his club announced on Tuesday.

 

"From CD Tenerife, we announce the tragic passing, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00 am, of Jesús de Miguel Alameda," the club said in a statement.

De Miguel was challenging for the ball in midfield during Monday’s match when he was struck in the chest by Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during the final minutes at Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López.

The 30-year-old player was taken to hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was suspended in the 108th minute.

Tenerife initially reported in a statement that he was “stable, despite the severity of his condition,” in the intensive care unit of the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz.

The club said in a statement that it was "heartbroken."

Since making his debut in 2015 with Leganés B, de Miguel played for eight other clubs in Spain, including Tenerife, where he arrived last year.

This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

World.title: Vivienne Jolie legally drops estranged dad Brad Pitt’s name
World.content:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie's 18-year-old daughter Vivienne has officially changed her surname and will now be known as Vivienne Jolie.

 

Vivienne filed the paperwork in Los Angeles County Superior Court on 12 July and she becomes the fifth of the former couple’s six children to no longer go by “Jolie-Pitt.”

It is not known whether Vivienne’s twin brother Knox has legally changed his surname, but he did publicly use the name “Knox Jolie” when he graduated from high school in June.

Shiloh, 20, was the first of the children to be granted a name change in 2024 - now going by the name Shiloh Jolie. In July this year, Maddox, 25, and Zahara, 21, also removed the actor’s surname from their names.

Pax Jolie-Pitt, 22, is the last of the children still using the double-barreled surname. He is reportedly the only one who remains in contact with Pitt’s family.

Angelina Jolie poses with her children Shiloh Jolie-Pitt, from left, Zahara Jolie-Pitt, Vivienne Jolie-Pitt, Maddox Jolie-Pitt and Knox Jolie-Pitt - 2021 AP Photo

Jolie, 51, and Pitt, 62, split in 2016 after more than a decade together.

The family divide is believed to have come following a 2016 airplane altercation in which Pitt allegedly got into a heated argument with his family. The Oscar winner allegedly was “verbally abusive” and “physical” with one of his kids.

Jolie filed for divorce the day after the incident, while an FBI investigation into child abuse allegations cleared Pitt of all charges.

The couple's divorce was finalized in December 2024.

World.title: Hungary is not blocking Ukraine's EU accession talks, Kyiv's ambassador insists
World.content:
Hungary has raised no new substantive objections to Ukraine's EU accession talks, Kyiv's new ambassador to the European Union, Taras Kachka, told Euronews, expressing confidence that the remaining two negotiating clusters could open before the end of the year.

 

In his first interview since taking up his new post Kachka spoke exclusively to Euronews' morning show Europe Today on Tuesday, a day before the European Commission publishes its latest enlargement assessment.

"I think that this word block misleads us," Kachka said when asked about Hungary's position, explaining that Budapest had requested additional time to examine the documents underpinning the next stage of negotiations.

His comments follow reports that Hungary withheld approval of the screening results for the remaining two clusters at EU Council working group meetings on October 20 and 27, despite lifting its objections to two other clusters earlier that month.

According to Kachka Hungary's government wants more time to examine the details.

Asked whether Budapest's position was still linked to minority education rights, a longstanding source of tension between the two countries, Kachka insisted that the issue had been resolved.

"There are no substantive requirements, disagreements or concerns," he said, describing the remaining delays as a matter of reviewing several hundred pages of documentation.

Ukraine amended its minority education legislation in October, paving the way for the opening of two additional negotiating clusters and bringing the total to four out of six.

Kachka confirmed that the amended rules were already being implemented in Ukrainian schools that issue was long sorted.

Ukraine sticks to 2027–28 accession timetable

Kachka also reaffirmed Kyiv's ambition to complete EU accession negotiations by 2027 or 2028, potentially sooner if domestic reforms progress faster than expected.

"I still stick to this 2027-2028 years as years of completion of negotiations and maybe even faster depending on how the situation will develop in Ukraine," he told Euronews.

He said Ukraine's sense of urgency differed from that of EU member states because of Russia's ongoing war, with daily attacks and fighting on the frontline adding pressure to accelerate the process.

Kachka acknowledged criticism over delays in adopting EU-related legislation in Ukraine's parliament but rejected suggestions of a deliberate slowdown, pointing to the difficulties of legislating during wartime, including parliamentary sessions interrupted by air raid alerts and Russian attacks on Kyiv.

Nevertheless, he said cooperation between the government and parliament has strengthened in recent weeks and expected the pace of reforms to accelerate.

"I see no challenges on substance," he said, adding that he hoped the Commission's enlargement assessment would confirm Ukraine's ability to adopt the necessary legislation by the end of 2027.

Kyiv rejects associate membership alternative

Kachka also reiterated Ukraine's rejection of associate EU membership as an alternative to full accession, even as similar arrangements have been discussed for countries such as Canada.

He argued that Ukraine, alongside Moldova, Montenegro and Albania, remained among the frontrunners for full membership.

"The EU sees us as a frontrunner, so that's why we don't need to shift to any alternatives," he said.

Kachka suggested that associate membership was better suited to countries seeking closer partnerships with the EU without intending to join the bloc.

He acknowledged, however, that proposals for closer cooperation before accession, particularly in defence, security and financial support, could be useful without replacing the objective of full membership.

Agriculture remains a major hurdle

Agriculture, one of the most sensitive areas of Ukraine's accession negotiations, would be among the most complex issues to resolve, Kachka acknowledged.

However, he rejected the need for lengthy transitional arrangements or broad restrictions on Ukrainian agricultural products entering the EU market.

"I believe that there are no necessity for any lengthy transitional period," he said.

While recognising that sensitive products such as wheat could require specific arrangements, Kachka argued that most agricultural goods should not face additional limitations.

He said consultations with EU member states and agricultural stakeholders were continuing, with Kyiv seeking to demonstrate that Ukraine's accession would strengthen the bloc's agricultural sector.

World.title: Child dies in New York’s first measles-linked death in over 30 years
World.content:
The New York State Department of Health and Lewis County Public Health announced the measles-related death on Monday, as a measles outbreak continues across the United States. That’s a fourth measles-related death this year, as the country battles its worst outbreak in decades.

 

There are 4,666 confirmed measles cases this year as of 30 October — roughly twice the total reported last year. New York reported 178 cases this year, covering the period up to 24 October.

Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency four weeks ago in response to the outbreak, enabling the expansion of the pool of healthcare professionals authorised to administer measles vaccines and facilitating access to additional resources.

State health officials said they were working with county authorities and local partners to provide vaccinations to unvaccinated people, while stepping up case monitoring and contact tracing.

“Measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious complications and death,” the joint statement said, adding that vaccination remained the best protection against the virus.

People can transmit the virus for around four days before the characteristic rash appears, meaning they may travel across borders before realising they are ill.

"We urge New Yorkers to ensure they are up to date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and speak to their healthcare provider about immunizations,” authorities said.

One dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine provides 93% protection against measles, while two doses provide 97%, according to the state health department.

The public health warning comes amid a wider debate over vaccination policy under the Trump administration.

In August, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order backing a recommendation to separate the combined MMR vaccine into three individual shots, rather than administering them together. The proposal drew criticism from health experts, who warned that requiring multiple appointments could create additional barriers to vaccination and increase the risk of children missing doses.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has also faced criticism over his comments questioning vaccine safety and promoting claims linking vaccines to autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal association between vaccines and autism.

Situation in Europe

The US is not the only country where measles continues to circulate. The biggest outbreaks currently are in Bangladesh, with cases surpassing 65,430, Indonesia with 46,578 and Guatemala with 31,222 cases.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews last week that the risk for Europeans remains moderate for infants under 12 months, children aged one to five and immunocompromised people. For older unvaccinated children and adults, the risk is estimated to range from low to moderate. People with immunity from vaccination or previous infection are considered to have a low risk of measles, as per its latest assessment.

In Europe, measles is endemic in twelve countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, France, Georgia, Germany, Italy, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Poland, Romania, Russia, Türkiye and Ukraine.

Romania reported most of the cases, with numbers reaching 30,692 in 2024, up from 3,371 in 2023.

Six European countries: Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan have re-established endemic measles transmission based on the number of cases in 2024 earlier this year.

World.title: Russia pounds Ukraine with 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles in overnight strikes, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Russia pounded Ukraine with overnight strikes, Ukrainian authorities said on Tuesday, as a flare-up in fighting dashed hopes of progress towards peace in the nearly five-year war.

 

The strikes rained down across the country, killing dozens of people, forcing patients to evacuate a medical facility and triggering a wave of ballistic missile alerts.

In Russia, Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said nearly 500 drones heading towards the capital region were destroyed.

The attacks followed a rare pause in the fighting between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson, which ended on Sunday.

The truce, which was the longest in the war that erupted in February 2022, enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

Hours after the local ceasefire ended, Russia targeted a village in Zaporizhzhia in southeastern Ukraine, killing at least 26 people, the acting regional governor said.

On Tuesday, authorities in Zaporizhzhia said Russian bombing had killed 29 people.

The result of air strikes across Ukraine as posted by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, 3 November, 2026 X/@ZelenskyyUa

The head of Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, Ivan Fedorov, accused Moscow of "striking people who had come to receive humanitarian aid".

In the northeastern city of Kharkiv, the regional military administration's head Oleg Synegubov said a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people, forcing around 200 patients to evacuate and damaging a building, windows and cars.

Ukraine's army warned of ballistic missiles heading towards Kharkiv and various other parts of the country, including the capital Kyiv, Dnipro and Sumy.

Dnipropetrovsk's regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said a Russian strike hit critical infrastructure in the Dnipro, as well as in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown Kryvy Rig.

Russia's defence ministry said on Tuesday it had carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine and port infrastructure in the Odesa region.

Ukraine's neighbour Poland said it activated air defences aimed at protecting its airspace, particularly in border areas.

Abu Dhabi talks

In a fresh push for diplomacy as the conflict grinds through its fifth year, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Tuesday that Washington-led talks between Russia and Ukraine were set to resume next week.

"The United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, advancing President Trump's mission to end the war," Wikoff wrote in a post on X.

President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the war but there has been no breakthrough.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy slammed the deadly Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia on Monday, which he said hit a school distributing humanitarian aid.

"There was a moment when the next steps (after the Oleshky truce) could have shown that progress toward peace was possible," he said.

The result of air strikes across Ukraine as posted by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, 3 November, 2026 X/@ZelenskyyUa

"With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings. There must be a response to this."

Acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram that two rescue workers and four police officers were among the dead.

Last week's ceasefire, which was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, enabled an evacuation of people in Russian-occupied Oleshky to both Ukraine-controlled territory and Moscow-annexed Crimea.

A senior Ukrainian figure told the AFP news agency on Sunday that Russia refused a Ukrainian offer to extend the truce.

Ukraine's military also alleged that Moscow had used the pause in fighting to "fortify its positions".

The Kremlin did not deny the accusations, with its spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters Monday: "This is a completely normal practice in such situations."

He alleged the Ukrainian army had also used pauses in fighting in the past to regroup.

Moscow saw the Oleshky humanitarian mission as "successful", Peskov added, praising the "good cooperation between all sides" and singling out the role of its human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova.

Lantratova oversaw the ceasefire alongside her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets in one of the most substantial instances of Russian-Ukrainian cooperation since the start of the war.

The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned "at the moment".

World.title: Top destinations and most bookings: Where did Europeans travel to in 2026?
World.content:
A new report has revealed which destinations European travellers booked trips to in 2026, with Spanish cities dominating the most popular holiday spots.

 

The “year in travel 2026” report by online travel agency eDreams ODIGEO analysed search and booking data for travellers across Germany, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, the UK and the USA to find the trends of 2026 and what might shape travel next year.

Globally, Barcelona, Madrid, Paris, Palma de Mallorca and London were the top five most booked destinations in 2026. Top searches in 2026 included Paris, London, Tokyo, New York City and Bangkok.

In terms of the top five growth destinations, travellers preferred “far-flung” places such as Durban (80%), Melbourne (57%), Cape Town (55%), Johannesburg (50%) and Sydney (48%).

This reveals an appetite for "Southern Hemisphere escapes that offer the best of many worlds: vibrant cities, access to stunning beaches and outdoor activities", the report said.

On the other hand, Paris, London, Tokyo, New York City and Bangkok are where travellers are setting their sights for next year in terms of bookings, while Tokyo, London, Paris, Orlando and Cancun are the top five searches for 2027 travel, according to the data.

“People’s appetite for travel is as strong as ever, and we expect 2027 to be another big year based on the early signs," Dana Dunne, CEO of eDreams ODIGEO, said.

New insights on preferred destinations for hotels

For the first time, eDreams' research also looked into hotel booking data. Globally, European destinations including Barcelona, Madrid, Paris, Rome and Amsterdam were the most popular globally in 2026 for choosing where to book a hotel specifically.

Cities like Cagliari in Italy, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania have also seen growth of 78%, 76% and 74% respectively.

“Travellers are also balancing European favourites with a growing interest in second and even third-city destinations that offer new cultural experiences,” eDreams said.

Travellers from the UK have strong appetites for shorter breaks of one to two days (68%) that are closer to home, with top hotel booking destinations like Barcelona, Amsterdam and Paris. Brits also love a staycation much closer to home, with growth destinations including Manchester (112%) and Belfast (56%).

Rome, Barcelona, Paris, London, Madrid, Battery Park in New York, Bangkok, Rio de Janeiro, Amsterdam and Sevilla remain “perennial favourites” among travellers, with 2027 bookings so far showing “strong interest in European city breaks”. Cultural immersion, food and adventure were among the main reasons cited for bookings.

Top booked destinations: Where Europeans travelled to in 2026

French travellers

For travellers from France, the top three booked destinations in 2026 featured Marrakech, Barcelona and Lisbon. Palma de Mallorca and Madrid, also featured on the list, alongside Porto, Tunisian island Djerba, and closer to home, Nice.

World.title: Collins English Dictionary reveals their 2026 Word of the Year: Do you know what 'Mogging' means?
World.content:
The Collins English Dictionary has announced a Word of the Year since 2013, a term selected by a team of lexicographers who look at "how often words are used" and who "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.

 

Following the likes of "permacrisis", "AI", "Brat" and last year's "vibe coding", we now have this year's pick: "Mogging".

The slang word is a popular term among Generation Z and Alpha, and means outperforming, outshining, or upstaging someone or something.

It went mainstream this year, with a 210 per cent increase in its usage.

Alex Beecroft, the managing director of Collins, said: “The selection of ‘mogging’ as Collins’ word of the year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language."

“It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and ‘mogging’ the rest of us.”

Mogging Collins

Like Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year "Maxxing", it has a darker side.

While "looksmaxxing" refers to efforts to optimise appearance, "mogging" implies more of a comparison, as it often refers to outclassing someone.

Where its sinister undertones surface is in its origins. "Mogging" can be traced back to the acronym AMOG, which stands for Alpha Male of the Group. In the past, it has been associated with bodybuilding forums as well as the manosphere - the toxic network of online websites, forums and social media accounts that promote aggressive masculinity and anti-feminism.

Nowadays, the new generations have moved the word on from its toxic subculture roots and usually employ it in a playful or teasing way.

For instance, if your friend says to you that you’re "mogging everyone in this room", you know you're doing something right at the party.

"Mogging" is listed by Collins as a noun but, like "maxxing", can be used as a suffix, with declinations including "stylemogging", "carmogging" and "lifemogging" - the latter meaning creating and leading a more impressive life compared to others.

It seems that no matter how ironically or playful the usage is, a sense of hierarchy still prevails...

"Mogging" saw off competition from other words such as “Manchesterism” (a term associated with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham), “carspreading” (which refers to automobile manufacturers increasing the length and width of vehicles), and “hydration break” - the latter having been made famous by this year's controversial World Cup.

Other runners up this year include "Ghost jobs", referring to vacancies that are advertised by employers who have no intention to fill them; “Bixie", a hairstyle that is shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut; and "P(doom)", an estimation of the probability that AI will bring about the collapse of human civilization.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy to make surprise Berlin visit this Tuesday, Merz says
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Ukrainian president is due to arrive in Germany around midday amid a renewed push for peace talks with Moscow.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would visit Berlin for talks on Tuesday.

The meeting comes as Kyiv seeks more missiles to defend against Russian ballistic strikes and asks European governments for an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) in funding next year.

Merz told Berlin's Chamber of Commerce and Industry that he expected to meet Zelenskyy around midday. The visit had been kept under wraps for security reasons.

What is on the agenda in Berlin?

Military and financial support is expected to be a focus of the talks. Ukraine needs more missiles for systems such as the US-made Patriot. Germany has already supplied the Patriot systems it says it can spare without weakening its own air defenses.

Zelenskyy set out Ukraine's funding needs at an EU summit in October. How to raise the money is expected to come up at future EU meetings as governments discuss the bloc's long-term budget.

Lavrov sets conditions for talks with Zelenskyy at G20 meeting To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin also plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine later this month to discuss further support ahead of winter.

How does the visit fit into the peace talks?

Shortly before Zelenskyy's expected arrival, US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced that advisers from Ukraine, Russia and the United States would meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 to discuss postwar security, steps to reduce tensions and humanitarian aid.

US envoys are due to discuss security guarantees and reconstruction with European and NATO representatives in Brussels this week. Berlin expects European representatives to be present in Abu Dhabi, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the negotiating table.

World.title: US midterm election: How it works, why it's important and races to watch
World.content:
US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.

On November 3, United States citizens will vote in the midterm elections. These won't decide who gets to sit in the White House; instead, Americans will be voting on who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power." If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

President Donald Trump's approval ratings have sunk to an all-time low: More than 60% of Americans view him negatively Image: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

Who are Americans electing in the midterms?

All the seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election. Its 435 members are elected by eligible voters across the country. Each member represents one electoral district. These are allocated based on population size. As a result, relatively large US states where few people live, such as Wyoming, have only one seat in the House of Representatives. New Jersey, a much smaller state by surface area but with a larger population, has 12. Representatives are elected for a two-year term of office.

US senators, on the other hand, are elected for a six-year term. The Senate, the other chamber of the US Congress, has 100 seats: two for each of the 50 US states, regardless of size. Around one third of these senatorial seats come up for election every two years. This year there are 35, meaning that not every state will be electing a senator in these midterms.

Separately, voters in 36 states will elect their governor, whose term of office is four years in most states. Many decisions in the US are taken at state level, on everything from abortion law to education and electoral procedure. It can therefore make a considerable difference to people's lives whether Democrats or Republicans are the ones making these decisions in their state.

Who currently has a majority in the US Congress?

At present, the Republicans, the party of President Trump, have a majority in both houses of Congress — but its margin is slim.

The House of Representatives currently has 218 Republican deputies, 214 Democrats, and one independent, who usually votes with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant. Observers think it likely that the Democrats will seize the majority in this chamber in the upcoming elections. "It would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House [of Representatives]," Coleman told the American broadcaster CBS at the end of October.

In the Senate there are currently 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independent senators who usually vote with the Democrats. When a vote in the Senate is deadlocked 50:50, the US vice president has the deciding vote. This means that currently, Trump's Vice President JD Vance would tip the scales if there were a tie in a Senate vote.

Republicans and Democrats are vying for seats in the two chambers of the US Congress Image: Graeme Sloan/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Why are the midterms so important?

Voter turnout is typically lower for midterms than for presidential elections, but the results will decisively influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.

It is therefore considerably easier for Trump to govern the country as he chooses if the Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress. If the Democrats win a majority in one or both chambers, it will be more difficult for him to make changes to either domestic or foreign policy.

Which races are crucial?

The Democrats only need to win four more seats in the House of Representatives to gain a majority. They would then have 218 representatives. Out of the 435 races, only a few are still considered toss-ups. These include districts in Iowa, Virginia and Montana.

One senatorial race to watch is the one in Texas. Current polls put Democrat James Talarico level with his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. The Democrats need four more seats in the Senate to win a majority. The possibility that Texas could be one of them is already a sensation. No Democrat has won here at state level since 1994. Talarico now even has the support of some members of the Bush family, the Texas Republican dynasty of former presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, his son.

Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the gubernatorial elections it is possible that, for the first time in US history, a Black woman could become state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the Black Republican Lisa DeMuth are vying for the position, while in Georgia the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against the Republican Rick Jackson.

DeMuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota: The state generally votes Democrat, and Klobuchar, who has been state senator there for almost two decades, is much better known than her rival. In Georgia, however, the latest polls suggest it's neck-and-neck. Bottoms has a realistic chance of winning.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany news: Ukraine in focus at Berlin Security Conference
World.content:
Markus Söder, the leader of Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and premier of the southern state, has said Europe should establish a free trade area with Arab countries.

On the sidelines of a visit to the United Arab Emirates, Söder, whose party is allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), said, "I believe that further free trade areas are needed to facilitate all the investments that can be made there."

He said other Arab countries other than the Emirates would also be interested.

In September, the Emirati head of state, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, announced investments worth up to tens of billions in Germany during a state visit, with €10 billion ($11.1 billion) intended for Bavaria.

Söder is to visit Qatar on Tuesday as part of his trip.

World.title: India news: Cyclone Murasu wreaks havoc after landfall
World.content:
11/03/2026 November 3, 2026 Indian Navy rescues crew members from hijacked Iranian ship

The Indian Navy coordinated a 48-hour operation and rescued 20 crew members from the Iranian fishing vessel Azini after it was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Somalia.

In response, the Indian Navy tasked a mission-deployed warship to intervene, supported by a maritime reconnaissance aircraft.

The vessel was seized by Somali pirates on October 29.

According to officials, the operation was carried out 3,000 km from Mumbai in the Arabian Sea.

"Executing a swift and well-coordinated tactical intervention, the Indian Navy secured the vessel, overcame the pirate threat and ensured the safe release of all 20 crew members," the Navy said.

Iran thanked the Indian government for rescuing the crew.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in New Delhi expresses its sincere appreciation to the Government of India, the Indian Navy and the Indian Air Force for their successful operation to rescue the 20 Iranian crew members of the fishing vessel Azini from pirates," the Iranian mission said in a post on social media.

World.title: North Korea denies role in record Binance hack, calls US charge 'provocation'
World.content:
Kim Yo Jong dismissed FBI claims that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, as the exchange began reopening withdrawals on more networks.

North Korea has hit back at US accusations that its hackers drained more than $6 billion (more than 5.36 billion euros) from cryptocurrency exchange Binance. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called the charge "a grave political provocation," according to state media agency KCNA.

Kim described the US claim as "absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”

What do we know about the hacking?

The accusation came from the FBI, which blamed a state-tied hacking group called TraderTraitor over the weekend.

This was reportedly the biggest crypto-exchange heist on record, well above the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit raid in 2025, which was also attributed to North Korean hackers. TRM Labs linked the attack to the same group and said it shifted most of the money out within 20 minutes, German news agency DPA reported.

Cryptocurrency giant Binance hit by $6.3 billion hack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video





Kim Yo Jong said Pyongyang now had "issues to reconsider" because of Washington's hostility.

North Korea has so far stayed silent on Trump's overtures about reviving summit talks. Analysts in Seoul told Reuters news agency the speed of the denial points to concern that Washington could step up efforts to cut off a funding source widely believed to bankroll arms development.

Is Binance working again?

Separately, Binance announced Monday that withdrawals will restart for additional assets across several blockchains, among them Binance Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP and Sui, from 04:00 GMT Tuesday.

Selected tokens on Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base are part of the same rollout.

Binance said it replaced most of the stolen assets out of its own funds.

World.title: US: Trump labels Democrats 'dangerous' ahead of midterms
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said the Democrats nominated "the most extreme and dangerous" candidates in US history in the midterms. He also lowered expectations by saying a sitting president "doesn't win" the midterms.

US President Donald Trump labeled the upcoming midterm elections as the most important "in our lifetime."

Trump seemed to lower his supporters' expectations on Monday, saying that an incumbent president "doesn't win the midterms," while also adding that his Republican party "gave this a very strong shot."

"Usually, whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president. For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms," Trump said.

According to the US president, the Democrats nominated "the most extreme and dangerous" list of candidates in the country's history.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, responded to Trump's accusation by calling his last message ahead of the midterms "pathetic."

"Donald Trump's pathetic closing message as his illegal war rages, his corruption mounts, and the inflation he caused persists," Schumer posted on his X account.

Trump's last-minute attempt to block 20,000 California ballots was rejected by the US Supreme Court.

Trump spoke in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he also discussed rusty pipes and algae extensively. Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

US carries out Iran attack: report

Ahead of the midterms, the US carried out a strike at Iran's Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing US sources.

The US Central Command did not officially confirm the attack.

This comes despite the Trump administration voicing optimism that the talks with Iran could lead to progress on ending the war between the two countries.

Vice President JD Vance earlier said that the goal remains to prevent Iran from securing nuclear weapons.

"We do think that there is a pathway there, but it really does require a firm commitment and a verifiable commitment that they don’t rebuild that nuclear program," Vance said, also labeling the US' conversations with Iran "good."

Referendum on acting president

This comes as voters are set to decide control of Congress for the rest of Trump's term as president on November 3.

Millions of voters will head to the polls, with surging costs of living and energy prices as a result of the Trump-led war in Iran taking center stage.

Trump said he hoped that voters would realize the risks of Iran having nuclear weapons heading to the polls.

"If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way," he argued.

Oil prices dropped significantly as the US and Iran renewed the talks over ending the war between the two countries.

The midterms are largely seen as a referendum on the current US president's policies.

The Democrats are expected to retake the House of Representatives from the Republicans' control, but the fight for the Senate is considered to be close.

The election's outcome is bound to influence both parties' strategies going ahead to the 2028 presidential election.

World.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block 20,000 California ballots
World.content:
The Trump administration had appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens.

On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump made a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail-in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.

The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, has claimed to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls.

In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations, which was rejected by a California district court.

On Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.

However, hours after the appeal was filed, the Supreme Court said it would decline to stop California from counting the votes.

When the initial lawsuit was filed by the Trump administration earlier in October, Los Angeles District Judge David Carter had warned that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.

"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote in rejecting the initial suit.

Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.

Battle for US midterm elections heats up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.

Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.

Trump's fixation on voter fraud

Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.

For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.

The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.

California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.

World.title: Ukraine: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center
World.content:
Skip next section Zaporizhzhia: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center

At least 26 people were killed and five more injured on Monday when the Russian air force launched repeated strikes on a school which was functioning as an aid distribution center in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia.

The multiple attacks, in which Russian planes reportedly launched more than 10 glide bombs, took place in the village of Komyshuvakha, about 35 kilometers (31 miles) east of the city of Zaporizhzhia and a dozen kilometers away from the frontline.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attacks as "utterly horrific" and accused Russia of being well aware of the humanitarian purpose of the site.

"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on social media.

"The Russians could not have been unaware that every week, local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid at that very location."

Ukrainian emergency services said two ‌members of ⁠a ⁠rescue crew were among the dead after falling victim to the so-called "double-tap" strike in which a location is targeted again with the aim of hitting first responders.

The attacks came less than 24 hours after a localized six-day humanitarian ceasefire in and around the town of Oleshky in the neighboring region of Kherson had expired.

Zelenskyy said the temporary truce could potentially have led to further steps toward a possible deal to end the ongoing Russian invasion, but said after Monday's strikes:

"This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of ​de-escalation or any real justice... With these killings, Russia has sent a completely opposite signal; Russia is counting on further killings."

The Zaporizhzhia region has been targeted repeatedly for months by heavy Russian airstrikes.

World.title: Puente se enfrenta a su comparecencia clave con un plan de medidas para reforzar la seguridad de los trenes
World.content:
El Gobierno tiene este martes jornada política decisiva para ver cómo es capaz de gestionar la grave crisis de credibilidad provocada por el segundo accidente mortal en nueve meses en la alta velocidad española. Óscar Puente, el ministro de Transportes, presentará por la mañana en el Consejo de Ministros un paquete de medidas con dos patas: una, la de las ayudas a las víctimas, que ya apuntó Pedro Sánchez este martes en su intervención en el foro World in Progress (WIP) organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Barcelona, y otra, la de las mejoras en seguridad.

Puente ha estado todo el fin de semana trabajando en estas reformas con su equipo, en especial con el presidente de Adif, el ingeniero de Caminos Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña, también con apoyo del Gabinete del presidente del Gobierno. Según diversas fuentes, no será una revolución, pero sí habrá cambios importantes en protocolos, para garantizar que nunca pueda repetirse una confusión como la que llevó al accidente de Urda (Toledo), en la que el tren que iba detrás recibió la orden de arrancar “a marcha normal”, esto a 200 kilómetros por hora, cuando tenía delante otro tren detenido, y sea absolutamente obligatoria la “marcha a la vista”, a un máximo de 40 kilómetros por hora. Pero las medidas también incluyen cambios en recursos humanos, con más personas para vigilar los trenes y mejores condiciones para los que trabajan ahora, que se quejan de saturación. Además, habrá innovaciones técnicas también para ofrecer más garantías.

01:29 Sánchez: “Debemos recuperar la confianza en la alta velocidad" Sánchez, este lunes durante su intervención en el foro WIP organizado por el Grupo Prisa en Barcelona. Foto: [ALBERT GARCIA] EL PAIS | Vídeo: EPV

Sobre la cuestión de la limitación a 40 kilómetros por hora cuando se cae el sistema de seguridad LZB en la línea Madrid-Sevilla, el personal jurídico de Adif y del Ministerio de Transportes es de la opinión de que “sí se puede articular de inmediato en forma de instrucción interna entre Adif y las tres operadoras que explotan la alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla”, argumenta un técnico al tanto de los detalles. Ese mandato, en el que también ha estado inmersa Renfe, es más restrictivo que el propio reglamento ferroviario.

Una segunda decisión es analizar y mejorar las condiciones de trabajo en la veintena de centros de regulación y control del tráfico de Adif, cuatro de ellos para la red de alta velocidad. Se incidirá en elevar los tiempos de descanso o en reducir y separar los turnos de noche. De forma paralela, Transportes va a ordenar refuerzos en esos puntos de seguimiento y conexión con los trenes, lo que llevará más tiempo, a la vista de que ha de realizar una oferta de empleo público, formar al personal y habilitarlo.

Otra de las reformas en la lista, anoche aún bajo estudio, se refiere a la infraestructura e incidiría en reforzar el balizamiento en el trazado Madrid-Sevilla para reducir la longitud de los cantones (segmento de vía entre señales) cuando se pierde el sistema de seguridad LZB y entra en juego el ASFA. Acortar la distancia de esos segmentos de vía, a través de mayor densidad de señalización, puede elevar las garantías de separación entre convoyes con pérdida del LZB.

Con el sistema ERTMS ya instalado en la Madrid-Sevilla, también se va a tratar de acelerar su activación, prevista para el inicio de 2027. Los trabajos de implantación se han llevado cinco años por parte de Hitachi Rail y las pruebas se efectúan en franjas de mantenimiento nocturno los fines de semana. Un ritmo que pretende elevarse.

En Adif se ha estudiado durante el fin de semana incluso la opción de instalar cinturones de seguridad, remedio menos claro como garantía de la seguridad de los viajeros y que tampoco se usa en otros países: “¿Qué pasaría en caso de colisión o frenazo a más de 250 kilómetros por hora con los viajeros anclados por cinturones de tela?”, se pregunta una de las fuentes consultadas. Este asunto ha sido materia de estudio por distintas instituciones sin que existan claras recomendaciones a favor. Sí es de interés para el caso del transporte en alta velocidad en España, como opción a medio plazo, un mayor aseguramiento del equipaje alojado en los portamaletas de los coches de viajeros.

Se han analizado desde los intervalos de salida de los trenes (los dos accidentados en Urda partieron desde Madrid hacia Sevilla con seis minutos de diferencia, a las 7.54 y 8.00 de la mañana), por si fuera preciso aumentarlos, hasta tecnología japonesa que comunica unos convoyes con otros para evitar que lleguen a encontrarse en la vía cuando viajan en el mismo sentido de la circulación. También están bajo estudio tecnologías avanzadas de geolocalización para tener ubicado el material rodante en los centros de control al milímetro y en tiempo real.

Prácticamente toda la dirección de Adif ha trabajado para que la batería de medidas sea de posible aplicación, más o menos inmediata, y no entre en conflicto con regulaciones nacionales ni europeas, tampoco con recomendaciones de instituciones de renombre en el sector ferroviario.

Los detalles finales serán avanzados en La Moncloa por el propio ministro que, lejos de dimitir, como le reclama buena parte del arco político, incluidos algunos socios importantes del Ejecutivo, ha optado por dirigir la crisis y afrontar de forma directa los golpes de las críticas masivas que está recibiendo la gestión de la alta velocidad, la joya de las infraestructuras españolas. Después de la rueda de prensa del Consejo de Ministros donde anunciará las medidas, Puente se irá al Congreso para enfrentarse a una dura sesión de la Diputación Permanente en la que casi todo el arco parlamentario le pedirá su dimisión.

El ministro parece decidido a seguir, incluso después de esa dura sesión, porque cree que una dimisión sería un reconocimiento de culpa injusto y con un efecto político demoledor para el Gobierno, pero la última palabra la tiene Pedro Sánchez. El presidente de momento le ha pedido al ministro que resista y que no dimita, después de que este pusiera su cargo a disposición tras la tragedia, pero algunos miembros del Gobierno creen que esa decisión no es definitiva y podría cambiar en los próximos días si se constata que la presión sobre Puente es tan fuerte que inhabilita por completo la posibilidad de volver a la campaña y tratar de recuperar un discurso en positivo.

Como momentos centrales de la semana, además de este martes con la prueba de fuego de Puente, están la rueda de prensa de Sánchez el jueves, al concluir la Cumbre Iberoamericana, y, después, los mítines del líder del PSOE el viernes y el sábado, donde recuperará la campaña.

El presidente ha animado a Puente en privado a seguir, según ha explicado él mismo, y ha decidido respaldarle porque si no ya no estaría en el Gobierno, pero públicamente aún no ha lanzado ningún apoyo político expreso a su ministro. No lo ha hecho porque en todos estos días no ha aceptado una sola pregunta de la prensa, pero el jueves está obligado a contestar y tendrá que hacerlo sobre su apoyo a Puente. Por eso algunos en el Ejecutivo especulan con la idea de que podría haber decisiones antes de este jueves, aunque en el entorno del presidente insisten en que la decisión de que Óscar Puente continúe es firme y no va a cambiar.

La parte de las medidas para mejorar la seguridad será sin duda una de las grandes novedades del Consejo de Ministros de este martes, y la que más interés está generando entre los profesionales y los expertos que analizan qué ha podido fallar en este nuevo accidente ferroviario, pero la que afecta más directamente a las víctimas de la tragedia de Urda es la de las ayudas. Sánchez avanzó en el WIP en Barcelona que el Gobierno aprobará un paquete basado en cuatro ejes, similar al que se planteó tras el incidente de Adamuz: primero, ayudas para duplicar la cuantía del seguro obligatorio para accidentes en vigor; segundo, un anticipo de las indemnizaciones para las víctimas; tercero, una mejora de los esquemas de incapacidad temporal para mejorar su cobertura y cuarto, la creación de oficinas de atención integral para afectados.

World.title: Amancio Ortega, Sandra Ortega y Juan Roig lideran la lista Forbes de las mayores fortunas de España
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

El patrimonio de los 100 españoles más ricos bate nuevo récord y llega a 300.530 millones

Amancio Ortega, fundador de Inditex, su hija mayor, la empresaria Sandra Ortega, y el dueño de Mercadona, Juan Roig, ocupan este año el Top 3 de las grandes fortunas españolas, según la nueva edición de la lista de Los 100 españoles más ricos que publica cada año Forbes España.

El patrimonio conjunto de estos 100 millonarios ha batido un nuevo récord y ha alcanzado los 300.530 millones de euros después de crecer un 16,1%, el doble que el año pasado, lo que ha sido posible gracias a la buena evolución de la Bolsa, al crecimiento económico, a la revalorización de activos y a la mejora de sus ingresos y beneficios.

El empresario gallego Amancio Ortega, de 90 años, lleva más de una década encabezando esta clasificación, y este año su fortuna ha aumentado un 13,9% en comparación con 2025, recuperando con fuerza lo que la corrección bursátil le restó el año anterior gracias al gran desempeño de Inditex.

Ortega atesora 125.200 millones de euros y concentra él solo el 41,7% de la riqueza de la lista española. También es el europeo más rico, a día de hoy, por delante de Bernard Arnault, propietario del Grupo LVMH al que pertenecen enseñas como Louis Vuitton, según el ránking de Forbes USA.

El segundo puesto sigue siendo para la hija mayor de Amancio Ortega, Sandra Ortega, que se mantiene como la mujer más rica de España con una fortuna de 11.500 millones de euros.

En tercera posición se sitúa el presidente ejecutivo de Mercadona, Juan Roig, con una riqueza de 9.800 millones de euros; seguido del banquero Juan Carlos Escotet, presidente de Abanca, con 8.100 millones de euros; y cerrando el Top 5, el presidente de Ferrovial, Rafael del Pino, con 7.800 millones de euros.

España se enfrenta en los próximos años al mayor relevo de herencias corporativas de su historia, explica el informe de Forbes, que añade que el recambio será estructural, pero que todo apunta a que el poder económico no cambiará de sectores ni de manos en el mercado abierto, sino que se mantendrá dentro de los mismos árboles genealógicos.

La edad media, 70 años

La edad media de la lista ha subido hasta los 70 años, lo que ratifica que la consolidación de la riqueza en España sigue requiriendo décadas de acumulación.

El más veterano es Amancio Ortega, seguido de históricos de la empresa española como Miguel Fluxà Roselló (87 años), que atesora 4.100 millones con Iberostar; Juan Abelló (83 años), que posee 3.100 millones con Torreal.

Los septuagenarios mantienen un peso clave en los primeros puestos, destacando Juan Roig (76 años), su esposa Hortensia Herrero y Florentino Pérez (79 años), quien este año irrumpe con fuerza en el top 10 general.

En el segmento de los sexagenarios, Rafael Del Pino (67 años) y Juan Carlos Escotet (66 años) lideran un grupo dominado fuertemente por las infraestructuras y la banca tradicional, mientras que entre los millonarios en la cincuentena destaca Sandra Ortega (57 años).

Más peso de las mujeres

Las mujeres han afianzado su peso este año en la élite empresarial española y este año ocupan el 26% de las posiciones del ránking.

Las féminas más ricas de la lista suman 64.779 millones de euros, un 14% más que el año pasado, con Sandra Ortega a la cabeza, que concentra ella sola casi una quinta parte de todo el patrimonio femenino del país.

En el sexto puesto global y en el segundo entre las mujeres, se encuentra la vicepresidenta de Mercadona, Hortensia Herrero, con una riqueza valorada en 5.550 millones de euros.

Una de las grandes novedades de este año es el desembarco en la lista de Fernando Masaveu y su familia. El presidente de la Corporación Masaveu entra directamente en el puesto 30 con un patrimonio de 1.700 millones de euros, la mayor irrupción en el ranking desde 2021.

Otras entradas destacadas son las de José Manuel Cortizo, fundador de Aluminios Cortizo, en el puesto 76, con 750 millones de euros; Enrique Riquelme, del Grupo Cox, que se coloca en la 90ª posición con 620 millones y es, además, el más joven de la lista, con 37 años.

También debuta este año la presidenta del Banco Santander, Ana Botín, en el puesto 97 con 550 millones de euros.

Asimismo, Madrid se consolida como el territorio con más fortunas de la lista, con un total de 33 y una riqueza conjunta de 54.600 millones de euros; seguida de Cataluña, con 26 fortunas y una riqueza de 33.040 millones de euros, aunque Galicia sigue siendo la comunidad española que más dinero acumula con 147.050 millones de euros entre cinco fortunas, gracias al “efecto Inditex”.

El análisis de Forbes España no tiene en cuenta sólo la riqueza de estas personas, sino cómo gestionan su capital y estudia también el valor de mercado de sus empresas, sus propiedades inmobiliarias y suntuarias y la liquidez de la que disponen, entre otros factores.
