World.title: Un agente inmobiliario quiere cobrarnos por enseñarnos un piso. ¿Es normal?
World.content:
Pregunta. Vivimos en Zaragoza y queremos comprar un piso. La persona que nos lo enseña nos dice que, en caso de venta, sus honorarios son un porcentaje del valor o una cifra que va desde 5.000 hasta 9.000 euros más IVA. ¿Enseñarnos el piso implica que lo hemos contratado y debemos pagar lo que pide? P. Pérez

Respuesta. Lo habitual es que el servicio de intermediación inmobiliaria sea contratado por el vendedor, que es quien pone la vivienda en el mercado y acuerda con la agencia las condiciones de la venta, incluyendo la comisión a abonar mediante el correspondiente contrato de encargo. Por ello, lo normal es que sea el vendedor quien asuma estos honorarios. El comprador, por regla general, no debe pagar comisiones a la inmobiliaria, salvo que exista un acuerdo previo, expreso y transparente, formalizado mediante la firma de un contrato de mediación.

El mero hecho de que una agencia inmobiliaria le enseñe una vivienda no implica que exista una relación contractual con el comprador ni genera, por sí solo, la obligación de abonar honorarios. La agencia está prestando un servicio al propietario del inmueble, que es quien la ha contratado para gestionar la venta. En consecuencia, la realización de visitas forma parte de los servicios incluidos en dicho encargo.

No obstante, resulta especialmente importante revisar con detenimiento cualquier documento que se firme durante la visita, en particular la denominada hoja o parte de visita. En ocasiones, estos documentos pueden incluir cláusulas o menciones relativas al pago de una comisión por parte del comprador en caso de adquisición del inmueble.

Asimismo, debe tenerse en cuenta que los tribunales vienen considerando que la incorporación de este tipo de cláusulas en una simple hoja de visita puede resultar abusiva y, por tanto, nula, cuando no ha existido una negociación individual previa. En este sentido, el parte de visita tiene como finalidad principal acreditar que la vivienda ha sido mostrada al interesado, pero no constituye, por sí mismo, un contrato de prestación de servicios entre el comprador y la inmobiliaria.

Por ello, si la agencia pretende cobrar una comisión al comprador lo recomendable es que dicho compromiso quede recogido en un contrato específico, claro y debidamente firmado por las partes. Si únicamente le comunican de forma verbal la obligación de abonar las cantidades indicadas, conviene solicitar que le faciliten por escrito un desglose detallado de los importes reclamados y de los servicios concretos que, en calidad de comprador, van a prestarle y justificarían el cobro de dichos honorarios.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: El Santander supera los dos billones de activos tras la compra de Webster y pugna por el trono de la banca europea
World.content:
El Banco Santander ha dado un gran salto con la adquisición del estadounidense Webster. De acuerdo a las cuentas del tercer trimestre —las primeras que recogen la adquisición de la entidad norteamericana, dado que la adquisición de esta se cerró en agosto—, el banco ha alcanzado los 2,1 billones de euros en activos, desde los 1,9 billones que tenía hace tres meses y de los 1,8 billones con los que inició el año.

La abultada cifra permite al Santander consolidarse en la tercera plaza como mayor banco de la Unión Europea, por detrás de los franceses BNP Paribas y Crédit Agricole. Deja atrás a las entidades galas BPCE y Société Générale, en los 1,7 billones cada una. La toma del banco estadounidense por 12.000 millones, además, también acerca al Santander al dúo de cabeza: recorta la distancia con Crédit Agricole a menos de 400.000 millones, si bien se queda todavía a algo más de un billón de BNP Paribas.

Resulta paradójico cómo se altera la clasificación cuando se atiende al correlato en Bolsa. Según la capitalización, el Santander es el mayor banco Europeo con una gran diferencia y con cerca de 150.000 millones de tasación bursátil. El segundo es el BBVA, con 117.000 millones, seguido por los italianos Unicredit (112.000) e Intesa San Paolo (103.000). Para encontrar al primero banco francés, BNP Paribas, hay que bajar a la cuarta posición.

La tortilla se ha dado la vuelta frente a lo que ocurrió hace más de una década, durante la Gran Recesión, cuando los países del sur de Europa despertaban los recelos de los inversores, que preferían a los del norte. Ahora, las entidades más valoradas por la Bolsa son los bancos españoles e italianos, por encima de franceses y alemanes. Así, el Santander cotiza a 1,3 veces su valor en libros, e Intesa, a 1,6 veces, mientras que las acciones de BNP Paribas lo hacen con descuento.

Las razones detrás de este fenómeno pueden ser múltiples. Es cierto que el Santander ha experimentado en los últimos tiempos intensas subidas en Bolsa. Así, en los últimos 12 meses suma un 17% y desde enero de 2025 más que duplica su valor. BNP Paribas, en cambio, se revaloriza un 32% en 12 meses y un 50% desde principios de 2025. En los últimos meses ha pesado sobre el valor las dudas hacia la economía francesa, por su alto nivel de deuda y la necesidad de emprender una senda de consolidación fiscal ante nuevas subidas de tipos y de encarecimiento del coste del pasivo público. También se teme la inestabilidad política ante las próximas elecciones.

Por el lado de abajo de la tabla, el BBVA consigue colarse en la décima posición, si bien se queda cerca de lograr el billón de activos. Es posible que sea desplazado del puesto esta misma semana, cuando sus inmediatos competidores Intesa San Paolo y Unicrecit presenten resultados. Los tres están prácticamente empatados justo por debajo del billón. Los primeros lo harán este martes, 3 de noviembre, y es posible que sobrepasen esa cota. Y los segundos, el lunes próximo, 9 de noviembre. A su favor, y en contra del banco español, está que ambos se encuentran inmersos en sendas operaciones coporativas que les meterán esteroides a la cifra de manera inorgánica. El primero, con la controvertida opa sobre Monte dei Paschi Siena y el segundo, en hacerse con el alemán Commerzbank. El BBVA, sin embargo, fracasó en su opa por el Sabadell hace un año y apuesta por crecer en solitario, un proceso mucho más lento.

Paralelamente, la operación de Webster sí permite al Santander alzar el vuelo como el banco español más grande. Con esos 2,1 billones más que duplica el tamaño del BBVA. La diferencia en capitalización es menor, de unos 30.000 millones; y en beneficios, computando las ganancias de este año hasta septiembre, de unos 11.000 millones. Al crecimiento del Santander también contribuye la adquisición del británico TSB al Sabadell, que se rubricó en mayo y empezó a computar en los resultados del primer semestre, y le resta la venta de su negocio en Polonia a Erste, igualmente cerrada en este ejercicio 2026.

En cualquier caso, todas estas clasificaciones son juego de niños cuando se amplía el foco. Ni con la toma de Webster o TSB el Santander consigue colocarse entre los bancos más grandes del mundo por activos. La clasificación está dominada por los chinos, que ocupan las cuatro primeras posiciones, seguidos por bancos estadounidenses como JP Morgan y Bank of America, el quinto y sexto. El primer banco de la zona euro es BNP Paribas, en la séptima posición, con Crédit Agricole en la novena y el Santander, en la decimoquinta.

El escaso tamaño de los bancos europeos para competir con entidades estadounidenses y asiáticas es una preocupación compartida tanto por las instituciones europeas como por el sector, si bien las soluciones son distintas. Los bancos ponen el foco en las crecientes demandas de capital en Europa, que afirman les impide competir de tú a tú con entidades de otros lados del mundo. Para instituciones como el Banco Central Europeo (BCE) o la Autoridad Bancaria Europea (EBA) la cuestión está en los recelos de los bancos por acometer grandes fusiones transfronterizas para construir gigantes bancarios paneuropeos.

Este debate se está teniendo actualmente en el seno de la Comisión Europea, que se ha comprometido a proponer un paquete legislativo a principios del año próximo en su intento por simplificar la normativa bancaria. Los bancos intentan que reorganice los cálculos de capital y establezca un límite ara estos requerimientos, mientras también aspiran a reformas que completen la unión bancaria y faciliten esas fusiones transfronterizas. En concreto, se fija como prioridad la construcción de un fondo de garantía de depósitos común.

World.title: Dual passports issue continues to plague Dutch-based footballers
World.content:
Dutch-born footballers who were called up to play for former colonies such as Suriname and Indonesia are still in limbo over their national status, six months after the “passportgate” crisis first flared up.

Suriname’s parliament passed a law in September enabling players who are selected for the national team to gain citizenship automatically.

But the Dutch immigration service IND said the law passed in Suriname made no difference to the rules on dual nationality in the Netherlands.

“The fact that Surinamese nationality has been obtained by legal means is not enough on its own to qualify for one of the exceptional categories under our law,” a spokesman for the Dutch justice ministry told broadcaster NOS.

The law was intended to settle the question of dual nationality for footballers, which arose last March when NAC Breda challenged the eligibility of Go Ahead Eagles defender Dean James.

James took Indonesian citizenship last year after accepting an invitation to play for the national team, but under Dutch dual nationality rules he was required to give up his original passport.

KNVB investigation

The Dutch football association KNVB launched an investigation into the employment status of players who were called up by countries such as Suriname, Cape Verde and Indonesia. In the meantime it arranged for Dutch-based players to be given temporary work permits so they could keep playing for their clubs.

Losing Dutch nationality also stripped them of their EU citizenship, meaning they would need to obtain visas and meet stricter criteria, such as an annual salary threshold of €600,000, to be eligible to play in the Eredivisie.

Several players have passed up invitations to join the Surinamese squad because of the uncertainty, including Danilho Doekhi of Lazio, Milan van Ewijk of Coventry City and Jayden Oosterwolde of Fenerbahçe.

National team manager Henk Fraser said it was “inexplicable” that players’ livelihoods were being damaged by their desire to play international football.

“Both countries have to get together and clarify the situation,” he told NOS. “This is a straightforward case of people following their hearts and wanting to play for Suriname, but not knowing where they stand.”

“Sports passports”

Some players said they felt misled by the Surinamese football association, which told them they were playing for the national team on “sports passports” that allowed them to remain Dutch citizens.

Former Feyenoord winger Jean-Paul Boëtius said he only discovered after he was first called up for Suriname last year that he had inadvertently renounced his Dutch citizenship as a result.

Shortly afterwards he received a letter from the city council in Rotterdam telling him to hand in his Dutch passport, which he had recently renewed, because it was no longer valid.

“I now have a sticker in my Surinamese passport that says I have a residency permit allowing me to live in the Netherlands,” he told NOS. “But that’s only for a year. It’s a very difficult situation. I want to become Dutch again. I was born and brought up here.”

World.title: Double shooting in Rotterdam leaves one dead, one injured
World.content:
One man has died and another is seriously injured after a shooting in Rotterdam on Monday evening, police have said.

The shooting happened at around 8pm in the Ooosterflank area of the city. While investigations are ongoing, reports say that the victims were in a car, along with two others, when someone opened fire. The driver was killed.

Several ambulances and a trauma helicopter were sent to the scene. Police said they could not yet say what had happened.

The three surviving people in the car fled after the shooting and were arrested shortly after. They are being treated as suspects, including the seriously injured man, broadcaster NOS reported. They are a 60-year-old Rotterdam resident and two men (35 and 54) of no fixed address.

World.title: Dutch pensions could rise by up to 25% for 2 million retirees
World.content:
Around 2 million pensioners could see their monthly pension go up by between 12% and 25% from January, when 37 pension funds move to the new Dutch pension system.

The estimate comes from a calculation by pension consultancy Aon for public broadcaster NOS. Across the 10 biggest funds making the switch, pensioners would gain 17% on average.

In the new system, everyone gets their own pension pot instead of sharing one big fund, and pensions move with investment returns. When funds make the switch, they share out the money they have left over as a one-off boost.

Civil service pension fund ABP, the largest by far, has about 1.09 million pensioners, and Aon expects them to get 13.9% more. Estimates for the other funds range from 12.6% to 22.4%.

The figures depend on markets over the next two months, as falling interest rates or share prices would leave less to share out. “The last two months of the year are still uncertain,” Corine Reedijk of Aon told NOS.

The rise applies from January 1, with the first months paid retroactively once the final calculations are done.

World.title: KNMI launches more accurate local weather warning system
World.content:
The Dutch meteorological service KNMI is changing the way it issues weather warnings, replacing the system of provincial alerts with more accurate regional bands.

At the moment the KNMI issues code red, amber and yellow warnings for each province, plus a separate alert for the Wadden islands, with red being the most severe.

Icy roads in the north of Friesland or sea fog on the Zuid-Holland coast would lead to a weather warning for the whole province, even if conditions were completely different further inland.

Under the new method meteorologists will be able to draw lines across the map based on actual weather conditions, giving a more accurate reflection of where conditions are most hazardous.

Upgraded app

The institute has also improved its app so that users can zoom in for more detailed forecasts of the impact in their local area. Organisations will be able to download the data so they can use it on their

A new law came into effect on May 20 allowing the KNMI to issue warnings for smaller areas rather than entire provinces. The method was first used at the end of August to inform people in Middleburg about a storm approaching the Zeeland town.

Remmy van Lisehout, director of crisis management at Amsterdam-Amstelland safety region, said the new system would make it easier for responders to prepare for storm damage.

At the moment an alert for Noord-Holland province means authorities have to take precautions for falling trees in Amsterdam when a storm is passing through Den Helder, 80km to the north.

“All being well, from November we will hear: ‘It’s in Den Helder and not Amsterdam’,” she said.

World.title: Private rental sector loses 22,000 homes as landlords sell up
World.content:
Private landlords are continuing to sell their properties, leaving fewer homes to rent. The number of homes let by individual landlords fell by 37,000 last year to 492,000, the national statistics office CBS said on Tuesday.

Across the private rental sector as a whole, which also includes companies and organisations, there were 22,000 fewer homes.

Owning and renting properties is no longer a profitable business for most landlords. Vastgoed Belang, which represents private landlords, warned in September that sales would continue because the cabinet had announced no measures to ease the tax on their investments.

It has also campaigned against rent controls, which were extended to mid-market homes in July 2024.

Most of the homes were sold to people who now live in them, some 57,000 over the past two years, CBS said.

The private rental sector as a whole, which also includes homes owned by companies and organisations, shrank by 22,000 to 1.16 million. In 2024 it lost just 3,000.

Utrecht saw the biggest shift. Some 15% of homes let by individuals in the city became owner-occupied over the two years, compared with 12% in Amsterdam and 11% in Rotterdam and The Hague. In Limburg and Zeeland the figure was 6% to 7%.

The homes being sold are at the pricier end. Their average WOZ valuation, used for local property tax, was €375,000, against €327,000 for all homes let by individuals. They are also more likely to be newer, bigger family houses.

Housing corporations, meanwhile, added 14,000 homes last year.

World.title: Council of State strongly criticises Heinen’s income tax reform
World.content:
The Council of State has delivered a withering verdict on finance minister Eelco Heinen’s plans for a capital gains tax system, saying the proposal had been drawn up too hastily and without proper consideration.

The administrative court said the deadline of 2028 for implementing the law was unrealistic because it would not give the tax office, banks and other institutions time to adapt their systems.

The report from the Council of State, which acts as the government’s constitutional advisor, is the latest setback for the cabinet as it tries to steer its budget for next year through parliament.

Heinen had hoped to speed up the reform of the income tax system to prevent the government losing more money from the current Box 3 mechanism, which the Council of State struck out in 2021 when it ruled that it unfairly discriminated against some savers.

Coalition and opposition parties are divided on how to reform Box 3, the section of the tax return form which calculates the tax due on assets savings based on an estimated rate of return.

D66, CDA and the left-wing opposition parties wanted to formalise this by taxing investors on their actual gains, but Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, and opposition groups such as JA21 favour a capital gains tax instead.

€10 billion shortfall

The latter option would create an estimated €10 billion shortfall in the immediate term because assets will not be taxed until they are sold.

The existing mechanism is costing the state €3.5 billion a year in lost revenue because savers can reduce their tax bill if they show their actual returns were lower than the estimated figure, but do not have to pay more if it is higher.

The Council of State criticised the minister’s decision to use a “novelle”, a device that allows legislation to be amended after it has been passed by the Lower House but is still wating to be approved by the senate.

Heinen said that would allow capital gains taxes to be levied on real estate and startup business in 2028 as a stepping-stone towards introducing the tax on all assets from 2030.

But the Council of State said the plans were too complicated, would only affect around 10% of all asset wealth and would have to be enacted at “very high speed”. It would be better to change the entire system in one go in 2030, the report said.

World.title: Drought may be cracking Groningen’s medieval churches
World.content:
Medieval churches in Groningen may be cracking because of drought as well as earthquakes, according to a study reported by broadcaster NOS.

Researchers from water and soil research institute Deltares and the Hanze University of Applied Sciences looked at how drought affects the wierden, man-made dwelling mounds, under churches in Oostum and Den Ham, northwest of the city of Groningen.

The study was commissioned by the province and the Old Groningen Churches Foundation (Stichting Oude Groninger Kerken).

The research began after new damage appeared in the church at Oostum in 2018, two years after suspected earthquake damage there had been repaired. There have been no major quakes in the area since, but the damage appears to be getting worse.

The nave of the Oostum church has stood for 800 years. “It’s not a given that this church will still be here in another 800 years,” researcher Floris Boogaard told NOS, “because it is ageing very fast now.”

Boogaard said lab tests showed the church stands on clay that swells when wet and shrinks during drought, while peat in the ground oxidises and compacts as groundwater levels fall.

He said increased traffic, changes to the surroundings and earthquakes all contribute to cracking, but that drought is the only one of those factors to have changed significantly in recent years, while the cracks have become much worse.

“The climate is changing,” he said. “Dry periods are significantly longer: in 2018 it was dry for two months, and that really does have an effect.” This year also had exceptionally long dry spells and droughts.

The two-year study is still underway, and the researchers say longer-term research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. They warn that other historic buildings face the same problem.

Possible solutions are still being examined, but the researchers say the churches need stable water levels around them. At Oostum, pits could be dug around the church to collect rainwater, which would then slowly seep into the ground.

World.title: Banning the infinite scroll: Pro MP files bill on addictive apps
World.content:
Social media platforms, games and dating apps should be banned from using designs like the infinite scroll that keep users online and push them into spending money, according to a bill being submitted to parliament on Monday by Pro MP Barbara Kathmann.

Kathmann told broadcaster NOS her bill would class manipulative features in the design of online platforms as “unfair commercial practices”, which are already illegal under Dutch consumer law. She says the current rules are geared to physical products, but online platforms have become “the new high street or marketplace”.

“If a doll is unsafe, we take it off the market,” she said. “If social media platforms are unsafe, they have to go back to the drawing board and be adapted.”

The proposal also covers chatbots. Kathmann said these products contain tricks “that make us addicted and tempt us into spending money, so that a handful of tech billionaires earn a fortune”.

She would prefer the issue to be tackled at EU level, but that would take too long, and hopes a Dutch law will prompt Brussels to act. She is working with MPs in Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Italy and Portugal who want similar legislation.

Last year, a Dutch court ordered Meta to let Instagram and Facebook users in the Netherlands set a chronological, non-algorithmic feed as their default, in a case brought by digital rights group Bits of Freedom. The appeals court upheld the order in March.

A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two. World.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned from his position, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw. All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS. Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation. All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026 On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021. Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively. While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK. Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau. Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022. On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS. Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”. The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court. It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government. Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own. The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023. This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful. Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law. "On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court. He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal. Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid. While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026 On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year. Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries. The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology. The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males. The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added. “I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.” Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas. With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps. The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees. “Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.” The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers. Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022 The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out. The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites. World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners. Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki. @PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute. Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted. On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”. Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki. “One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia” – sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026 While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added. Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Prezesem @TK_GOV_PL jest nadal Bogdan Święczkowski, a Wiceprezesem Bartłomiej Sochański. Pani Anna Korwin-Piotrowska nie jest sędzią Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026 The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister. She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered. Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening. Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”. Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland. Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”. Our most tracked flight right now: A Polish government aircraft en route to Senegal is now returning to Warsaw. https://t.co/YdLhQmV8pl pic.twitter.com/Dz9KPgI3eI — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 30, 2026 Tusk, however, issued a statement on social media defending what was taking place at the TK. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity. The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures. The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years. Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆 ❓Czym jest OPRO? ✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich… — Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026 Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly. Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days. The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels. Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”. The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly. Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects. EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late. Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU. However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish Left seeks to end state funding of clergy’s social contributions as government reform stalls
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund. However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted. 📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️ Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️ ✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026 The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings. It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty. Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half. For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.” At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found. In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025 An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained. Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law. “I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”. Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled. Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed. Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners. A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church. Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025 Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance. In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement. Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities. The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy. A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
