World.title: 56,000 People in Croatia Diagnosed With a Disability in One Year
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – There has been a staggering increase of 56,000 people across Croatia diagnosed with some kind of disability in just one year. As things currently stand, every fifth person in Croatia is disabled.

In just one single year, the number of recorded persons with disabilities in Croatia rose by as many as 56,000, according to a new report by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ). Ivana Krnic reports for Jutarnji that according to the report, on 28 September this year there were 730,987 persons with disabilities living in Croatia, compared with 675,213 one year earlier. In other words, almost every fifth resident of Croatia is now officially recorded as a person with a disability.

Such a worrying and high increase is primarily, according to those familiar with the matter, a consequence of the introduction of the inclusive allowance. Namely, the Register of Persons with Disabilities is actually a database of persons who exercise some right on the basis of disability: persons who have not been assessed or do not exercise any right cannot be in that database, regardless of their actual disability.

Since the criteria for obtaining the inclusive allowance are incomparably milder than the criteria for the personal disability benefit or the allowance for another person’s assistance and care — rights that preceded the inclusive allowance — the number of persons receiving the inclusive allowance is significantly higher than the number of persons who previously received cash assistance. Specifically speaking, before the introduction of the inclusive allowance, around 150,000 persons received the personal disability benefit and the allowance for another person’s assistance and care, while the inclusive allowance is now received by around 240,000 persons, with around another hundred thousand applications still pending. The majority of persons receiving the inclusive allowance had the same or very similar difficulties earlier, but did not meet the strict criteria for receiving cash assistance and were therefore not registered as persons with disabilities.

The HZJZ response also confirms that the new rights have significantly increased interest in assessments.

new rights prompted an assessment increase

“It covers a wide range of rights and that has attracted a large number of persons who hadn’t previously been assessed to undergo assessment and try in this way to exercise some of the mentioned rights,” doc. dr. sc. Tomislav Benjak, assistant director of the HZJZ for the quality of healthcare and author of the Report on Persons with Disabilities, told Jutarnji list.

In addition to the inclusive allowance, he also mentions other rights, such as priority in employment, transport privileges, scholarships and tax reliefs, which can be exercised on the basis of an established disability. The method of collecting data also influenced the increase. Today almost all findings and decisions arrive digitally, practically immediately after the assessment, whereas previously they were partly delivered by post. Such a system did not guarantee that all of the data was indeed recorded in the Register. The largest part of the increase relates to persons over the age of 65. Their number rose in one year from 317,164 to 358,806, i.e. by 41,642 persons. That is almost three quarters of the total annual increase.

Today almost half of all persons recorded in the Register are over 65 years old, and disability has been established in approximately 40 percent of the population of that age. Benjak says that the ageing of the population is one of the main reasons for the long-term increase in the number of persons with disabilities. In older age, difficulties with mobility, impairments of sight and hearing, and the consequences of chronic diseases occur more frequently. However, part of the increase also stems from the fact that persons who were already recorded eventually move into the older age group.

“The natural transition from the age group up to 65 years into the age group of 65 years and over affects this distribution by approximately 30 percent,” he explains. Croatia is also not helped by the health habits of the population. Benjak warns of the high frequency of cardiovascular and malignant diseases, smoking, obesity and insufficient physical activity.

how much does croatia actually deviate from global trends?

Despite this, he emphasises that Croatia does not deviate significantly from international trends. When the first Register data was published back in 2007, the share of persons with disabilities was 10.7 percent, and today it is 18.9 percent. According to the data he cites, the World Health Organisation estimates that persons with disabilities make up around 16 percent of the world’s population, while Eurostat for the European Union cites 23.9 percent. These data, however, are not necessarily completely comparable because they are based on different methods of establishing disability. The new HZJZ report for the first time also brings a division according to the severity of disability. According to that classification, 106,724 persons have severe disability and 142,722 persons have more severe disability. Together that is almost 250,000 people. However, for as many as 206,902 persons, or 28.3 percent of all those recorded, the severity of disability has not been classified.

Benjak explains that these are mostly persons who were assessed many years ago, when the findings from the then social welfare centres did not contain the data needed for today’s classification.

Interestingly, a large part of these persons, despite the possibility of exercising these new rights, have not undergone a new assessment. It is also possible that they are not sufficiently informed. “What somehow surprises us as well is that around 200,000 persons assessed at that time with rights from social welfare and elements for entry into the Register have not requested new assessments in order to exercise the right to, for example, the inclusive allowance or rights in transport,” Benjak is also surprised.

He emphasises that this is not a matter of double entries or of deceased persons. Every person is tracked by personal identification number (OIB), and the HZJZ also has data on deaths. He confirms that all 206,902 persons are alive and that there is a legal basis for their entry into the Register. The new division according to the severity of disability serves exclusively for statistical purposes and does not affect the exercise of rights. Nevertheless, the fact that data needed for classification are missing for more than a quarter of the recorded persons shows how difficult it is to obtain a complete picture of the structure of disability in Croatia.

huge differences on a county by county basis

There are also large differences among counties. In Šibenik-Knin County disability is recorded in 24.4 percent of the population, almost twice as much as in Istria County, where that share is 12.3 percent. The range is even greater among those over 65 years of age. In Šibenik-Knin County 49.6 percent of the population of that age have a disability, in Požega-Slavonia County 49.5 percent, and in Istria County 25.1 percent.

Data for children and young people in Sisak-Moslavina County are particularly worrying. There the prevalence of disability in the age group up to 19 years rose from 17.9 to 20.5 percent, while the Croatian average is 12.3 percent. This means that disability is recorded in approximately every fifth child or young person in that county. Asked why the differences are so large, Benjak says that a special study would need to be conducted. Nevertheless, he warns that Sisak-Moslavina is one of the most deprived Croatian counties, with lower wages, weaker employment, higher unemployment and unfavourable demographic trends.

“All of the above certainly also has as a consequence the occurrence of disability and developmental difficulties in children,” Benjak believes. Without additional analysis it is not possible to determine how much health and social conditions, and how much the availability of diagnostics, assessments and the method of recording, influence such a high prevalence.

the case with children across croatia

Another seemingly unusual piece of data appears in the report. Although the total number of children and young people with disabilities is rising, the number of persons for whom decisions on an appropriate form of schooling arrived in the Register has decreased from 57,703 to 49,847. Nevertheless, it seems that the reason is not necessarily a smaller number of children with difficulties, but a change in the records.

According to Benjak’s explanation, the Ministry of Education requested the deactivation of records of persons up to the age of 21 whose only basis for entry into the Register was a decision on an appropriate form of schooling, and who after 2015 weren’t ever reassessed. Among them are persons who during childhood had developmental difficulties such as dyslexia, dysgraphia, behavioural disorders or learning difficulties, which over time may have decreased or disappeared. Changes in the records also explain the decrease in the number of Croatian war military invalids. Their number fell from 54,640 to 46,132, i.e. by 8,508 persons.

According to instructions from the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, only persons who are in its official database remain in the HRVI category. Some previously recorded persons no longer appear in that database, so their HRVI status in the Register has been deactivated. Despite such changes, Benjak claims that the annual reports have been prepared using the same methodology and that it is possible to track trends. In fact, the only novelty in the 2026 report is the additional statistical division according to the severity of disability. However, precisely the changes in the records of children and veterans show how much administrative decisions can influence the statistics.

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.

World.title: 135 Years of the Zagreb Tram – From Horses to Modernity
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – 135 years is the time period during which the now iconic blue Zagreb tram has snaked through the capital city. From being pulled by horses to new vehicles, let’s look back at the history of what we now know as ZET.

Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that frequent trams have been circulating Zagreb’s streets for 135 years now. They have become the blue symbol of the city, living history on the rails, and transport without which Zagreb can hardly function, something Zagreb residents felt most clearly during the recent multi-day ZET workers’ strike, which caused days of traffic problems until a court declared it illegal and banned it.

horse-drawn trams named after vineyard pests…

The first tram circled Zagreb back in 1891. It was pulled by horses and was far from the technical modernity we know today. Zagreb’s trams were once yellow and ran on only a few lines through the very city centre. People affectionately called them “konjka” (horse-tram), but also mockingly “filoksera”, after the notorious wine louse (phylloxera) that was ravaging vineyards in those years, because the workers laying the tracks had dug up and torn apart half the city. Before the trams, passengers were transported around Zagreb by omnibuses that resembled stagecoaches from Western films. They ran from the city centre to the bathing spots on the Sava and from the railway station to a few hotels. As ZET explains, “the city fathers in Zagreb began discussing the need to introduce a horse-drawn tram as a means of transport” in 1885.

French engineer Raoul Pierre Alexandre Gautier proposed a contract for the introduction of tram traffic to the Zagreb City Magistrate on the 20th of June 1887. The city municipality accepted his offer and on the 26th of March 1889 issued him a permit to build a tram line on the ground of the city streets. The Association of Engineers and Technicians allowed the construction of a 76-centimetre-wide track, and the Tramway Company, a special private enterprise, began work. The first tram depot was built on the site of today’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum.

ilica, zagreb’s modern main artery, was dug up

zagreb.hr

The first lines were built from the corner of Ilica and Mandaličina Street to Maksimir, from the corner of Ilica and Frankopanska Street to the Sava Bridge, and from the corner of Ilica and today’s Republic of Austria Street to the Western Railway Station. Construction began in May 1891, and the trams started running a few months later. Historian Lelja Dobronić, in the article “Old Notes on the Zagreb Tram” published in the magazine Kaj, cites a document from the 17th of August 1891: “Since the long-awaited rails from England and the carriages from Graz (in Austria) have finally arrived, Upper Ilica has been being dug up since last Thursday, and from today Frankopanska Street as well, so that the rails can be laid. Certainly by this Sunday the rails will be laid through the whole of Ilica and Jelačić Square. Up to 500 workers are working a day.”

At the time when Zagreb’s trams were pulled by horses, there were ten closed and six open vehicles available, manufactured at the Weitzer factory in Graz. The average speed of the horse-drawn tram cars was 7.5 km/h. Zagreb’s horse-drawn tram also carried passengers in Velika Gorica, where the joint-stock company Horse Railway was founded back in 1907. They had a seven-kilometre line from the railway station, through the centre of Velika Gorica, to Novo Čiče. It was called “konjača.” After 1945 the horses were replaced by a small diesel locomotive.

electrification and expansion

The electric tram started in August 1910, but horse-drawn trams continued to operate for the following year. Zagreb’s trams changed colour in 1923. They became blue instead of yellow, while the vehicles were reconstructed. A new model, the M-24, manufactured in Zagreb and running on the right-hand track, also appeared on the streets. Summer open-air trams soon became available as well. During the time of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), Zagreb’s trams ran with increasing difficulty because of bombing, and services were suspended in 1944. Traffic resumed after liberation, and in the autumn of 1945 tracks were built through Vodnikova and Mihanovićeva streets. From then on, the tram lines had numbers. In the following years lines were built towards Žitnjak as well as the Mihaljevac–Dolje line. A building for ZET workers was constructed in Puljska Street.

bull, czech and katica…

At the beginning of the 1950s, Zagreb’s residents also received the first domestically produced tram, built in the ZET workshop. It was prototype 101 with 95 passenger seats. This was followed by cooperation with the “Đuro Đaković” wagon factory from Slavonski Brod and the purchase of M-201 vehicles.

The last example of the M-201 tram, nicknamed “Đuro” or “Bik” (Bull), ran until June 2024 on line 9. Its predecessor, the M-24, ran from 1924 to 1977. Today it is used as the Christmas tram. In 1977 Czechoslovak trams from the ČKD-Tatra factory in Prague were purchased. The Czech T4 model trams, known as “Čeh” (Czech), ran for years on lines 4, 6 and 14. Years later the Tatra KT4YU trams, better known as “Katice,” also arrived. An important date in the history of the Zagreb tram was the 25th of November 1979, when the line along Držićeva Street, across the Bridge of Youth, to New Zagreb was opened. That was when the tram crossed the Sava. In 1980 a tram-bus terminal was built at Črnomerec on the site of a former brickworks. In November 1985 the tram also started running across the Adriatic Bridge towards New Zagreb. Further development of ZET includes the abolition of the conductor’s job in 1996 (conductors had been cancelling and selling tickets in the vehicles for 105 years) and the extension of tram routes to Dubec and Prečko.

and then came končar…

Over the last thirty years or so the old trams, Bulls, Czechs and Katicas, have been replaced by trams manufactured at Končar, Zagreb’s technological giant.

“In more than 30 years of operation on Zagreb’s tram network, Končar trams have covered more than 140 million kilometres, confirming their quality, reliability and indispensable role in the lives of Zagreb residents,” Končar told Index. The company had already begun manufacturing electric rectifier stations for ZET back in 1954. “After almost three decades of cooperation on energy infrastructure, ZET and Končar began joint development of tram vehicles. Production of the TMK 2100 series trams began in 1993, and the prototype was presented on the 5th of September 1994 and immediately put into regular service,” the company notes, also recalling the TMK 2200 trams. “From June 2010 a total of 140 TMK 2200 series trams and two shorter TMK 2200-K trams (which carry the designation TMK 2300 in ZET’s fleet) have been produced for Zagreb,” Končar says. The company later also manufactured shorter trams for the Latvian city of Liepāja.

zagreb’s blue trams

In order to fill gaps in the timetable until the delivery of new vehicles, ZET bought 11 used GT6M trams from Augsburg, Germany, at the end of 2023 and during 2024. This sparked lively public debate because of their age and the fact that the passenger areas are not air-conditioned. The newest Zagreb trams, the TMK 2300, have been in service since February 2025, and there will be forty of them. Through their rich history Zagreb’s trams have become the city’s blue symbol, a mark of the development of domestic technology, and an indicator of Zagreb’s expansion ever further from its historic centre. Zagreb is, along with Osijek, the only Croatian city with tram traffic. Trams once also ran in Pula (from 1904 to 1934), Dubrovnik (from 1910 to 1970), and Rijeka and Opatija.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Accuses EU of Wanting to be a Superstate
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian President Zoran Milanović has accused the EU of wanting to become a superstate, adding that Montenegro, with which Croatia has multiple open issues, is otherwise welcome to join.

President Zoran Milanović stated that Montenegro is welcome to become a full member of the European Union, while at the same time criticising the direction in which the EU is developing. Index reports that the president believes the EU is increasingly trying to become a superstate, whereas it should focus on free trade, freedom of movement and the harmonisation of rules among member states.

Milanović spoke at the 27th Lučindan Gatherings in Zagreb, a traditional meeting of the Montenegrin community in Croatia. The event was also attended by Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović, who is on a working visit to Croatia. The two presidents discussed relations between the two countries and Montenegro’s European future.

“montenegro is welcome to join”

“Montenegro is a candidate for membership of the European Union, it is moving towards the EU and let it come. As far as I am concerned, it is welcome,” Milanović said. Nevertheless, he repeated his criticisms of the European Union, which he believes is exceeding the powers and possibilities on which it was originally founded. In his view, the EU should stick to economic cooperation, free movement and the alignment of rules, rather than striving to create a superstate.

Milanović told Montenegrins that the greatest value they have is their state. He emphasised that Montenegro has realised its statehood and that its future success does not depend exclusively on membership of the European Union. “The greatest thing you have is your state. Montenegro has realised itself, and everything else consists of greater or lesser advances that do not stand in the way of Montenegro being successful, well-governed and relatively prosperous,” Milanović said. He wished Montenegro to continue on its own path and develop as a successful and well-governed state. He concluded his address with verses by the Montenegrin ruler and poet Petar II Petrović Njegoš.

trust between croatia and montenegro must be strengthened

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović assessed that Croatia and Montenegro are friendly countries and that Montenegro’s membership of the European Union is in the interest of both countries. He stressed that improving relations requires continuing political dialogue and resolving existing open issues.

“It is our shared responsibility to build good-neighbourly relations, foster open dialogue, overcome current challenges and strengthen mutual trust,” Milatović said. He emphasised that a common European future implies political and economic cooperation, mutual respect and a willingness to resolve disagreements. He thanked the Montenegrin community in Croatia for preserving national identity, culture and ties with the home country.

The Lučindan Gatherings are a traditional event dedicated to preserving Montenegrin cultural identity, tradition and ties with Montenegro. They bring together members of the Montenegrin national minority in Croatia as well as representatives of the cultural and public life of the two countries. According to the 2021 census, 3,127 members of the Montenegrin national minority live in Croatia, or 0.08 percent of the total population.

World.title: Before You Apply: The Legal Deadline Blocking Croatian Descendants
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – There is a somewhat unknown legal deadline blocking Croatian descendants from obtaining their Croatian and as such EU passport.

That issue relates to the exact reason your family left the former Yugoslavia, and why exactly this could throw a spanner in the works of your EU future. Let’s turn the clock back to October the 8th, 1991… If you’re exploring your eligibility for Croatian citizenship by descent, you have likely come across a specific date repeatedly, and that date is October the 8th, 1991. In the (often confusing) world of Croatian citizenship law, this is the ultimate historical line in the sand. Under the descent and emigrant pathways of the Croatian Citizenship Act, your ancestor must have left the territory of what is now the recognised territory of Croatia before this exact date to grant you a pathway to a Croatian and therefore EU passport of your own.

For many second- and third-generation descendants of those who left what was then Yugoslavia, this seems straightforward at first glance. They look at their family history, note that their parents or grandparents moved to the United States 1960s, 1970s, or 1980s, and check the box. However, many “DIY applicants” face rejections from the Croatian side of the fence because they fail to realise that the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) enforces strict, hidden caveats regarding why and how your ancestor left when they did. Simply proving your family departed before the clock struck 1991 is not quite enough. To secure your Croatian citizenship, you must prove the exact legal nature of their exit. That is where, quite understandably, many people become unstuck and their citizenship applications get shoved to the back of a shelf somewhere to gather dust.

what exactly does croatia deem to be an emigrant?

The Croatian side evaluates citizenship applications based on a highly specific legal definition of what they deem an emigrant to actually be. Under the law as it stands, an emigrant is someone who left the territory of Croatia with the clear, permanent intention of abandoning their domestic residence and resettling somewhere abroad. Because of this ultra-narrow definition that leaves very little wiggle room, there are two major legal traps that routinely catch DIY applicants by surprise.

the so-called internal migration problem

If your ancestor was born in Croatia but moved to another republic within former Yugoslavia, such as Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Slovenia, and then moved across the pond to North America, Croatia’s authorities may not view them as a legal emigrant from Croatia because of that, regardless of the fact that they still ended up in the USA. If that person’s initial move was treated as an internal migration within the same federal state, the chain of continuity for Croatian descent can be heavily compromised or, as is often the case, simply rejected outright.

the curse of the Croatian gastarbajteri…

A Monument to Croatian Emigrants – Anglogermantranslations

During the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of people left the former Yugoslavia to work abroad as temporary economic migrants, often referred to as gastarbajteri (guest workers). Many of these individuals retained their active residency rights, property registrations, and legal ties to Croatia and as such to Yugoslavia, fully intending to return after a few years. If MUP reviews your ancestor’s file and determines that their departure was legally categorised as a “temporary economic migration” rather than a permanent severance of domestic ties, your application under the emigrant track can be denied.

verifying permanence…

Commons/Bain News Service

When you submit your application to a Croatian consulate, the reviewing officers will thoroughly inspect your paperwork to determine the legal permanence of your ancestor’s departure. A simple plane ticket or family story will not suffice. To build an airtight case, you must present a synchronised paper trail that cross-references multiple things.

The first is what’s known as a foreign naturalisation timeline. This works to document precisely when your Croatian ancestor applied for and received citizenship in their new country, showing a definitive shift in legal allegiance. Then come the international arrival records. These are official historical maritime or flight manifests matching the timeline of their permanent resettlement. Last but not least comes the so-called letter of motivation. This might seem odd, but there should always be an explicit structure built up of your family’s narrative, framing their historical departure to meet the rigid legal thresholds expected by Croatia.

for croatia, the year 1991 represents a minefield in several ways…

Proving the legal nuances of a person’s departure that took place forty or fifty years ago is a massive bureaucratic challenge. It requires a deep understanding of historical (and of course needlessly complicated) Yugoslav exit laws, international naturalisation records, and precise legal phrasing in the Croatian language. This is exactly why the structured service provided by Croatian By Descent is an essential safeguard for diaspora families.

croatian by descent‘s experts understand the complexities of the former state

Rather than treating your citizenship application like a roll of the dice, their team conducts an exhaustive upfront document review. They analyse your family’s specific migration timeline, identify potential vulnerabilities in how your ancestors left Yugoslavia, and help you with your application package. By coordinating the procurement of records and managing the precise drafting of your legal motivation letter, they ensure that the Ministry views your family’s departure as a definitive, permanent emigration. They handle the heavy administrative legal lifting, protecting your application from common 1991 cutoff traps and turning your family history into a submission package. Outsource the endless guesswork and verify your eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent.

World.title: State IT authority spokesperson: Motives for Selver fridge hack not yet known
World.content:
Motives behind Monday's cyber attack on a supermarket's refrigeration equipment are not yet clear, an Information System Authority (RIA) spokesperson said.

Mai Kraft, head of RIA's Cyber Security Center, told "Aktuaalne kaamera" there is currently no evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) was used in, nor are

Is there reason to suspect AI was involved in this attack?

This morning, Selver notified RIA about cyberattacks targeting its refrigeration system, but as of now we have no information indicating that the attack was caused by AI.

This is part of a major wave of attacks that we have seen across Europe. What characterizes this attack – was it simply a so-called random security vulnerability that was exploited, or is there reason to suspect some kind of larger malicious plan?

The main factor in these attacks is that devices with security vulnerabilities are visible on the internet, and attackers maliciously exploit them. The motives behind the present attacks are currently unknown.

How many other stores in Estonia have been attacked – there was talk that at least two other stores were known to have been hit?

RIA received one notification from Selver today. We have not heard of any other incidents today.

What actually bars a similar attack from being carried out against, for example, a hospital or a heating system?

Such attacks are likely to be carried out when unsecured systems are visible on the internet and companies and institutions have not made effort to level up their cybersecurity

How many vulnerable devices are actually connected to the network in Estonia – we are not talking about hundreds, but rather hundreds of thousands, aren't we?

If we are talking specifically about refrigeration control systems, we have identified fewer than ten of them today. If we speak a little more broadly about how many vulnerable devices there are in Estonia's cyberspace overall, then according to RIA, there are more than 30,000.

What other attacks have targeted our information systems recently?

We are seeing a variety of types of cyberattacks, most frequently denial-of-service attacks against Estonian information systems. At the same time, all the various scams and phishing campaigns remain widespread, and in addition, we have observed quite a few incidents involving the compromising of websites over the summer.

You say that we have more than 30,000 devices with security vulnerabilities. In what areas are these devices, and which sectors in Estonia are in a vulnerable state?

This figure incorporates the whole of Estonia's cyberspace and includes private individuals and companies alike. Exactly which sectors are affected is currently being analyzed.

Background:

Monday's cyber attack hit one branch of supermarket Selver in Estonia, with hackers accessing a computer controlling refrigeration and changing a freezer setting to 50 degrees above zero. The incident was responded to promptly.

Similar attacks were reported on Monday in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg. This followed incidents in France and the Netherlands last month where supermarket refrigeration systems were also interfered with. In the case of Sweden, spoiled produce had to be disposed of.

World.title: AI makes it harder for young people to land their first job
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is eliminating many of the tasks that once helped young people start their careers, raising concerns about how future workers will gain experience as employers seek more seasoned talent.

Marketer and entrepreneur Hando Sinisalu said some jobs will disappear as AI takes over certain tasks, but new jobs will also emerge. He noted that the nature of work is already changing in fields such as marketing.

"Simple tasks, such as creating basic texts and visuals and automating certain marketing activities, are areas where AI is already doing the work today," he said. Sinisalu added that some people have undoubtedly already lost their jobs as a result.

Many young people are currently studying marketing and advertising at universities. Sinisalu said life could become more challenging for them. Under the traditional model, a young person moves from school into an entry-level job or internship, starts with simple tasks, and gradually advances their career. Sinisalu said those simpler tasks are often more efficiently handled by AI, which may leave young people without the initial experience they need.

Young people's first experience in question

"At the same time, young people have an advantage because they learn faster," Sinisalu said.

He explained that today's middle school graduates, who will enter the labor market several years from now, have grown up with AI and have been using it since childhood. The question, however, is what kind of first work experience young people will need in the future.

Sinisalu said the marketing sector increasingly needs skilled editors who can assess AI-generated text or images and improve them. The same applies to visual content.

"We are currently seeing a huge wave of AI-generated visuals, and a large share of them are bad, unattractive, and tasteless," he said.

Organizations now need editors or curators with good judgment and experience who can distinguish quality work, assign tasks to AI systems, and reject unsuitable results.

"That requires experience and good taste, and it requires people who are better, smarter, and more skilled than AI," he said.

AI-generated work can outperform human work

In the past, agencies and designers had to create large numbers of s and other practical informational materials, and clients paid for that work. Today, AI can produce the same output quickly and cheaply, and the result may not be worse than human work. In some cases, it may even be better.

Ann Hiiemaa, a partner at communications consultancy Meta Advisory, said AI has increased the value of experienced communications professionals in the public relations sector. At the same time, she noted that people whose work has focused primarily on content creation are more easily replaced.

"This means that those who can put a company's business, target audiences, customers, and broader social changes into context and generate growth for companies as a result are worth far more than before," Hiiemaa said.

"But those whose work has mainly involved writing or producing average-quality content are likely facing a certain degree of pressure on their jobs," she added.

Distinguishing important information is critical

Content can include press releases, articles, memos, and analyses. Hiiemaa said the key is being able to synthesize important information from that content and place it in context.

Still, she believes communications will remain highly valued now and in the future because people's attention spans continue to shrink.

"That means packaging information in a way that people can understand and embrace remains extremely valuable," she said.

Hiiemaa said obtaining a first job may become more difficult for young people because many entry-level tasks can be replaced by AI.

"I think young people will also have new opportunities to create content, move away from long articles, and think more about the formats people actually consume," she added.

Gert Tiivas Autor/allikas: Kirke Ert/ERR

Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund CEO Gert Tiivas said AI will increasingly affect the work of everyone who performs office-based jobs. He added that people should prepare early rather than wait for a larger wave of AI-driven job displacement.

"The way to prepare is to start educating ourselves," he said.

Tiivas said the organization is also ready if a larger wave of layoffs occurs. He noted that AI will reshape multiple sectors and that people working in IT companies, telecommunications firms, banks, law offices, and the public sector should be considering its impact and preparing for the changes ahead.

World.title: Estonia to cut doctor-led ambulance crews as medics split over plan
World.content:
The Ministry of Social Affairs plans to cut back on Estonia's 13 doctor-led ambulance crews, a move which has divided medics and left potential job losses unclear.

Arvi Vask, head of South Estonian Hospital (õuna-Eesti haigla), argues the doctor-led crews are not sensible and that nurses can do the job just as well.

Estonia has 13 ambulance crews that include a doctor as well as a nurse, in addition to mobile intensive care units, paid for by the Health Insurance Fund at higher rates.

"As far as I know, there is one doctor-led ambulance crew in Annelinn because it was once claimed that Annelinn is very far from the university hospital, so there must be a doctor-led crew in Annelinn. That's nonsense. In Otepää, it has been claimed that there are many international events there, so there must be a doctor-led crew there," Vask told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

According to the hospital director, this is a waste of doctors' resources. The Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa) pays €15,000 more per month for a doctor-led crew than for a nurse-led crew, which Vask says is precisely why there is reluctance to give them up, although not all of that money goes toward doctors' wages.

"Instead of these doctor-led crews, there could be more ambulance crews, because today a doctor-led crew is much more expensive. These top doctors who work in ambulances could replace family doctors in primary care, or work in hospital emergency departments," Vask said.

Tuuli Paju, a member of the management board at the Tartu Ambulance Service, which covers much of South Estonia, said the proposal may be motivated by staff shortages at smaller hospitals, which it is hoped ambulance doctors could help alleviate.

"I know that, first of all, some of these people already work in emergency departments and hospitals, and secondly, there are specialists working in the ambulance service who would not go to work in a county hospital emergency department," Paju said.

Tartu Ambulance Service has doctors on duty in Paide, Viljandi, Põltsamaa and Räpina, as well as Tartu itself,, with one crew alternating between Otepää, Jõgeva and Tartu. Paju said smaller places cannot rely on separate doctor-led support crews because of the distances.

The Ministry of Social Affairs confirmed doctor-led crews will not be scrapped, just that there are plans in place to reduce their number.

"We want to review how many of them are actually needed and where, so that they are not predominantly responding to calls that a nurse could actually handle, allowing us to use our resources optimally. We are not giving them up completely, and some will remain," said Nikita Panjuškin, head of the ministry's healthcare services department.

New ambulance service arrangements are expected to be made public in the coming weeks.

Estonia plans to shift to mostly two-person ambulance crews, down from three, by 2028 in any case. The Health Board and Health Insurance Fund say the new model will position crews closer to demand and reduce regional disparities. Under the 2028 plan there will be 63 three-person and 43 two-person crews by day, and 63 three-person and 30 two-person crews at night.

World.title: Estonia's Ott Tänak to make WRC comeback in 2027 with Toyota
World.content:
Estonian rally driver Ott Tänak is set to return to the World Rally Championship (WRC) next season with Toyota, the team announced on Tuesday.

Tänak, 39, stepped down from WRC competition at the end of the 2025 season and so was not competing in 2026. He will rejoin Toyota, the team he won his sold drivers' title with in 2019, and will be joined with his Estonian co-driver Martin Järveoja.

"It is a great honor to be back at Toyota, the team with which Martin and I became world champions. We have very good memories of this team, and I have great respect for the people here and everything they have achieved," Tänak said via a Toyota press release.

The WRC reported Toyota is also to bring back the Celica name to the WRC in 2027 as part of a major expansion that will see the Japanese manufacturer field two separate teams and two different cars under the championship's new technical regulations, with six drivers named across the operation.

Tänak and Järveoja will be driving for Toyota again, over seven years after leaving the team. Source: American Rally Association/Facebook

Toyota is also retaining the Yaris Rally1, which Tänak and Järveoja will be driving alongside two-time champion Kalle Rovanperä (Finland) and Takamoto Katsuta (Japan).

New world champion Elfyn Evans (Wales) will be number on driver for Toyota Racing in the all-new GR Celica Rally1, joined by Norwegian-Swedish driver Oliver Solberg and another Finn, Sami Pajari.

Rally portal Dirtfish reported Tänak said he was "probably a bit relieved" when he stepped away, and that the decision came during a period when "things were not really going as smooth as you would have expected."He added that he began to miss the championship during Monte Carlo, though he was "still happy not to be there on Thursday evening, worrying about the tires."

Toyota's 2027 team launch can be watched by clicking on the video player below.

As for the upcoming season, Tänak said: "It has been really nice to work with them again this year on developing the car. I have enjoyed my time away from rallying, but the desire to drive has remained strong. It is a new beginning for everyone and there are still many unknowns, but I am looking forward to returning to the rally stages."

Tänak drove for Toyota in 2018–19, winning the title in his second season and ending Frenchman Sébastien Ogier's dominant six-year reign. The pair won 10 WRC rounds during that spell. He then spent 2020–22 and 2024–25 with Hyundai, interspersed by a single season at M-Sport Ford in 2023. While he took 10 more wins after leaving Toyota including before a home crowd at the inaugural WRC Rally Estonia, he did not win a second world title up to 2025.

The Estonian announced exactly a year ago that he was putting his career on hold and did not compete in any WRC rounds in 2026, saying he wanted to be present for his children and to "reset, recharge my batteries and refocus."

Tänak, at left, with two of his new teammates at Toyota, Takamoto Katsuta and Kalle Rovanperä. Source: TOYOTA GAZOO Racing/X.com

Dirtfish reported Toyota's approach came through existing contacts within the team, who "have my number," Tänak said. Discussions began early in the season when the team realized its current drivers would be busy with the championship and the new car needed development driving. italics

According to Dirtfish Tänak called new WRC regulations "quite a challenging regulation" and said the rules will make the season "so open" he first wants to see how the cars compare to Rally2 machinery. italics

The Celica, central to Toyota's 1990s dominance, is being developed in parallel with the Yaris in Jyväskylä in central Finland, with homologation in December.

The 2027 season starts January 21 as per tradition with Rally Monte Carlo and ends 15 rounds later in Saudi Arabia in late November.

New technical regulations replace the 2022–2026 rules, with WRC27 cars using Rally2 engines, suspension, running gear and brakes, and Rally2 manufacturers able to homologate an aero kit to compete in the top class. Two new teams are due to compete at selected races alongside Toyota and Ford, while a question mark hangs over Hyundai's status for the 2027 season.

World.title: 3 new exhibitions mark Black Nights Film Festival's 30th anniversary
World.content:
Three exhibitions have opened in Tallinn's Telliskivi Creative City, looking back at the history of the Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), which opens its 30th edition on November 6.

The exhibition at the Three Trees outdoor gallery (Kolme puu õuegalerii) focuses on the festival's atmosphere and shows moments that have shaped the PÖFF.

Festival Director Tiina Lokk said PÖFF has developed rapidly over the past three decades, but it must continue to keep pace with changing global circumstances and demands.

"We have stabilized, we know our place, we more or less know our identity, and we know what we need to preserve about this festival. Now the next decade is very exciting, to see where we develop from here," she said.

Triin Tramberg took over as PÖFF's artistic director this year and is working to ensure that the festival will still be held 30 years from now.

"For us to be a good A-list festival, we need funding, and right now, name one sector that isn't facing a shortage of it. We are still trying to do something big here," she said.

The creative city's outdoor gallery is also hosting a photography exhibition titled "Stars in the Night," featuring 20 portraits of major figures from the film world who have visited the festival. Big names will also be attending this year, and films from a record number of countries will be screened.

"It simply shows our diversity and, in fact, how many good films are made around the world. We are very happy to have films from 87 countries. This allows us to show how different stories are told by different directors and to take our audiences on a journey," Tramberg added.

The third exhibition brings together all of PÖFF's posters for the first time. The newest on display is a poster by animation director Priit Pärn, which he designed especially for PÖFF's anniversary.

"It is very difficult to create an image that captures the meaning of a film festival. A film festival is like life itself: try showing what life is in a single image. I started from the idea that it had to be original and totally different from what a poster is. As if it were a 'Poster' with a capital P," Pärn said.

PÖFF begins on November 6 and runs until November 22.

World.title: PPA: Illegal immigration to Estonia has fallen, but may rise next spring
World.content:
The number of migrants crossing from Belarus into Latvia and Estonia has fallen over the last week, but the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) already expects the problems to return in the spring.

Thousands of migrants from Africa and the Middle East have crossed the Belarusian border into Latvia this year, as part of a long-running "hybrid attack" orchestrated by the regime in Minsk.

Almost 400 have been found in Estonia as smugglers try to move them on to Scandinavia, after Poland and Germany tightened checks at their borders to stop migrants traveling further west.

So far, 148 of the 388 migrants found to be in Estonia illegally have been handed back to Latvia, under EU rules. Fifteen people have been apprehended on suspicion of smuggling.

But while PPA Director General Egert Belitšev said on October 8 that the migration pressure could increase significantly before winter to beat the freezing temperatures, this has not been the case.

Indrek Aru, head of the Border Guard Bureau of the Northern Prefecture, said both Latvia and Estonia have seen the numbers fall. "Last week, we actually caught only 14 migrants," Aru told the "Uudis pluss" radio show. But an uptick cannot be ruled out ahead of the winter, he said

Indrek Aru. Source: ERR

Migrants travel covertly

In recent weeks, migrants have only been caught in Tallinn. Aru put this down to migrants traveling covertly, and smugglers do not want the police to detect their activities either.

"When people are in vans, enclosed spaces without windows or hidden under a carpet on the back seat of a car, then naturally it is not easy to catch them," he explained.

Spot checks are carried out on the Estonian-Latvian border and in Estonia, but the PPA cannot check every vehicle.

Smugglers often come from Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, or Ukraine. But some come from further afield and are in the Schengen Area legally. "They often arrived here a few years earlier, obtained a residence permit and are now trying to help their relatives or fellow citizens follow them," Aru said.

Conflicts in detention centers

Aru said tensions have risen in detention centers due to the uptick in residents. In most cases, arguments are about everyday matters, such as the television remote control or the queue for food.

"Today, we are also seeing tensions beginning to escalate between different ethnic groups," he added.

No very serious incidents have occurred so far, and no major attacks against officials have been observed. "These are more like squabbles among themselves," Aru explained.

Currently, illegal migrants have been temporarily accommodated at the detention facility in Pärnu.

A PPA swoop on suspected illegal migrants in the Nõmme district of Tallinn in July. Source: ERR

Deportation is a lengthy process

Deporting migrants from Estonia is a long process. Aru said gathering evidence is complicated, as the individuals need to be identified, as well as where they entered the Schengen Area and other circumstances.

If someone requests international protection from the Estonian state, the PPA must carry out separate procedures and assess their need for protection.

"Considering that they speak languages that we do not speak in Estonia, we have to carry out the procedures with the help of several different interpreters, and all of this takes time," Aru stated.

The Social Insurance Board and local governments have had to spend considerable time and resources establishing the origins of people who themselves claim to be minors. Kaja Rattas, head of the substitute care department at the Social Insurance Board, said communication with the minors' countries of origin takes place through the PPA.

However, some people have arrived in Estonia claiming to be minors but without documents to prove it. Local governments act on behalf of minors in PPA proceedings, which are necessary to establish the facts of their cases.

Determining age is difficult

Rattas said many experts are involved in the age verification process, which also includes interviews with the minors. The PPA has created an age assessment committee, which includes a child protection expert, a medical professional, a psychologist and a migration expert from the Tallinn Migration Center.

The Social Insurance Board has been assisting local municipalities, such as Rae near Tallinn, which have said they are struggling with the situation. Rattas said the agency has assisted outside of working hours, such as evenings and on weekends.

"Increasingly, the Social Insurance Board has also taken on representation procedures during normal working hours, precisely to reduce the burden on local governments," she added.

Since mid-October, the Social Insurance Board has taken responsibility for all representation of unaccompanied minors in PPA proceedings. This arrangement will continue in the future to relieve the pressure on local councils.

The PPA's Aru said that statistical data from previous years indicate that the situation eases with the arrival of winter.

"However, it is also relevant that Poland and Lithuania have significantly strengthened their control measures this year, which is why the illegal migration route has shifted further north," he said. This has led to greater pressure on Estonia. He believes that the number of illegal migrants will continue to rise in the spring of next year.

World.title: Drivers waiting until first frost to change to winter tires
World.content:
Car workshops in Tartu are ready for the seasonal tire change, but many drivers still seem to hope the warm weather will continue, and winter tires will not be needed for some time.

Mechanics say summer tires begin to lose grip at temperatures of 7 degrees Celsius. As the temperatures are already falling below 10 degrees Celsius, drivers should make the change now, several mechanics told Monday's "Aktuaalne kaamera" evening news show.

"People are already coming in and changing their tires, but you can still definitely get an appointment during the day," said Mihhail Mayastrishin, owner of the A-velg workshop.

"Last year, I think there was already snow on the ground at this time. Right now, it's a real slow period, to be honest," said Pärt Loskit, owner of the Tiremarket tire center.

Ideally, drivers should change their tires before the winter weather arrives.

"Many people who live outside the city of Tartu inevitably experience overnight frosts, roads can be slippery in places, and that's the main concern. Knowing Estonian weather, one moment it's 20 degrees outside and the next moment there's snow on the ground," said Kevin, a tire fitter at Rehvidtartus24.

While there are plenty of tire workshops in Tartu, there is a rising trend for people changing their own at home to save money.

"Usually, either the bolts have been tightened too much and can no longer be loosened, or there are problems with balancing," Loskit said, listing some of the problems that can arise.

Due to tariffs imposed on Chinese tires, the prices of cheaper tires have risen by almost half this year.

World.title: Tartu's 'self-service bar' scrutinized over underage and takeout drinking fears
World.content:
A Tartu bar where no staff work on site and drinks are bought from vending machines is being investigated by the city government, over whether it complies with alcohol laws, Tartu Postimees reported .

Merle Pau, chief specialist at Tartu City Government's business development department, said the city has opened a state supervision proceeding against the business, to establish whether the establishment, called Nuti baar, is violating alcohol law requirements.

Since there is no permanent staff member on site, there is no one to bar off-site sales – banned between the hours of 10 p.m. and 10 a.m. the following day – if patrons take the drinks they bought away from the bar, while fears have also arisen of under 18s being able to buy alcohol there.

Diana Lints, head of the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority's (TTJA) services supervision bureau, said no complaints have been received, but the authority is assessing whether the circumstances need further checking. "What matters is not only what the point of sale is called or what notices it has, but also how alcohol sales actually take place," she said.

Bar promoter Margus Tomp called Estonian law "outdated," and explained the Nuti baar is a private club, for this reason.

Tomp said the machine's ID verification is secure enough to prevent sales to minors, noting face recognition tech is used as well.

News of the bar's opening was shared on social media, where posts indicated an access code is needed to get in — though during Tartu Postimees said when it visited the door was open and entry was possible without this code.

Tomp said similar staffless bars exist elsewhere in the world, though Nuti is the only one in Estonia to his knowledge - there have been no issues with customers, he said.

Police in Tartu are aware of the bar's activities, and have also reported no incidents there up to now.

World.title: US dollar rates hold steady near 168,000 dinars across major Iraqi markets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate of the U.S. dollar against the Iraqi dinar maintained relative stability across parallel markets in major commercial centers on Tuesday morning, November 3, 2026, with retail selling prices hovering near the 168,000-dinar threshold per $100.

According to morning trading data, exchange desks in Baghdad posted retail selling rates at 168,000 dinars against buying bids of 167,500 dinars per $100.

In Erbil, counters registered selling quotes at 167,950 dinars alongside purchase offers of 167,500 dinars. Across local markets in Basra, foreign currency desks recorded retail selling prices at 168,250 dinars and purchase bids at 167,750 dinars per $100.

The parallel market spreads continue to trade at an elevated premium over the Central Bank of Iraq’s official benchmark rate, which remains set at 152,000 dinars per $100 (1,520 dinars per dollar).

World.title: Iraq targets 2028 WTO accession as ITC proposes national trade strategy
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi federal government is actively accelerating its accession procedures to join the World Trade Organization (WTO), targeting full membership compliance by 2028, according to Executive Director of the International Trade Centre (ITC) Pamela Coke-Hamilton.

Speaking on the Dinar Iqtisadi program broadcast by Al-Iraqiya News, Coke-Hamilton confirmed that the ITC continues to support Baghdad through technical reviews of domestic trade legislation, regulatory alignment, and capacity-building across both public institutions and the private sector.

Following Iraq’s submission of its market access offer on goods in September, authorities are finalizing the corresponding services offer. Coke-Hamilton noted that strong political commitment was evident in her high-level consultations with Iraq’s foreign and trade ministers, identifying the reform implementation schedule as the primary challenge.

Full WTO accession is projected to bolster international investor confidence by institutionalizing transparent, predictable commercial frameworks.

Coke-Hamilton outlined a formal proposal submitted to the Iraqi government to establish a comprehensive National Trade and Investment Strategy linked directly to Iraq’s National Development Plan (2024–2028).

Designed to identify promising non-oil sectors and expand employment for youth and women, the initiative responds to critical structural vulnerabilities highlighted by recent transit volatility in the Strait of Hormuz, where a single maritime disruption can yield an estimated $60 billion in economic shocks.

To insulate the sovereign economy from severe hydrocarbon price shocks, Coke-Hamilton emphasized priority diversification toward construction, tourism, information technology, and agro-industrial manufacturing.

Highlighting that micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) drive roughly 90% of Iraq’s domestic economic activity, Coke-Hamilton detailed the tangible footprint of ITC programs on the ground.

The SAAVI project, launched in 2020, has supported over 4,000 Iraqi farmers, generating a 70% increase in agricultural yield and exports, while ongoing programs like “Jobs” and “Masar” continue expanding vocational and technical apprenticeships in solar installation, green construction, and hospitality.

Iraqi produce—including commercial potato, tomato, and poultry varieties—has met modern retail standards to secure shelf placement in supermarket chains like Carrefour.

However, Coke-Hamilton warned that Iraqi agro-food exports remain constrained by the absence of internationally accredited domestic testing laboratories, forcing local exporters to send food samples abroad for testing at substantial logistical cost.

In the commercial sector, she noted that the Iraqi National Trade Fair facilitated more than $83 million in sales, attracting multinational conglomerates including Siemens, Alcatel, Nokia, and General Electric, reflecting Iraq’s emerging position as a viable regional hub for cross-border investment and trade integration.

World.title: Pandora to open at Baghdad Boulevard as modern retail expands in Iraq Gate
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Baghdad Boulevard is accelerating its commercial expansion within the Iraq Gate mixed-use development in central Baghdad, securing an agreement to bring global Danish jewelry house Pandora into its growing lineup of international retail tenants.

The upcoming branch marks another notable entry for multinational fashion and lifestyle brands establishing formal retail presence in the capital.

Situated on the grounds of the former Muthanna Airport complex in central Karkh, Iraq Gate has become one of Baghdad’s primary integrated urban projects, blending modern high-rise residential towers with pedestrian-friendly commercial arcades designed to capture rising domestic consumer demand.

The arrival of Pandora builds upon a curated tenant mix anchored heavily by premium specialty food and beverage operators. The boulevard currently hosts popular regional and local brands including international specialty chain Espressolab, heritage Iraqi coffee roaster Ridha Alwan, Grinders, Vanilla, and tech-lifestyle retailer DNA.

The clustering of established dining concepts alongside international personal-luxury brands illustrates a deliberate commercial strategy to build sustained, high-value foot traffic by pairing leisurely café culture with experiential shopping.

Beyond a single brand launch, the expansion reflects broader structural shifts in Baghdad’s commercial real estate landscape.

Private capital is increasingly flowing into managed, open-air lifestyle strips and secure mixed-use compounds that offer structured parking, pedestrian promenades, and standardized property management—amenities rarely available in the capital’s legacy commercial corridors like Mansour and Karrada.

As global brands seek stable franchise environments, modern developments like Baghdad Boulevard are serving as the primary launchpads for international retail investment in postwar Iraq.

World.title: Fly Baghdad resumes twice-weekly flights between Iraq and Pakistan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi airline Fly Baghdad has restarted operations to Pakistan, with twice-weekly flights between Baghdad and Karachi beginning October 21, 2026.

The Iraqi airline commemorated its return to the Pakistani market with an introductory flight and a ceremony celebrating the restoration of air connectivity between the two nations.

Fly Baghdad now runs two flights per week to Karachi and intends to add a twice-weekly service to Lahore in the near future.

The airline said that the extension intends to improve travel connections between Iraq and Pakistan, notably for religious pilgrims, tourists, and other passengers traveling between the two nations.

Amson Travel International, Fly Baghdad’s General Sales Agent in Pakistan, worked with the airline’s management and operational staff to resume services.

World.title: Barzani inaugurates three landmark automotive projects in Zakho
World.content:
Zakho (IraqiNews.com) – Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) Prime Minister Masrour Barzani officially inaugurated three landmark commercial, industrial, and motorsports projects in the Zakho Independent Administration, marking a significant milestone in advancing northern Iraq’s automotive infrastructure and domestic logistics capabilities.

The developments feature a newly completed central warehousing and logistics complex for Nissan Iraq, established to anchor nationwide distribution networks and streamline supply chains for vehicles and genuine spare parts across all Iraqi governorates.

Alongside the logistics facility, Barzani unveiled dedicated assembly and manufacturing facilities for prominent Chinese automotive brands JETOUR and HONGQI, representing a calculated shift toward localizing vehicle production, technology transfer, and industrial job creation in the region.

Complementing the commercial and industrial projects, the inauguration included the launch of the Zakho Motorplex, a purpose-built motorsports venue engineered for competitive closed-circuit racing, drifting exhibitions, off-road trials, and community automotive events.

The integrated launch positions Zakho as an emerging automotive gateway and trade hub, leveraging its strategic border geography to draw private investment and diversify the regional economy beyond the hydrocarbons sector.

World.title: US signals progress in Iran talks to avert flare-up
World.content:
Washington – US President Donald Trump signaled progress on Monday in talks with Iran to avoid a return to war, as Tehran reported “intensive” exchanges while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.

The fresh diplomatic signals came ahead of US midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Trump’s Republican Party is pushing to retain control of Congress, faced with voter dissatisfaction over the conflict and the soaring fuel prices it has triggered.

A deal with Tehran “could happen,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

“Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.”

But hours later, Washington’s diplomatic overtures were dashed by a report that the United States had attacked Iran, in what the Wall Street Journal said was the latest in a string of limited strikes it secretly carried out against the Islamic republic in recent weeks.

Iranian state media reported five explosions in rapid succession on Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US Central Command did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.

Earlier, oil prices plunged by more than seven percent on Monday on optimism over a possible end to the eight-month-old conflict.

The WSJ report came shortly before polls opened in the midterms, in which Democrats expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on Trump for the first time in two years.

– Reopen the strait –

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that indirect talks with Washington were taking place via mediators.

“Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive,” Araghchi told state media.

“Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active mediating role in these negotiations.”

Vice President JD Vance said both he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement.

“We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more,” Vance told reporters on Monday.

China also urged a return to diplomacy, while Iran’s security chief discussed the conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, marking the highest-level move in months.

Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said the messages received from Washington were “an acknowledgement of our victory.”

A senior Iranian official said that Tehran was ready to open the Hormuz strait, an export conduit for the energy-rich Gulf, within two days — as long as Washington agreed to its list of demands.

In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, with demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

“The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach,” Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters at a briefing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping also discussed the war with Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing on Monday — the first visit to China by the Gulf nation’s head of state since diplomatic ties were established.

“The two sides called for resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, urging the United States and Iran to pursue a peaceful path, achieve a ceasefire (and) prevent war entirely,” an Omani statement said.

– ‘No compromises’ –

China held meetings with Iranian and Saudi officials in Beijing on Monday as well.

Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security,” Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.

Bagheri told Wang that “Tehran’s stance on defending its national security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remains unchanged, and that Iran will make no compromises in this regard,” state TV reported.

In an interview with Al Jazeera released on Sunday, Araghchi said Washington must accept a new route agreed between Iran and Oman for transiting the strait.

He said Washington must also remove sanctions imposed recently and reduce American troop numbers in the region.

Trump has kept up his threats against Tehran, saying on Sunday that the United States may have to give Iran “the hammer” at some unspecified time.

On Saturday, the US leader said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets including Pickaxe mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.

Baqaei warned that any act of aggression against Iran “will be met with a powerful, immediate and comprehensive response.”

World.title: Stocks mostly down as AI concerns top plunge in oil prices
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stock markets struggled Tuesday following another AI-fuelled tech selloff on Wall Street that overshadowed a plunge in oil prices and signs of a possible breakthrough in talks to end the Iran war, with eyes also on the upcoming US midterm elections.

Investor fears about the vast sums being invested in the artificial intelligence complex have cast a pall over trading floors in the second half of the year, with many questioning firms’ profitability.

Earnings reports from titans including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft have shown they will keep pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips even as investors grow impatient for returns.

Monday saw Apple post forecast-topping sales and profits but warned that its gross margin — the percentage of sales left after output costs — would drop in October-December.

Earlier, leading AI firm Anthropic posted a more than 1,100 percent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly $900 billion in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month.

The investment pledges come amid a surge in borrowing costs, which have raised concerns about some companies’ financial positions owing to their huge debts, adding downward pressure to stock prices.

After a tough run last week, the selling continued at the start of this week with losses in Asian giants followed by their US counterparts on Wall Street where the Nasdaq ended 1.1 percent off.

And there was not much improvement Tuesday — Seoul-listed SK hynix and Samsung tanked around four percent, dragging the Kospi down more than two percent.

There were also losses in Taipei, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington, though Hong Kong, Manila and Jakarta edged up. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.

Even a more than seven percent plunge in oil prices Monday was unable to provide support.

The “collapse in crude should have been rocket fuel for the battered growth trade”, said SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“Cheaper energy takes heat out of inflation, eases the rates pressure and normally gives long-duration tech a meaningful updraft.

“Instead, the Nasdaq handed back the entire opening bounce and broke Friday’s lows, a fairly ugly sign that the selling is now being driven by something deeper than oil, yields or the dollar.”

Crude extended the losses in early Asian trade as the US and Iran sounded notes of optimism.

US President Donald Trump on Monday signalled progress in talks as Tehran said “intensive” exchanges were underway while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.

“But here’s the thing: we’re dealing from total strength. We can end it at any time. If I can make a deal, I’d rather do it, save a lot of lives.”

Vice President JD Vance separately said that both he and the president were optimistic about securing an agreement.

“We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more,” Vance told reporters on Monday.

That came after the Axios news outlet said he had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, the highest-level move from the White House in months.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government had been granted more authority by the country’s supreme leader to pursue peace talks.

Still, National Australia Bank’s Rodrigo Catril offered a word of caution.

“It is worth noting that the US and Iran’s positions have not materially changed,” he wrote in a commentary.

“Iran wants US restraint and economic relief (i.e. an end to hostilities, the lifting of the US naval blockade, relief from oil sanctions and the unfreezing of at least $12 billion in assets) before delivering the concessions Washington seeks, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

“The US is demanding concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme, but Iran wants to deal with the nuclear issue in separate talks at a later stage.

“Bottom line: for the stalemate to end, somebody needs to give ground, and it is unclear if either side is willing to do so.”
