IRAN FOREIGN MINISTER. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi attends a press conference at the Iranian embassy in New Delhi, India, May 15, 2026.

Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate as the powerful militia advances towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint that lies on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz

DUBAI, UAE – Talks between Iran and Saudi Arabia are ongoing as Tehran aims to reach new regional security arrangements for countries in the region without foreign military involvement, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on X on Tuesday, November 3.

Last week, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran, the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations since August. The US-Israeli war on Iran started in late February and since then, fighting has spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Riyadh said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to “prevent the return of military escalation,” as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis had intensified in recent weeks.

Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalated as the powerful militia advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint that lies on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis have also attacked Saudi oil facilities and airports including Riyadh’s international airport, disrupting flights and oil exports and drawing Saudi airstrikes on Yemen in response.

Impoverished Yemen has been mired in a civil war since the Houthis pushed the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government out of the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Ramps Up Civilian Airstrikes as ASEAN Envoy Visits
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime continued bombing civilian targets even as it hosted ASEAN’s special envoy last week, killing more than a dozen people and wounding over 50 across four days.

Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro visited the southern Shan State capital of Taungyi on an October 28-30 humanitarian mission, meeting the regime’s foreign minister during her trip.

Meanwhile, The Irrawaddy recorded nine regime airstrikes from October 29 to November 1, resulting in 16 deaths and 51 injuries. Over half of the attacks occurred in Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the ethnic Arakan Army (AA).

On Sunday, regime warplanes targeted Rakhine’s Kyaukphyu, a hub for China-backed projects and gas pipelines, along with AA-controlled townships of Kyauktaw, Pauktaw, and Mrauk-U.

In Mrauk-U, five people including a baby were killed and nine wounded when cluster bombs shattered a temporary maternity clinic.

The clinic was established after a December 10 bombing raid destroyed Mrauk-U District Hospital, killing at least 33 patients, caregivers and medical staff and injuring around 70.

Sunday’s airstrikes killed at total of 12 civilians and injured 32 others across Rakhine, according to an AA statement.

They came two days after the Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO) and a coalition of 70 local and international Rakhine groups called on the UN Security Council, ASEAN, international governments, and global humanitarian agencies to enforce a no-fly zone over Rakhine State.

In Karenni State’s Loikaw, three children were killed and eight injured when two regime fighter jets and a Y-12 aircraft bombed their school in Wanngawt village as holiday meals were being served on Sunday.

Any hope of a break in the bombing campaign as the regime pushes for regional reintegration was shattered the day Lazaro arrived. As the special envoy touched down on Wednesday, blasts hit Tawkyaunglay village monastery in Sagaing’s Chaung-U Township, where around 60 worshippers were gathered for Patthana chanting. The attack wounded a 57-year-old monk. Bombs struck a former prisoner-of-war camp in Chin State’s Hakha on the same day, but no casualties were reported.

On Saturday, an airstrike on a temporary shelter at Thaezalauk village monastery in Sagaing’s Homalin Township left seven displaced people injured. The attack came shortly after resistance forces captured the local regime outpost. Elsewhere in Sagaing, a woman was killed and three residents injured when a pair of gyrocopters attacked Duhtauk village in Salingyi Township despite the absence of clashes on the ground.

Human rights activists criticized Lazaro’s visit as bid to create an image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded regime to mask the reality of daily civilian atrocities and mass displacement.

According to data collected by the parallel National Unity Government, a total of 6,467 civilians have died in regime airstrikes since the February 2021 coup.

World.title: Regime, Thailand Discuss Russian LNG Supply Route via Dawei
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime and Thailand have discussed importing Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Myanmar and sharing supplies to help meet growing energy demand in both countries, according to regime media.

The proposal emerged during separate meetings in Bangkok on Saturday between junta Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin, Thai Energy Minister Akanat Promphan and Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov.

According to the regime, discussions focused on a trilateral energy cooperation framework under which Russian LNG would be shipped to Myanmar and distributed to Thailand. Officials also examined the possibility of building an LNG terminal in Dawei and utilizing existing gas pipeline infrastructure linking Myanmar and Thailand to transport imported gas.

The latest discussions follow Akanat’s visit to Naypyitaw on October 19, when he met regime chief Min Aung Hlaing and held separate talks with Ko Ko Lwin on expanding bilateral cooperation in the energy and natural gas sectors.

During those meetings, officials reportedly discussed plans for a Myanmar-Thailand-Russia energy trade network centered on the Dawei area.

The proposal has gained momentum in recent months. In August, Ko Ko Lwin met his Thai counterpart in Bangkok alongside prominent Myanmar oil magnate Michael Moe Myint, whose companies cooperate with the regime in the oil and gas sector.

The inclusion of Russia’s economic development minister in the latest round of talks suggests the three sides are moving to advance the Dawei-based energy trade initiative.

Analysts note that the interests of all three parties largely align. Myanmar and Thailand face growing energy needs, while Russia is seeking new markets for its abundant natural gas exports amid Western sanctions.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Russia in August, Myanmar and Russia signed memorandums of understanding covering the power and oil and gas sectors. Russian President Vladimir Putin said energy would remain a key pillar of bilateral cooperation and highlighted significant potential for LNG exports to Myanmar, including possible re-exports to third countries.

The junta has already signed several agreements with Russia covering fuel imports, including LNG, and says it expects to conclude an energy cooperation pact with Thailand in the near future.

The effort is also linked to the junta’s attempt to revive the long-delayed Dawei Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project, which has struggled to attract investment amid political instability and Western sanctions.

During his Russia visit, Min Aung Hlaing described the Dawei deep-sea port, special economic zone, and energy cooperation package including an LNG terminal, oil refinery, power plants and gas-based infrastructure projects as strategic pillars of Myanmar-Russia economic cooperation.

For Russia, closer ties with Myanmar could provide opportunities to expand investment and access new markets in Southeast Asia, which Moscow expects would offset economic restrictions imposed by Western countries.

Min Aung Hlaing has repeatedly portrayed Myanmar as a reliable partner for Russia in Southeast Asia, telling Putin that Myanmar stands ready to support deeper cooperation.

Thailand has long been involved in Myanmar’s energy sector through major offshore gas projects such as Yadana and Zawtika. Since the 2021 military coup, Thai companies have become some of the most significant foreign investors in Myanmar’s oil and gas industry after the withdrawal of several Western firms.

The junta also awarded the Min Ye Thu offshore project, the first new offshore project approved since the coup, to Thailand’s Gulf Petroleum Myanmar Co., Ltd.

Located off the coast of Tanintharyi in southern Myanmar, the Dawei Special Economic Zone is envisioned as a strategic hub incorporating a deep-sea port, industrial estate, power facilities and transport infrastructure, while giving Thailand direct access to the Indian Ocean.

In recent months, both Min Aung Hlaing and his deputy Nyo Saw visited Dawei to inspect “regional development tasks”. Myanmar military Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin also toured military commands in Tanintharyi Region in June, stressing the need to secure strategic projects including the Dawei deep-sea port and key transportation corridors.

However, analysts say ongoing armed conflict and instability in the region remain major obstacles to the realization of the Dawei project and broader energy cooperation plans.

World.title: China Reopens Trade Through Border Crossings Controlled by Armed Groups
World.content:
China has lifted restrictions on the flow of key goods into territories along the border that are controlled by ethnic armed organizations with ties to Beijing, allowing fuel, construction materials, medicines and other previously banned imports to enter Myanmar.

Residents and traders say China has recently relaxed some restrictions imposed when the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) and Kachin forces seized key border trade routes during anti-regime Operation 1027 in 2023–4.

At the military regime’s request at the time, Beijing blocked the flow of construction materials, machinery, electrical goods, fuel, medicines and explosives through those crossings.

“In Muse, previously restricted items can now be imported through Kyin San Kyawt border gate,” a Muse resident told The Irrawaddy. “Restrictions remain in place at the Sinphyushin and Nandaw gates that are still controlled by the regime.”

At the Namhkam border crossing controlled by the TNLA, trade has not yet fully resumed. TNLA spokesman Lway Yay Oo said only food and household goods are being allowed in to help improve living conditions for locals.

“The border gates have not fully reopened yet,” she told The Irrawaddy. “The relaxation benefits people living in border areas, but whether the crossings are fully reopened depends entirely on the Chinese government’s policy decisions.”

She added that a full reopening of border trade would help reduce shortages of fuel and medicine in the region.

The cash-strapped regime is furious that it can no longer tax imports and tries to intercept them elsewhere if they make their way further inland. In a cabinet meeting on Oct. 28, putschist president Min Aung Hlaing warned that smugglers are indirectly financing armed groups by paying them taxes, thereby strengthening their capacity and obstructing his own “peace” efforts.

In northern Shan itself, Chinese products are now plentiful and relatively cheap, but once they pass through Hsipaw, Kyaukme and Nawnghkio and onward to Pyin Oo Lwin, Mandalay and Yangon, it is a different story.

Transport operators say frequent inspections, unofficial payments and cargo checks at checkpoints have increased both delivery times and transportation costs, pushing up prices for consumers.

One transporter cited the example of a car tire that sells for around 380,000–400,000 kyats in the northern Shan capital of Lashio but can cost as much as 850,000–900,000 kyats in Mandalay.

“If the regime genuinely wants to reduce prices for consumers, it can establish a customs checkpoint in Lashio and allow legal imports with proper tax payments,” he said. “That would improve the flow of goods and bring prices down.”

Instead, Min Aung Hlaing has urged his ministers to intensify the crackdown on “smuggling” and ensure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through regime-controlled channels.

World.title: ASEAN Envoy’s Farce: Humanitarian Aid as Smokescreen for Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Special Envoy and Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro has staged a farcical “humanitarian mission” in Taunggyi, a safe city in a military-controlled part of Shan State, where there has been no fighting or war-related destruction since the military coup in 2021.

Meanwhile, her hosts, the Myanmar military junta, continue to send paramotors, gyrocopters and fighter jets to bomb villages, schools, hospitals, markets, Buddhist monasteries and residential houses, killing and maiming women, schoolchildren, babies and displaced civilians.

What Lazaro has done is a grotesque spectacle, a cynical manipulation of humanitarian aid and a shameful betrayal of the people of Myanmar.

Let me be absolutely clear: Lazaro is not an innocent diplomat who has been deceived or manipulated by the junta. She knows perfectly well what is happening in Myanmar. She knows about the daily airstrikes, the massacres of civilians and the deliberate obstruction of humanitarian assistance to communities most desperately in need.

She knows what she is doing. She has willingly played her part in this cynical, carefully choreographed farce.

The purpose of this theatrical humanitarian performance is to manufacture a false image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded military regime and provide ASEAN with another opportunity to rehabilitate Min Aung Hlaing and lift its ban on the criminal junta’s political representatives attending the bloc’s summits.

The junta decided where Lazaro could go, what she could see and whom she could meet. She was not allowed to meet Aung San Suu Kyi, despite repeated requests from the Philippines. She did not meet representatives of the National Unity Government, ethnic revolutionary organizations, local administrations or the civil society networks delivering humanitarian assistance in areas beyond junta control.

The military controlled the stage. Lazaro knowingly played her assigned role. She happily posed for photographs. And the junta collected the political dividends.

Her photographs from peaceful, junta-controlled Taunggyi are part of a carefully constructed smokescreen intended to conceal the reality of Myanmar: daily atrocities against civilians, relentless aerial bombardment, mass displacement and the systematic obstruction of humanitarian assistance precisely where it is needed most.

I do not object to food reaching people displaced by the junta’s deliberate burning of villages and bombing of towns and cities. Every bag of rice matters to those who receive it.

What is outrageous is that ASEAN’s special envoy has played along with this farce, allowing humanitarian aid to be used as a propaganda instrument to whitewash the very military responsible for creating Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe.

What did Lazaro achieve?

No meaningful breakthrough in humanitarian access to resistance-controlled areas, where atrocities continue, hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, and millions of internally displaced people remain beyond the reach of international aid. No access to Aung San Suu Kyi. No genuine engagement with all relevant stakeholders. No commitment by the military to stop bombing civilians.

Instead, the junta proudly announced that its foreign minister had discussed with Lazaro the restoration of Myanmar’s “original role and rights” within ASEAN.

There it is. The real political dividend of this entire farce.

ASEAN’s own Five-Point Consensus requires an end to violence and engagement with all concerned parties. Yet Lazaro allowed the junta to dictate the terms of her mission, select her interlocutors and exploit humanitarian assistance for its campaign of international rehabilitation.

We should refuse to pretend that this was merely another unsuccessful diplomatic initiative undertaken with good intentions. Lazaro was not simply a spectator in this shameful performance. She was an informed and willing participant. She chose to cooperate in a spectacle that served the junta’s political interests.

She cannot hide behind diplomatic language about dialogue, humanitarian assistance and constructive engagement.

While Min Aung Hlaing’s forces continue their campaign of aerial terror against the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s special envoy has knowingly helped project an image of his regime as a legitimate and cooperative partner deserving renewed international acceptance.

Instead of exposing and confronting the perpetrators of Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe, Lazaro has willingly participated in a performance that helps polish their bloodstained image.

The people of Myanmar do not need ASEAN’s humanitarian theater. They need humanitarian assistance that actually reaches those most in need. They need protection from the military’s relentless airstrikes. They need ASEAN to stop providing diplomatic cover and opportunities for international rehabilitation to those responsible for their suffering.

Igor Blazevic is a senior adviser at the Prague Civil Society Centre. Between 2011 and 2016 he worked in Myanmar as the head lecturer of the Educational Initiatives Program.

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers. Chinese state-linked firms provided raw materials and equipment for Myanmar’s ordnance factories including aircraft parts and explosives precursors used in attacks on civilians.

A milestone for China’s cross-Myanmar pipeline

The Myanmar–China crude oil pipeline has transported more than 100 million metric tons of crude oil since it began operations in 2017, PipeChina announced earlier this week. Stretching 771 km from embattled Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State through northern Shan State to Yunnan Province, the twin oil and gas pipelines are strategic lifelines that reduce Beijing’s dependence on the congested and vulnerable Malacca Strait.

One of China’s four major energy import corridors, the pipelines traverse 22 townships across Rakhine, Magwe, Mandalay and Shan, and today ethnic armed organizations such as the Arakan Army (AA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) control substantial sections there.

Myanmar is projected to receive around $1.5 billion annually from the pipelines, though the exact profit structure is unclear. It certainly receives a fixed, annual right-of-way payment of $13.81 million for both pipelines plus $1 per ton of crude transiting through the country—PipeChina reckons at an average rate of 35,000 tons a day, most of it disgorged at Kyaukphyu from the Middle East. PipeChina and CNPC own 51 percent, while state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49 percent.

The gas pipeline, meanwhile, started operation in 2013 and carries output from the offshore Shwe fields, with a a design capacity of 12 billion cubic meters per year. China National Petroleum Corporation holds a controlling 50.9 percent stake and MOGE just 7.365 percent. Sales of natural gas from Shwe to China are estimated to generate around $1 billion annually.

To finance its stakes, MOGE borrowed around $1.5 billion from the China Development Bank at an interest rate of 4.5 percent, according to Sandhi Governance Institute. Nobody knows how much of that has been paid back or ever will be.

Chinese aid bottleneck throttles Myanmar regime’s budget

Myanmar’s military regime faced severe fiscal strain in the 2025–2026 fiscal year when China withheld approval for multiple projects under the Lancang–Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Special Fund. Naypyitaw’s budget deficit shot up amid overspending by ministries and loss‑making state enterprises.

Deputy Planning and Finance Minister Kyaw Htin admitted that the deficit was exacerbated by failure to secure expected grants, project approvals, and technical resources from Beijing. The Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development did submit proposals for LMC financing in 2025, but the response was deafening silence. Likewise, the Industry Ministry budgeted for computer hardware and technical equipment for Chinese experts who were to come to Myanmar for a technology transfer, but they never turned up and the equipment was not delivered.

The reasons are shrouded in mystery. In a recent article in regime newspapers, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia claimed China had backed 140 development projects in Myanmar through the LMC Special Fund. In March, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said the country benefited from 132—worth $38.6 million—since 2017.

Either way it would be the biggest handout to any Mekong country.

Some older Chinese projects are already falling to pieces. Kyaw Htin admitted that power transmission lines from two China‑backed hydropower plants—the 240 MW Dapein Hydropower Station in Bhamo, Kachin State and the 600 MW Shweli 1 Dam in Namhkam Township, northern Shan State—were damaged and could not be repaired due to “security conditions,” depriving the regime of projected electricity revenues.

Russian grant money that had been promised was also not forthcoming, Kyaw Htin said. The rest of the world has suspended official development aid since the 2021 coup.

More trouble in Shan over Kokang ‘Sinicization’

The past two weeks have seen growing tensions between Shan communities and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) that is consolidating its control in territories it has seized over the past three years.

The Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—comprising the armed Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the civilian Shan Nationalities League for Democracy, and other Shan opposition groups—issued a statement accusing the MNDAA of undermining ethnic rights, erasing Shan cultural heritage, and imposing Chinese language and governance systems there.

The MNDAA rejected the allegations as “baseless” and “politically motivated” and accused the SSJAC in turn of stirring the ethnic pot.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations also released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and stability on the Chinese border. And in April, Ta’ang civil society groups condemned the MNDAA after it seized Kutkai, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

Founded in 1989 from the remnants of the Communist Party of Burma, the MNDAA is rooted in Kokang, an enclave that is 90 percent ethnic Chinese. Once limited to Laukkai and Kongyan townships, the group has expanded its territory west of the Salween River since Operation 1027, and locals report a great deal of painting over of signboards and other attempts to suppress their languages and identities by their brash new masters.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Hosts Russian Mining Billionaire After Approving Gold Ventures
World.content:
Russian mining billionaire Vladislav Sviblov — head of Russia’s Areal Group — met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Wednesday to discuss cooperation in mineral exploration and mining between the two Western-sanctioned actors.

According to regime media, both sides spoke of “mutual trust and friendly relations” between Myanmar and Russia and discussed cooperation in education, science, and technology.

Formerly known as Highland Gold Mining Limited, Areal Group rebranded after expanding beyond precious metals into base, rare, and strategic minerals. Areal and its owner have been under U.S. and EU sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Similarly isolated by international sanctions after the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing and his regime have been courting economic and diplomatic support from Russia.

On the day that Sviblov arrived in Naypyitaw, Myanmar’s Investment Commission approved 16 new investment proposals — including large‑scale gold mining ventures. The green lights came just weeks after Min Aung Hlaing invited investment in Myanmar’s mineral sector at the Russia–Myanmar Economic Forum in August, touting “value‑added mineral products” as a new export base.

Russia’s sanctions‑hit companies have leaned toward Asian markets since 2022, while Myanmar’s regime, starved of foreign currency, is eager to attract Russian capital.

Regime insiders suggest rare earths may have been on the agenda of Wednesday’s meeting, given the presence of natural resources minister Khin Maung Yi, while Sviblov himself spoke on on rare earths at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.

Myanmar boasts rich deposits of the critical minerals, exporting roughly half of the world’s heavy rare earth elements over the border to China.

Meanwhile, the U.S.’s recent reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that a global scramble for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. Regime supporters now boast that the junta has a “rare earth card” to play, pointing to parallel interest from India.

However, almost all of Myanmar’s estimated 600 rare earth mines lie beyond the regime’s control in territory overseen by ethnic armed groups. Despite repeated invitations by the regime and talk of “strategic partnerships,” Russian [mining?] businesses have yet to make any substantial investments in Myanmar.

World.title: Japan, UNDP Commit $ 3 Million to Greener Mining in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Japan and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) provide Kazakhstan with $3 million to strengthen environmental oversight and promote sustainable development in its rare metal and rare earth mineral sector under a new initiative launched Oct. 30, reported the UNDP’s press service.

Funded by Japan, the project will be implemented by UNDP in partnership with Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction.

Kazakhstan has identified more than 120 rare-metal and rare-earth deposits nationwide. As global demand for critical minerals grows, ensuring that their extraction and processing meet environmental standards is becoming increasingly important.

The initiative will help Kazakhstan develop the analytical, regulatory and technological foundations for sustainable rare metal and rare earth mineral supply chains. It will focus on integrating environmental standards and digital monitoring at an early stage to identify and address environmental risks before large-scale industrial development begins.

“This joint initiative with UNDP and Japan will allow us to significantly strengthen our efforts by integrating advanced green technologies and international environmental standards into our production chains,” said Olzhas Alibekov, deputy chair of the Industry Committee at the Ministry of Industry and Construction.

According to Yasumasa Iijima, Japan’s ambassador to Kazakhstan, the initiative aligns with Japan’s priorities of Green and Resilience and Connectivity, announced at the December 2025 Central Asia-Japan Summit.

“Japan intends to provide comprehensive support for the project,” he said.

“The growing demand for critical minerals brings new economic opportunities, but it also calls for greater environmental responsibility. Strong environmental governance, pollution prevention and the protection of local communities must be central to the sector’s development,” said Katarzyna Wawiernia, UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan.

“Through this partnership, UNDP aims to help Kazakhstan strengthen the standards, expertise and monitoring needed to manage environmental risks and ensure that development benefits people while safeguarding ecosystems,” she added.

Japan has long partnered with UNDP to advance sustainable development and resilience in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

UNDP and Japan are currently implementing four joint initiatives in Kazakhstan focused on flood risk management at dams, addressing the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level, improving urban resilience to climate and disaster risks, and strengthening disaster preparedness in Central Asia.

The new project is the fifth initiative under the partnership and expands cooperation to environmental governance and sustainable natural resource management.

World.title: Kazakhstan Restores Oil Flows Through Key Export Pipeline
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has resumed oil transportation through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline after suspending operations following drone attacks on facilities in Russia, according to the Kazakh Ministry of Energy.

The pipeline returned to operation after specialists inspected the infrastructure and confirmed that the equipment was safe to use.

Oil transportation was suspended at 6:09 a.m. Astana time Monday, following drone attacks on facilities at the Samara production and dispatch center.

No casualties were reported, and the situation remains under the ministry’s control, according to the statement.

The Atyrau-Samara pipeline is Kazakhstan’s second-largest oil export route by transportation volume, after the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) system.

World.title: Global Tech Weekend 2027 to Launch in Tbilisi With Startup Pitches
World.content:
ASTANA – Global Tech Weekend (GTW) will hold the official launch event of its 2027 program on Dec. 5 at Mtatsminda Hall in Tbilisi. The event will feature an unconventional pitch session, with startup founders presenting their ideas to international investors aboard the Mtatsminda Ferris Wheel.

The ferris wheel session will be the evening’s main highlight. Each selected startup founder will have six minutes, or one full rotation of the ferris wheel, to pitch their business idea to investors. The pitches will also be livestreamed, allowing audiences beyond the venue to follow the presentations.

The winner will be announced later that evening during an awards ceremony.

According to the organizers, the format is designed to create opportunities for direct engagement between startup founders and investors while moving beyond traditional pitch sessions.

“The tech ecosystem has many promising startups whose growth depends, in part, on meeting the right investors, securing funding, and expanding internationally. The ‘Pitch in a Ferris Wheel’ experience is designed to facilitate these connections: six minutes, one rotation, and a direct conversation between a founder and an investor,” said Medea Janjghava, CEO of Global Tech Weekend.

Following the session, GTW will present its full calendar for 2027, along with its plans to expand its international network and establish new partnerships.

The event is expected to bring together representatives from more than 10 sectors, including technology, finance, international organizations, corporate leadership, creative industries and media.

In 2026, Global Tech Weekend expanded its activities across San Francisco, Tashkent and Tbilisi. Its Tbilisi festival, held June 19-21, brought together more than 10,000 attendees, 250 speakers, 300 investors and 150 partners from more than 12 sectors, according to the organizers.

The Global Tech Weekend 2027 Official Launch Event will be held in a closed format, with attendance available by prior registration only through Global Tech Weekend’s official Luma page.

More information is available on the Global Tech Weekend website.

World.title: Erdoğan Sends Warm Message to Tokayev While Flying Over Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent greetings to Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev while flying over Kazakhstan en route to South Korea, Aibek Smadiyarov, the Kazakh president’s press secretary, said on his Telegram channel on Nov. 2.

“On my way to the Republic of Korea for an official visit, I am flying over the territory of our historical ancestral homeland, friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan. The successful outcomes and warm memories of my visit to Kazakhstan in May this year, as well as your recent visit to Ankara to attend the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, remain fresh in our minds,” Erdoğan wrote.

“Taking this opportunity, I would like to extend my sincere greetings and best wishes for your good health and personal happiness, as well as continued prosperity and well-being for the brotherly people of Kazakhstan,” he added.

Tokayev thanked Erdoğan for the warm welcome extended to the Kazakh delegation during its official visit to Ankara and the OTS Summit.

“I express my heartfelt gratitude to Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for his attention and hospitality in Ankara. I am confident that the friendship and strategic partnership between our countries will continue to grow stronger,” Tokayev wrote on his X account.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Annual Inflation Slows to 9.2% in October
World.content:
ASTANA – Annual inflation in Kazakhstan slowed to 9.2% in October, down 3.4% from 12.6% in the same month last year, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

Consumer prices rose 0.5% month on month in October, compared with 0.6% in September. Annual inflation stood at 8.5% in October 2024 and 12.6% in October 2025. Food prices increased 7.6% year on year in October, while non-food goods rose 10.4% and paid services became 10.3% more expensive.

On a monthly basis, food prices increased 0.2%, non-food goods rose 0.8% and paid services climbed 0.5%.

Among food products, the largest annual price increases were recorded for sausages and meat products, up 11.2%, non-alcoholic beverages, up 10.1%, eggs, up 9.9%, and fermented milk products, up 9.4%. Some food prices declined. Fruits, berries and nuts became 2.2% cheaper year on year, while sugar prices fell 2.9%.

Annual inflation in non-food goods reached 10.4%. Clothing prices rose 11%, footwear increased 11.1%, and personal goods became 11.3% more expensive. Gasoline prices climbed 8.6%.

Paid services recorded annual inflation of 10.3%. Housing rents saw one of the steepest increases, rising 17.4%, while the cost of housing maintenance and repairs increased 12.3%. Housing-related services, water, electricity, gas and other fuels became 11.2% more expensive over the year. Some utility costs declined, with cold water prices falling 1.7% and wastewater services becoming 0.8% cheaper.

Inflation varies across regions

Regional inflation rates differed considerably in October. The Aktobe Region recorded the lowest annual inflation at 7.5%, followed by the Mangystau and Pavlodar regions at 7.7% each and the Abai Region at 7.9%.

Annual inflation reached 10% in Astana, 9.2% in Almaty and 8.8% in Shymkent. The highest rate was recorded in the North Kazakhstan Region at 10.9%, followed by the Akmola Region at 10.8% and the Zhetisu Region at 10.3%.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans to Build Strategic Uranium Reserve of 150,000 Tons by 2050
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is considering the creation of a state strategic uranium reserve to secure fuel supplies for future nuclear power plants, with a target of reserving at least 150,000 tons of uranium by 2050, Almasadam Satkaliyev, chairman of the Agency for Atomic Energy, said at a parliamentary committee meeting, reported the Kazinform news agency.

The target is outlined in Kazakhstan’s Nuclear Industry Development Strategy through 2050, which also supports the development and approval of a framework for establishing the reserve.

Speaking at a meeting of the Kurultai Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Energy, Satkaliyev said the agency was reviewing its approach to uranium resource management, treating uranium not only as a raw material but also as a strategic resource for the country’s future economic development.

“To ensure that future nuclear power plants have the fuel they need, the creation of a state strategic uranium reserve is under consideration,” Satkaliyev said.

The agency is currently developing approaches and mechanisms for building the reserve, taking into account Kazakhstan’s long-term nuclear energy needs. The proposed reserve would be a multi-layered system covering the entire nuclear fuel supply chain, from setting aside uranium resources in the ground to establishing physical stocks of natural uranium and reserves of ready-to-use nuclear fuel.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev previously called for the creation of a state strategic uranium reserve in his address to the nation.

World.title: Alatau City Secures $ 1.3 Billion in Deals During London Investment Roadshow
World.content:
ASTANA – Nine agreements with international partners worth a combined $1.3 billion were signed during an investment roundtable for Alatau City in London on Nov. 2, as Kazakhstan launched a European roadshow to attract foreign investment for the city’s development.

The agreements cover infrastructure and investment project financing, the development of educational and medical facilities, and expanded international cooperation.

The parties plan to explore projects to establish educational institutions in partnership with the University of Exeter, Brighton College and Repton Group. Cooperation with AstraZeneca and Crescent Meditours will focus on medical infrastructure, investment and scientific exchange.

Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev led the Kazakh delegation and presented Alatau City’s development concept, investment opportunities and prospective infrastructure projects to representatives of international companies and financial institutions.

Bozumbayev emphasized the city’s strategic importance.

“We are not starting the roadshow in London by chance. It is one of the world’s leading financial and legal centers. The United Kingdom is our strategic partner. Alatau City is a national project launched at the initiative of the head of state. We are creating a new center for business, finance, technology and logistics that is expected to become an important link in economic cooperation between Europe and Asia,” Bozumbayev said.

The city’s key advantages include a special legal regime established under a constitutional law. It provides for the application of principles of English and Welsh law, investment protection mechanisms and a predictable business environment.

An expert session featured international law firms Norton Rose Fulbright, Reed Smith and Boies Schiller Flexner. Discussions focused on investment-related legal frameworks, public-private partnerships, international arbitration, digital asset regulation and commercial dispute resolution. Participants also discussed plans to establish a specialized investment court in Alatau City based on the principles of English law.

The program included meetings with executives from the London Stock Exchange, Brookfield Asset Management, Société Générale, J.P. Morgan and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Discussions focused on attracting institutional capital, project financing and potential participation by international financial institutions in developing the city’s energy, transport and engineering infrastructure.

Alatau City’s investment portfolio includes 67 projects valued at approximately $6.9 billion, expected to create around 55,000 jobs. The city is also implementing 26 engineering and transport infrastructure projects worth 35.3 billion tenge (US$7.8 million), covering electricity, water and gas supply, sewerage networks and roads.

The roadshow will continue with meetings with UK government agencies, financial institutions and strategic partners. Germany will be the next stop on the European roadshow.

World.title: Central Asia Needs More Than Power Lines to Build Regional Electricity Market, EDB Report Finds
World.content:
ASTANA – Central Asia could unlock significant economic benefits from closer cooperation between its electricity systems, with a developed regional architecture potentially generating up to $640 million in annual gross benefits, according to a new report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB). However, the region’s ability to realize this potential will depend less on building new power lines alone than on addressing grid bottlenecks, improving operational coordination and establishing reliable rules for cross-border electricity trade.

The report, titled Energy Without Borders: The Architecture of Power Connectivity in Central Asia, prepared in cooperation with the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), notes that the region is not starting its energy integration from scratch. Yet what was designed for a different energy reality is increasingly struggling to accommodate rising demand, new renewable energy capacity and changing patterns of electricity consumption.

The problem goes beyond generating capacity

The Central Asia Power System (CAPS), which connects Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan and southern Kazakhstan, had an installed capacity of 38.6 gigawatts as of Jan. 1, 2025. In 2024, the system generated 125.4 billion kilowatt-hours, while consumption totaled 142.2 billion kilowatt-hours.

Regional electricity trade has recovered considerably, increasing from 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours in 2010 to 12.1 billion kilowatt-hours in 2024. Nevertheless, its share of consumption remains below historical levels, at about 8.5% compared with 13% in 1990, and is about half the level observed in the European Union (EU), the report reads.

The EDB identifies a distinction that is particularly important for understanding the region’s energy constraints: installed capacity does not necessarily translate into electricity that can actually be supplied. During critical hours, generating capacity may be unavailable because of fuel shortages, hydrological limitations, equipment conditions, thermal power plants operating in cold reserve or insufficient transmission capacity.

Around 6.6 gigawatts of capacity was unavailable for various reasons during the 2024 annual peak, illustrating why the region cannot rely on installed generation figures alone when assessing its energy security.

Transmission infrastructure presents another constraint. During the 2024-2025 winter operating period, actual electricity flows on several monitored transmission interfaces exceeded allowable levels, with the actual-to-permissible ratio ranging from 102% to 123%.

In Kazakhstan, the North-South transit corridor operated at 2,395 megawatts against an allowable 2,100 megawatts, or 114% of its permissible level. The Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan interface also recorded flows of 1,600 megawatts against allowable levels of 1,100-1,300 megawatts.

“Physical interconnection does not equal commercially available transmission capacity,” the report emphasizes, explaining that a power line between two systems does not automatically mean additional electricity can be transmitted safely or commercially at any given moment.

For regional electricity trade to expand, transmission capacity must be assessed against stability requirements, voltage conditions, emergency protection systems and existing power schedules.

Why Kazakhstan’s North-South Corridor matters

The report places southern Kazakhstan among the region’s major electricity load centers, highlighting its dependence on the North-South transmission corridor that connects it to the country’s northern power system.

The electricity balance of southern Kazakhstan is covered roughly equally by domestic generation and electricity flows from northern Kazakhstan, meaning that the transmission corridor is not simply a route for regional electricity trade but an essential part of the country’s domestic energy security.

An emergency shutdown of the North-South line would deprive the southern regions of approximately 2,000 megawatts of power flows, significantly complicating the system’s ability to respond to an outage. At the same time, imbalances elsewhere in the Central Asian power system can place additional pressure on the corridor, increasing the risk of overloads.

Kazakhstan also participates in seasonal electricity exchanges with Kyrgyzstan, receiving electricity during the agricultural growing season under reciprocal arrangements linked to irrigation water supplies and providing electricity during other periods. In recent years, Kazakhstan’s electricity exports to Kyrgyzstan have exceeded imports, reflecting lower water levels in the Toktogul Reservoir and growing domestic demand in Kyrgyzstan.

This makes the reliability of Kazakhstan’s internal transmission network directly relevant to the broader regional system. The report identifies strengthening northern and southern transmission corridors, as well as the Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan interconnection, as important priorities for improving the availability of electricity transfers across the CAPS.

Among the possible longer-term solutions, the report discusses an approximately 1,500-kilometer, 2,000-megawatt high-voltage direct current link from Ekibastuz GRES-1 toward the Zhambyl or Shymkent area, as well as a potential back-to-back HVDC connection between the CAPS and Kazakhstan’s Unified Power System. Both options would require separate feasibility assessments.

Renewable energy requires more flexibility

The expansion of solar and wind generation is adding another dimension to the challenge. While countries across Central Asia are increasing renewable energy capacity, the region’s transmission infrastructure, storage and balancing capabilities are not developing at the same pace.

Uzbekistan’s renewable energy capacity could reach 25 gigawatts by 2030 under announced plans. However, under conservative assumptions, the country’s renewable electricity curtailment is projected to rise from about 2.2 billion kilowatt-hours in 2026 to 3.5 billion kilowatt-hours in 2028.

Curtailment occurs when electricity generation must be reduced because the power system cannot absorb or transmit the available energy. This means that newly installed renewable capacity may not translate into an equivalent increase in usable electricity, while financial obligations under power purchase agreements may continue even when generation is curtailed, depending on contractual terms.

The EDB notes that regional integration could help address this problem by expanding the area where electricity surpluses can be used, providing access to flexible hydropower generation, and allowing neighboring systems to balance fluctuations in solar and wind output.

Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are particularly important in this regard. Their hydropower plants, including the Toktogul Reservoir, the Naryn Cascade and the Nurek hydropower plant, provide peak support, operating reserves and seasonal flexibility to neighboring systems.

However, the report stresses that hydropower flexibility should not be treated as a free resource automatically available to downstream countries. Water is also essential for irrigation, food security and interstate water-management obligations. Providing electricity on demand or adjusting hydropower generation to balance renewable sources involves operational costs and constraints that must be recognized and compensated.

The report therefore recommends treating hydropower flexibility as a measurable ancillary service, with payment mechanisms that reflect the value of balancing capacity while respecting national water-management responsibilities.

Integration could bring $120 million in annual net benefits

The economic case for regional cooperation extends beyond increasing the volume of electricity traded between countries. According to the EDB, the potential benefits come through four main channels: electricity trade arbitrage, shared reserves, reduced renewable energy curtailment and lower emergency-support costs.

Its preliminary scenario-based assessment estimates that partial integration could generate an annual gross system-wide effect of $193 million, against annualized costs of $75 million, for a net benefit of about $118 million.

Under a deeper integration scenario, the gross effect increases to $398 million, while annualized costs reach $275 million, producing a net benefit of approximately $123 million.

An advanced regional architecture could generate up to $640 million in annual gross benefits. However, the associated annualized costs would also rise to approximately $600 million, bringing the estimated net effect to around $40 million in the central case.

These figures suggest that deeper integration does not automatically translate into proportionally greater economic returns. The EDB identifies diminishing marginal returns as an important consideration, noting that relatively inexpensive improvements in coordination and the use of existing infrastructure can deliver substantial gains, while later stages require much larger investments in transmission networks, digital systems and institutions.

The report’s authors stress that these calculations are preliminary screening estimates rather than forecasts or guaranteed financial returns for individual countries, utilities or investors. Under unfavorable conditions, particularly when infrastructure utilization is low and investment costs are high, the net effect could even become negative, especially under the advanced integration scenario.

The distribution of benefits is another issue to address. One country may benefit from reduced renewable energy curtailment, another from transit revenues, while another may receive payments for hydropower flexibility or reduce its emergency electricity costs. Without transparent arrangements for allocating expenses and benefits, a project that makes economic sense for the region as a whole may still prove difficult to implement politically.

Regional market without a supranational regulator

Rather than recommending the immediate creation of a fully integrated regional electricity market or a supranational regulator, the EDB proposes a phased approach that builds on existing bilateral arrangements while gradually introducing more sophisticated trading and balancing mechanisms.

The first stage, covering 2026-2028, focuses on the operational foundations: settlement metering, secure data exchange, coordinated dispatch schedules, a registry of cross-border transactions, rules for settling electricity imbalances and accounting for emergency supplies.

The next stage, for 2028-2030, would introduce a pilot day-ahead electricity market, subject to confirmed available transmission capacity, alongside priority grid upgrades, improved automatic generation control and payment mechanisms for balancing energy and ancillary services.

After 2030, provided the necessary technical and institutional conditions are in place, the region could move toward full-scale real-time balancing, regional assessments of resource adequacy and mechanisms recognizing reliable cross-border contributions to electricity supply. Importantly, national system operators would retain full control over their domestic power systems throughout the process.

The report also considers the region’s external electricity connections as part of a broader portfolio of opportunities, including the northern route linking Kazakhstan with Russia and the Eurasian power system, the CASA-1000 southern corridor to South Asia, the eastern route toward China and the proposed Trans-Caspian Green Energy Corridor. Their commercial potential, however, depends on the reliability of the internal Central Asian system, available generation and external political and regulatory conditions.

Ultimately, the report’s argument is that the future of regional energy cooperation will depend on whether countries can move beyond physical connectivity toward predictable operating rules, transparent data exchange and a credible system for sharing both costs and benefits.

“Central Asia already has power lines. What is still lacking is an ‘architecture of trust’ among countries, operators, and investors,” reads the report, warning that without these foundations, existing infrastructure may remain little more than lines on a map.

World.title: Karabakh: Why have only 40,000 of planned 140,000 Azerbaijanis returned?
World.content:
Return of Azerbaijanis to Karabakh

Azerbaijan will mark Victory Day on 8 November. The first state programme, known as the “Great Return”, is due to conclude at the end of this year. According to data from the State Statistical Committee, 40,520 former internally displaced persons (IDPs) had returned to Karabakh and East Zangezur as of 1 October.

However, under the programme, 140,000 people were expected to return by the end of 2026. With just three months remaining before the programme’s conclusion, only around 29% of the target had been met.

In 2025, JAMnews reported on the social problems associated with the return of displaced people. This time, we examine a different question:

Why has less than a third of the target been achieved as the first programme nears its end, and what could the second programme change?

What do the figures show?

Indicator Target

Latest figures

Number of former internally displaced persons (IDPs) who have returned

Around 140,000 people

40,520 people (as of 1 October)

Number of settlements 100 47 (as of September)

Area cleared of landmines 280 000 hectares

Around 300,000 hectares (as of September)

Funding

More than 32bn manats (approx. $18.8bn)

More than 25bn manats (approx. $14.7bn) (2020–2026)

Sources: Official government portal, State Statistical Committee, Prime Minister Ali Asadov and Azerbaijan National Agency for Mine Action (ANAMA).

The pace of returns is increasing. At the beginning of the year, the number of returnees stood at 26,014. This means that a further 14,506 people returned to the region over nine months. If the current pace continues, it will take another five years for the remaining roughly 100,000 people to return.

The frequently cited figure of 96,068 refers to the total number of people living, working and studying in the region. In January, President Ilham Aliyev said that “120,000, 130,000 or 140,000 people” could be living and working there by the end of the year. However, he also acknowledged that implementation of the programme could take longer than expected:

“I have told everyone, and I can tell the public now, that I have never set any deadlines.”

Nevertheless, the programme itself sets the end of 2026 as the deadline for achieving its target.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, told Meydan TV that around 20 of the 47 settlements had been rebuilt, while the remainder were villages that came under Azerbaijani control in 2023.

That same year, around 100,000–120,000 ethnic Armenian residents of the region were forced to flee to Armenia. Yerevan describes the events as ethnic cleansing, while Baku maintains that Armenians can return if they accept Azerbaijani citizenship.

What has the money been spent on?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that more than 25bn manats (approximately $14.7bn) had been allocated from the state budget for the reconstruction of the region since 2020.

This year’s budget earmarked 3.5bn manats (approximately $2.06bn) for reconstruction. According to Finance Ministry figures, 1.76bn manats (approximately $1.035bn) was spent over the first nine months of the year. Of this amount, 891.8m manats (approximately $524.6m) went towards infrastructure development, while a further 692.5m manats (approximately $407.35m) was allocated to projects in education, healthcare and culture.

Ilham Aliyev explained the distribution of funds, saying: “As infrastructure projects are implemented, more funds will naturally be allocated to housing construction.”

However, critics argue that the main problem is a lack of transparency. According to Meydan TV, annual progress reports on the programme’s implementation are not publicly available, while the website of the centre responsible for monitoring the programme does not publish its findings.

How serious an obstacle do landmines remain?

According to Azerbaijan’s Mine Action Agency (ANAMA), 979 landmines and 3,070 unexploded ordnance items were discovered in October alone. The agency had previously reported that 421 people had been injured or killed by landmines and other explosive devices between November 2020 and April 2026, including 72 fatalities. In September, ANAMA chairman Vugar Suleymanov said there had also been cases of previously cleared areas becoming contaminated with landmines again as a result of flooding.

Journalist Tapdig Farhadoglu told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that much of the territory could become habitable within 10–15 years, while the full restoration of mountainous areas could take 20–30 years.

Economist Natig Jafarli, meanwhile, considers the current pace of returns justified. Speaking to the same outlet, he expressed confidence in the official statistics and noted that a phased return of displaced people made it easier to ensure their safety. He argued that too much emphasis should not be placed on deadlines and numerical targets, saying that “these are not Soviet five-year plans”.

Housing is available, but what about jobs?

Analyst Togrul Juvarli told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that the 1,200-square-metre plots of land provided with houses were insufficient for viable farming. Meanwhile, large agricultural enterprises offer local residents low-paid jobs. Economist Natig Jafarli also pointed out that internally displaced persons had not received land plots during the agricultural reforms of the late 1990s. He believes they should now be granted private ownership of land.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, described the situation in an interview with Meydan TV:

“If a village has housing but no jobs, opportunities to use land are limited, starting a business is difficult, and people have to leave again to find work in other cities, it is hard to call this a genuine Great Return.”

Aytaj Amirjanli, who relocated to the village of Vangli in Aghdara district, told Radio Liberty that she had been registered with the employment service for ten months. According to her, the village has neither a pharmacy nor public transport. She claimed that “most residents are already locking up their homes and leaving for Baku”.

Meanwhile, presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev advised residents to submit complaints directly to government officials rather than record and circulate videos expressing their grievances.

On 30 October, MP Agil Abbas told parliament that around 10,000 people originally from Aghdam were not registered in the city and did not have internally displaced person status. Parliamentary Speaker Sahiba Gafarova objected, saying: “So much work has been done. Why are you trying to discredit it?”

What could the second programme change?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that the draft of the second programme had been submitted to the president. He also described the implementation of the first programme as successful. The targets of the new programme have yet to be made public. According to Finance Ministry projections, 13.2bn manats (approximately $7.765bn) is expected to be allocated to the region’s reconstruction between 2027 and 2030.

Under amendments approved in July, anyone who refuses housing offered by the state loses their status as an internally displaced person. Human rights defenders argue that this violates the principle of voluntary return, while pro-government media portray the changes as a restoration of property rights.

Razim Amiraslanli has called for a comprehensive audit of the first programme. He believes the new programme should focus not on the number of buildings constructed, but on the number of people who have found employment and families who have received land plots.
