World.title: Beaconsfield miner Todd Russell to 'see out' last days at home amid health battle
World.content:
Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has announced he is leaving hospital treatment and will "see out his days" at home surrounded by his family.

Mr Russell, 54, was one of two Tasmanian miners thrown into the world spotlight after becoming trapped underground by a rockfall at the Beaconsfield gold mine, in northern Tasmania, on Anzac Day 2006.

He and co-worker Brant Webb were presumed dead after the body of a third miner, Larry Knight, was found.

They were discovered alive six days later, setting off a rescue operation that lasted another eight days and had the world captivated.

Todd Russell survived 14 days underground when the Beaconsfield mine collapsed in 2006. (ABC/Docker Media)

In July 2024, it was announced that Mr Russell had received "some unfortunate health news and has been unwell".

In October last year, Mr Russell posted an image from hospital, announcing he has started treatment for an undisclosed illness and was hoping to "get back to my old self".

Today, Mr Russell took to social media to announce that "after years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give".

"The time has come, medically and physically, where there are no further options on either front for me, and there is no more fight left in me.

"I will leave hospital tomorrow after eight and a half months for the last time to see out my days in my own home surrounded by my wife, kids, loved ones and friends.

Mr Russell posted a "massive thank you to the incredible staff at the Launceston General Hospital" for their "overwhelming support, care and kindness have helped to soften the daily grind of what has been an incredibly difficult journey".

Mr Russell was up until recently active in his local community, as a firefighter and also having a career as a motivational speaker talking about his ordeal at the mine.

He has also openly discussed his battle with mental health challenges following the experience at Beaconsfield.

World.title: Indian national killed, New Zealander injured in Mount Everest helicopter crash
World.content:
An Indian national is dead and a New Zealander injured after two helicopters collided in Nepal's Mount Everest region, officials have said.

The two helicopters collided while trying to land below Mount Everest's South Base Camp on Tuesday.

The aircraft were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking to the base camp during one of the busiest seasons for the hike.

Heavy snow had covered the route before the weather improved on Sunday and thousands of trekkers were able to move around.

A 47-year-old tourist from India was killed in the crash, according to officials from the Solukhumbu district.

A passenger from New Zealand was injured and was being transported to the capital, Kathmandu, for treatment. A Nepali pilot sustained injuries but was treated locally.

The crash comes during peak trekking season in Nepal. (Supplied: X@kumarsubodh_)

The helicopters were operated by two private firms, Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air.

Fishtail Air said in a statement that its helicopter was carrying passengers who had been rescued from the Everest region.

An official from Dynasty Air said its helicopter was carrying only cargo

The helicopters crashed at Pheriche village, which sits at 4,200 metres above sea level.

The Indian national and the New Zealander on board were both tourists, according to a spokesperson for Fishtail.

There are no roads on Mount Everest, and helicopters are the only way to bring trekkers and guides who cannot make the downward journey.

The Mount Everest base camp trek lasts up to two weeks and goes from the only airstrip in the area.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Scientists hope $28m 'waterless barrier' will stop the spread of cane toads
World.content:
The latest bid to halt the ongoing cane toad invasion of northern Western Australia is set to begin after final funding and approval.

The current estimated front line of the toad's spread has the pests around 100km from Broome, 2,200km north of Perth.

Scientists are now hoping a "waterless barrier" across WA's northern Pilbara will help halt the further spread of the invasive species.

Scientists, traditional owners, pastoralists and Rio Tinto have teamed up in an attempt to stop the cane toad reaching the Pilbara. (Supplied: Lily Youngsmith)

The barrier proposal, to be implemented south of Broome, will see artificial watering holes such as dams and storage tanks cut off, in turn removing the toads' water supply.

This project involves modifying water points across six pastoral stations, which cover 7,500 square kilometres of land.

An additional $28m funding injection from Rio Tinto and the Rhodes Ridge joint venture will see official work on the containment zone start next year.

Locations of the various water points across the Kimberley. (Supplied)

A 'national tragedy'

The toads have already killed millions of Australian native animals, ranging from snakes to goannas and crocodiles.

"The loss of these animals from across that landscape is a national tragedy and it's a loss of natural heritage and cultural heritage for Indigenous landowners," Curtin University biologist Ben Phillips said.

"The Pilbara is another region of Australia chock-full of plants and animals found nowhere else on the planet. Cane toads will thrive in the Pilbara."

Professor Phillips said the project represented the best opportunity to prevent the worst from happening.

Judy Dunlop has been involved with the project for three years. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Curtin University ecologist Judy Dunlop said toad-proofing water points had proven successful in other locations.

"By removing the critical thing they need, which is water, we prevent them from continuing their spread," Dr Dunlop said.

"The build itself will take the next two to five years and we will be doing a lot of work on the sidelines as well as monitoring animals."

Protecting native wildlife

Karajarri Traditional Lands Association chief executive Martin Bin Rashid said traditional owners had been consulted throughout the process.

"We've got a ranger program, we have a heritage team that are going to assist the project leads and construction workers," he said.

"Making sure we also look after those special water holes that hold significant stories and Dreamtime stories for our people and give life to country."

Martin Bin Rashid says it is crucial to act now. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

The region's pastoralists are also on board.

"It's a big station so there's plenty of water points; it ends up being about 100 waterless barriers," Anna Plains Station owner David Stoate said.

"It took a bit of time to come around to the idea of the project because it's such a big job.

"A journey of 1,000 miles starts with a single step, so that's very much what we're doing with this project."

David Stoate manages Anna Plains Station, which covers an area of 3,600 square kilometres. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Funding commitment

The state government allocated about $340,000 in funding for community consultation in 2024.

Funding for the conservation initiative initially reached $12 million, with the Rio/Rhodes Ridge contribution, to be allocated over five years, more than doubling that figure.

Rio Tinto's Chris Osborn said the Pilbara was a special place and important to protect.

"I think it's a model for how really critical problems can be solved when you get the right partners involved," he said.

"Science-based solutions with practical input from traditional owner groups, from pastoralists, [that] will help this project be a success."

World.title: Car slams through supermarket wall 'like a sonic boom'
World.content:
A worker at a supermarket in Adelaide's western suburbs has had a narrow escape after a car reversed through the building.

Emergency services were called to the Woodville IGA supermarket on Port Road about 1:30pm on Sunday.

The store's owner Marc Schirripa told 891 ABC Adelaide he was checking stock when the car ploughed through the wall of the store, sending shelving and packages flying.

The car left a hole in the side of the building. (Supplied: SA Police)

"It felt like a big wave shooting up behind me, hitting me from behind, pushing me up against the shelves," Mr Schirripa said.

"It was like a sonic boom just flashing behind me.

"A car reversed through the wall quite fast, smashed into the wall and blew everything on top of me."

CCTV from inside the store captured the moment of impact in the aisle that included snacks and confectionery.

Marc Schirripa was standing in one of the aisles when the car crashed into the store. (891 ABC Adelaide: Troy Sincock)

Mr Schirripa was examined by paramedics at the scene.

Police said the driver, a 31-year-old woman, and her passenger were not injured.

"She was a little bit shook up, and I'm OK," Mr Schirripa said.

"I'm a very lucky man."

The aftermath of the crash. (Supplied: IGA Woodville)

Mr Schirripa said his family members were among those who rushed to see what caused the commotion.

"My wife and my dad were actually quite scared. They heard the boom from the other side of the shop and came running over to see what it was," Mr Schirripa said.

"It's going to take a couple of weeks to get repaired.

"We've only been here a month open."

The driver has been fined for "reversing further than necessary", SA Police said.

World.title: Chinese embassy suggests military-grade explosive is actually a wine bottle
World.content:
A large Chinese military-grade explosive found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea is a legitimate weapon, the ABC can reveal, despite Chinese government officials suggesting the object was a wine bottle.

Four Chinese nationals were arrested and taken into custody on Friday after the suspected artillery round was located at a major wharf in Port Moresby.

PNG police and military explosives experts secured the device and took it away for analysis.

The projectile was removed from the wharf for analysis. (Supplied: Facebook)

Today, the Chinese Embassy in Port Moresby posted on social media, saying a company linked to the incident had conducted an "on-site verification" and found the object was a shell-shaped wine bottle.

"According to the company involved and following an on-site verification, the object in question — reported as an 'artillery shell' — is in fact a shell-shaped wine bottle," the statement reads.

" It poses no danger at all. "

They also downplayed the feasibility of a Chinese-made military weapon being trafficked into Papua New Guinea.

Chinese officials said they were keeping PNG police "fully updated on the developments" while awaiting official findings of the police investigation.

High-level sources told the ABC a police report finalised today identified the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse.

An X-ray machine that Australia donated to the Royal Papua New Guinea Police was used to analyse the 32-kilogram device.

Sources said the police report had been provided to criminal investigators handling the case.

China responds to Australia's defence treaty with PNG China has urged Papua New Guinea not to sign any deal that might exclude or restrict third parties from cooperating with the Pacific nation, as Australia scrambles to clinch a landmark defence treaty.

Last week, PNG's Police Commissioner David Manning praised the work of officers involved in responding to the incident.

"Police acted quickly upon receiving information that the artillery round had been discovered. The area was secured to prevent the risk of harm in the surrounding area," he said.

"This enabled police and military explosive disposal experts to move in, examine the device and have it safely moved to be stored in a secure facility."

The Chinese nationals arrested in relation to the case remain in custody in Port Moresby.

World.title: Quick hits: A-listers, mistakes and the king's Melbourne Cup connection
World.content:
The 2026 Melbourne Cup race day has provided on-course action and off-track celebrities.

With a generous A-lister shouting fans dinner, a heartfelt message from MND sufferer Nathan Charles and the royal connection to race winner Point of Law, there was a little bit of everything at Flemington.

Here's the quick hits from the race that stops a nation.

1. Waller fined $50,000 for 'honest mistake'

Chris Waller was fined heavily for an error. (AAP: James Ross)

Some mistakes are more costly than others on Melbourne Cup Day, and it's fair to say that Chris Waller paid dearly for an error made by a member of his team on race day morning.

The New Zealand horse Asterix was found to have had Penetrene administered to both forelegs in its stable just hours before the race.

"Unfortunately, there was a topical treatment applied to the horse this morning which is allowed during the week but not on race day," Racing Victoria chief steward Rob Montgomery told Nine.

"It just is an honest mistake but unfortunately has big consequences."

Penetrene is used to relieve muscle soreness and inflammation and is permitted for use, but not on race days.

Waller was fined $50,000 for the error, but said there was no blame for the incident.

"It's a very basic liniment most stables use and I guess the pressure of race day, the person that looks after the horse, put it on his legs right in front of the security guard," Waller said.

"Nothing was hidden … as soon as it happened we knew there was a problem.

"It's not [the stablehand's] fault, I've got to wear the responsibility, it's my team."

2. The Generous Mr Foxx

Jamie Foxx has been particularly generous in Melbourne of late. (Getty Images: Sam Tabone)

The Melbourne Cup is known for attracting everyone and anyone who wants to be seen in high society and this year is no exception.

Hollywood A-lister Jamie Foxx has been in Melbourne shooting his latest film, Deadlocked.

Between takes though, he has been mixing it with the Melbourne public, including at the evocatively named Maison Bâtard where, according to The Age, he paid for several people's dinner by surprise.

He was at Flemington and told the Daily Mail Australia that he was taking his girlfriend, Alyce Huckstepp, and her family to the races as a surprise.

What a generous guy.

3. Nathan Charles flipping the script

On a more serious note, former Wallaby Nathan Charles was also at Flemington today.

The 37-year-old has recently been diagnosed with motor neurone disease and, despite the shock of such a devastating diagnosis, is intent on raising the profile of the disease and living his life to the full at the same time.

"In life, everyone has adversity. I've always been a believer in you should be judged not by how you fall over, but instead how you stand back up. And it's a really unfortunate circumstance," he told Nine.

"But it is my journey and I've just got to keep on moving forward.

"I sort of took the week to get my emotions together.

"And then I just thought, you know what, I gotta flip the script.

"Instead of doing things for the last time I want to start doing things for the first time.

"And I want to provide inspiration and hope to young Australians that they can achieve in the face of adversity."

4. Robbie Williams still entertains us

Robbie Williams wowed onlookers with his pre-race performance. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Racegoers were given a real musical treat ahead of the race, with 52-year-old British legend Robbie Williams performing both pre and post-race at Flemington.

Ahead of his latest Australian tour, which starts at Adelaide Oval on Saturday, Williams performed singalong favourites Feel, Rock DJ, Angels and then Let Me Entertain You.

The crowd at Flemington were up on their feet.

And they'll have another opportunity to enjoy the British legend later on too, when he performs another set at the course.

5. From King Charles to Coaster

Point Of Law claimed the Melbourne Cup, having previously been owned by King Charles III. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Racing Photos)

Cup winner Point of Law has had quite the colourful past.

The four-year-old, who was sired by unbeaten British legend Frankel, formerly belonged to King Charles III, who sold the colt earlier this year.

King Charles's mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, was a noted horse racing fan, with her gleeful celebration of Estimate's victory in the 2013 Ascot Gold Cup a particular highlight.

She even finished sixth in the 1997 Melbourne Cup with Frankie Dettori on Arabian Story.

One can only guess how she'd have felt about her son selling a horse that would go on to win the race later that same year…

A consortium of Australians bought Point of Law, among them legendary West Coast and Carlton superstar, Chris Judd.

6. The Cinderella Horse

The Melbourne Cup offers something for everyone each year.

Sure, there are plenty of punters who study the form guide intently, listen to all the shows, read all the previous and make an educated selection based on all those factors and more.

And then there's the rest of us, who pick the horse with the name they like best or whose colours remind you of your favourite flag.

For tangential sports fans, there may have been one name that stuck out: James J Braddock.

James J Braddock, boxing's Cinderella Man. (Getty Images: Keystone France/Gamma-Rapho)

Film buffs may well recognise this name better than sporties, because James J Braddock was the subject of the 2005 biographical film, Cinderella Man, starring Russell Crowe.

Braddock was an American boxer in the 1930s who, due to persistent hand injuries, jacked in his ring career to work in the docks during the Great Depression.

He came back to the ring though and, after a couple of impressive victories, managed to land a fight against the heavyweight champion of the world, Max Baer, at Madison Square Garden in 1935.

So monumental was the upset and the way he had come back from near retirement, that the press christened him the Cinderella Man.

Braddock's next fight was against Joe Louis, who knocked him out in the eighth round of their bout in Chigaco in 1937.

As for his equine namesake, he finished a credible seventh in the Cup.

World.title: Polls show Trump's party could lose control of Congress but they may be wrong
World.content:
If the midterm elections polls can be believed, the Democratic Party could be about to seize control of the US Congress.

Polling predicts a crushing victory for Democrats in the House of Representatives, where they need to gain four seats.

There is even the possibility of Republicans losing their majority in the Senate, where the Democrats need to defend four seats in tight races and win four more to wrest back control.

Historically at midterm elections, control of the House can flip. But a path to the Senate for Democrats is quite a turnaround for the party that started out having to "pitch a perfect game", as Jessica Taylor from the Cook Political Report puts it.

Mr Trump's decision to launch a war on Iran has been pivotal in his sliding popularity.

"Typically the president's party loses seats and certainly President Trump's approval ratings were not great before March, but pursuing an unpopular war that drove prices, especially on gasoline and diesel, further up has only put his party in more peril," Ms Taylor said.

Loading

Democrats now look competitive in Senate races in red states such as Texas, Kansas, Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

They are widely considered likely to win a North Carolina Senate seat off the Republicans, and polling is very tight in the swing state of Michigan, which backed Mr Trump in the presidential race two years ago.

But Ms Taylor cautions that polls are only a snapshot of voter sentiment at a moment in time.

"I think this is why we look at polls holistically, rather than one poll, because you can have an outlier ... but we see most of the polls trending in the same direction. I mean, a lot of these polls are just very, very close."

Ms Taylor says Democrats should not interpret the positive numbers as an endorsement.

Many analysts, including the founder of the Cook Political Report, are characterising the numbers as more of a "red undertow" than a "blue wave".

"It's Republicans that are in power and voters have a strong anti-incumbent sentiment right now. It's more like a pox on both their houses," Ms Taylor said.

Donald Trump's Republican Party is expected to struggle at the midterm elections. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Polls look 'genuinely bad' for Republicans

Many polls are extremely close and within the margin of error (a measure that accounts for how likely it is to be wrong).

This is similar to the 2024 presidential polls, which were mostly too close to call. Mr Trump ended up sweeping all the swing states, but that was not particularly outside what polls had predicted.

"National polls always under count support for Republicans, and with President Trump barnstorming the country and driving our voters to the polls, Republicans are ready to fight, defy history, and protect our majorities," Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre said.

Charles Franklin, the director of the respected Marquette Law School Poll, recently told Politico that one of the largest fears for pollsters was that not enough Republicans were responding.

"We've done a lot over this past decade to try to improve the control we have over those kinds of errors, but ultimately we can't force people to do polls, and so this remains always a background fear factor," he said.

This graph shows how polls have changed this year.

But Republican pollster and strategist Patrick Ruffini said the environment was "genuinely bad" for Republicans.

"They look weaker this late in a cycle than I can remember," he told the ABC.

He said there also were complications with where the Democrats were leading.

"The Senate battleground runs through red states like Iowa, Ohio and Texas and these are states that Republicans consistently carry by solid margins, or that the polls have a hard time getting right."

Loading...

Mr Ruffini recently examined more than 3,000 Senate polls from the past eight years to assess their track record.

He found 73 per cent of them had overstated the Democrat candidate. In Iowa, Ohio and Michigan, the Democrats were overstated 93 per cent of the time.

"That doesn't mean it will happen again. Democrats are still gaining in the polls this year," he said.

"The bigger risk is uneven error from state to state, where the national picture is right but some states miss.

"Polls have been more accurate in the Sun Belt than in the Rust Belt, so I'd believe a blue Texas before a blue Iowa."

Massive spending ahead of midterms

It is not always the Republicans who defy polls. In what the US calls off-cycle elections, the Democrats running in high-profile governor races in New Jersey and Virginia have outperformed their polling and won easily.

Even with the extraordinary unpopularity of Mr Trump, Democrats are reluctant to consider the midterms sewn up.

Former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel recently stressed to The New Yorker that he felt only "cautiously optimistic" about the Senate, although he was more confident about the House.

It is possible to read some tea leaves about where money is pouring in.

The analytics firm AdImpact calculated that Republicans were out-spending Democrats in 10 battleground Senate races a week out from the election.

The Republican war chest was significantly boosted by MAGA Inc, a political action committee, or PAC, associated with the president.

PACs are organisations formed explicitly to raise and spend money on election races.

In the final sprint of campaigning, Mr Trump promised that he would unleash a further $US100 million ($142 million) to back Republican candidates, adding to more than $US300 million MAGA Inc had already spent.

Other mega-donors like Elon Musk are also using PACs to put money behind favored candidates.

The closely fought Texas Senate race has been flooded with cash, with spending surpassing $US500 million.

In North Carolina, where the former Democratic governor Roy Cooper looks set to easily convert a Republican Senate seat, the top campaign spending organisation for Senate Republicans pulled its funding at the start of October.

That suggests the party considered the seat lost even then. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat senator since 1932, ad spending increased tenfold in the weeks leading up to the election.

Observers are also reading in to Mr Trump's travel schedule. He has mainly held rallies in deeply red areas.

And the president, of course, does not believe the polling.

"Look, the polls are fake," he said last week. "I don't rely on the polls, but polls mean something. But a lot of the polls are rigged, just like the journalists are rigged."

World.title: Lamarre-Condon asked police not to judge him, jury told
World.content:
Accused double murderer Beau Lamarre-Condon became emotional and told police that he was "not a bad person" after revealing the location where he left the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a jury has heard.

The 31-year-old former officer is facing trial on two counts of murder, accused of shooting the couple with his police pistol inside Mr Baird's Paddington share house in February 2024.

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

Their bodies were discovered in surfboard bags near a monastery in Bungonia, south of Sydney, more than a week after the deaths. Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty and is arguing self-defence.

Jurors in the Supreme Court trial have previously seen body-cam footage of the moment Mr Lamarre-Condon handed himself in at Bondi Police Station four days after the men died.

Detective Sasha Pinazza, the officer in charge of the investigation, was with the accused as he was taken to another station, the court heard on Tuesday.

Mr Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Luke Davies, left, and Jesse Baird, right. (Instagram)

She advised him that it may be in his best interests to speak to his lawyer regarding the 'no body, no parole' legislation.

"I explained that legislation excluded a person convicted of murder from release on parole in circumstances where the victims had not been located, and the accused had failed to assist," Detective Pinazza said in her statement, which was read to the court.

When he was told that police had information about the men's bodies being in a dam or on a farm near Goulburn, he did not comment and cited legal advice.

The court heard he spoke about having an "outer body experience".

'I don't want you to judge me, I'm not a bad person'

In an interview room, he was crying and became emotional as he talked about mental health and claimed to have PTSD, Detective Pinazza's statement said.

The detective said he claimed previous work-related matters had "messed me up" and said he was sent to Youth Command as punishment.

She recalled the accused stating: "I don't want you to judge me, I'm not a bad person."

He also asked whether police were close to finding the men's bodies.

The court heard that four days later, Detective Pinazza and colleagues attended Silverwater prison and advised the accused that they only wanted to speak to him about the location of the bodies.

After speaking to his lawyer, he said the location was in the same area as a Bungonia farm police had been searching.

Police conducting a line search at the site where the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were found. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Jurors heard that police showed Mr Lamarre-Condon maps on a laptop and he indicated the roads he had travelled to a monastery, before describing its gates.

He was then shown images of a property police believed he had gone to.

"The accused believed to the best of his recollection this to be location where he left the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies," Detective Pinazza said in her statement.

"The accused was emotional and implored that he was not a bad person."

He also asked to wait while investigators attended the location.

"The accused expressed a hope that he would one day be able to talk to Jesse and Luke's families," her statement recorded.

"He was emotional and stated, 'I'm not that person'."

That day, police located the bodies near the entrance of a monastery in surfboard bags, partially covered by sticks and rocks.

The court has previously heard he allegedly attempted to sink the bags in a dam at a Bungonia farm, using quick-set cement and weights, after transporting them in a white hire van.

The jury has heard evidence about his movements in the week of the alleged murders, which the Crown alleges involved deliberate steps to cover up his involvement in the deaths.

Mr Lamarre-Condon's lawyers have indicated that his case will be that he "panicked" after two separate struggles involving the gun, which resulted in the two deaths.

The Crown is expected to close its case shortly in the trial, which is now in its seventh week.

The trial is expected to run for three months

World.title: WA minister shares vile voice message as concerns grow over MPs’ safety
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament WA minister shares vile voice message as concerns grow over MPs’ safety Hamish Hastie and Andrew Du November 3, 2026 — 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk has shared a vulgar message left on her office answering machine in a demonstration of the regular vitriol West Australian MPs and their electorate office staff face. Speaking at a Business News breakfast on Tuesday morning, McGurk vented her frustration at the current state of political debate in Australia, revealing the frequent aggression MPs and political staff received. Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk. Hamish Hastie The message shared by McGurk was from an American man seemingly upset at the member for Fremantle’s past commentary about US politics. He opens with the greeting, “Hello, you horrible f----ing witch”, before telling her to “shut up about American politics”, and describes Australia as a “prison colony” and “inbred”.



McGurk said it was important people understood the sort of vitriol and aggression that many elected representatives and their staff received. “I think women get it in particular, but it really does extend to a lot of elected representatives,” she said. “It’s really vulgar. It’s aggressive. It’s unacceptable by any measure. Sadly, that then extends to real life, where in my electorate office we will often get calls.” McGurk said on Monday afternoon a staff member was called an “f---ing c---” over the phone.



“Staff that are working in our electorate offices just don’t deserve that sort of abuse,” she said. Editor's pick Fishing What life will look like for WA’s fishers after controversial ban lifts The safety of WA MPs has become a priority issue after federal Victorian independent MP Helen Haines lost both her legs after being rammed allegedly by a constituent driving a four-wheel drive while she was outside her office. Days later, WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley’s Victoria Park electorate office was forced into lockdown when a man allegedly brandished nunchucks. One Nation’s WA leader Rod Caddies also said a man threatened to kill him while he was driving home from parliament one night.



Concerns over MP safety resulted in a meeting between all party leaders and WA Police at parliament on October 22. The state will likely conduct an audit of electorate office safety, and they are considering allowances available to MPs to upgrade security. McGurk’s comments came the same day a Victorian One Nation volunteer was allegedly attacked by a man and a teenager with a baseball bat on his front lawn in a coastal town on the Great Ocean Road. Victoria Police said in a statement on Tuesday the 60-year-old was recovering from serious, non-life-threatening injuries after he confronted a 14-year-old boy who was allegedly damaging a corflute outside a home in Torquay on Sunday evening. McGurk said the overall temperature in public debate was at an all-time high.



“I don’t think we’re just seeing this in the WA or in Australia. I think we’re seeing it around the world,” she said. “I really want people to think about when they are feeling impatient or angry, just to take a step back and take a breath and not to take that out on the people around them.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. “My technique for dealing with these robotic receptionists (C8) is to not say a word until a human eventually appears on the line,” advises Dave Horsfall of North Gosford. “Being in IT for decades, I regard computers as my vassals, not my equals.”

“When the Herald transitioned from broadsheet (C8) to a compact size (I dare not call it ‘tabloid’), I had a letter published in the very first, smaller edition which said: ‘Those of us with shorter arms salute you’,” says Alicia Dawson of Balmain. “I still stand by that.”

“In the 1950s and for many years following, the Leaving Certificate (HSC equivalent) started on the first Tuesday in November – Melbourne Cup Day,” says Kathy Earls of Hunters Hill. “My sister was a boarder at a school in Glebe. Students caught the tram to the old Fort Street High School where many schools gathered to sit the final exams (C8). The English paper commenced after lunch. At about 3pm the students were told to put their pens down, the wireless was turned on, and they listened to the Cup. When the race ended, they were directed to pick up pens and continue the exam. I wonder if the same will happen in 2026 for Investigating Science and French Continuers students.”

Aidan Cuddington of Umina Beach says that, “like Sally Deves (C8), I was taught mental arithmetic at an early age (and it was the only branch of mathematics at which I excelled), but my ability to calculate unit prices was greatly enhanced by a lifetime of darts and cribbage.”

“Why is it that interest rates are hiked, yet water levels are raised, blood pressure is elevated, danger is heightened, search efforts are expanded, the debt is enlarged, and threat levels are escalated?” We’ll get back to you, Geoff Goodfellow of Moss Vale.

World.title: Changing the way teachers see the world
World.content:
NationalHigh school Editorial Changing the way teachers see the world The Herald's View Editorial November 3, 2026 — 8:00pm

November 3, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The NSW government’s innovative opening up of western Sydney schools to trainee teachers to demystify the stigma around public education is the sort of blue-sky thinking that can change ordinary lives. Herald education reporter Emily Kowal has tracked some of the 50 university students attending schools with teacher shortages and complex needs where teachers’ roles go far beyond the curriculum. Kingswood High maths teacher Natalie Benson said some high schoolers, for diverse reasons, did not value education. “It’s our job to work with that,” she said. “You have to show you care; we have to adapt our lessons to be worthy of them. You can’t just give them something and expect it to work. Meet them where they are at.” Students such as these University of Sydney graduates experience a raft of positive and benefit outcomes. Louie Douvis One student teacher, Saajidah Reijerink, said her week-long placement helped shed preconceptions about teaching in so-called “deficit” areas. “Kids who don’t receive love at home will come to school to receive it … creating an environment in which kids feel supported and accepted will then support them to do better academically and to thrive here,” she said.



Related Article Exclusive

Education The classroom moment changing how new teachers see western Sydney This sensible move to inspire frontline educators is a reminder of education’s promise. Yet the innovation comes as governments are so distracted by multiple crises that excellence appears to have taken a back seat. Structural failures have been causing a measurable decline in student outcomes. Consistently poor results in PISA and NAPLAN demand urgent action. As a consequence, year 5 students are set to return to pen and paper for NAPLAN writing tests next year as, under growing criticism from parents opposed to widespread use of devices, the sheen goes off Australia’s embrace of technology. Federal Liberal education spokesman Julian Leeser has warned it is time to move beyond arguments about school funding and socio-economic status in school policies and implement a root and branch reform of the national curriculum (NSW has its own curriculum).



But the Albanese government had been hedging, putting off a review until 2032. On Monday, federal Education Minister Jason Clare and his state and territory counterparts agreed to merge four of Australia’s key secondary education agencies in a restructure it hoped would help address the decline in student NAPLAN results and boost attendance. It is a start, but Canberra has put the next tier of education – tertiary education – well down the priority list. And that is a problem for Australia’s education and even political divide. According to the 2026 McKinnon Index, a striking chasm has opened between graduates from universities and high school graduates over their satisfaction with Australian democracy and the integrity of elections.



Related Article Exclusive

Mental health From homework to big kids: What keeps primary school students up at night It extends far beyond lack of trust in politicians and the system. More than 80 per cent of university graduates said they understood how Australian democracy works, compared with fewer than two-thirds of high school graduates. The McKinnon Index illustrates the need for big ideas to improve our education system. Education is transformative for an individual but also important for the country. Frontline experience for potential recruits can help the next generation of teachers to inspire the next generation of students to embrace education, for their own sake and that of the wider community. World.title: Hollywood star Jamie Foxx cuts a rug while Don Farrell schmoozes US ambassador
World.content:
SportRacingCBD Hollywood star Jamie Foxx cuts a rug while Don Farrell schmoozes US ambassador Fiona Byrne and Christine Lacy November 3, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you don’t ask, you won’t get. In what was an epic coup for Crown Resorts and its private equity owner, Blackstone, the casino company landed new US ambassador to Australia David Brat at Flemington on Tuesday. US ambassador David Brat (left), Trade and Tourism Minister Don Farrell (taking a selfie) and US consul-general Colin Crosby outside the Crown marquee. Penny Stephens When Crown asked if Brat, who started in his role as Donald Trump’s man Down Under in August, would like to be at the track and attend its Birdcage marquee, he said yes and diplomacy swung into action. It was the first visit to Melbourne for Brat, who was joined by his wife, Laura. The couple were accompanied to the track by US consul-general Colin Crosby and his wife, Vivian.



After lunching in the VRC Committee Room, Brat told CBD he was loving the Cup spectacle. He said Victorian Governor Margaret Gardner had encouraged him to punt on what she told him was the King’s horse, Point Of Law, which went on to win the $10.2 million race. The horse was previously owned by King Charles. Crown Resorts CEO David Tsai, Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Sally Curtain and Crown Resorts chairman John Borghetti on Cup Day. Penny Stephens Brat said he would vote in the US midterm elections, which begin on Tuesday night (AEDT), via email and that being sent to Australia by Trump was “the best posting there is”. Elsewhere in Crown’s enclosure, chairman John Borghetti played host to pollies and high rollers alike.



Taro Squires, head of real estate in Australia for international private equity giant Blackstone, was at his first Melbourne Cup, after taking on his new post in July. Squires was previously based in Tokyo and is now living in Sydney, from where he will oversee the casino asset. Caitlin Donaldson from Qantas and Michael Photios, Liberal Party powerbroker, arriving at the Birdcage. Penny Stephens He was in the house with Crown Resorts chief David Tsai and head of Crown in Melbourne Ed Domingo. Lobbyist and former NSW Liberal minister Michael Photios was in from Sydney with Qantas government relations operative Caitlin Donaldson, while National Gallery of Victoria director Tony Ellwood, federal Trade and Tourism Minister Don Farrell, VECCI boss Sally Curtain, Melbourne Airport chief Lorie Argus, and Crown Melbourne chair and former racing minister Martin Pakula were also present. A Wylie win



Before the feature race, veteran investment banker and former chair of the Australian Sports Commission John Wylie was striding the Birdcage bitumen with his wife, Myriam. Together, they own 10 per cent of Point Of Law. John Wylie, former chair of the Australian Sports Commission, and his wife, Myriam Wylie, had plenty to celebrate. Penny Stephens John ducked in and out of Crown before heading for the mounting yard. By the end of the day he was back at the company’s marquee celebrating

the horse’s win in a back room with his fellow owners. Bishop’s blessing for Jess Wilson Julie Bishop, Australia’s minister for style, and her partner, Stephen Grey, were the epitome of Birdcage diplomacy on Cup Day, floating from one marquee to another.



Julie Bishop calls this Dior dress “my French look”. Getty Images Dressed in “timeless Dior – this is my French look”, Bishop paused for a moment from her marquee-hopping to throw her support behind Jess Wilson in this month’s Victorian election. “I have always been impressed by Jess. She is a very confident, smart, inspiring woman, and I hope she is given the opportunity to lead this state,” Bishop said. “She is an impressive talent. I think she is a star.” Last month CBD reported that Bishop, who also has a role with the United Nations, had hitched her wagon to a Trump-linked advisory firm in the US.



“I have maintained my interest in foreign affairs, Australia’s place in the world and global strategic matters,” she said. Bishop’s advisory firm, Julie Bishop & Partners, has inked a “strategic alliance” with American Global Strategies, a company chaired by Robert O’Brien, a former US national security adviser and current member of Donald Trump’s President’s Intelligence Advisory Board. Foxx tears up the dance floor There have been rumours for days that Oscar winner Jamie Foxx would make it out to Flemington at some point during Cup Week, and when he arrived at the Don Julio marquee just before 1pm on Cup Day, a real Hollywood buzz went through the Birdcage. Hollywood star Jamie Foxx was ready to live it up on the dance floor. Eamon Gallagher



The Collateral star attracted a huge media scrum when he turned up at the tequila bolthole, and he wasn’t boring – chatting to everyone, doing oodles of selfies and busting some moves on the dance floor. Foxx is in Melbourne for a couple of months filming Deadlocked, an action movie that has been shooting at various locations around the city. He is staying at disgraced media mogul Antony Catalano’s St Kilda penthouse. Foxx’s partner, Australian fitness instructor Alyce Huckstepp, is in Melbourne with him. While many visiting international stars like to fly under the radar while in town, Foxx has been embracing our golf courses and our hospitality scene. He has been a regular at Maison Batard, the high-end restaurant in the Melbourne CBD operated by Chris Lucas, and as evidenced by his Birdcage enthusiasm, loves a selfie with fans. He is a vibe. Pour one out for Mumm



Over in the Mumm marquee, the definition of celebrity was quite loosely applied. Jules Neale’s “tap, tap” moment”. Getty Images In what has seemed like a real-life episode of Days of Our Lives, the bubbles brand has this week played host to both halves of the soap opera-like disintegration of footballer Lachie Neale and newly minted influencer ex-wife Jules Neale’s marriage. Jules was Mumm’s big-name guest on Cup Day and did the daily “tap, tap” champagne shower on the steps of the marquee for the cameras. Questions about her marriage implosion were off-limits, minders stipulating she could only be asked about fashion and racing.



Adelle Petropoulos at the Caulfield Cup last month. Penny Stephens Asked how she was feeling about being at the track, she said: “I will be honest … I don’t know anything about the racing,” adding she was there for the fashion. Lachie, a former Brisbane Lions star and now new Collingwood recruit, and his current girlfriend, Emma Field, were guests of the champagne house on Saturday, Derby Day. On Tuesday, another new-age celebrity guest was influencer Adelle Petropoulos, who came to public notice last year after she split with her fiance. Petropoulos bounced back in March by wearing what was to be her wedding gown to the Australian Grand Prix’s Glamour on the Grid party and has been riding a social media wave ever since.



Also turning heads in the marquee was Chelsea Becirevic, who is known as “Australia’s hottest WAG”. Becirevic is dating retired AFL player Ivan Soldo. “There are worse things to be called, so I’ll take it,” she quipped. Lunch is served The hallowed Committee Room was once again the most exclusive venue at Flemington, a strictly invitation-only location. Victoria Racing Club chair Neil Wilson and his wife, Stephanie, the VRC board and club chief executive Kylie Rogers hosted dignitaries, politicians, board members of other race clubs, sponsors, and owner representatives of runners in the Melbourne Cup.



Related Article CBD Daicoses, partners and a camera-shy premier’s wife: The eclectic social mix in the Birdcage As well as Governor Margaret Gardner, US ambassador David Brat and US consul-general Colin Crosby, also joining the Committee Room lunch were Victorian Racing Minister Anthony Carbines, state Treasurer Colin Brooks, Sport Minister Steve Dimopoulos, retiring Nationals MP Tim Bull and Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece. Pollies take Birdcage flight The Birdcage was a grab bag of political, business and showbiz identities on Cup Day. In our travels, CBD came across member for Mallee Anne Webster, member for Nicholls Sam Birrell, federal member for Maribyrnong Jo Briskey and new federal director of the Liberal Party Lincoln Folo in the Mumm marquee.



At TAB, the company’s heavy hitters were out in force in traditional morning suits, including chairman Brett Chenoweth, chief executive Gil McLachlan and non-executive director David Gallop. Senators Sarah Henderson (left) and Jane Hume. Eamon Gallagher Many politicians declined invitations to join the fun in light of the Reserve Bank’s decision on interest rates at 2.30pm – just the sort of optics our elected officials are keen to avoid. A few still got along, including NSW politician Mark Latham and federal Nationals MP Michael McCormack. Also enjoying the betting shop’s hospitality was former Melbourne Racing Club chair John Kanga and former Bill Shorten adviser Ryan Liddell, who now runs his own outfit, Principle Advisory.



At Lexus, Australian Industry Group chief Innes Willox was enjoying the day with partner Jane Devereux, while at Nine senators Jane Hume and Sarah Henderson were in attendance. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ethan Brown reconsidered riding after his brush with death. Now he’s a Melbourne Cup champion
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup Ethan Brown reconsidered riding after his brush with death. Now he’s a Melbourne Cup champion Peter Ryan November 3, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A heart-to-heart over a couple of beers with trainer Ciaron Maher about two years ago sowed the seeds for 27-year-old jockey Ethan Brown’s Melbourne Cup win on Point Of Law. After nearly losing his life in a massive fall off Maximillius in the 2023 Australian Guineas, and a stop-start return to riding, Brown wondered whether he should continue in the toughest of capers. Ethan Brown and girlfriend and fellow jockey Celine Gaudray celebrate with the trophy after Point of Law won the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images The injuries were significant, and that was before the emotional toll was considered. Brown suffered a grade-five lacerated liver and severed artery, damage to his right kidney, significant internal bleeding, and hairline fractures to three vertebrae in his lower back. He lost more than five litres of blood. The fall was in the March, and he returned to the races that August.



“By the time I got [back] to the races, I still wasn’t ready,” Brown said. “I was tricking myself into telling myself I was ready, so I rode for a month and thought, ‘I am not ready for this’, and took a step back. That was the stage I wondered whether I would get back.” Loading He contemplated training, but Maher – who became a trainer after a short-lived career as a jumps jockey – set him straight over a drink with Brown. The pair’s relationship went way back, with Brown riding the horse he learnt to ride on in Alice Springs, Here to There, to victory at Caulfield in 2017. Maher told him he was a rider, not a trainer. Brown and Ciaron Maher embrace after the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images



“He was very firm about that. He said, ‘You are delusional mate, get back riding’,” Brown said. Brown took the advice on board, but still took time to commit. “I woke up one morning. I was hungry again, and it was full-bore,” Brown said. Maher – who on Tuesday became the first trainer to claim the Melbourne Cup trifecta with Point Of Law, Zahrann and Juja Kibo – had merely passed on the wisdom he had gathered over his time in the business, recognising Brown’s talent was as a rider, and backing him in. Loading



“He’s a very dedicated man, and he was just a bit lost because he is a bit of an overthinker,” Maher said. “I rode at a very low level, and it was the greatest time of my life just booting around with my mates and riding, and he was just a bit down, and he was going to be a trainer. I thought, ‘Riding is much more fun’ and I just told him my thoughts.” A stint in Hong Kong gave Brown the confidence he needed to compete with the best, having grown up in Alice Springs where he started riding under Greg Connor before becoming an apprentice to Michael Kent. “He’s always been a grounded lad,” Connor said. “He still is.” Ethan Brown celebrates winning the Melbourne Cup on Point Of Law. Justin McManus At the same time, he recognised that the only way of being a jockey was to devote himself to the craft, showing the same traits he revealed as a teenager when he modified his diet after being told he had heavy legs.



“I have just matured a lot in the last 12 months. Mentally I have grown up ... staying quiet, not going out [and a] bit of sacrifice here and there. It has paid off,” Brown said. “When I came back it was like a switch, ‘I’m back to ride and that is all I am doing’. When you make those sorts of decisions you’re not half-hearted. You’re not back to just push around for your riding fee. It was, ‘I am going in full-bore’ and it was a moment like this I dreamt of, and it has happened.” Related Article Melbourne Cup Eileen had lunch with King Charles at Windsor Castle. It delivered her son a Melbourne Cup It didn’t just happen, though. Brown had to choose between Point Of Law and his other potential mount, Zahrann, in the lead-up. It was not a call he took lightly, but he opted for Point Of Law due to the horse’s X-factor. He then took on board Maher’s decisions to work Point Of Law hard to have him peaking for the race, finding the balance between being worked hard enough to relax in the run and fresh enough to quicken when called upon. Former hoop Simon Marshall, who has worked with him for 12 months, helped get him in the right frame of mind and if he needed further advice, his partner Celine Gaudray had ridden Torranzino to fifth place in the 2025 Melbourne Cup.



Brown had not ridden Point Of Law before the Geelong Cup, but he got off the horse in the winner’s stall and whispered to Maher it might be the best horse he has trained. Then he made early visits to Werribee to ride Point Of Law in trackwork, which gave him an understanding that he was on the best horse of the race. He could win as long as he could get him to settle in just his sixth race start. Editor's pick Analysis

Melbourne Cup ‘I looked up and thought, oh god’: The split-second choice that delivered Point Of Law’s historic Cup triumph He did it beautifully, timing his run to perfection as he reeled in, and then roared past, Royal Supremacy who looked to have opened up a winning lead entering the straight. With 350 metres remaining and Royal Supremacy still five lengths ahead, Brown knew it was all over. “He quickened like a sprinter at the end of 3200. When he hit that top gear, I knew we had won,” Brown said. The question of whether it was all worth it had been answered, and Brown was looking forward with a bank full of memories.

World.title: There’s a creepy problem with mince pies. It goes deeper than hot cross buns
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsChristmas Opinion There’s a creepy problem with mince pies. It goes deeper than hot cross buns Nicola Redhouse Writer Updated November 3, 2026 — 7:33pm , first published 7:00pm

Updated November 3, 2026 — 7:33pm ,first published 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s spring – a wondrous time for allergic rhinitis and for complaining about Christmas mince pies already being in the supermarket. The Mince Pie Creep, as I have come to think of it, might be less notorious than the Hot Cross Bun Creep (no longer even ubiquitous with Easter, now a completely non-denominational carbohydrate), but I feel deeper unease about its presence. I no longer believe the Christmas mince pie is an innocent little pastry designed to bring cheer – that it holds enough sugar to induce a diabetic-grade thirst is another matter. Rather, it is what animal behaviourists call a sign stimulus: a specific environmental cue that triggers instinctive behaviour. Mince pies are an innocent treat as we approach Christmas, right? Wrong. Steven Siewert For monarch butterflies, shorter days and colder temperatures are a sign stimulus to swivel their antennae compasses and head to the butterfly equivalent of Copacabana. The red belly of the male three-spined stickleback fish is a sign stimulus to other male sticklebacks to launch a vicious attack. And the Christmas mince pie signals to Homo sapiens with a shopping centre or the internet within reach to launch themselves into a mindless consumer frenzy. It’s possible the early spring Christmas mince pie harbours something like the alien spore pods in The Body Snatchers, which released tiny mind-controlling pathogens. I cannot otherwise explain why, in the face of every shred of evidence that we are burning down this planet, come October – the very same time the pies now appear – the average human brain starts accommodating two separate realities to justify frittering away money on more crap that has racked up a zillion carbon emissions and will end up in landfill.



Related Article Opinion

Supermarkets I found the best supermarket. It treats you like it’s a communist dictatorship Nicola Redhouse Writer We know that the Arctic is melting, bushfires are raging and average temperatures are climbing. That significant weather events are making us uninsurable, that disasters such as the Nepal flood are happening more often and that microplastics are clogging every waterway from our oceans to our tear ducts. Some of us even feel terror in the dark of night thinking of the future for our children and our children’s children, as well as guilt for the knowledge they will not be ones to suffer the worst – in fact that will be those in countries with less infrastructure, less money. But, understandably, we prefer to stay in our own little house of fun, where we can find joy in having five strands of single-use candy cane fairy lights twinkling around our necks and line our pockets with multiple Festive Pokémon figurines and dance with our limited-edition Christmas tunes robotic vacuum. In our house of fun, we can justify our purchases with thoughts such as, “Well, how could I possibly make a difference to this catastrophe” and “Well, it’s all so terrifying and sad I might as well enjoy my few hundred latex-filled giant-eyed squishy toys.” Psychoanalyst Adam Phillips says that modern life now demands we be happy. “It’s as though we’re phobic of frustration, so the moment there is a feeling of frustration it’s got to be filled with something,” he has said. Ours is a world in which we escape the terror generated by the consequences of capitalism and consumerism by purchasing more from Temu. The problem is, we need to feel pain, frustration, sadness, fear to take action. No civil rights activist ever emerged from a life of pina coladas on the riviera.



As Phillips writes: “It may be that when catastrophic change is inflicted upon us … we may become more able and willing to … create the kind of change we would like, the kind of change that we realise we need in order to get the lives we want.” Related Article Opinion

Cars My car kept making a thucka-thucka noise, but no one else could hear it Nicola Redhouse Writer Lord knows I am prone to the occasional impulse purchase of a dancing voice-activated cactus or tuba for a good dopamine hit. But as the festive season approaches this year, I want to do better. I’m going to buy from businesses that are using renewable energy, actively reducing their waste, and going for sustainable materials. I’m also going to try to give things that are good for the planet: things that grow, like plants and seedlings, and mushrooms and my washing pile. I’m going to give with actions, like cooking meals for friends who are stretched for time or money. I’m going to try to find gifts that offer low-emission experiences or op shop finds. I might even make my own mince pies.



Nicola Redhouse is a Melbourne writer and author of Unlike the Heart: A Memoir of Brain and Mind. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: WA minister shares vile voice message as concerns grow over MPs’ safety
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament WA minister shares vile voice message as concerns grow over MPs’ safety Hamish Hastie and Andrew Du November 3, 2026 — 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk has shared a vulgar message left on her office answering machine in a demonstration of the regular vitriol West Australian MPs and their electorate office staff face. Speaking at a Business News breakfast on Tuesday morning, McGurk vented her frustration at the current state of political debate in Australia, revealing the frequent aggression MPs and political staff received. Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk. Hamish Hastie The message shared by McGurk was from an American man seemingly upset at the member for Fremantle’s past commentary about US politics. He opens with the greeting, “Hello, you horrible f----ing witch”, before telling her to “shut up about American politics”, and describes Australia as a “prison colony” and “inbred”.



McGurk said it was important people understood the sort of vitriol and aggression that many elected representatives and their staff received. “I think women get it in particular, but it really does extend to a lot of elected representatives,” she said. “It’s really vulgar. It’s aggressive. It’s unacceptable by any measure. Sadly, that then extends to real life, where in my electorate office we will often get calls.” McGurk said on Monday afternoon a staff member was called an “f---ing c---” over the phone.



“Staff that are working in our electorate offices just don’t deserve that sort of abuse,” she said. Editor's pick Fishing What life will look like for WA’s fishers after controversial ban lifts The safety of WA MPs has become a priority issue after federal Victorian independent MP Helen Haines lost both her legs after being rammed allegedly by a constituent driving a four-wheel drive while she was outside her office. Days later, WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley’s Victoria Park electorate office was forced into lockdown when a man allegedly brandished nunchucks. One Nation’s WA leader Rod Caddies also said a man threatened to kill him while he was driving home from parliament one night.



Concerns over MP safety resulted in a meeting between all party leaders and WA Police at parliament on October 22. The state will likely conduct an audit of electorate office safety, and they are considering allowances available to MPs to upgrade security. McGurk’s comments came the same day a Victorian One Nation volunteer was allegedly attacked by a man and a teenager with a baseball bat on his front lawn in a coastal town on the Great Ocean Road. Victoria Police said in a statement on Tuesday the 60-year-old was recovering from serious, non-life-threatening injuries after he confronted a 14-year-old boy who was allegedly damaging a corflute outside a home in Torquay on Sunday evening. McGurk said the overall temperature in public debate was at an all-time high.



“I don’t think we’re just seeing this in the WA or in Australia. I think we’re seeing it around the world,” she said. “I really want people to think about when they are feeling impatient or angry, just to take a step back and take a breath and not to take that out on the people around them.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. “My technique for dealing with these robotic receptionists (C8) is to not say a word until a human eventually appears on the line,” advises Dave Horsfall of North Gosford. “Being in IT for decades, I regard computers as my vassals, not my equals.”

“When the Herald transitioned from broadsheet (C8) to a compact size (I dare not call it ‘tabloid’), I had a letter published in the very first, smaller edition which said: ‘Those of us with shorter arms salute you’,” says Alicia Dawson of Balmain. “I still stand by that.”

“In the 1950s and for many years following, the Leaving Certificate (HSC equivalent) started on the first Tuesday in November – Melbourne Cup Day,” says Kathy Earls of Hunters Hill. “My sister was a boarder at a school in Glebe. Students caught the tram to the old Fort Street High School where many schools gathered to sit the final exams (C8). The English paper commenced after lunch. At about 3pm the students were told to put their pens down, the wireless was turned on, and they listened to the Cup. When the race ended, they were directed to pick up pens and continue the exam. I wonder if the same will happen in 2026 for Investigating Science and French Continuers students.”

Aidan Cuddington of Umina Beach says that, “like Sally Deves (C8), I was taught mental arithmetic at an early age (and it was the only branch of mathematics at which I excelled), but my ability to calculate unit prices was greatly enhanced by a lifetime of darts and cribbage.”

“Why is it that interest rates are hiked, yet water levels are raised, blood pressure is elevated, danger is heightened, search efforts are expanded, the debt is enlarged, and threat levels are escalated?” We’ll get back to you, Geoff Goodfellow of Moss Vale.

World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Next airport rail stop: Spaghetti Junction November 3, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
