Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. AIRPORT LINK The article ‴⁣⁣Tulla rail planned ‘doctored’ in secret Sunshine push” (3/11) was interesting reading. I think the decision to go for the Sunshine option was a wise one because it didn’t require tunnelling. You only have to look at the Hydro 2.0 project initiated by the federal Liberal Party under Malcolm Turnbull to see how its costs have blown out.

Other factors in this case are that the Maribyrnong defence land is contaminated, and a decision to develop it into housing has stalled over decades. The extent and depth of contamination is unknown, and the costs of decontaminating it will need an open cheque book.

The Craigeburn route has public bus 901 which already connects Broadmeadows station with Tullamarine airport. The Sunshine hub offers access to regional people who would not have to travel into congested Southern Cross station.

It will be interesting to see what the royal commission brings, and what decisions the government of the day makes based on these many factors, Labor and Liberal alike.

Margaret Forster, Aberfeldie No such thing as ″⁣no cost″⁣

The categorisation of the private consortium bid to build the Melbourne Airport Rail Link as no cost to the public is misleading. The consortium wanted 127.8 hectares of public land in return. That is not ″⁣no-cost″⁣ and would have led to protests about private developers gaining free access to that land.

There was another bid to build and operate the railway, presumably similar to the expensive Heathrow Express in London which is not used as much as the normal tube lines. The best link is the one that is part of the existing system, and which maximises potential customers by linking to regional rail.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster



Less government listens to private vested interests the better

The article ″⁣City to the Airport in 18 Minutes″⁣ (3/11) searches for a controversy where there isn’t one. I would think there are all sorts of private developer plans put to the government on a regular basis.

No doubt they would be very favourable financially to the various developers all eyeing off potential ways to make money. The West Gate link is a prime example of this, and we know how that turned out. And let’s not forget that we are all now paying for the folly of the Kennett Liberal government who sold off all our utilities and closed way too many schools.

Private consortiums have one aim, and that is to make money, and often we find out the hard way that the best interests of the community are not in focus.

The less the government listens to private vested interests the better, and that includes the so-called expert opinions being quoted in this article.

Michael Cormick, Carnegie The cost of bias and vested interests

It appears that earlier governments ignored the need of travellers to reach the airport as soon as possible and not have to go on a winding route through the government’s favourite places. We’ve all lost out to their madness, bias and vested interests, and yet again, Melbourne becomes a lesser place to be.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn And connecting a link to regional cities?

The Age article on the proposal to build a private rail line to Tullamarine Airport reports the private line would be nine minutes faster to the airport for Melburnians than the line from Sunshine now being constructed.

Would The Age please ascertain how much longer the journey to the airport from Ballarat, Bendigo, Geelong, and the fastest growing population centres such as Melton and Wyndham, would be with the privately owned line?

Robert Toogood, Ballarat THE FORUM Elite school ecosystem

It’s disappointing that the spiralling escalation of private-school fees (″⁣Fees at prestigious Victorian school surpass $100,000 for one year level″⁣, 3/11) is even further from what ordinary Australian wage earners can ever afford, an affront to an egalitarian Aussie ethos.

Oddly though, I feel somewhat sorry for this privileged demographic. Firstly, what pressures is the upcoming generation subjected to in return for this substantial investment? And families are locked into not only an inflexible, expensive and arguably monocultural educational journey once they have commenced at a certain school, but also narrowly standardised lifestyle expectations of exclusive addresses, prestige cars and overseas holidays that are inevitably part of this elite ecosystem. How is this ever to cultivate young people to be broadly knowledgeable, humbly selfless and empathetic to a wide range of social experiences?

Marish Mackowiak, Ormond



Private school buildings

Re “Parents face record fee increases at top girls schools”. The contrast between private school construction and public school infrastructure should spark a debate on educational equity and sustainability. While families face fee increases at elite private institutions, these schools simultaneously embark on multimillion-dollar, ultra-modern building programs.

It could be argued that these expansive architectural projects heavily drive up fee costs, placing a greater financial burden on parents. This stands in stark contrast to the public school system, where staff frequently navigate outdated buildings, lacking facilities, and challenging working conditions. The divide is further compounded by federal funding models, which critics claim favour independent schools and frees their budgets for these premium developments.

Ultimately, this disparity raises questions about social sustainability. If public infrastructure strains while private institutions build increasingly luxurious campuses, the educational gap threatens to widen. Surely, our society’s future depends on its ability to equitably and sustainably educate all young people. Ensuring that funding and infrastructure support the entire community, rather than widening the educational divide, remains vital for long-term social cohesion.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Keep them honest

Like your lead correspondent (Letters, 3/11), I campaigned for my local independent, for similar reasons. But unlike her, I recognise that the major parties still have a role because government requires balancing competing priorities. The major parties have developed mechanisms for that process, while the independents can aim at “keeping them honest” in integrity, climate change and DEI.

Peter Greig, Colac Trump no example

OK, the Americans are as concerned as the rest of the world about the cost of fuel, and the rising cost of living. Some Americans seem to be concerned about the war with Iran, but why aren’t they appalled about Trump’s foul mouth, and not being an example for young people to follow, to make their country great again?

Ruth Murphy, Pipers Creek American fate

I’m a 26-year-old American living in Melbourne for the last few years. I came here with rose-coloured glasses, and after witnessing the brutal Nazi attack on Camp Sovereignty, realised they’d lost their tint.

Reading Brielle Kohlbeck’s story (″⁣Escaping Trump″⁣, 1/11), I saw my own sentiments laid out before me.

I, too, have filled my online ballot for the blue state of Washington, voting on measures such as No.IP26-645 which seeks to repeal a 9.9 per cent wealth tax on income over $1 million dollars during a cost of living crisis; No.IL26-638 which would require the verification of children’s biological sex to compete in certain school sports and activities; and No.IL26-001 which would repeal a child’s right to attend school in an environment that is free of discrimination of any kind, a parent’s right to know if their child has been a victim of physical or sexual abuse, and seeks to repeal the requirement of teaching sex education.

It’s true things are much better over here, but looking around I see complacency mixed with those who would willingly see Australia share the fate of the US. Sure, there’s a protest every now and then where attendees can pat themselves on the back and feel like they’ve accomplished something.

But, then we allow the likes of white supremacist Thomas Sewell out on bail. The naivete is appalling. Every opportunity that is not taken to deliberately move away from fascism, is an opportunity for fascism to catch up. And I pray that young people see that.

Through electing the likes of Zohran Mamdani and the late MP Tim Read, we push Australia towards a better and brighter future for us all. And, I look forward to seeing the needle pushed in this direction for the US as well.

Abigail Carnell, Kensington Gun controls

It is a conundrum. Do the police wearing visible guns increase or decrease the threat of violence from gun-bearing antagonists?

Meg Paul, Camberwell



DC reflection

What a gift for cartoonists! Narcissus gazing into the Trump Reflecting Pool ... There are several versions of the myth, and I await cartoonists making play with them.

Of course, its correct title is the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool: that ‘memorial’ bit is the part to focus on.

Pam Cupper, Dimboola Stopping the nation

Yet another brilliant cartoon by Megan Herbert (3/11). She encapsulates two sides of the same coin of the Victorian racing calendar. The enthusiastic glamour and the addiction to gambling and alcohol which can negatively affect individuals and families.

Added to this is the recent euthanasia of a horse after an accident in a race. One wonders whether the race that ‘stops the nation’ now reflects more on the growing divisions and values in our nation.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading Market forces win

There’s another scenario beyond that described by your Letters correspondent (″⁣What stops a nation″⁣, 3/11) for the Cup Day race. The ‘Party Policies’ horses may well be flagging. But wait, here comes one accelerating through the pack. It’s the people’s horse, Market Forces, surging ahead with its low-cost gear and speedy take-up.

It’s a one-horse race and the others are left struggling, ruing the day they ignored the approach of this popular horse to getting ahead and thus hitting the net zero target without really trying.

Carolyn Ingvarson, Canterbury Watch the nags

It’s disappointing that your correspondent’s ″⁣call of the climate card″⁣ for the Melbourne Net Zero Cup did not include any independent nags as qualifiers (Letters, 3/11).

With a vested interest in the outcome of the net zero race, but no qualifications in either horse racing or politics, I’d happily put my money on the staying prospects of any of the current independent stable ahead of all the party hacks.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor Black humour

Your correspondent (Letters, 2/11) questions violent costumes for Halloween. Yesterday, I saw outside a home with young children, a very large toy teddy bear, with a rope around its neck, hanging from a tree.

What a sick world we live in when someone thinks this is funny.

Marie Teague, Ocean Grove



Hound party

The most bizarre Halloween costume-wearing I’ve encountered was in a local park where a joyously manic party of Italian greyhounds bedecked as witches, bats, ghosts, spiders and a fairy were having a fabulous frolic. The crazily energetic little hounds, accompanied by their more sedately dressed humans, clearly loved being the stars of the show.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East Tasty bedeckment

Agree about the violence trend in Halloween costumes. I was delighted when my grandson was bedecked as a hot dog.

Susie Holt, South Yarra We want attention

Re Letters, ″⁣Motorcycle awareness″⁣, 3/11. I have been riding motorcycles for more than 50 years and the most important thing I know is I am completely invisible.

If I ride at the same speed as the traffic around me them 50 per cent of the threats come from behind me and these are difficult to spot. Riding faster than the traffic shifts the threats to the front, which are easier to spot as I’m better at looking forward.

I’ve also found that riding ″⁣in your face″⁣ means I become more visible. If you are in your car and see me and exclaim ″⁣Stupid motorcyclist″⁣ then that means it worked and you saw me.

Laurens Meyer, Richmond Real world economics

I can see why economics is known as the dismal science and ipso-facto economists are depressingly pessimistic about the world. The language used by this profession of gloomy prognosticators is revealing as it barks about the likelihood of recession, higher unemployment, cost of living pressures etc.

Whatever the RBA does, it inevitably will be a bad day as one way or another the sky will be falling. My solution is to go for a walk and look at the real world which doesn’t seem to look bad after all.

Pier Paolo De Carlo, Ascot Vale AND ANOTHER THING



Matt Golding State politics

One Nation’s Warren Pickering “vows transparency, refuses to release costings” (3/11). Would I buy a car from this man? No.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill I might have lost confidence in the major political parties, but it is a step too far to endorse or support a political party which is led by a former, admitted illicit drug user and multiple DUI offender.

Michael Gamble, Belmont Here’s a thought for the councils going around painting potholes pretty colours. Perhaps if they take the equipment to fill the potholes as well, they might save on the paint cost.

John Cain, McCrae Furthermore

While thousands wait for decent healthcare, our government gives away billions of dollars of free gas to overseas interests. A 25 per cent tax on export gas would mean Albo romps home in 2028.

Wendy Baker, Lilydale



Is Zuckerberg promising there will be no “human error” if everyone has their own personal AI assistant? (“Data breach sinks $50 million hospital tender due to ’human error‴⁣⁣, 3/11).

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne Target Time: With so much doom and gloom in the world, could the nine-letter word be more joyful, like ″⁣happiness″⁣, not ″⁣terrorist″⁣ or ″⁣depressed″⁣ as in recent days.

Lyn Bayley, Kyneton Why won’t cricket commentators applaud South Africa’s brilliant victory? It’s not cricket.

Alan Williams, Port Melbourne Melbourne Cup

Cup Day has come and gone. Let’s hope we’re one year closer to banning animal cruelty dressed up as a respectable sport.

Mark Cherny, Caulfield North Megan Herbert makes her point very clearly in her Cup Day cartoon (3/11), however, she, too, wears blinkers by ignoring the pleasure the day brings to millions of Australians.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South



Re Megan Herbert’s cartoon: Talk about a wet horse blanket.

Damien Ryan, Berwick The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

If you don’t ask, you won’t get. In what was an epic coup for Crown Resorts and its private equity owner, Blackstone, the casino company landed new US ambassador to Australia David Brat at Flemington on Tuesday. US ambassador David Brat (left), Trade and Tourism Minister Don Farrell (taking a selfie) and US consul-general Colin Crosby outside the Crown marquee. Penny Stephens When Crown asked if Brat, who started in his role as Donald Trump’s man Down Under in August, would like to be at the track and attend its Birdcage marquee, he said yes and diplomacy swung into action. It was the first visit to Melbourne for Brat, who was joined by his wife, Laura. The couple were accompanied to the track by US consul-general Colin Crosby and his wife, Vivian.



After lunching in the VRC Committee Room, Brat told CBD he was loving the Cup spectacle. He said Victorian Governor Margaret Gardner had encouraged him to punt on what she told him was the King’s horse, Point Of Law, which went on to win the $10.2 million race. The horse was previously owned by King Charles. Crown Resorts CEO David Tsai, Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Sally Curtain and Crown Resorts chairman John Borghetti on Cup Day. Penny Stephens Brat said he would vote in the US midterm elections, which begin on Tuesday night (AEDT), via email and that being sent to Australia by Trump was “the best posting there is”. Elsewhere in Crown’s enclosure, chairman John Borghetti played host to pollies and high rollers alike.



Taro Squires, head of real estate in Australia for international private equity giant Blackstone, was at his first Melbourne Cup, after taking on his new post in July. Squires was previously based in Tokyo and is now living in Sydney, from where he will oversee the casino asset. Caitlin Donaldson from Qantas and Michael Photios, Liberal Party powerbroker, arriving at the Birdcage. Penny Stephens He was in the house with Crown Resorts chief David Tsai and head of Crown in Melbourne Ed Domingo. Lobbyist and former NSW Liberal minister Michael Photios was in from Sydney with Qantas government relations operative Caitlin Donaldson, while National Gallery of Victoria director Tony Ellwood, federal Trade and Tourism Minister Don Farrell, VECCI boss Sally Curtain, Melbourne Airport chief Lorie Argus, and Crown Melbourne chair and former racing minister Martin Pakula were also present. A Wylie win



Before the feature race, veteran investment banker and former chair of the Australian Sports Commission John Wylie was striding the Birdcage bitumen with his wife, Myriam. Together, they own 10 per cent of Point Of Law. John Wylie, former chair of the Australian Sports Commission, and his wife, Myriam Wylie, had plenty to celebrate. Penny Stephens John ducked in and out of Crown before heading for the mounting yard. By the end of the day he was back at the company’s marquee celebrating

the horse’s win in a back room with his fellow owners. Bishop’s blessing for Jess Wilson Julie Bishop, Australia’s minister for style, and her partner, Stephen Grey, were the epitome of Birdcage diplomacy on Cup Day, floating from one marquee to another.



Julie Bishop calls this Dior dress “my French look”. Getty Images Dressed in “timeless Dior – this is my French look”, Bishop paused for a moment from her marquee-hopping to throw her support behind Jess Wilson in this month’s Victorian election. “I have always been impressed by Jess. She is a very confident, smart, inspiring woman, and I hope she is given the opportunity to lead this state,” Bishop said. “She is an impressive talent. I think she is a star.” Last month CBD reported that Bishop, who also has a role with the United Nations, had hitched her wagon to a Trump-linked advisory firm in the US.



“I have maintained my interest in foreign affairs, Australia’s place in the world and global strategic matters,” she said. Bishop’s advisory firm, Julie Bishop & Partners, has inked a “strategic alliance” with American Global Strategies, a company chaired by Robert O’Brien, a former US national security adviser and current member of Donald Trump’s President’s Intelligence Advisory Board. Foxx tears up the dance floor There have been rumours for days that Oscar winner Jamie Foxx would make it out to Flemington at some point during Cup Week, and when he arrived at the Don Julio marquee just before 1pm on Cup Day, a real Hollywood buzz went through the Birdcage. Hollywood star Jamie Foxx was ready to live it up on the dance floor. Eamon Gallagher



The Collateral star attracted a huge media scrum when he turned up at the tequila bolthole, and he wasn’t boring – chatting to everyone, doing oodles of selfies and busting some moves on the dance floor. Foxx is in Melbourne for a couple of months filming Deadlocked, an action movie that has been shooting at various locations around the city. He is staying at disgraced media mogul Antony Catalano’s St Kilda penthouse. Foxx’s partner, Australian fitness instructor Alyce Huckstepp, is in Melbourne with him. While many visiting international stars like to fly under the radar while in town, Foxx has been embracing our golf courses and our hospitality scene. He has been a regular at Maison Batard, the high-end restaurant in the Melbourne CBD operated by Chris Lucas, and as evidenced by his Birdcage enthusiasm, loves a selfie with fans. He is a vibe. Pour one out for Mumm



Over in the Mumm marquee, the definition of celebrity was quite loosely applied. Jules Neale’s “tap, tap” moment”. Getty Images In what has seemed like a real-life episode of Days of Our Lives, the bubbles brand has this week played host to both halves of the soap opera-like disintegration of footballer Lachie Neale and newly minted influencer ex-wife Jules Neale’s marriage. Jules was Mumm’s big-name guest on Cup Day and did the daily “tap, tap” champagne shower on the steps of the marquee for the cameras. Questions about her marriage implosion were off-limits, minders stipulating she could only be asked about fashion and racing.



Adelle Petropoulos at the Caulfield Cup last month. Penny Stephens Asked how she was feeling about being at the track, she said: “I will be honest … I don’t know anything about the racing,” adding she was there for the fashion. Lachie, a former Brisbane Lions star and now new Collingwood recruit, and his current girlfriend, Emma Field, were guests of the champagne house on Saturday, Derby Day. On Tuesday, another new-age celebrity guest was influencer Adelle Petropoulos, who came to public notice last year after she split with her fiance. Petropoulos bounced back in March by wearing what was to be her wedding gown to the Australian Grand Prix’s Glamour on the Grid party and has been riding a social media wave ever since.



Also turning heads in the marquee was Chelsea Becirevic, who is known as “Australia’s hottest WAG”. Becirevic is dating retired AFL player Ivan Soldo. “There are worse things to be called, so I’ll take it,” she quipped. Lunch is served The hallowed Committee Room was once again the most exclusive venue at Flemington, a strictly invitation-only location. Victoria Racing Club chair Neil Wilson and his wife, Stephanie, the VRC board and club chief executive Kylie Rogers hosted dignitaries, politicians, board members of other race clubs, sponsors, and owner representatives of runners in the Melbourne Cup.



Related Article CBD Daicoses, partners and a camera-shy premier’s wife: The eclectic social mix in the Birdcage As well as Governor Margaret Gardner, US ambassador David Brat and US consul-general Colin Crosby, also joining the Committee Room lunch were Victorian Racing Minister Anthony Carbines, state Treasurer Colin Brooks, Sport Minister Steve Dimopoulos, retiring Nationals MP Tim Bull and Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece. Pollies take Birdcage flight The Birdcage was a grab bag of political, business and showbiz identities on Cup Day. In our travels, CBD came across member for Mallee Anne Webster, member for Nicholls Sam Birrell, federal member for Maribyrnong Jo Briskey and new federal director of the Liberal Party Lincoln Folo in the Mumm marquee.



At TAB, the company’s heavy hitters were out in force in traditional morning suits, including chairman Brett Chenoweth, chief executive Gil McLachlan and non-executive director David Gallop. Senators Sarah Henderson (left) and Jane Hume. Eamon Gallagher Many politicians declined invitations to join the fun in light of the Reserve Bank’s decision on interest rates at 2.30pm – just the sort of optics our elected officials are keen to avoid. A few still got along, including NSW politician Mark Latham and federal Nationals MP Michael McCormack. Also enjoying the betting shop’s hospitality was former Melbourne Racing Club chair John Kanga and former Bill Shorten adviser Ryan Liddell, who now runs his own outfit, Principle Advisory.



At Lexus, Australian Industry Group chief Innes Willox was enjoying the day with partner Jane Devereux, while at Nine senators Jane Hume and Sarah Henderson were in attendance. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ethan Brown reconsidered riding after his brush with death. Now he’s a Melbourne Cup champion
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup Ethan Brown reconsidered riding after his brush with death. Now he’s a Melbourne Cup champion Peter Ryan November 3, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A heart-to-heart over a couple of beers with trainer Ciaron Maher about two years ago sowed the seeds for 27-year-old jockey Ethan Brown’s Melbourne Cup win on Point Of Law. After nearly losing his life in a massive fall off Maximillius in the 2023 Australian Guineas, and a stop-start return to riding, Brown wondered whether he should continue in the toughest of capers. Ethan Brown and girlfriend and fellow jockey Celine Gaudray celebrate with the trophy after Point of Law won the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images The injuries were significant, and that was before the emotional toll was considered. Brown suffered a grade-five lacerated liver and severed artery, damage to his right kidney, significant internal bleeding, and hairline fractures to three vertebrae in his lower back. He lost more than five litres of blood. The fall was in the March, and he returned to the races that August.



“By the time I got [back] to the races, I still wasn’t ready,” Brown said. “I was tricking myself into telling myself I was ready, so I rode for a month and thought, ‘I am not ready for this’, and took a step back. That was the stage I wondered whether I would get back.” Loading He contemplated training, but Maher – who became a trainer after a short-lived career as a jumps jockey – set him straight over a drink with Brown. The pair’s relationship went way back, with Brown riding the horse he learnt to ride on in Alice Springs, Here to There, to victory at Caulfield in 2017. Maher told him he was a rider, not a trainer. Brown and Ciaron Maher embrace after the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images



“He was very firm about that. He said, ‘You are delusional mate, get back riding’,” Brown said. Brown took the advice on board, but still took time to commit. “I woke up one morning. I was hungry again, and it was full-bore,” Brown said. Maher – who on Tuesday became the first trainer to claim the Melbourne Cup trifecta with Point Of Law, Zahrann and Juja Kibo – had merely passed on the wisdom he had gathered over his time in the business, recognising Brown’s talent was as a rider, and backing him in. Loading



“He’s a very dedicated man, and he was just a bit lost because he is a bit of an overthinker,” Maher said. “I rode at a very low level, and it was the greatest time of my life just booting around with my mates and riding, and he was just a bit down, and he was going to be a trainer. I thought, ‘Riding is much more fun’ and I just told him my thoughts.” A stint in Hong Kong gave Brown the confidence he needed to compete with the best, having grown up in Alice Springs where he started riding under Greg Connor before becoming an apprentice to Michael Kent. “He’s always been a grounded lad,” Connor said. “He still is.” Ethan Brown celebrates winning the Melbourne Cup on Point Of Law. Justin McManus At the same time, he recognised that the only way of being a jockey was to devote himself to the craft, showing the same traits he revealed as a teenager when he modified his diet after being told he had heavy legs.



“I have just matured a lot in the last 12 months. Mentally I have grown up ... staying quiet, not going out [and a] bit of sacrifice here and there. It has paid off,” Brown said. “When I came back it was like a switch, ‘I’m back to ride and that is all I am doing’. When you make those sorts of decisions you’re not half-hearted. You’re not back to just push around for your riding fee. It was, ‘I am going in full-bore’ and it was a moment like this I dreamt of, and it has happened.” Related Article Melbourne Cup Eileen had lunch with King Charles at Windsor Castle. It delivered her son a Melbourne Cup It didn’t just happen, though. Brown had to choose between Point Of Law and his other potential mount, Zahrann, in the lead-up. It was not a call he took lightly, but he opted for Point Of Law due to the horse’s X-factor. He then took on board Maher’s decisions to work Point Of Law hard to have him peaking for the race, finding the balance between being worked hard enough to relax in the run and fresh enough to quicken when called upon. Former hoop Simon Marshall, who has worked with him for 12 months, helped get him in the right frame of mind and if he needed further advice, his partner Celine Gaudray had ridden Torranzino to fifth place in the 2025 Melbourne Cup.



Brown had not ridden Point Of Law before the Geelong Cup, but he got off the horse in the winner’s stall and whispered to Maher it might be the best horse he has trained. Then he made early visits to Werribee to ride Point Of Law in trackwork, which gave him an understanding that he was on the best horse of the race. He could win as long as he could get him to settle in just his sixth race start. Editor's pick Analysis

Melbourne Cup ‘I looked up and thought, oh god’: The split-second choice that delivered Point Of Law’s historic Cup triumph He did it beautifully, timing his run to perfection as he reeled in, and then roared past, Royal Supremacy who looked to have opened up a winning lead entering the straight. With 350 metres remaining and Royal Supremacy still five lengths ahead, Brown knew it was all over. “He quickened like a sprinter at the end of 3200. When he hit that top gear, I knew we had won,” Brown said. The question of whether it was all worth it had been answered, and Brown was looking forward with a bank full of memories.

World.title: There’s a creepy problem with mince pies. It goes deeper than hot cross buns
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsChristmas Opinion There’s a creepy problem with mince pies. It goes deeper than hot cross buns Nicola Redhouse Writer Updated November 3, 2026 — 7:33pm , first published 7:00pm

Updated November 3, 2026 — 7:33pm ,first published 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s spring – a wondrous time for allergic rhinitis and for complaining about Christmas mince pies already being in the supermarket. The Mince Pie Creep, as I have come to think of it, might be less notorious than the Hot Cross Bun Creep (no longer even ubiquitous with Easter, now a completely non-denominational carbohydrate), but I feel deeper unease about its presence. I no longer believe the Christmas mince pie is an innocent little pastry designed to bring cheer – that it holds enough sugar to induce a diabetic-grade thirst is another matter. Rather, it is what animal behaviourists call a sign stimulus: a specific environmental cue that triggers instinctive behaviour. Mince pies are an innocent treat as we approach Christmas, right? Wrong. Steven Siewert For monarch butterflies, shorter days and colder temperatures are a sign stimulus to swivel their antennae compasses and head to the butterfly equivalent of Copacabana. The red belly of the male three-spined stickleback fish is a sign stimulus to other male sticklebacks to launch a vicious attack. And the Christmas mince pie signals to Homo sapiens with a shopping centre or the internet within reach to launch themselves into a mindless consumer frenzy. It’s possible the early spring Christmas mince pie harbours something like the alien spore pods in The Body Snatchers, which released tiny mind-controlling pathogens. I cannot otherwise explain why, in the face of every shred of evidence that we are burning down this planet, come October – the very same time the pies now appear – the average human brain starts accommodating two separate realities to justify frittering away money on more crap that has racked up a zillion carbon emissions and will end up in landfill.



Related Article Opinion

Supermarkets I found the best supermarket. It treats you like it’s a communist dictatorship Nicola Redhouse Writer We know that the Arctic is melting, bushfires are raging and average temperatures are climbing. That significant weather events are making us uninsurable, that disasters such as the Nepal flood are happening more often and that microplastics are clogging every waterway from our oceans to our tear ducts. Some of us even feel terror in the dark of night thinking of the future for our children and our children’s children, as well as guilt for the knowledge they will not be ones to suffer the worst – in fact that will be those in countries with less infrastructure, less money. But, understandably, we prefer to stay in our own little house of fun, where we can find joy in having five strands of single-use candy cane fairy lights twinkling around our necks and line our pockets with multiple Festive Pokémon figurines and dance with our limited-edition Christmas tunes robotic vacuum. In our house of fun, we can justify our purchases with thoughts such as, “Well, how could I possibly make a difference to this catastrophe” and “Well, it’s all so terrifying and sad I might as well enjoy my few hundred latex-filled giant-eyed squishy toys.” Psychoanalyst Adam Phillips says that modern life now demands we be happy. “It’s as though we’re phobic of frustration, so the moment there is a feeling of frustration it’s got to be filled with something,” he has said. Ours is a world in which we escape the terror generated by the consequences of capitalism and consumerism by purchasing more from Temu. The problem is, we need to feel pain, frustration, sadness, fear to take action. No civil rights activist ever emerged from a life of pina coladas on the riviera.



As Phillips writes: “It may be that when catastrophic change is inflicted upon us … we may become more able and willing to … create the kind of change we would like, the kind of change that we realise we need in order to get the lives we want.” Related Article Opinion

Cars My car kept making a thucka-thucka noise, but no one else could hear it Nicola Redhouse Writer Lord knows I am prone to the occasional impulse purchase of a dancing voice-activated cactus or tuba for a good dopamine hit. But as the festive season approaches this year, I want to do better. I’m going to buy from businesses that are using renewable energy, actively reducing their waste, and going for sustainable materials. I’m also going to try to give things that are good for the planet: things that grow, like plants and seedlings, and mushrooms and my washing pile. I’m going to give with actions, like cooking meals for friends who are stretched for time or money. I’m going to try to find gifts that offer low-emission experiences or op shop finds. I might even make my own mince pies.



Nicola Redhouse is a Melbourne writer and author of Unlike the Heart: A Memoir of Brain and Mind. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Two dead in plane crash near Nelson
World.content:
Two people have died in a plane crash near Nelson.

The plane left the city at about 9.10am on Tuesday morning and was reported overdue just before midday.

Two rescue helicopters had been searching at the plane's last-known location north-east of Nelson.

On Tuesday evening Nelson Area Commander Steven Collins said the plane was found in the remote search area, south of Castor Peak.

"Work is ongoing to recover the deceased and to examine the crash scene, which will be done in conjunction with investigators from Civil Aviation Authority."

A Cessna 172P Skyhawk took off from Nelson Airport and crashed near Castor Peak on Tuesday, 3 November. Screengrab / FlightRadar24

Flight tracking data on the website FlightRadar24 showed a Cessna Skyhawk taking off from Nelson Airport at 9.10am and flying into the hills near Whangamoa before its tracking data stopped.

Earlier, mayor Nick Smith said the Cessna could carry four people.

It "...got to an altitude of 3100ft but suddenly dropped to 1800ft when it was lost off radar near the Byrant Range 35 km north east of Nelson", he said.

Smith said Nelson was "anxiously hoping and praying" for those on board.

World.title: Psychiatrist exits public health system after Hillmorton Hospital patient murders woman
World.content:
A psychiatrist has told the family of a woman murdered by a patient at Christchurch's Hillmorton Hospital that her death has changed their life forever.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home in June 2022.

Hussein was jailed for life, with a 13-year non-parole period, in November that year, and had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

At the time of Waka Tunidau's death, Hussein was allowed to leave Hillmorton Hospital on unescorted community leave.

Laisa Waka Tunidau RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The second phase of an inquest into the death resumed in Christchurch on Tuesday in front of coroner Alexandra Cunninghame.

More than 20 doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses who were part of Hussein's care were due to give evidence during the inquest.

A clinician who treated Hussein between 2015-2022 began their evidence on Tuesday afternoon.

Their identity was suppressed.

Before beginning their testimony, the clinician addressed Waka Tunidau's family seated in the public gallery, saying how deeply sorry they were for what happened.

"What happened on 25 June has changed my life, and not a day goes by when I don't think about Ms Waka and her family.

"I have children myself and I just notice in the moments that we share, I'm constantly just thinking about what happened to Ms Waka, but what's happened to her family in the moments with her that you guys should still be sharing.

"I'm so conscious that, through that time, I've been able to return to the everyday moments of my life with my family, whereas you've had to live with the absence of someone who you should still be sharing those moments with."

The court heard how Waka Tunidau's death, coupled with broader sector concerns, had prompted the psychiatrist to depart the public health system altogether.

"Ms Waka's death had a profound effect on me and changed the direction of my career.

"Alongside the concerns I had about the service during that period, it was a very significant part of why I felt I couldn't continue working within clinical medicine essentially, but at Health New Zealand and for the local forensic service."

The clinican raised concerns in a letter to the director of mental health in January 2022, where instances of two acutely unwell patients being returned to prison, alongside "incidents" following efforts to move patients to less secure units, were outlined.

Stephanie Grieve Counsel assisting coroner RNZ / Nate McKinnon

There were also wider difficulties with staffing facilities, and pathways between forensic and general adult mental health services, the witness said.

"We were trying to meet increasingly complex needs with limited resources, while staff were working under considerable strain.

"I was concerned about the care we could provide and about the sustainability of what we were asking of staff.

"I stepped down from the leadership roles in that context."

Counsel assisting the coroner Stephanie Grieve KC asked the clinician about the decision-making process around permitting Hussein for unescorted leave within Hillmorton's grounds in early 2022.

They said it was decided that Hussein would shift towards a rehabilitation-based pathway.

"I know that's perhaps going to be something that's going to be challenged, the very idea that he was someone who was deemed for rehabilitation... to not be locked up indefinitely in a ward.

"To my mind, you know, we reflected on five months successfully living in the community, three years prior to that of no violence, and saw capacity in him to try and move his life forward."

World.title: National and Labour increase support in final 1News-Verian poll before election
World.content:
National and Labour have both increased their support in the final 1News-Verian poll before the election.

Meanwhile ACT and New Zealand First have lost support, despite campaigns to increase their party vote at the expense of National's.

National is up one point to 30, with Labour on their heels on 29, up two points.

The Greens are up one point to 16, ACT is down two points to 10, and New Zealand First is down two points to eight.

Opportunity is unchanged on six, while Te Pāti Māori is up 0.3 points to 0.4 percent - but the party is openly running an electorate-only campaign.

On those numbers, National would have 36 seats, ACT would have 12, and New Zealand First 10 - giving the coalition 58 seats: not enough to govern without Opportunity, which has seven seats.

On the other side, Labour would have 35 and the Greens 20.

The poll makes two assumptions. One assumes Te Pāti Māori would have four seats and Te Tai Tokerau Party would have one. The other assumes Te Pāti Māori gets one seat.

Under the former assumption, it would give the left bloc 60 seats in a 125-seat Parliament. With Opportunity's seven, it rises to 67 seats - four more than needed.

The latter assumption would give the left bloc 56 seats. Opportunity's seven would give it 63 seats in a 121-seat Parliament.

In the preferred prime minister stakes, Christopher Luxon is down one point to 23 percent, while Chris Hipkins is up one point to 19 percent.

Between October 29 and November 2 2026, 1006 eligible voters were polled by mobile phone (500) and online using online panels (506). The maximum sampling error is approximately ±3.1%-points at the 95 percent confidence level. Party support percentages have been rounded up or down to whole numbers, except those less than 4.5 percent, which are reported to one decimal place. The data has been weighted to align with Stats NZ population counts for age, gender, region, ethnic identification and education level. The sample for mobile phones is selected by random dialling using probability sampling, and the online sample is collected using an online panel. Undecided voters, non-voters and those who refused to answer are excluded from the data on party support. The results are a snapshot in time of party support, and not a prediction.

World.title: Historic shortcomings in forestry regulation need to be recognised, says iwi
World.content:
Gisborne District Council needs to acknowledge historic shortcomings in the regulation of the forestry in the region, Ngāti Porou says.

An independent review into the council's approach to the industry found no evidence of anti-forestry bias, and says it acted in good faith.

But the review highlighted a lack of oversight - in the years ahead of 2017 - which contributed to poor industry practice and a resistance to scrutiny.

The region had been plagued by slash and debris, damaging infrastructure and putting life and property at risk, following severe storms.

Te Rūnanganui o Ngāti Porou chief executive Henare Walker said landowners and communities were caught between local and central government arguments over who was responsible for the future of forestry in the region.

"We are being left in the middle while our landowners and communities deal with the consequences. We need local and central government working with us on solutions, not pointing at each other," Walker said

He said the report identified unresolved issues around forestry slash discharges and transition away from forestry on erosion prone land.

"The Crown has been part of this story for decades and the report is clear it has an important role in what happens next," he said.

Walker said Te Rūnanganui o Ngāti Porou was calling for transparent scrutiny of the Council's historic monitoring performance and a jointly developed

approach to regulatory improvement and long-term land-use transition.

"We cannot keep dealing with this one consent, one clean-up or one programme at a time. We need to be thinking about what we want our whenua and our rohe to look like in 30, 50 or 100 years, and making decisions now that take us towards that future," Walker said.

World.title: Consumer Reports doubles down on demands for Millie Moon nappy recall
World.content:
A US consumer group is standing by its demand for nappy brand Millie Moon to recall its products, after learning that a child, who reportedly used the nappies, might require skin grafts.

The US-based Consumer Reports said it had received 700 reports about Millie Moon nappies since January 2026.

There had been five New Zealand reports of a rash or blisters forming, after using the nappies.

On social media, Millie Moon, which was part of the Zuru Edge group, said testing of its diapers and training pants, including batches linked to complaints, by six independent laboratories found no product-related cause for reported negative reactions.

Consumer Reports senior policy analyst Gabe Night said some parents who used the nappies on their children in the US had reported very severe injuries.

"Parents are reporting all sorts of skin reactions, not just rashes, but severe burns, bleeding, blisters, welts and peeling skin. Unfortunately, in a few cases, parents have had to seek medical attention.

"There have been at least three emergency room visits reported, and we were informed last week that a two-year-old was given fentanyl and oxycodone for his pain, and he may eventually need skin grafts, if he doesn't improve."

Night said Millie Moon needed to issue a voluntary recall, until the cause of the skin reactions was determined.

Until then, she said Consumer Reports would advise US customers not to purchase the nappies.

"We have never seen this number of incidents reported in such a short time period. We know that Millie Moon is doing their own investigation.

"Unfortunately, though, we still don't have answers. Parents are still left wondering what's going on.

World.title: Saudi Arabia Asian Cup postponed due to conflict in Middle East
World.content:
The Socceroos will have to wait another year for the chance to win a second Asian Cup, with the 2027 tournament postponed by nearly a year.

Scheduled to be played in Saudi Arabia in January and February of 2027, the tournament will now be played from December 23, 2027 to January 21, 2028.

The new dates are pending approval from FIFA.

The decision has been forced by conflict in the Middle East, with Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis claiming responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.

A strike on Riyadh's international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.

"The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," an AFC statement read.

The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through its Public Investment Fund in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the World Cup in 2034.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, with golf's Asian Tour postponing the Saudi International indefinitely, while cycling's Urban World Championships were also cancelled.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December and FIFA postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in Jeddah until an unspecified future date.

World.title: Melbourne Cup 2026 finishing order from first to last
World.content:
Race favourite Point Of Law has run down Royal Supremacy to lead a trifecta for trainer Ciaron Maher in the 2026 Melbourne Cup.

Here is the full finishing order for all 23 horses that ran in the 166th Melbourne Cup at Flemington.

Finishing order of the 2026 Melbourne Cup

WINNER: Point Of Law (Number: 20, Barrier: 8, Jockey: Ethan Brown, Trainer: Ciaron Maher)

2. Zahrann (15, 10, Ben Melham, Ciaron Maher)

3. Juja Kibo (11, 13, Sam Clipperton, Ciaron Maher)

World.title: This Samoan superman is the World Cup's greatest comeback story
World.content:
As he prepares to lead his nation into a World Cup semifinal against Australia, sometimes Ronald Volkman still can't believe this is happening.

He'd have settled for one NRL game this year with Parramatta and after what he's been through, that really would have been enough.

But instead the best season of his budding career will continue when he lines up for Samoa against the Kangaroos with a World Cup final berth up for grabs, standing on the shoulders of giants with the whole rugby league world watching.

It still feels more like a fantasy than a reality for the 24-year-old, even as he's living it.

"I didn't see myself playing NRL and I didn't see myself playing for my country, in a World Cup, on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"I grew up watching this, I'm still pinching myself that I got to get on these fields.

Ronald Volkman will start in the halves for Samoa against Australia this weekend. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"The players in this team, you look left, you look right, you see guns. It gives you so much confidence in what you can do and that you can take it to the next level."

It has been a long journey. It was only a few years back that Volkman thought his football career was over.

Bad shoulder and hip injuries in 2023 scuppered a move from the Warriors to St George Illawarra the following season, sending Volkman to rock bottom in a full year out of the sport.

The physical pain was such that Volkman could barely move and without the game he loved he lost his way.

He stopped training and put on weight. He didn't know himself and when he was out and about, he'd pull his hood up so nobody would know him.

Mates would reached out to support him, but Volkman often ignored them, trapped in a downward spiral with a heart set on suffering, haunted by football dreams he could barely remember.

At his lowest depths, he leant on the things that mattered most to him.

Ronald Volkman's career and life fell apart after he left the Warriors. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"A big one for me was my faith. I fell down to that faith, my God, my loved ones, my family and my partner family," Volkman said.

"They were there for me during those tough times and it'd be slack for me not to take the opportunity I've had this year and showcase my talent, not for myself but for my loved ones.

"They've been through it as much as I have."

There's a lot of loved ones to repay.

Volkman is one of eight siblings and Samoan on both sides of the family. Growing up they'd go back to the islands every second year.

His father, Tas, wept tears of joy when his son debuted for the Warriors in 2022 and did so again when Volkman made his rugby league return in a pre-season trial for Parramatta last year.

Volkman did the same during the Samoan anthem on Sunday night but Emeline, Tas's mother, doesn't give as much away.

She still lives in Samoa, in a village called Vaitele Tai in the western outskirts of Apia, where she watched her grandson come on against Tonga and score a key try.

Loading Instagram content

Volkman played the final 27 minutes after Chanel Harris-Tavita strained his hamstring while kicking for goal, sparking a Samoan revival that just fell short despite the Toa outscoring Tonga four tries to three.

"I got rattled in the ribs early and struggled to breathe for about five minutes, but it's so good to be out there with my usos (brothers)," Volkman said.

"The first thing I thought was about Chanel. You never want to see a teammate go down like that and to me the way to honour him, to show respect, was to get on and do a job.

"He did a pretty good job for the majority of the game and it made my job easy."

Ronald Volkman has rebuilt his NRL career with Parramatta this year. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Volkman's play — the sharp feet, quick hands, a nose for the tryline and a big shot on Tongan backrower Siua Wong — would have been familiar to any Parramatta fans in the record-breaking crowd.

He made his NRL return for the Eels last year and just getting back at all and having his shoulder hold up was a blessing, even if they lost the two games by a combined total of 88-24.

This season, with the highly-rated Jonah Pezet arriving for one year, Volkman didn't expect to play any first grade.

But instead he relieved the injured Pezet in Round 6 and never looked back, playing every game for the rest of the season and signing a new two-year deal with the Eels in September.

He finished the year a blue and gold fan favourite, with Volkamania running wild among the Parramatta faithful.

In 2027 he'll act as a back-up to Mitchell Moses and Jarome Luai, but the latter has already had an impact on Volkman through Samoa camp.

"He's given me confidence to do what I do," Volkman said.

"The way he trains and prepares himself during the week is relentless.

"He's such a competitor but that's all I can say, because if he hears this he'll think I love him."

Tonga and Samoa can be Origin for the new century The scale and spectacle of Tonga's Rugby League World Cup win over Samoa was not just an instant classic, it proved a demand for this clash that rugby league must find a way to supply.

But before Volkman and Luai are club teammates they will be brothers in arms against Australia, starting in the halves together as the masters of Samoa's chaos.

A win over the Kangaroos would be a glittering prize at any time but with a World Cup final berth on the line the stakes are even higher it shapes as the biggest night of Volkman's career.

It would be Samoa's second and Volkman remembers watching the first four years ago and dreaming of being a part of it. Now, against all odds, that dream is real and the best could still be yet to come.

"I'd just started my first pre-season with the Warriors and it was mind-blowing, to see Samoa on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"We have the chance to do it again next week, so let's do it. I can't wait."

World.title: Opals veteran opens door to Australian return after WNBA retirement
World.content:
Opals Star Bec Allen has kept the door ajar for a return to Australia's domestic women's basketball competition after ending a glittering 11-year tenure in the WNBA.

The 33-year-old's decision to leave the top women's basketball competition in the world has raised questions about whether she is preparing to finish her career back home in the WNBL.

"It's something that I'm not saying a hard no on. Right now the answer is no, purely because my body just needs rest," Allen told AAP.

Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven Australia's Izzy Borlase falls just short of a title as her Atlanta Dream are beaten by Golden State Valkyries in game seven of the WNBA Finals.

"After a year, maybe I'll get a call from Cheryl [Chambers] or a good friend like that, and I'll jump back in and play in Geelong or something like that.

"I just know that I want to be in Melbourne.

"I want to be in Australia and you can't say a hard no to anything."

Allen has a sparkling history in Australia's top domestic league, debuting with the Dandenong Rangers in the 2010-2011 campaign and playing in the competition until 2016.

She claimed the league's Defensive Player of the Year award in 2014, before signing her first WNBA contract with the New York Liberty in 2015.

The WNBL's chief operations officer, Justin Nelson, said he had no doubt some clubs had inquired about securing her signature.

"Bec is an incredible role model, an incredible athlete. She's done so much for girls and women in basketball," he told AAP.

Bec Allen was a member of the Opals squad at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

"All of the fans around Australia would love nothing better than to see her playing in the WNBL, and if the league or I can do anything to help make that happen, we'd love to see Bec playing."

Allen has plans to become a player agent and pursue commentary, but the Tokyo Olympian is currently relishing in some much-deserved rest, having represented the Connecticut Sun, Phoenix Mercury and Chicago Sky before coming back to New York for one final season in 2026.

Reuniting with her past team proved the right move as Allen won the WNBA Commissioner's Cup in June and reached the semi-finals last month.

"My first [WNBA season] was in 2015, and I had impostor syndrome at the beginning, and then I got to realise after years that, hey, I belong here," Allen said.

"I never thought that when I started, I'd play 11 years in the league.

"Body, mind, heart … I've given the game all of myself in those capacities, and so now it's time for the next chapter."

AAP

World.title: Maxwell retires from international cricket but continues franchise T20 career
World.content:
Australian short-form cricket star Glenn Maxwell has retired from the international game.

The 38-year-old retired from one-day international cricket in 2025, but has now hung up his bat and gloves for Australia's Twenty20 team and his state team.

"Post the last one-day game for Victoria, speaking to my teammates and letting them know that was gonna be my last game for the state was probably harder than I thought it was going to be; got a little choked up," Maxwell said on The Final Word.

Maxwell represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka earlier this year and, across his career, played 130 T20 internationals, scoring 2,897 runs at 28.97 and with a strike rate of 154.42.

He also took 51 wickets and claimed 62 catches, with a career-high score of 145 not out against Sri Lanka in 2016.

"I'm grateful for the time I was able to play for my country," he said.

"If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Vic change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.

"I'm extremely grateful to have played that much for my country and to hopefully inspire some kids who want to take the game up, to want to play differently and to be open and vulnerable and to not shy away and be themselves.

"It was pretty incredible when even getting my first Test cap, well and truly before I was probably ready.

"It was pretty exciting, and I'm glad they took a gamble on me, and I'm glad I could, at different stages, repay the faith and be afforded the chance to play as much, for as far, as I did."

Maxwell also played seven Tests for Australia and 149 ODIs, and enjoyed an expansive and productive First Class and List A career with Victoria, too.

He will continue to play Twenty20 franchise cricket, including for the Melbourne Stars in the upcoming Big Bash League.

AAP

World.title: Ciaron Maher becomes first trainer to sweep Melbourne Cup placings
World.content:
Point of Law, a horse sold by King Charles III in July, has won the Melbourne Cup in just its sixth start.

The three-year-old colt trained by Ciaron Maher firmed as the favourite just before the jump, taking the tag away from Hopewell Rock, which began the day as the most fancied to win the famous 3,200m race.

Ridden by Alice Springs native Ethan Brown, Point of Law stormed home late, chasing down long-time leader Royal Supremacy with 150 metres to go, to win ahead of Zahrann and Juja Kibo.

Mahar became the first trainer in Melbourne Cup history to train the trifecta.

Point of Law, the son of famous champion Frankle, was bred in England and owned by King Charles III before being sold in August to an Australian consortium following his Group 3 Bahrain Trophy win at Newmarket.

Its two runs in Australia have both been victorious after winning October's Geelong Cup, becoming just the fourth horse to claim the Geelong-Melbourne Cup double after Media Puzzle (2002), Americain (2010) and Dunaden (2011).

Earlier, Chris Waller-trained Asterix was scratched from the Cup after stewards deemed medication had been used on the horse today. Waller explained it was a simple mistake in the heat of the moment.

Look back at all the action of Melbourne Cup Day at Flemington in our live blog below.

World.title: Addo-Carr's future in Parramatta's hands as B-sample returns negative
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr's immediate playing future is in the hands of the Parramatta hierarchy after police advised the winger his second result from a roadside drugs test had come back negative.

Addo-Carr met Eels officials at a board meeting on Monday afternoon to respond to a breach notice after it was widely presumed the former Test and State of Origin star would be sacked.

The Eels released a statement afterwards.

Eels star Addo-Carr allegedly returns positive test for cocaine NRL player Josh Addo-Carr is being investigated by police after allegedly returning a positive test for cocaine.

"Josh and his legal team were given the opportunity to respond to the notice," the Eels said.

"The club will consider their submission and make a decision in due course."

The 31-year-old allegedly tested positive to cocaine at a random roadside test in September.

But police have confirmed to AAP that no further action will be taken, leaving Addo-Carr to potentially earn a stay of execution.

"About 11.10pm on Friday [11 September 2026], officers attached to Inner West Police Area Command were patrolling Enmore Road, Newtown, when they stopped the driver of a vehicle for random testing," a NSW Police spokeswoman said on Monday: "The driver — a 31-year-old man — was subjected to a roadside breath test, which returned a negative result. "The driver underwent a preliminary drug wipe, which allegedly returned a positive indication for cocaine. An oral fluid sample was obtained and sent away for forensic testing. Following the testing the result has returned a negative result. No further police action is expected."

Addo-Carr has scored 27 tries in two seasons with the Parramatta Eels. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Addo-Carr was sacked by Canterbury almost two years ago to the day for testing positive to cocaine.

He declined to talk to media after leaving the club's headquarters at Belmore about 6pm.

But his lawyer, Elias Tabchouri, thanked the club for being "generous with their time".

"The club were able to allow us to express our thoughts in relation to this situation," Tabchouri said.

"We remain positive in relation to the negative finding for the B test, and we remain committed to the club."

Pressed on whether Addo-Carr would remain with the Eels in 2027, after bagging 27 tries in his first two seasons in blue and gold, Tabchouri said: "That's a matter for the club right now. We're waiting for the outcome".

"Josh has always maintained — and still maintains — a commitment to the Parramatta club."

AAP

World.title: Cats' rise well overdue as AFLW finals loom
World.content:
Co-captain Nina Morrison has always felt Geelong had the potential to be among the AFLW's best teams.

And she is not surprised by teammate Georgie Prespakis's rise to super stardom that has helped remove Geelong's underachievers tag and catapult the Cats to new heights.

Geelong has thrived under former Melbourne mentor Mick Stinear this year and will face the Demons in Saturday's qualifying final at Princes Park.

The Cats (11-1) are the highest-scoring regular-season AFLW team of all time and only finished second behind North Melbourne on percentage.

"We've been disappointed the last couple of seasons, to be honest, about where our performance has been," Morrison said.

"I feel like I've always looked at the group that we've had and the list profile and thought that we could be playing better footy.

"So in that sense, I would look at our performance and it doesn't feel like it's come out of the blue.

"We've probably just unlocked a few things that were already there and it's just about being able to do that all together and at the right time."

Georgie Prespakis is one of the superstars of the AFLW. (Getty Images: AFL Photo/Michael Willson)

Explosive midfielder Prespakis, the runner-up in the 2025 AFLW best and fairest, has gone to another level.

The 23-year-old has averaged 30.6 disposals, 8.1 clearances and eight score involvements.

"She's put in a body of work off-field as well to get herself in the right mindset coming into games to be able to perform well," Morrison said.

"She's obviously a star of the competition and I stand back in awe sometimes at the things she's doing on-field.

"She's an amazing player but her ability to bring her teammates into a game has always been a strength, but [she's] riding the ebbs and flows of that a bit better this season.

"To be someone that can do such incredible things but then also be such a great teammate has been her real growth this year."

Saturday will be the first time Stinear leads Geelong against Melbourne.

Tyla Hanks and Melbourne's impressive midfield will pose a tough test for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Wiltshire)

Morrison, who will play her 75th game, played down how much his inside knowledge could help against a star-studded midfield led by Kate Hore, Tyla Hanks and Olivia Purcell.

"We haven't played them, clearly, this year so I'm looking forward to the challenge of going up against one of the best mids in the comp, just seeing how we stack up against them," Morrison said.

"Obviously they're a pretty well-rounded team and Mick will know them pretty well as well.

"I'm sure he'll have some little things that we can draw on but I think a big focus for us over the course of the year has been how we focus on us and do us well. I'm sure that'll be no different this week."

Morrison insisted having to play at Princes Park instead of home ground Kardinia Park — booked out for a dirt bike event — was not on players' minds.

AAP

Tech.title: Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple CEO John Ternus doesn’t have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is “working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this ​point, we’re not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Apple launched its first foldable last month for $1,999, featuring a 5.4 outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen. Preorders for the iPhone Duo quickly sold out, with some shipments expected to arrive in 2027. Apple also made a limited number of iPhone Duo models available in-store at launch.

In his interview with Reuters, Ternus also addressed reports about cracked screens, saying “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duos were returned for this issue, and that Apple is replacing them.

The company has contended with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs for months now. This resulted in price increases across its product lineup, along with higher iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus said during Apple’s Q4 2026 earnings call on Monday. Ternus added that the company expects to see “even higher memory costs” during Apple’s December quarter but notes that this is “partly offset” by recent price increases.

Even without a standard iPhone 18 model, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone revenue at $57.58 billion during its fourth quarter.

Tech.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products. Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027. “We saw higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, and that was partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on non-memory components,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during an interview with CNBC.

Apple reported a 12 percent increase in revenue overall, ballooning to $114.5 billion. Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.

Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks. It made a big push into the smart home space with its first smart home display and a series of video doorbells, security cameras, and door locks, made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Tech.title: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027. Apps that support the Quest 2 or Quest Pro can also be submitted through December 2027, Meta says.

Meta is calling the Quest 3 and 3S “now the baseline for Meta VR gamers.” The company is announcing this shift ahead of the planned release of its new VR Glasses, which are set to launch sometime in spring 2027.

“Quest 2 and Quest Pro laid the foundation for this platform, and millions of people still play on them,” Meta says. “Quest 3 and Quest 3S give your apps more performance headroom and mixed reality built in, and apps built for them carry forward to Meta VR Glasses, which run on the same OS and SDKs.”

Tech.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.

The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

Related Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army

It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”

Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

Tech.title: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow.

The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. On the highway, BMW will allow drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel — but on local roads, they’ll need to keep their hands on the wheel.

BMW is the latest automaker to commit to releasing a partially autonomous city driving feature to its customers, as the industry races to keep up with Tesla and its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. BMW, in particular, recently introduced its next-generation Neue Klasse platform, which includes a driver assist system partly powered by Qualcomm’s technology. And with hands-free highway driving now widely available in many mass-market vehicles, the next frontier is a safe and capable city driving feature that rivals FSD.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: BMW

BMW says its system works cooperatively with drivers rather than fighting their control, which means they can steer, brake, or speed up at any point to adjust their driving without shutting the system off. At the same time, the car shows what it sees and what the assistance system is doing right in your line of sight through the heads-up display and in a clear 3D map on the main dashboard screen.

The necessary cameras and sensors already come built into models like BMW’s 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3, and iX4. BMW can activate the feature through an over-the-air software update. The system follows new European safety rules that let cars suggest and make automated driving moves on city streets for the first time. BMW says that outside experts have already road-tested the setup and confirmed it meets the technical standards, with final official government approval expected in early 2027.

With more cars equipped with partial automation hitting the road, safety researchers are growing increasingly worried about driver attention and the potential for these systems to cause crashes. There is compelling evidence that, regardless of the company, most driver-assist systems are less safe than normal human driving. Drivers tend to develop an overreliance on these systems to drive the car for them — even after a short period of use. And when it’s time to take back control of the vehicle, their reaction times are slower than what’s considered safe.

BMW is entering risky territory with the adoption of a Level 2 driving feature. Much like Tesla, the company is emphasizing that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle even while using the partially autonomous system in urban environments. Tesla does the same for its FSD feature, but some customers have successfully argued in court that the company bears some responsibility for crashes when they occur.
