Tech.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.

In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”

“We know that trust is earned.” — Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer

The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.

Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.

Previous Next





1 / 4

To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.

It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

Tech.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
Tech.content:
Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmellow, and robotaxi Mooves.

On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.

“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”

The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”

As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.

However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.

Still Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”

Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it pour £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.

“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”

Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.

Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”

“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.

She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mistusi and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”

“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

Tech.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
Tech.content:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.

The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.

Image Credits:Apple

However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.

Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.

With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.

Image Credits:Apple

Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.

When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.

These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.

The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.

Image Credits:Apple

Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.

Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.

This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.

At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.

This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too.

Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.

Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.

The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.

Image Credits:Apple Watch

The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.

To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards).

The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.

Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.

Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

Tech.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
Tech.content:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.

On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.

Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.

Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.

Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.

In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.

Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.

That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish.

Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content.

Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system.

Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder.

Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear.

Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.

Tech.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
Tech.content:
Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure. The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth.

However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.

When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.

Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.

During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory.

“We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.”

Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.”

TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds.

Tech.title: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them
Tech.content:
In Brief

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

Tech.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
Tech.content:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.

“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.

On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.

He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”

As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.

For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”

Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.

“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”

But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

Tech.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
Tech.content:
Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan as its parent company Match Group looks for new ways to get users to pay for dating apps at a time when people are increasingly tired of subscriptions and, in some cases, dating apps altogether.

During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Monday, Match Group said the new Hinge tier will include features such as additional filters and custom location boundaries, giving users more control over who they see and where they meet people.

“It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” said Steve Bailey, chief financial officer of Match Group. “Remember that Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.”

Match Group didn’t share how much the new subscription will cost. TechCrunch has reached out to the company for more details.

The move comes as dating apps continue to struggle to convince people to pay for services they’re growing tired of using. Between subscription fatigue, endless swiping, and frustration with the overall dating experience, users are increasingly questioning whether premium dating features are worth the money.

Interestingly, Hinge is making this move despite being one of Match Group’s strongest performers. The app had a much better quarter than Tinder, with global monthly active users growing 12% year over year, direct revenue increasing 19%, and paying users rising 23% to 2.3 million. The app generated $221 million in direct revenue and had 2.3 million paid subscribers as of the end of the quarter. Direct revenue is money earned from subscriptions and in-app purchases.

By comparison, Tinder brought in $480 million in direct revenue but experienced a slight 2% decline year-over-year, although it has 8.9 million paid users, a 4% decline from a year earlier.

The lower-priced subscription could help Hinge build on that momentum by converting more users into paying customers without requiring them to spend as much upfront.

The move also marks a shift in Hinge’s subscription strategy. In 2023, the company experimented with a more expensive tier aimed at users willing to pay extra for features designed to help them get more out of the app. Now, it’s testing whether a more affordable option could appeal to a broader audience.

Still, cheaper subscriptions alone are unlikely to solve the bigger problem facing dating apps: user fatigue. Match Group says it’s seeing some signs of improvement, partly thanks to efforts to make its platforms feel less like traditional dating apps.

Recent initiatives include Group Hangouts and Events, which offer users alternative ways to connect beyond the usual one-on-one matching experience. Match Group plans to ramp up those efforts in the fourth quarter.

Another initiative on the horizon is real-time adaptive recommendations, which the company plans to begin testing in the fourth quarter. Announced during its CEO Connection presentation in September, the feature will allow Tinder to respond to user actions within seconds rather than hours, with the goal of making recommendations more relevant and personalized.

Tech.title: Apple says it’s ‘hard to predict’ when iPhone Duo constraints will improve
Tech.content:
Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan acknowledged the shipping delays plaguing the new iPhone Duo during the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, but offered little clarity on when customers can expect relief.

The delays were just one point of concern during an earnings call filled with questions about the rising costs of memory chips, driven by soaring demand from the AI industry.

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan said.

Customers who didn’t wait in line at an Apple Store or immediately jump on preorders are now seeing ship times stretch into next year. Meanwhile, Verizon has been apologizing to its customers for the delays by offering gift cards.

In an October report from Financial Times, Apple described demand for the Duo as “nothing short of extraordinary,” after the device sold out on the company’s website within hours of going on sale, pushing delivery dates into next year.

The prolonged shipping delays are notable given Apple’s reputation for its highly efficient supply chain. But the company is hardly alone in facing supply pressures. Soaring demand for memory chips from the AI industry has driven up component costs for hardware makers across the board, threatening to push device prices even higher.

Apple, too, has raised prices on a number of products, Khan noted on the call, adding that those decisions were made “reluctantly.”

In another sign of the company’s efforts to meet demand for the Duo, Apple said it’s “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer for supplying materials for the new foldable device.

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during his opening remarks.

Tech.title: Uber Eats Promo Codes: $15 Off│November 2026
Tech.content:
Uber began as a modern alternative to taxis, letting riders order through a phone app, track the driver’s route in real time, share their location with contacts, and even split the fare in the app—it was the convenience-obsessed answer to the old way of hailing cabs. Then in 2014, Uber leveled up with Uber Eats. Much like Uber was the convenient, modern answer to taxis, Uber Eats was the equivalent for food delivery.

Instead of calling a local restaurant and enlisting a delivery driver from that restaurant, Uber Eats draws from hundreds of participating restaurants, cafes, and stores in your area, tailoring deals and picks to your location and preferences. So if you want fresh sushi from your favorite local spot for a date night in, or just need some Advil and Gatorade after a night out, Uber Eats delivers the goods in minutes flat. Whether you’re new to the service or a longtime devotee, we have an Uber Eats promo code and other Uber Eats coupon codes to help you save big—and stay at home.

Uber Eats Coupon Code for New Users

One of the easiest ways to save big on Uber Eats is to create a new account. First-time Uber customers can save 30 to 50% on their first order, plus new offers with up to $20 off rides or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber Eats promo code to get this steep discount—this offer applies automatically when you create your account and book your first trip or delivery.

Save More With Uber One Membership

If you use the rideshare app often or order takeout multiple nights a week, an Uber One membership will pay for itself within a few weeks. At $10 per month, it offers major perks that add up over time if you use the service frequently. You’ll get tons of perks across rides and food delivery, including $0 delivery fees on eligible food, grocery, and retail orders, up to 10% off eligible Uber Eats orders, 5% back in Uber One credits on eligible rides, and automatic surge savings. Uber One members save $29 on average every month.

Uber Eats Promo Code: 50% Off Your First Uber Ride

As mentioned above, the simplest way to save big with Uber is to be a first-time user. You’ll save 30 to 50% on your first ride, including up to $20 off all rides or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber promo code. Uber welcome discounts apply automatically once you create your account and book your first trip. Trust me, you’ll get used to the convenience of a rideshare app and a food and delivery service app, all in one place—in the palm of your hand.

Share the Gift of an Uber Eats Gift Card

One of my go-to gifts lately is an Uber Eats gift card. I find it especially thoughtful and useful as a convenience gift, whether that’s after a death, loss, birth, or a big life change. An Uber Eats gift card is more than just a gift card. It takes another thing off someone’s plate and offers an easy, comforting meal, especially during times of grief or celebration. Uber Eats gift cards start at $15 and can be purchased from participating retailers or sent instantly through the app to friends and family.

Unlock an Uber Eats Student Discount

Being a student often means tight budgets, long nights, and limited kitchen space (and culinary knowledge). Investing in an Uber One account may be a good idea—for only $10 per month, you can get, on average, $30 in savings on Uber rides and Uber grocery and meal delivery. You won’t have to worry about meal planning or expensive takeout bills. With Uber One discounts and promos, you can get multiple meals for the week at a lower cost. And if you’re a student, you can try Uber One for free for four weeks to make sure the service is a fit. After that, the service is half off at only $5 per month. No Uber Eats coupon code necessary. Just verify your student status to get the four weeks for free and $5 per month after.

Get Your Groceries Delivered with Uber Eats

If you’re not in the mood to eat out, stay in and get groceries delivered with Uber Eats. Uber Eats partners with hundreds of grocery stores near you—including your favorite supermarkets—for same-day delivery in as little as 25 minutes. Using your location, Uber Eats offers fast delivery from drugstores, grocery chains, and local stores, so whether you need toilet paper or a gallon of milk, Uber Eats delivers.

Deliver With Uber Eats

If you’re looking for a side hustle or gig work where you set your own schedule, delivering with Uber Eats is a great way to earn extra cash. It's flexible in so many ways. You can deliver with a car, a bike, or on foot, for an hour, a day, or daily. Uber Eats makes it easy to see what you’ll earn and what your day will look like. You’ll be able to see how much you’ll earn by delivering before you accept a job, and the tips you get are all yours. With Instant Pay, you can cash out up to 6 times a day for a fee, and weekly earnings are automatically transferred to your bank account. The possibilities (and flexibility) are endless—you can sign up to deliver food and packages, as well as “Shop & Deliver,” which allows you to earn by shopping for customers and delivering the order.

Get Your Starbucks Delivered With Uber Eats

If you’re like me and need about 40 oz. of coffee to get through the day, you know how important it is to have caffeine at a moment’s notice. With Uber Eats’ vast network, you can now get your Starbucks delivered. Starbucks delivery with Uber Eats couldn’t be easier. There are hundreds of Starbucks locations across the country, with both delivery and pickup available through the convenient app. Enter your zip code to see the nearest matching pickup location. Whether you’re catering for a big meeting or just want a quick breakfast.

FAQs

Does Uber Eats Offer Promo Codes for New Users?

Yes, Uber Eats regularly offers first-order discounts for new customers, often a percentage off or a capped dollar amount (like $15–$25 off) on your first delivery.

How Do I Apply a Promo Code on Uber Eats?

In the app, go to your account menu, select "Promotions" (or "Add promo/gift card" at checkout), enter the code, and it should apply automatically if valid and still active.

Does Uber Eats Offer Discounts on Grocery or Convenience Store Orders?

Yes, Uber Eats has expanded beyond restaurants to include grocery, convenience, and retail delivery, and many promo codes apply across these categories

Can I Use Uber Eats Codes With Uber (Rides) Credits?

No. Uber Eats and Uber rides promo codes/credits are generally separate, though Uber One membership benefits apply across both rides and Eats.

Tech.content:
What if I told you Brooks Running started out making ballet slippers and bathing shoes? Founded in 1914, the Seattle-based company spent decades making just about everything except running shoes, moving from baseball cleats to roller skates, football cleats, children’s shoes, and softball cleats. It wasn’t until 1972 that Brooks made running its focus, and the company has been refining the category ever since.

Brooks introduced one of the industry’s earliest uses of EVA foam, developed the first running shoe with a breathable GORE-TEX upper, and introduced the Kinetic Wedge, an innovative design tailored to women’s anatomy.

So, while Brooks may not be the trendiest brand, it has built a reputation for dependable support, comfort, and durability. Here at WIRED, Brooks has plenty of fans, especially for trail and gravel running. The company also offers apparel we regularly recommend, including sports bras, outerwear, and running bottoms.

If you’ve never ordered from Brooks’ website before, new customers get 20% off their first order after subscribing to email. You can apply the one-time Brooks coupon code to top-selling shoes, like the Caldera 7 and Adrenaline shoes, as well as other gear and apparel. It’s an easy way to save on some of their top products and take your road and trail running game to the next level.

Should You Hike in Boots or Trail Runners? Lightweight shoes now dominate the trails, so do you still need boots? Here’s how to choose the right footwear for your outdoor adventures.

Brooks makes so many iconic running shoes that it’s hard to list them all. I’m currently running in the Brooks Glycerin Max, which is one of the cushiest shoes I’ve ever tried. I don’t feel particularly stable on uneven terrain, but the padding is noticeably springy and cushy if you’ve been putting in some serious miles. WIRED director Michael Calore is a fan of the Brooks Ghost line, and if you’re planning to hit the trails in the cold, wet Pacific Northwest, I’d suggest the Brooks Cascadia Gore-Tex. This shoe has light, springy cushioning that helps propel you forward, whether that’s competitive trail racing, Sub-ultras, VKs, or ultras.

Upcoming Brooks Sale Events to Watch Out For

Do you have a runner in your life? The odds are they’re taking stock of their winter apparel and shoes, deciding whether these leggings will make it through another winter. The best time to save is during seasonal sales, with discounts on footwear and apparel, including popular items like the Ghost 16 running shoes.

If you’re looking for a new pair of shoes but don’t have the cash to invest in a brand-new, high-end pair, look no further than Brooks’ restock page, where gently used Brooks shoes are on sale at deeply discounted prices. Some of the best benefits Run Club offers include a 20% discount on apparel when you join and an annual birthday gift. You’ll just need to log in or join the club to get the discount code.

All you have to do is verify your status by signing in or creating an ID.me account to confirm your qualifications. Then, you’ll get a steep 40% discount on the first $1,000 spent on eligible items in Brooks Running online orders (it resets every January 1).

Tech.title: Take Care of That New iPhone Duo, Because Repairs Could Cost Up to $1,500 Without AppleCare
Tech.content:
The first iPhone Duos are now in customers’ hands, and we’re seeing in real time what happens when years of confidential Apple design meets the real world for the first time. Although reports still seem limited, several just-unboxed units are suffering from dramatic cracks on the inner screen. CNET is doing our own testing of the phone’s hinge by continuously opening and closing an iPhone Duo — which is now up to more than 200,000 times.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

Apple has already promised to replace cracked units, a repair that also falls under the phone’s one-year warranty, but what if a crack or some other defect appears outside that window of time? Should owners and potential buyers add AppleCare Plus for their new Duo? (Or at the very least, an iPhone Duo case?) Based on Apple’s repair prices, it might not be a bad investment — unless you’re JerryRigEverything, whose warranty is most definitely voided.

After all, the iPhone Duo starts at expensive and goes up to exorbitant for its higher-capacity configurations. If something happens and you need a repair, the costs could be substantial without AppleCare coverage.

More from CNET

The base 256GB storage option is priced at $1,999, but if you want to max out Apple’s new foldable phone with 2TB of space, it’ll cost $3,199. That’s pricey by iPhone standards, compared to the iPhone 18 Pro that begins at $1,199, though in line with the retail prices of Android folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Adding AppleCare coverage on top of the iPhone Duo’s price is an ongoing cost in addition to the price of the phone, but in terms of potential repairs, it does make sense. Because if you don’t fork out for a plan, and the inner display of your iPhone Duo gets crunched, expect to pay $999 to get it replaced, according to Apple’s support documentation. These are prices for repairs made directly by Apple, not third-party services.

The range of repairs starts at a modest $49 for “cover layer damage” and jumps all the way up to $1,499 for “other damage,” though it’s not clear what the latter entails. Here’s the breakdown:

Cover layer damage: $49

Back glass damage: $199

Battery service: $229

Rear camera damage: $229

Outer display damage: $379

Outer display and back glass damage: $509

Inner display damage: $999

Other damage: $1,499

AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss is priced at $20 per month or $200 per year until canceled and includes “unlimited repairs for accidents like drops and spills” and theft and loss coverage for up to two claims every 12 months. It also features Express Replacement Service, which gets you a new iPhone Duo instead of waiting for a repair.

Alternatively, the AppleCare One service costs $20 a month until canceled and applies AppleCare Plus to up to three devices. It also adds a third theft-and-loss coverage event in the 12-month span.

If something happens to your iPhone Duo under AppleCare, the repair pricing ranges from zero for battery service to $149 for theft or loss. The list of repair services doesn’t match up exactly to the ones noted without coverage. Here’s what Apple details as estimated costs:

Battery service: $0

Cover layer damage: $19

Back glass damage: $29

Outer display damage: $29

Inner display damage: $99

Other accidental damage: $99

Theft or loss: $149

Keep in mind these are the amounts provided by Apple’s services. If you’re purchasing the iPhone Duo through a wireless carrier, it might have different warranty options.

We’re looking forward to testing not just how well the iPhone Duo works, but how resilient Apple’s most complex iPhone will be. In the meantime, be sure to check out our review of Apple’s first foldable and ask yourself if the iPhone Duo is really for you.

Tech.title: Starbucks Drive-Thru AI Could Know What You Want Before You Do
Tech.content:
Could an AI barista know you’re craving an iced caramel macchiato? Starbucks says it will begin testing artificial intelligence for drive-up ordering — including recognizing customers as they approach — as the company focuses on integrating more automated tech, CEO Brian Niccol said on last week’s fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call.

The idea is to make ordering “faster, more convenient and more personal” for drive-up customers, which account for roughly half of all Starbucks patrons, according to Niccol. The company would begin testing background AI models for drive-thrus sometime during fiscal year 2027, which ends Sept. 28, 2027. There were no specifics as to where the testing would take place or how it would affect food and drink prices.

Niccol said AI would help input orders “more accurately and efficiently” while the baristas talk to drive-up customers to increase personal connection and speed up service.

More from CNET

The AI could also know what you want, or might want, before you even engage with the human barista. Niccol said the company is exploring ways for automated systems to recognize repeat customers as they drive up and offer “personalized digital menus,” possibly including suggested purchases.

While the exact kind of systems that would be tested to recognize customers weren’t specified, possible methods could include facial recognition, license plate reading or perhaps mobile app detection. It also remains to be seen which methods would require explicit customer consent or offer an opt-out mechanism. In an email to CNET, a Starbucks representative did not confirm which specific technology would be employed.

The representative said that Starbucks is already using AI in its operations through Green Dot Assist, which helps workers look up drink recipes, troubleshoot equipment issues and coordinate staffing. The company also uses Smart Queue to figure out sequencing of orders that come in via in-store, drive-thru, mobile app or delivery.

Do customers even want more AI?

Several major fast-food chains are using or testing AI to process drive-thru orders, including McDonald’s, Taco Bell, KFC, White Castle and Wendy’s. Customer reviews have been mixed so far, with the main problems being botched orders, lengthy processing and the inability of bots to answer questions, according to customer research from restaurant tech website Canopy.

Burger King, meanwhile, decided to pull back on using AI for drive-thru because some customers drove off rather than place their orders with a bot. The company is still testing AI but said it wants to give people the option of ordering from a human.

It’s unclear what Starbucks’ goal is or what customers the company is trying to appeal to, said Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan, AI researcher and associate professor at the University of Washington. But there’s plenty to be skeptical about.

“AI in face-to-face customer service will fail in many edge cases and has many potential PR problems with no clear benefits,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “It is better to defer until there is a broader general acceptance among the public.”

Ananthakrishnan said one flaw of using bots is voice recognition — many AI models are trained on general US accents and don’t perform well with non-native speakers or international accents. Surrounding noise from vehicles and weather can also affect how well the bot understands the customer through a kiosk microphone. That could pose health risks, Ananthakrishnan said, if, for example, someone is allergic to nuts and the AI misinterprets the request as “no nuts.”

McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru experiment with IBM in 2024, when bots were unable to understand various accents and dialects. The fast-food giant recently launched a new experiment with AI bot Archy as part of an $8.5 billion modernization plan. There was also a fake order that went viral when someone ordered 18,000 waters at a Taco Bell, and the AI processed it.

Most of Ananthakrishnan’s students have said they don’t want to talk to AI during their customer service interactions. However, more people might accept drive-thru AI if they know that mistakes will be rectified quickly, Ananthakrishnan said.

In a Bluesky post by More Perfect Union, an Emmy-winning nonprofit newsroom that advocates for workers, the reaction to Starbucks’ AI plan was overwhelmingly negative, with commenters complaining about privacy violations and pointing to the potential for “dynamic pricing” based on customer behavior and algorithms

Starbucks has said it doesn’t use surveillance pricing, a discriminatory method that’s been increasingly used by hotels, airlines and retailers. Still, a 2025 report in The Washington Post indicated that loyal customers using the Starbucks app more often might be getting fewer promotional deals.

More AI, fewer workers?

In a 2026 statement on the use of AI, the company says: “Our business is rooted in human connection — and our technology is designed to strengthen it, not replace it.” But Starbucks’ human connection with its workers has been problematic, and AI isn’t known for improving labor relations.

Since initiating a major organizing blitz starting in late 2021, Starbucks employees have formed unions at nearly 700 stores in the US, demanding higher pay and more robust staffing levels. Workers say they are not given enough hours so the company can avoid providing benefits, and are often given very short notice about shift changes. Last year, the NLRB said Starbucks “engaged in a scorched earth campaign and pattern of misconduct in response to union organizing.”

Since taking over as CEO in September 2024, Niccol has cut more than 2,000 employees as part of his Back to Starbucks strategy, which has resulted in simplified menus, reduced wait times and the closure of some shops.

In August, Starbucks Workers United, which represents 12,000 baristas, announced an open-ended national consumer boycott against corporate-owned Starbucks locations. The call accused the company of violating US labor law and attempting to break up the union, while also criticizing the corporate push for AI. “Starbucks has repeatedly demonstrated a lack of care for the workers who fuel the company’s profits by wasting millions of dollars on AI and technology that doesn’t work, launching countless gimmicky drinks designed to distract from real problems, and inventing pointless policies that do nothing but make workers’ jobs harder,” the call read.

In a 2025 interview with Current Affairs, union organizer Jason Woods said the company was trying to use AI to place orders but couldn’t handle staffing when an employee calls out. “They want to use algorithms to deploy our plays,” he said. “It’s inhumane. It’s anti-worker, anti-labor.”

Starbucks Workers United didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Anthropic Addresses Video Game Cloning With Minor Claude Update
Tech.content:
One of AI’s biggest selling points is its ability to build things quickly. AI models can help users sort through mountains of files, generate videos that have Hollywood studios worried, and create everything from websites and businesses to custom video games. With what’s called vibe coding, ordinary people can build playable video games in minutes using simple text prompts in popular AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

But the AI company Anthropic appears to be drawing a line in the sand about what kinds of games its AI model Claude can make. If a Claude user is trying to recreate someone else’s intellectual property, the AI tool will decline to build it.

That’s according to Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic who posted on X. He was responding to concerns that Anthropic had changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games, which could violate copyright rules and the company’s usage policy.

More from CNET

“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” Osmani said. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.



Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to… — Addy Osmani (@addyosmani) October 30, 2026

He offered to review cases where amateur game developers believe Claude wrongly refused their requests.

A representative for Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Homage versus infringement

Anthropic’s stance, as expressed by Osmani, acknowledges that using AI to try to clone a video game, even a simple one, could constitute intellectual property infringement, an issue that predates the rise of AI tools like Claude.

Even with the change, Claude will still generate video games that resemble popular hits from the past few decades. A CNET request to build a game “that resembled Breakout but with the word Claude on each brick” yielded a playable web version of the arcade classic, but not one that any video game fan would mistake for the original.

The same thing happened after Flappy Bird became a hit in 2014, spawning a wave of copycat games in app stores. Copyright infringement of games is complicated, said David Kocan, an intellectual property lawyer at Nixon Peabody who co-leads the firm’s esports and gaming team.

“This is something courts have wrestled with long before AI came along,” Kocan said. “The basic distinction has always been that copyright protects a game’s original creative expression, but generally not its underlying ideas, rules, or gameplay mechanics. Copyright protects the game you created, not the genre you helped popularize.”

You can’t copyright the concept of, say, a battle royal game or a side-scrolling platformer, which is why when a new type of game emerges as a hit, you’ll see many similar games.

“That distinction may sound straightforward in theory, but in practice, the line between borrowing an idea and copying someone’s creative expression can be blurry,” Kocan said. “That’s particularly true in gaming, where so much of the experience combines functional mechanics with creative expression.”

RTB Ruhan, founder and CEO of Null Station, an animation and video game art studio, said that AI has made it”fast and cheap” to cross the line into infringement, allowing people with no art or design skills to clone a popular game. But that doesn’t mean someone can publish or sell a cloned game without running into trouble.

“‘(Claiming) AI made it’ won’t protect them,” Ruhan said.

His studio uses a simple test.

“Remove the title and logo and ask whether a player could still tell the two games apart,” Ruhan said. “If they can’t, you’ve crossed the line.”

Are AI companies responsible for game clones?

Legal experts CNET spoke with said there are no laws requiring AI companies to outlaw game clones on their tools. But adding those guardrails could prevent trouble down the road, said Eric Blatt, a corporate, securities and intellectual property lawyer at Scale and a former examiner at the US Patent and Trademark Office.

“Anthropic is prudent to tap the brakes here,” Blatt said. “If Claude — Anthropic-owned software operating on Anthropic servers — receives an instruction to copy a game, and if Claude then copies the game, there is a facially plausible argument that Anthropic performed the copying. The chat logs would be a gold mine for the plaintiff’s counsel.”

Blatt said that litigation hasn’t kept pace with AI’s growth, but he thinks lawsuits could quickly follow if a rebuilt game made with AI directly threatens a company’s business model.

But some of those attempts could be stopped before they start if AI models refuse to make exact copies.

“Ultimately, copyright law draws the legal boundaries,” Kocan said. “But AI companies have to decide where they’re comfortable drawing their own. And those aren’t necessarily going to be the same thing.”

Tech.title: Over 370,000 Dreo Space Heaters Recalled After 17 Catch Fire
Tech.content:
Keeping cozy this season comes with an important caveat. Dreo has recalled its DR-HSH015 space heater due to the risk of the unit catching fire.

The recall covers Dreo’s $100 model DR-HSH015, a 13-inch-tall, black ceramic electric heater that came bundled with a remote control. Regulators noted the issue is limited to units manufactured between April 2025 and January 2026, which consumers can verify by checking the date stamped on the bottom of the device.

DREO said it received 17 reports of space heaters igniting, three resulting in property damage and one in a burn injury to the hand.

More from CNET

The company sold over 370,000 units in the US and Canada. The space heater was available from outlets including Home Depot, Best Buy, Kohl’s and Costco, as late as October 2026.

Owners should stop using the recalled space heaters immediately, disconnect them from power, destroy them by cutting off the power cable and contact the company for a free replacement.

Space heaters are a popular way to heat cold rooms, and CNET’s own tests found that properly functioning units can help owners reduce their energy bills over winter.

Tech.title: GTA 6 Sneakers: Rockstar Games, Nike and Travis Scott Reportedly Team Up
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games is releasing the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 in just a few weeks, on Nov. 19, and rapper Travis Scott and Nike are reportedly getting in on the game’s hype. According to Sneaker News, Nike, Rockstar Games and Travis Scott are working together to release a set of Nike Air Force 1 ’07 sneakers themed around the upcoming game. Reports suggest the shoes will retail for $130 and be available on Nov. 19, the same day as the game’s release.

The shoes will reportedly be available in three colorways. Those palettes are supposedly “White/White/Fire Pink,” “Black/Black/Fire Pink” and “Multicolor/Pale Ivory/Black/Bold Berry/Fire Pink.” The sneaker account prm.stocks.01 shared images of what the black pair would look like if you want to take a peek.

The shoe will reportedly have the reverse swoosh logo traditionally seen on other Travis Scott sneakers, and the leather appears to feature a grid that looks like city blocks.

More from CNET

The shoes have six stars on the heels, the report says, a nod to the six-star wanted level, which makes its return to the Grand Theft Auto series in the upcoming game. Grand Theft Auto 5 replaced the six-star system with a five-star system.

The sneakers will also supposedly come with a $100 GTA-branded money band around the shoe’s toe box. Other Nike shoes, like the different colors of the Concepts x Nike SB Dunk Low Lobsters, have had removable rubber bands, too.

And the shoe’s midsole reportedly replaces the “AIR” lettering normally on all Air Force One models with the letters “GTA.” There are likely more details that reference the game hidden throughout the shoe.

Neither Nike nor Rockstar Games immediately responded to my request for comment.

While there will reportedly be three colors of this shoe available, I think Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott could have stopped at the black pair. I’m sure the other two colorways are fine, but it’s a joke that black Air Force 1 sneakers are used in various criminal and illegal activities, making that pair a perfect representation of the Grand Theft Auto series.

I appreciate the six-star and money band details we see in the photos, and the pink gives the pairs a nice hint of Vice City-coded color without being too much. The black pair of these shoes reportedly comes with black and pink laces, and I’d lace up the pink ones if I ever got these shoes.

However, since these are a collab between Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott, I’m not expecting to see them on my feet. Travis Scott and Nike collaborations usually release in limited quantities, so it’s difficult to get a pair. You could always buy the shoes on eBay, StockX or a similar marketplace, but some Travis Scott and Nike collabs sell on the aftermarket for more than $1,000, depending on your size. And I’m not spending that much on a single pair of shoes. I’ve got a mortgage to pay, thank you very much.

Tech.title: Jean-Luc in Blue Jeans: Picard Cosplay Taught Me How Much Patrick Stewart Is Loved
Tech.content:
Star Trek fans never doubted the amount of love the community had for Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at age 86. But I experienced that love firsthand. Back in 2021, my husband, Rob, dressed as Captain Jean-Luc Picard for Emerald City Comic Con in Seattle, and the adoration he received, simply for cosplaying Stewart’s beloved character, was overwhelming.

Our planning wasn’t complicated. Looking for a costume that would go with his shaved head, and being a big fan of the show, it made sense for him to put on a red and black Star Trek uniform shirt, pin on a combadge and four pips to denote the Starfleet rank of captain, and step into some black shoes. Except for his glasses (and mask since this was 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic), it was an eerily accurate look.



More from CNET

Once we walked into the Seattle Convention Center for the con, it was as if the real Patrick Stewart had shown up. The respect Stewart had built up for Picard transferred seamlessly to his lookalike. Just walking around with Rob made me feel like a celebrity escort. We couldn’t travel more than a few feet without someone noticing and calling out to him, always with glee, always with respect.

“Hey, Captain! Captain!”

“Jean-Luc!”

“Make it so, sir!”

“Engage!”

“Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!”

Rob didn’t even wear costume-authentic black pants. In a hurry to get out the door and not expecting this level of attention, he had just pulled on his jeans. That led to a few of the funnier comments.

“Hey Captain! Was it casual day on the bridge?”

Comic Con attendees go all out. There were eerily realistic characters from Star Wars, Pokemon creatures, groups of friends dressed as The Incredibles, at least five Spider-Men, the Doctor from Doctor Who and exquisite, elaborate characters from anime. Many, many people had put more time, money and sweat equity into their costumes than we did, but few received such a universally awed reception.



Other Star Trek characters were also portrayed, for sure. Two separate Will Rikers, Picard’s trusted “Number One,” raced up to us at different times to take photos with their captain. One woman cosplaying as Kathryn Janeway, captain of the USS Voyager from Star Trek: Voyager, also posed with Rob for a two-captain photo.

And then, they saw us. A group of Comic Con attendees dressed as the Borg, the villainous cyborgs who take Picard hostage to assimilate him and temporarily turn him into Locutus of Borg.

These Borg did not throw their costumes together last-minute. They could have walked off a Hollywood set. They had working lights on their outfits, ocular and cranial “implants,” corpse-like face makeup, arms built into cybernetic tools. Of the Borgs, three were towering men and one was a woman. The woman played the Borg Queen, her bald head covered in white makeup, elegant and terrifying.

The minute the Borg saw Rob’s Picard in the convention center crowd, they came after him. Resistance, as they say in the show, was futile.

Thankfully, they were a jollier sort than the television Borg, and after one joke about his casual-day jeans, they whisked him away to stroll around as a group and snap photos.

These Borg were so realistic that I felt a bit unnerved the entire time he was gone — and relieved when they returned him unharmed, thanked us, waved and headed on their way. I’m sure there were other serendipitous meetups between cosplayers at the convention, but this one was amazing to see and even more so to be even a small part of.

Rob poses in front of a number of Star Trek posters, including Picard and his famed “Make it so!” command. Gael Fashingbauer Cooper

We’ve been to Emerald City Comic Con other times. Our daughter has cosplayed a variety of characters, and Rob once went as Dr. Stone, a science prodigy with green-tipped white hair (which required a wig). People in the know enjoyed that cosplay, too, and he was similarly asked to pose for photos.

But the sheer love we experienced when he dressed as Captain Picard was like nothing I’ve ever felt. Since his death, I’ve seen Stewart called a generation’s space dad, and there’s truth in that. People at the convention were delighted to see their space dad, even if just a doppelganger. It buoyed us along on an unexpected high on that cold December day in 2021.

In the famous Star Trek: Next Generation episode Darmok, Picard is trapped on a planet with the Tamarian captain, Dathon. They can’t understand each other. The entire Tamarian language is constructed out of mythological and historical metaphors, none of which Picard knows

Slowly, Picard begins to comprehend. He figures out that one of the most frequent phrases, “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!” references Darmok and Jalad, warriors who united on the island of Tanagra and eventually became friends, just like he and Dathon.

But there’s another phrase I’ve been thinking of lately. “Kiazi’s children, their faces wet.” An online Tamarian dictionary translates it as “downplaying the severity of a perceived injury.”

There’s no downplaying this loss. We’re all Kiazi’s children today. Our faces wet.

Tech.title: Forget the AI Notetaker, Someone From Iceland Will Knit a Summary of Your Meeting
Tech.content:
Is there anything worse than a meeting that really should have been an email? Visit Iceland has a new, albeit quirky, way to combat increasing meeting fatigue.

Rather than turning to AI tools and notetakers to take your place or keep track of what’s important in meetings, a real, crafty person will show up to listen. The AI Knittakers initiative from Visit Iceland will let you book an authentic Icelandic knitter to join your virtual meeting who will knit a sign with a single word that sums up the meeting, like “align,” “pivot,” “reset,” “huh?” or, my personal favorite, “WTF?”

Meeting fatigue is real. A December 2023 survey of 5,000 workers found that 78% of respondents said work meetings make it hard for them to get their work done, and 76% said they feel drained on heavy meeting days, highlighting that the growing number of virtual meetings since the COVID-19 pandemic is both ineffective and exhausting. Many stressed-out workers (65%) are now turning to AI notetakers to sometimes attend meetings for them.

More from CNET

“An AI notetaker hears every word,” said Salka Sól Eyfeld, the program’s chief AI Knittaker. “A knitter hears the sigh. We listen for the one thing that actually matters, and then we knit it.”

The initiative is available now and will run through Nov. 20.

How to book an Icelandic AI Knittaker

The booking couldn’t be simpler: Pick an available Knittaker from the website, book them during a meeting when your schedules align and give your coworkers the surprise of a lifetime while you do something more fun. The AI Knittaker will also email you a photo of your knitted one-word meeting summary, with the option to have it shipped to you if you live in Europe or the US.

The best part? It’s completely free.

According to the press release, some Knittakers will also be available to attend meetings in languages other than English. Just explore the list of Knittakers to see their language capabilities.

Maybe the answer to meeting fatigue isn’t another AI tool, but an actual human in your place.

What’s behind the knitted sign

The idea of giving your coworkers a shock while also making a statement about your precious work time sounds appealing, but it also signals a broader global attitude.

People are drained by meetings, and AI tools exacerbate it. A recent study in Harvard Business Review found that certain uses of AI tools, such as switching between different chatbots, can lead to cognitive fatigue they call “brain fry.”

After conducting a survey that found that workers spend about 8 hours per month in meetings that they deem unnecessary, Visit Iceland wanted to remind you that there’s more to life than just work meetings. The solution is both deeply analog and deeply Icelandic.

Knitting is a big part of everyday life in Iceland, according to Visit Iceland, and is a common hobby for relaxation and socialization. Icelanders are often knitting lopapeysas, Iceland’s distinctive patterned jumpers made of lopi wool, in public and even during meetings. By joining the work call, the AI Knittakers will give you a glimpse of their culture and stunning surroundings, reminding you of how good life can be when it’s not dominated by work and technology.

“It’s easy to assume that every modern problem needs a technological answer,” said Sigríður Dögg Guðmundsdóttir, spokesperson for Visit Iceland. “In Iceland, we’ve found that some of the best answers are the simplest ones: a little more time, a little more nature and people who really listen to each other.

“With AI Knittakers, we’re sharing a little of that Icelandic perspective with the world, and we hope it inspires people to step away from their screens and perhaps come and experience Iceland for themselves,” she added.
